documents.s: Course B — Urban Mobility: Designing an SoS with CADL × SUMO

documents.t: Course A, the Textbook, used a robot-delivery SoS as the running example and generated Unity C#. This tutorial swaps both axes: Domain: urban mobility (taxis + passengers + a matching platform) Target runtime: SUMO (Simulation of Urban MObility) The CADL/SoS-DSL syntax is unchanged — that is the whole point. mobility_sos.cadl │ ├─ cadl check ← type-check ├─ cadl sim-ir ─► IR JSON │ │ │ ├─► cadl-explorer (Lifecycle View) │ │ │ └─► cadl_to_sumo.py ← ★ codegen │ ├─► SUMO sumocfg │ └─► contract constraints JSON │ └─ (demand CSV) ─► generate_sumo_routes.py ↓ SUMO ─► tripinfo.xml ↓ analyze_results.py (guarantee check) ↓ Iterate: revise CADL guarantees / deadlines The reference implementation lives in the cadl-mobility-sos-exercise repository. Repository availability cadl-mobility-sos-exercise is a private repository on GitHub and is not publicly available at present. If you have been given access, clone it as in the setup below; otherwise, place the copy you were given at ~/program/cadl-mobility-sos-exercise. Without either, this page can still be read as a worked example of applying CADL to a mobility SoS.

Same as Course A for cadl_repo and cadl-explorer (Section 2.4 of the Textbook). The new requirement is SUMO: cd ~/program # With access to the private repository: git clone https://github.com/ertlnagoya/cadl-mobility-sos-exercise # Without it, place the copy you were given at ~/program/cadl-mobility-sos-exercise. # Exercise venv cd cadl-mobility-sos-exercise python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python3 -m pip install --upgrade pip pip install -r requirements.txt # SUMO (pip is the simplest cross-platform way) pip install eclipse-sumo # CADL compiler: install the clone from Course A into this venv, # so that `cadl` and the exercise scripts run in the same shell pip install -e ~/program/cadl_repo cadl --version # cadl-explorer (cloned in Section 2.4 of the Textbook, Course A): install its # requirements into this venv too, so that `streamlit` runs in this shell (§4). # It keeps the cadl installed above, as in Chapter 6 of the Textbook. pip install -r ~/program/cadl-explorer/requirements.txt If z3-solver fails to build during pip install -e ~/program/cadl_repo, fall back to pip install --no-deps -e ~/program/cadl_repo followed by pip install lark pyyaml. This tutorial only needs cadl check and cadl sim-ir, neither of which uses Z3. For other install failures, see the setup troubleshooting in Section 2.4 of the Textbook.

Open cadl/mobility_sos.cadl and look at the actors: inside the sos: block (excerpt): sos: name: "MobilitySoS" type: Acknowledged actors: - id: PLATFORM autonomy: low # central matching authority - id: "TAXI[1..N]" autonomy: high # self-interested fleet - id: "PASSENGER[1..M]" autonomy: medium # service requesters How to read it: the platform is the central coordinator and has little freedom to act on its own (autonomy: low); the taxis are self-interested agents with high autonomy; passengers issue requests and decide whether to board. The same Acknowledged SoS type as the robot-delivery example. 🔍 Visualization Checkpoint 0 — What a structure-only spec gives you So far you have read only the structure (the actors). Check the file, and print how much of the contract's normative part the IR carries: cd ~/program/cadl-mobility-sos-exercise cadl check cadl/mobility_sos.cadl # → Type check passed: cadl/mobility_sos.cadl cadl sim-ir cadl/mobility_sos.cadl --format json \ | python3 -c "import sys, json; c=json.load(sys.stdin)['institution']['contracts'][0]; print('lifecycle =', 'present' if c['lifecycle'] else None, '/ monitors =', len(c['monitors']))" The file you are reading is the complete specification: its contract already carries the lifecycle: and monitors: blocks that §3 walks through, so the command should report a lifecycle. To see what the structure alone would give, make a scratch copy, delete the lifecycle: and monitors: blocks from it, and run the same two commands on the copy: cadl check still passes, but the IR has "lifecycle": null and no monitors, and the Contract Lifecycle page of cadl-explorer shows no diagram: only a warning that the contract does not declare a lifecycle: section, and a note that it declares no monitors. On the Designer page, the Message flow tab of the Structure view (cadl-explorer v0.5.5 or later) shows only "No messages yet": it takes messages from protocol steps, lifecycle events and information sharing, and the copy has none of them. That gap — structure alone cannot express deadlines, violations, or consequences — is what the blocks you read in §3 fill.

The contract in the same file (an excerpt: the assume: and incentives: blocks, the transitions after accept, and the monitors waiting_too_long and detour_guard are omitted; the # ... at the end of each list stands for its omitted entries; comments are removed and on_violation: / on_match: are written in flow style): contracts: - id: RIDE_SLA parties: [PLATFORM, "TAXI[*]", "PASSENGER[*]"] guarantee: - "waiting_time <= 300s" - "ride_time <= 1800s" lifecycle: states: [Requested, Matched, Accepted, PickedUp, Delivered, Violated, Cancelled, Terminated] initial: Requested terminal: [Delivered, Violated, Cancelled, Terminated] transitions: - id: match from: Requested to: Matched on: "PLATFORM -> TAXI[i] : match_assignment" deadline: 30s on_violation: { transition: Violated, severity: Major } - id: accept from: Matched to: Accepted on: "TAXI[i] -> PLATFORM : ack(accepted)" deadline: 5s on_violation: { transition: Violated, severity: Major } # ... monitors: - id: low_battery_guard observe: "TAXI[i].battery" sampling: periodic(500ms) rule: "TAXI[i].battery < 15 AND state == Accepted" on_match: { transition: Violated, severity: Critical } # ...

One lifecycle instance corresponds to one ride request. Answer the following. If the platform fails to dispatch within 31 seconds, what state does the contract enter? Whose responsibility is the accept deadline? State, in one sentence, when low_battery_guard fires.

In §3 you read the lifecycle: and monitors: blocks of the CADL source. Because the file contains them, cadl-explorer renders a meaningful picture. cd ~/program/cadl-mobility-sos-exercise cadl check cadl/mobility_sos.cadl cadl sim-ir cadl/mobility_sos.cadl --format json > cadl/mobility_sos.ir.json cd ~/program/cadl-explorer streamlit run app.py # Browser opens at http://localhost:8501 # Sidebar → "Contract Lifecycle" → drag mobility_sos.ir.json into the uploader You should see something like: Visual Meaning Double circle = Requested initial state Dashed grey = Delivered/Cancelled/Terminated normal terminals Dashed pink = Violated violation terminal Solid edge with Δ 30s / Δ 5s deadline-bearing transitions Red dashed edge labelled violation / Major (two lines) forced move to the on_violation target state Terminated stands alone in the diagram: the contract declares it as a terminal state, but no transition leads to it. If you open mobility_sos.cadl on the Designer page, the same fact is reported as a Lifecycle warning (State 'Terminated' cannot be reached from the initial state 'Requested'). cadl check passes regardless. This pattern repeats throughout the tutorial You will run edit CADL → cadl sim-ir → upload the IR to cadl-explorer again at every milestone (reloading the browser page clears the uploaded file): after reading the structure, after reading the contract, after codegen, after the simulation, after revising the contract. The whole point of the tutorial is to internalize that the picture changes in lockstep with the code.

In cadl/mobility_sos.cadl, change the match deadline from 30s to 60s, regenerate the IR, and upload it again. The edge label should change from Δ 30s to Δ 60s. Once verified, revert it back to 30s before continuing (later sections assume 30s).

scripts/cadl_to_sumo.py is the SUMO counterpart to cadl codegen --target unity-csharp: it consumes the IR JSON and emits SUMO configuration plus a contract-constraints JSON. cd ~/program/cadl-mobility-sos-exercise python scripts/cadl_to_sumo.py Example output (excerpt; the scripts print their progress messages in Japanese): [1/4] CADL.environment 検証 [OK] grid_size=5 は SUMO ネットワークと一致。 [2/4] contracts → constraints 抽出 - contract RIDE_SLA guarantees: 2 waiting_time <= 300.0s ride_time <= 1800.0s deadlines : 2 match 30.0s (violation→Violated, sev=Major) accept 5.0s (violation→Violated, sev=Major) monitors : 3 [3/4] sumocfg 生成 (CADL.time_step_ms / 終端を反映) ✓ step-length = 1.0s ✓ end = 4920s Produces: sumo/config/midtown.cadl.sumocfg — step-length from environment.time_step_ms, end = the last depart in sumo/routes/midtown.rou.xml + the larger of 1800 s and the ride_time guarantee + 60 s (3060 + 1800 + 60 = 4920 with the sample data). The repository ships sumo/routes/midtown.rou.xml, so this first run already gives 4920 s; without the route file end would be 3600 s. §6 re-runs this script after generate_sumo_routes.py, before run_sumo.py, so end follows the routes you generate. A tighter ride_time (as in §8) does not shorten end. sumo/cadl_constraints.json — the contract conditions (guarantees / deadlines / monitors) that analyze_results.py reads. 🔍 Visualization Checkpoint 2 — Post-codegen (CADL source is unchanged) cadl_to_sumo.py only reads the IR and writes SUMO config files; it never modifies cadl/mobility_sos.cadl. The lifecycle: and monitors: blocks are byte-for-byte identical to what they were in §3. Upload cadl/mobility_sos.ir.json to cadl-explorer again now and you should see the exact same picture as in §4. That invariance is what lets us treat CADL as the single source of truth: target-specific generators consume the spec without mutating it.

# Check the sample demand CSV python scripts/prepare_sample_data.py # Build the SUMO network (one time) netconvert -c sumo/network/midtown.netccfg # CSV → route file python scripts/generate_sumo_routes.py # Regenerate the sumocfg now that the route file exists (end = 4920 s) python scripts/cadl_to_sumo.py # Run SUMO (picks the CADL-derived sumocfg) python scripts/run_sumo.py # headless # python scripts/run_sumo.py --gui # with visualization This populates results/tripinfo.xml and results/summary.xml. The headless run needs nothing beyond the eclipse-sumo package. --gui starts sumo-gui, which is an X11 application: on macOS it needs XQuartz installed and running, and without it the run stops with FXApp::openDisplay: unable to open display. The same error appears right after installing XQuartz, until you log out and back in; to continue without doing so, start XQuartz (open -a XQuartz) and run export DISPLAY=:0 in the terminal first. In the SUMO window, press the play button to start the simulation. The rest of this course uses only the headless results.

python scripts/analyze_results.py Example output (excerpt; the header line is printed in Japanese): === CADL 契約 (cadl_constraints.json) との遵守チェック === contract: RIDE_SLA -- guarantees -- [OK ] waiting_time <= 300s (tripinfo.waitingTime) [OK ] ride_time <= 1800s (tripinfo.duration) -- deadlines (lifecycle) -- [SKIP ] match ≤ 30.0s (not-evaluated (matching/accept events not modeled in SUMO yet)) [SKIP ] accept ≤ 5.0s (not-evaluated (matching/accept events not modeled in SUMO yet)) -- monitors -- [SKIP ] waiting_too_long (not-evaluated (observed attribute not exported by SUMO)) [SKIP ] low_battery_guard (not-evaluated (observed attribute not exported by SUMO)) [SKIP ] detour_guard (not-evaluated (observed attribute not exported by SUMO)) What is actually checked here is the two guarantee clauses only; the deadlines and the three monitors are listed but not evaluated: Guarantees are evaluated against tripinfo.xml. ride_time maps directly to tripinfo.duration. waiting_time is compared with tripinfo.waitingTime, which is only a stand-in: it is the time a vehicle spent standing still during its trip, not the time a passenger waited for a taxi. In this pipeline each CSV row inserts one vehicle at the pickup point at the pickup time, so no passenger ever waits, and the value is 0 s for all 30 trips. This [OK] therefore holds by construction. Deadlines for matching/accept events are not modeled in SUMO yet — flagged SKIP. Monitors observe per-passenger waiting_time while Matched, battery, and route_deviation_ratio, none of which SUMO exports — flagged SKIP. 🔍 Visualization Checkpoint 3 — Post-simulation (spec ↔ outcomes) Each line of analyze_results.py's output traces back to something in cadl-explorer's diagram. With the explorer open beside the terminal, walk through the correspondence: analyze_results.py line Where it lives in cadl-explorer [OK] waiting_time <= 300s Not in the graph (a numeric guarantee, evaluated post-hoc) [OK] ride_time <= 1800s Same as above [SKIP] match ≤ 30.0s The Δ 30s label on the Requested → Matched edge [SKIP] accept ≤ 5.0s The Δ 5s label on the Matched → Accepted edge [SKIP] waiting_too_long / low_battery_guard / detour_guard First, second and third rows of the Monitors table SKIP is not a failure — it simply reports that SUMO has no observable for that signal. A stretch goal in §9 walks through closing one of these gaps via TraCI.
documents.s: 7. Check the results against the contract (10 min)

documents.t: This is the punchline. Edit a CADL guarantee, regenerate the IR, and the existing simulation result is re-evaluated against the new contract — without re-running SUMO. # Rewrite ride_time 1800s → 100s (for the experiment) sed -i.bak 's|ride_time <= 1800s|ride_time <= 100s|' cadl/mobility_sos.cadl # Regenerate the IR (no need to re-run the simulation) cadl sim-ir cadl/mobility_sos.cadl --format json > cadl/mobility_sos.ir.json python scripts/cadl_to_sumo.py # Re-evaluate the existing SUMO results python scripts/analyze_results.py | grep -E "OK|VIOLATED" Output (12 violations with SUMO 1.28.0; the run is deterministic, so the same SUMO version reproduces it exactly; the violation count and the taxis listed can differ with another SUMO version — what matters is the pattern: waiting_time stays OK while ride_time turns VIOLATED): [OK ] waiting_time <= 300s (tripinfo.waitingTime) [VIOLATED (12)] ride_time <= 100s (tripinfo.duration e.g. ['taxi_8', 'taxi_9', 'taxi_10', 'taxi_11', 'taxi_14']) OK: 分析完了。 The last line is the script's closing message ("analysis complete"); it matches the grep pattern because it starts with OK. 🔍 Visualization Checkpoint 4 — Post-revision (★ highlight) Upload the regenerated cadl/mobility_sos.ir.json to cadl-explorer again (the commands above already wrote it). The change you just made touches only a guarantee value (ride_time <= 1800s → 100s). You did not touch lifecycle: or monitors:, so the state-machine diagram itself is identical to §4 — same states, same transitions, same Δ labels. To change the diagram you would have to edit transitions: (you did exactly that in Exercise 4-1). The reason this checkpoint still matters is that, after editing the CADL source, you should consciously go back to the browser and see that the same spec that drives the diagram also drives analyze_results.py's verdict. That single-source correspondence is the whole goal of this tutorial: CADL source (mobility_sos.cadl) │ ├── Picture (cadl-explorer) ← visual understanding ├── Execution (SUMO) ← dynamic behavior └── Verdict (analyze_results.py) ← guarantee check That round-trip is the SoS-design feedback loop CADL is meant to enable. When you're done, restore the original guarantee: mv cadl/mobility_sos.cadl.bak cadl/mobility_sos.cadl cadl sim-ir cadl/mobility_sos.cadl --format json > cadl/mobility_sos.ir.json python scripts/cadl_to_sumo.py python scripts/analyze_results.py
documents.s: 8. Sensitivity analysis: edit the contract, re-evaluate (10 min)

documents.t: Task Hint Tighten the match deadline 30s→10s; how many trips realistically meet it? SUMO has no match event (one CSV row is one vehicle), and cadl_to_sumo.py only reads the IR, so the line stays [SKIP]. Extend analyze_results.py to use departDelay in tripinfo.xml as a proxy. With the sample data it is 0 s for all 30 trips, so first decide what a match event should be. Change num_taxis from 10 to 5 and find out whether anything changes. Nothing in the SUMO pipeline consumes num_taxis (demand comes from the CSV, one vehicle per row): the 30 <tripinfo> rows of tripinfo.xml are identical after the change (only the header comment with the generation time differs). Use the running time series in summary.xml (it peaks at 2 with the sample data) to argue what fleet size this demand needs, and what would have to be modelled for a capacity violation to appear. Add a new monitor surge_pricing_guard and follow it through the toolchain. Add it under monitors: and regenerate the IR. Confirm that it reaches the IR (4 monitors), the Monitors table in cadl-explorer and the [SKIP] list of analyze_results.py. Monitor rules are not evaluated by this pipeline, so there is no trigger pattern to observe yet. A/B visual diff: compare the before and after designs. In cadl-explorer, open the .cadl file on the Designer page, save a version under Versions, open the revised file and compare the two there. Saving the version selects it as A — baseline under Compare two designs, and the current design as B — compared (cadl-explorer v0.5.4 or later; with older versions, choose them yourself); a structured diff and a source diff are shown. To see two lifecycle diagrams side by side, open the Contract Lifecycle page in two browser tabs and upload one IR in each; a second instance on another port is not needed. Close one of the [SKIP] gaps by reading the relevant SUMO signal via TraCI: measure the match deadline. pip install eclipse-sumo does not make traci importable: run pip install traci, or add os.path.join(sumo.SUMO_HOME, "tools") to sys.path after import sumo (the shell variable $SUMO_HOME is not set by the pip install). Read traci.vehicle.getDeparture(vehID) (or traci.simulation.getDepartedIDList()) and compare it with the CSV's pickup_time. This measures insertion delay — a proxy for match, 0 s in the sample data — not a modelled match event.

Same CADL/SoS-DSL syntax; different domain (mobility vs robot delivery) and different runtime (SUMO vs Unity C#). The contract's deadlines / guarantees / monitors live in one place, the CADL source, and reach each tool through the IR that cadl sim-ir emits. How much of them a given runtime can evaluate differs: in this course the SUMO pipeline evaluates the guarantee clauses only, and reports the deadlines and monitors as [SKIP] because SUMO has no observable for them. Editing a CADL guarantee and re-running the analysis re-evaluates the existing results without re-simulating — a cheap, fast feedback loop for SoS design.
Course A (robot delivery): Textbook SoS-DSL spec: cadl-spec Appendix E SUMO project: https://eclipse.dev/sumo/

Course C is deliberately open-ended. It is given as an outline rather than as step-by-step exercises: you choose the domain, write the specification from a blank page, and decide how to exercise it. Treat it as a small self-directed project. Pick a domain other than robot delivery — recommended: food delivery (modelled as a Collaborative SoS); as a stretch, disaster response in its first hours, before any incident-command structure has formed (Virtual SoS) — and take it through the same five stages as the textbook (Chapters 4–9). The key difference: Course C does not give you a starting .cadl file. Identify actors and contracts (no template is provided). Decide which SoS type (Maier / ISO/IEC/IEEE 21841) the domain belongs to, and justify the type: you declare. Write lifecycle: and monitors: from scratch, pass cadl check, and inspect the result in cadl-explorer. Exercise the specification with a runtime of your choice. The suggested default is a lightweight Python discrete-event harness (for example SimPy) that replays the lifecycle from the IR JSON (cadl sim-ir --format json); Unity is not required. No harness is provided — writing it is part of the task. Sweep parameters and write a comparison report (the 3-page format of Exercise 9.4 in Chapter 9 of the textbook works well). Course C needs only the public repositories (cadl, cadl-explorer). For the academic positioning of this course (Maier criteria, ISO standards, taxonomy), see academic-background.md.
documents.s: Course C — Modelling a New SoS End-to-End

documents.t: ⬅ Back to Course A → Course A — Robot Delivery Audience: Students who have completed Course A (CADL/SoS-DSL basics). Course B is not required. Time: 120–150 minutes, plus optional stretch goals. You will leave with: KPIs written by a human in natural language, the LLM's amendment proposals and decision requests, the human's decisions with their reasons (in prose and in GSN), and the versions of the CADL rules and of the constitution that resulted, period by period.
documents.s: Course D — Robot Town: Amending Rules Toward a KPI

documents.t: Courses A and B write a contract once and check a simulation against it. In Course D the contract itself changes while the system runs. Three delivery companies (A, B, C; two robots each) share the 11-node road network of the Raspberry Pi Mouse simulator. After each simulated hour (one period), amendments to the rules are considered. A human, an LLM and a set of mechanical gates share the work: Who Does what Human (the service operator) Writes the service KPIs in natural language; the KPIs may change over time. Answers the LLM's decision requests and records the reason and the outcome, in prose or in GSN LLM Turns the KPI into measurable metrics and proposes amendments to rules, regulation and contracts toward it. When a question cannot clearly be settled, or when human stakeholders must agree, it does not decide: it asks the human and supplies what the decision needs Gates Check, constitution, improvement measured on the same random seeds, and the companies' vote. The LLM's own account is never trusted; only measured values count kpi.md (written by a human in natural language; may change per period) │ the LLM turns it into a measure; if it can be read several ways, the human picks ← request K<k> ▼ measure robot_town.cadl (version k) in this period's environment │ the LLM proposes amendments (rules, contract, regulation) │ gates: check → constitution → improvement (same seeds) → vote ▼ does any proposal raise agreement, contract, regulation, safety, KPI conflict or uncertainty, or did the LLM ask? ├ no → adopt automatically the gate-passing proposal with the best KPI └ yes → the LLM writes a decision request and the human answers ← request D<k> ▼ robot_town.cadl (version k+1) and the record of decisions (decisions.md, gsn.yaml) │ next period, the LLM reads the human's decisions and reasons before proposing The exercise lives in the public repository cadl-robot-town. It needs neither Unity nor SUMO: the town is a small Python simulation, and the norms are judged by the same reference runtime as Course A (contract_engine.py, copied from cadl-raspimouse-simulator). About the recorded LLM output §4–§8 can be followed without an API key by replaying the records in examples/steward-d-en/ (English) and examples/steward-goodhart/. They are records of real runs with Claude Opus 5.5 on 2026-10-29/30; examples/steward-d/ holds the same run in Japanese. The answers to the decision requests (answers.yaml) were written by Claude playing the human operator when the records were made; from §4 on, answer them yourself. Every number shown is measured by the gates and the simulation on replay. §10 shows how to run a real LLM with your own key.

All you need is the CADL compiler cloned in Course A (~/program/cadl_repo). cd ~/program git clone https://github.com/ertlnagoya/cadl-robot-town cd cadl-robot-town python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python3 -m pip install --upgrade pip pip install -e ~/program/cadl_repo # the cadl command and PyYAML If the install fails, see the setup troubleshooting in Section 2.4 of the Textbook. Only §10 (a real LLM) needs the Anthropic SDK and an API key. pip install anthropic town.steward --lang en prints English and asks the LLM to write in English. town.period, town.council and town.compare print Japanese only; each step below explains what you need from their output.

Open cadl/robot_town.cadl. The town has two contracts. DELIVERY_SLA: one instance per order. Pick up within 120 s and deliver within 120 s of pickup, or the order becomes Late. This is the promise to customers. ROAD_USE: one instance each time a robot stops on the road to wait for its next order. - id: DELIVERY_SLA parties: [TOWN_STEWARD, "ROBOT[*]"] guarantee: - "pickup_time <= 120s" # @amend:pickup_deadline - "dropoff_time <= 120s" # @amend:dropoff_deadline lifecycle: ... - id: pickup from: Assigned to: PickedUp on: "ROBOT[i].status == PickedUp" deadline: 120s # @amend:pickup_deadline on_violation: { transition: Late, severity: Major } ... - id: ROAD_USE parties: [TOWN_STEWARD, "ROBOT[*]", COUNCIL] authority: decision_holder: COUNCIL incentives: type: sanction lambda: 0.5 # @amend:sanction_lambda lifecycle: states: [Holding, Overstay, Released, Evicted] initial: Holding terminal: [Released, Evicted] transitions: - id: release from: [Holding, Overstay] to: Released on: "ROBOT[i] -> TOWN_STEWARD : node_released" deadline: 60s # @amend:hold_limit on_violation: { transition: Overstay, severity: Minor } monitors: - id: blocking_guard observe: "ROBOT[i].blocking" sampling: periodic(1000ms) rule: "ROBOT.blocking >= 3 AND state IN [Holding, Overstay]" # @amend:block_k on_match: { transition: Evicted, severity: Major } (Excerpt, simplified.) A line tagged # @amend:<name> holds a parameter that may be amended. When several lines carry the same name (the pickup guarantee and the pickup deadline), they must all hold the same value. Which layer a parameter belongs to and how far it may move is set by constitution.yaml: amendable: hold_limit: {layer: rule, min: 10, max: 120, step: 10} # seconds a robot may wait on the road block_k: {layer: rule, min: 1, max: 4, step: 1} # robots waiting behind it before eviction sanction_lambda: {layer: rule, min: 0.0, max: 2.0, step: 0.5} # sanction points per violation (Minor 1, Major 3) to_central: {layer: rule, safety: true, ...} # operating-mode switch (§9) pickup_deadline: {layer: contract, min: 60, max: 180, step: 30} # promised seconds to pickup dropoff_deadline: {layer: contract, min: 60, max: 180, step: 30} # promised seconds to delivery invariants: min_company_on_time_rate: 0.6 vote: quorum: 2 regulation: invariants.min_company_on_time_rate: {min: 0.5, max: 0.95, step: 0.05} vote.quorum: {min: 1, max: 3, step: 1} (Excerpt, simplified.) There are three layers of amendment: Layer Covers Who decides Rule ROAD_USE and the operating-mode switching conditions adopted automatically if it passes every gate; the switching conditions (safety: true) are decided by the human Contract DELIVERY_SLA (the promise to customers) customers have no vote, so the human decides Regulation values in the constitution (invariants, quorum) the human decides The three companies behave differently (town/policies.py): A always returns to its garage; B waits on the road for its next order but leaves 5 s before hold_limit, and does not wait on the road at all if a single waiting robot triggers eviction (block_k of 1); C waits until an order comes or it is evicted, unless sanction_lambda reaches 1.5, when it behaves like B. A robot stopped at an intersection blocks everyone who wants to pass through it.
documents.s: 2. Read the rules, the contract and the regulation (15 min)

documents.t: Which company can never be sanctioned under the current rules, and why? If the pickup promise (pickup_deadline) were extended to 150 s, what would you expect to happen to the number of on-time deliveries? And to how long customers actually wait? Why must an amendment to the contract layer not be settled by the companies' vote alone?

Fix the operating mode to distributed for now (§9 explains the modes): python -m town.period --mode DISTRIBUTED 需要: 各社の注文の平均間隔 75 秒 運用モード: DISTRIBUTED 規則: robot_town.cadl (hold_limit=60s, block_k=3, sanction_lambda=0.5) 定時配達 121.8 / 注文 132.2 未配達 0.0 ふさがれた時間 2404s （シード平均） 会社 定時率 遅配 道路で待った回数 ふさがれた秒数 罰点 効用 A 0.84 7.8 0.0 1352 0.0 38.4 B 0.94 2.6 38.0 849 0.9 38.9 C 1.00 0.0 39.6 203 14.8 28.8 違反（原因別，シード平均）: deadline:dropoff=2.6, deadline:pickup=7.8, deadline:release=23.0, monitor:blocking_guard=2.8 運用モード: 集中の時間 0% 切替 0.0 回（切替中の合計 0s，管理者による退去 0.0 台，安全条件の違反 0.0 回） The columns are: on-time rate, late deliveries, times waited on the road, seconds blocked by stopped robots, sanction points, and utility (on-time deliveries minus sanction points). The numbers are averages over five random seeds. C waits on the road, reaches every customer on time, and pays 14.8 sanction points for it; A, which never blocks anyone, is blocked for 1352 s and loses 7.8 deliveries. Every violation in the second-to-last line was detected by the contract runtime from the IR: deadline:* by lifecycle deadlines, monitor:blocking_guard by the monitor.

The human's first job is to write the KPI. In English it goes in kpi.en.md: ## From period 1 Deliver as many orders as possible across the town within the times we promised customers (120 seconds from order to pickup, 120 seconds from pickup to delivery). No company's customers should be kept waiting badly. ## From period 5 The quiet season begins and orders fall. On-time delivery still matters, but to keep the companies cooperating, no single company should gain or lose because of how the road is used. A ## From period k heading says when a KPI takes effect (the Japanese file, kpi.md, uses ## 第 k 期から). The loop re-reads the file at the start of every period, so you may edit it between periods. --lang en makes the loop's own text and the LLM's writing English. A natural-language KPI cannot rank proposals by itself. The LLM rewrites it as a combination of the metrics in town/kpi.py (on-time deliveries, late deliveries, unfinished orders, blocked time, the lowest company's on-time rate, the spread of the companies' utilities, total sanctions, and so on). This is the measure: a main goal (improvement is measured by it), watched goals (the human is told if they get worse by more than the noise) and conditions (which every amendment must keep). Replay the record and run one period. Without --answers, you answer decision requests in the terminal. python -m town.steward --lang en --mode DISTRIBUTED --rounds 1 --name try-d-en \ --llm replay --replay-dir examples/steward-d-en KPI (from period 1): Deliver as many orders as possible across the town within the times we promised customers (120 seconds from order to pickup, 120 seconds from pickup to delivery). No company's customers should be kept waiting badly. LLM: replay: examples/steward-d-en/p1-kpi.json (claude-opus-5-5, input 2428 / output 2266 tokens) Reading: The KPI has two parts. The main goal is to maximize the number of orders delivered town-wide within the promised SLA times (120 s order-to-pickup, 120 s pickup-to-delivery), which maps directly to on_time_deliveries. The second part, 'no company's customers should be kept waiting badly', is a fairness floor across companies A, B and C. (…) [1] Maximize town-wide on-time deliveries with a floor on the worst company: main goal on_time_deliveries (increase), min_company_on_time_rate (increase), unfinished (decrease), late_deliveries (decrease); conditions min_company_on_time_rate >= 0.8, unfinished <= 3 [2] Maximize the worst company's on-time rate (maximin fairness first): main goal min_company_on_time_rate (increase), on_time_deliveries (increase), unfinished (decrease); conditions unfinished <= 3 [3] Maximize town-wide on-time deliveries with a cap on the inter-company gap: main goal on_time_deliveries (increase), on_time_rate_gap (decrease), min_company_on_time_rate (increase); conditions on_time_rate_gap <= 0.15 Concern: 'Kept waiting badly' is not quantified. It could mean an absolute floor per company, a limit on the spread between companies, or no orders left undelivered. The numeric thresholds in the guards are provisional guesses and should be set from baseline measurements. Concern: on_time_deliveries is a proxy that ignores orders already past their deadline. Optimizing it alone could deprioritize late orders and leave them unfinished, which is exactly the badly-kept-waiting outcome the KPI forbids. (…) Concern: The promised times (120 s / 120 s) are part of the KPI and of DELIVERY_SLA. Raising the on-time count by loosening the SLA would game the metric, and any SLA change must be decided by humans as a contract amendment. (2 more) → Decision request K1 (the LLM recommends 1) Choose an id (1 / 2 / 3): This replays what Claude Opus 5.5 actually wrote on 2026-10-29. When a KPI has a single reading and no concern, the LLM uses its measure without asking. Here it found "kept waiting badly" unquantified and returned three measures with five concerns. The machine checks the metric names and the shape of every measure the LLM writes; one that uses an unknown metric is dropped from the choices. After you pick a number you are asked for a reason and for assumptions (GSN Assumptions; any number of lines, an empty line ends). The recorded answers (examples/steward-d-en/answers.yaml) were written by Claude playing the operator when the record was made: K1: choice: "1" reason: Follow the order of the KPI. Town-wide on-time deliveries are the main goal, and the worst company's on-time rate, unfinished orders and late deliveries are watched. The floors are provisional, as the LLM says; 0.8 keeps today's worst company (0.84) from falling further. (…) assumptions: - Customers cannot choose their delivery company
How do you expect the decision request in §5 to change if you pick measure 2? The last concern restates question 2 of Exercise 2-1. Where in the KPI's wording did the LLM find that?

After K1, the LLM proposes amendments and each passes through the gates: | id | proposal | layer | check | constitution | on-time | late | blocked s | road violations | lowest on-time rate | change in on_time_deliveries | seeds improved | KPI conditions | utility A / B / C | votes A B C | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | — | current | — | — | — | 121.8 | 10.4 | 2404 | 25.8 | 0.84 | — | — | — | 38.4 / 38.9 / 28.8 | — | | 1 | block_k 3 → 2 | rule | ○ | ○ | 131.0 | 1.2 | 985 | 34.0 | 0.98 | +9.2 | 5/5 | ○ | 45.4 / 37.2 / 19.0 | ○ × × | | 2 | hold_limit 60s → 50s | rule | ○ | ○ | 120.6 | 11.6 | 2468 | 28.8 | 0.86 | -1.2 | 2/5 | ○ | 38.8 / 37.6 / 27.2 | ○ × × | | 3 | sanction_lambda 0.5 → 1 | rule | ○ | ○ | 121.8 | 10.4 | 2404 | 25.8 | 0.84 | +0.0 | 0/5 | ○ | 38.4 / 38.0 / 14.0 | ○ × × | | R1 | invariants.min_company_on_time_rate 0.6 → 0.65 | regulation | — | ○ | | | | | | | | | | | (The "watched goals and conditions" and "notes" columns are left out here; the note on R1 reads "the current rules meet the new condition".) The LLM's first proposal, block_k 3 → 2 (evict a robot as soon as two robots wait behind it), adds 9.2 on-time deliveries but is voted down by B and C. It also proposed a regulation: raising the constitution's floor on every company's on-time rate from 0.6 to 0.65. It proposed no contract change, having read at K1 that loosening the promised times does not count as improving the KPI. The loop does not decide when a proposal raises any of the following (triage() in town/steward.py): Reason When Agreement it improves the KPI but is voted down, and beats every proposal that could be adopted automatically Contract it changes the promise to customers and improves the KPI Regulation it changes a value of the constitution Safety it changes an operating-mode switching condition and improves the KPI KPI conflict it improves the main goal but breaks a KPI condition or worsens a watched goal Uncertain it passes every gate but improves on fewer than 4 of the 5 seeds LLM the LLM itself said a human should decide (only for proposals that keep the constitution's invariants) Here proposal 1 raises agreement and R1 raises regulation. The LLM writes decision request D1, saved as runs/try-d-en/p1-request.md: → Decision request D1 (LLM: replay: examples/steward-d-en/p1-request.json (claude-opus-5-5, input 2712 / output 1957 tokens)) **Question**: Should we adopt the rule change block_k 3 → 2 even though B and C voted against it, raise the constitutional floor invariants.min_company_on_time_rate from 0.60 to 0.65, or keep the current rules (v1)? - **1**: block_k 3 → 2. (…) Adopting it means overriding the votes of B and C (votes ○ × ×). (stakeholders: Gains: customers of all companies, because late deliveries fall from 10.4 to 1.2 and the worst company's on-time rate rises to 0.98. Company A also gains (utility 38.4 → 45.4). Losses: Company C (utility 28.8 → 19.0) and, slightly, Company B (38.9 → 37.2). (…)) - **R1**: (…) The current rules (lowest on-time rate 0.84) already meet it, so nothing changes in operation now. It only blocks future changes that would let the worst company fall below 0.65. (…) - **keep**: no change. (…) The LLM recommends: R1 — R1 is low-risk: the current rules (0.84) and proposal 1 (0.98) both satisfy it. It strengthens the KPI's fairness clause without overriding anyone. Proposal 1 has the strongest measured KPI gain, but it failed the company vote, cuts C's utility by about a third, and raises road violations. I suggest not forcing it now. Instead, take it to B and C for negotiation, (…) and re-measure before deciding. The LLM does not know: Why C's utility drops sharply (28.8 → 19.0) under proposal 1 while the lowest company on-time rate rises to 0.98; the utility components were not broken down. The LLM does not know: Whether B and C would accept proposal 1 with compensation or a modified threshold, and how the companies would change their behaviour if it were forced through. The LLM does not know: Whether overriding a failed company vote is acceptable under the town's governance norms. (3 more) A request contains the question; why the LLM is not deciding; for each option what happens and who gains or loses; the LLM's recommendation; and what the LLM does not know. The options are the proposals that raised a reason, the proposal that could be adopted automatically (if any) and "keep"; the LLM cannot add options. The table of numbers is the gates' measurement, not the LLM's prose. The recorded answer goes against the LLM's recommendation and adopts proposal 1, overturning the vote: D1: choice: "1" reason: The intersections are a road shared by the three companies; waiting there is no company's right. Late deliveries fall from 10.4 to 1.2 and the worst company's on-time rate rises, so adopt it against B's and C's votes. Re-measure C's utility (28.8 to 19.0) and the road violations next period. The constitutional floor (R1) can wait; it changes nothing now. assumptions: - B and C keep delivering in town after the rules change The same period in Japanese (examples/steward-d/) produced no regulation proposal, and its recommendation changed when the request was sent a second time on the same numbers (first "1", then "keep"). A recommendation is the output of one request. The LLM laid out the material and showed that both choices had reasons; the human decided.

Each decision goes into two files in runs/<name>/: decisions.md: the prose record — for each decision, the measure, the LLM's assessment, why the human was asked, the LLM's recommendation and unknowns, and the human's choice and reason. gsn.yaml: a GSN (Goal Structuring Notation) tree, with a Mermaid diagram in gsn.md. GSN element What goes in it Goal the KPI written by the human (one per version) Strategy the decision of a period (the amendment adopted, or no change) Solution the measurement on the same seeds (p<k>-evidence.md) Context the measure of the KPI; the period's environment Assumption assumptions written by the human Justification the human's reason (or, for an automatic decision, its condition) Reasons may be written in prose or as GSN elements; in the --answers YAML, list elements (each with type: and text:) under gsn:. For example (the recorded answer to D2 gives its reason in prose): D2: choice: keep gsn: - type: justification text: Only 2 of 5 seeds improve; do not cut C's utility by 16 for an uncertain gain - type: context text: In D1 we decided to re-measure C's utility From the next period on, earlier decisions and the human's reasons are passed to the LLM. §6 shows how that changes its proposals and recommendations.

The same first period with the rule-based council (town.council), which tries every one-step amendment to the rules and adopts the gate-passing one with the best objective, never a vetoed one: python -m town.council --mode DISTRIBUTED 改正案 定時配達 違反 (道路) ふさがれた 検査 憲法 改善 投票(A B C) hold_limit 60s → 50s 120.6 40.4 (28.8) 2468s ○ ○ × ○ × × hold_limit 60s → 70s 124.2 31.6 (23.6) 2367s ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ block_k 3 → 2 131.0 35.2 (34.0) 985s ○ ○ ○ ○ × × ... → 採択: hold_limit 60s → 70s（目標 +2.4，賛成 ABC）。v2.cadl として保存。 (town.council prints Japanese only.) block_k 3 → 2, the best for the town, is vetoed, and a small amendment all three accept is adopted. The difference from D1 is who decided whether to overturn the veto, and whether the reason was recorded.
documents.s: Compare: a council with no human

documents.t: Answer keep (or R1) to D1 and rerun the first period. How do decisions.md and gsn.md change? B is itself blocked for 849 s, yet it votes against block_k 3 → 2. Explain why from the table in §3.

Run all six periods with the recorded answers: python -m town.steward --lang en --mode DISTRIBUTED --rounds 6 --name steward-d-en \ --llm replay --replay-dir examples/steward-d-en --answers examples/steward-d-en/answers.yaml scenario.yaml sets the demand of each period (normal, busy, quiet, with a mid-period rush in some). The current rules are re-measured in each period's environment before being compared. Period Reasons for the request LLM recommends Human's choice Result 1 (normal) agreement (block_k 3 → 2 vetoed by B and C); regulation (floor 0.6 → 0.65) R1 block_k 3 → 2, overturning the veto v2 2 (normal + rush) uncertain (block_k 2 → 1 improves on 2/5 seeds); LLM keep keep v2 3 (busy) none (the only proposal gains +0.6, below the noise of one delivery) — — v2 (automatic) 4 (busy + rush) none (the LLM proposes nothing) — — v2 (automatic) 5 (quiet) see §7 1 hold_limit 60s → 70s v3 6 (quiet) KPI conflict (hold_limit 70s → 80s widens the spread of on-time rates from 0.02 to 0.05) keep keep v3 The Japanese record (examples/steward-d/) ends with the same six outcomes, because the human answered the same way; the LLM's proposals and recommendations differ in places (see §10). Things to notice: Period 2: block_k 2 → 1 passes every gate, but only 2 of 5 seeds improve. The LLM also asked on its own, citing the human's promise in D1 to re-measure C's utility. It lists as unknown "Whether the A and B yes votes alone meet the quorum": in fact A and B's two votes reach the quorum of 2, so no override is needed. The decision-request call is not given the constitution, so the LLM did not know the quorum (the Japanese LLM, in the same period, wrongly called it an override). Periods 3–4: in the busy season there are few late deliveries left, so there is little room for the main goal. The LLM says so in its assessment and proposes nothing in period 4. No request; the GSN still records that the decision was automatic, and on what condition. Period 6: the LLM recommends keeping the rules, citing the human's reason for 70 s in D5 ("almost no cost to on-time delivery") and noting that it no longer holds at 80 s. A past reason became the ground for the next recommendation. Open runs/steward-d-en/gsn.md to see the tree of six periods of decisions (GitHub and the VS Code preview render it as a Mermaid diagram).

The rule versions runs/steward-d-en/v1.cadl to v3.cadl can be compared on the Designer page of CADL Explorer (v0.5.9 or later). Open v1.cadl under Open an existing CADL file, switch the view to Versions, type v1 as the name and press Save as a version. Do the same for v2.cadl and v3.cadl. Under Amendable parameters, upload this repository's constitution.yaml as the Constitution (Use the Robot Town constitution loads the same file). The table lists each # @amend: name with its value, layer, range, step and decided by: the checks for the rule layer, a person for the contract layer and for the safety-related operating-mode rules — the same division as in §2. Open History of the amendable values across the versions. block_k changes from 3 to 2 in v2 and hold_limit from 60 to 70 in v3: the amendments of periods 1 and 5 in the table above. Under Compare two designs, choose v1 as A and v2 as B. The amended parameter (block_k 3 → 2) is listed above the structural changes and the source diff. Explorer checks the values with the same rules as the constitution gate of this course: only numbers on # @amend: lines change, one name at a time, by one step, within the range. It does not run the other gates (the checks of cadl aside, it measures no improvement and holds no vote). Amending a value there (the Amend field) keeps the comments, but its decision record lasts only for the browser session unless you download it. The record of this course is decisions.md and gsn.yaml.
documents.s: Seeing the versions of the rules in CADL Explorer

documents.t: Copy examples/steward-d-en/answers.yaml, change D2 to "2", and pass the copy to --answers. The recorded LLM outputs assume the recorded answers; once an answer differs, every later replay prints "note: the request differs from the recorded one". At which gate is the LLM's period-3 proposal stopped, and why? What would happen with a real LLM (§10)?

From period 5, the other section of the KPI file takes effect. When the KPI changes, the LLM rewrites the measure and lists earlier decisions whose premises no longer hold: KPI (from period 5): The quiet season begins and orders fall. On-time delivery still matters, but to keep the companies cooperating, no single company should gain or lose because of how the road is used. [1] Fairness of utility first, on-time delivery watched: main goal utility_gap (decrease), on_time_deliveries (increase), on_time_rate_gap (decrease), sanction_total (decrease); conditions min_company_on_time_rate >= 0.8, unfinished <= 3 [2] Fairness of on-time rates first: main goal on_time_rate_gap (decrease), on_time_deliveries (increase), utility_gap (decrease), min_company_on_time_rate (increase); conditions min_company_on_time_rate >= 0.8, unfinished <= 3 [3] On-time delivery first, fairness watched: main goal on_time_deliveries (increase), utility_gap (decrease), on_time_rate_gap (decrease), late_deliveries (decrease); conditions min_company_on_time_rate >= 0.8, unfinished <= 3 Concern: A gap metric can be improved by levelling down: making the best-off company worse instead of helping the worst-off one. (…) Concern: 'No company should gain or lose' may mean no company ends up worse off than under the current rules. No available metric measures each company's change against today. (…) (2 more) To review: K1 — K1 made town-wide on-time deliveries the main goal. The new KPI puts fairness between companies first and on-time delivery second, so the main goal and its guards need to be chosen again. To review: D1 — D1 (block_k 3 → 2) was adopted against B's and C's votes, and C's utility fell from 28.8 to 19.0. The new KPI says no company should lose because of how the road is used. (…) → Decision request K5 (the LLM recommends 1) The recorded answer picks measure 1 (narrow the utility spread). This period's proposals: id Proposal On-time Late Main goal (utility spread) Seeds improved Utility A / B / C Votes A B C Watched values (excerpt) — current 80.8 1.8 — — 25.2 / 25.4 / 10.2 — on_time_rate_gap 0.03, sanction_total 20.0 1 hold_limit 60s → 70s 80.2 2.4 +1.7 4/5 25.0 / 24.7 / 11.5 ○ × ○ on_time_rate_gap 0.04, sanction_total 19.0 2 block_k 2 → 3 74.8 7.8 +7.5 4/5 23.0 / 23.6 / 15.9 × × ○ on_time_rate_gap 0.16, sanction_total 12.3 3 sanction_lambda 0.5 → 0 80.8 1.8 +12.0 4/5 25.2 / 27.2 / 28.4 ○ ○ ○ on_time_rate_gap 0.03, sanction_total 0.0 Proposal 3 (switch off sanctions) improves the main goal most and wins every vote. The LLM still asks, writing "This would make utility_gap look fair by switching off all road enforcement. (…) That may be exactly the Goodhart pattern the KPI warns against", and recommends proposal 1: The LLM recommends: 1 — Option 1 narrows utility_gap (+1.7, 4/5 seeds) and lowers sanctions without reversing D1's principle and without switching off enforcement. Its costs to customers and the conditions are small (on-time 80.8 to 80.2, lowest rate 0.95, well above 0.8). Option 2 buys fairness with about 6 more late deliveries and a lowest rate of 0.83, near the floor. Option 3's large gain comes from no longer pricing C's and B's road use, which leaves A carrying the cost of being blocked and looks like the Goodhart pattern the KPI warns against. (…) Proposal 2 (undoing D1) is vetoed by A and B (agreement) and worsens the watched on-time deliveries and spread of on-time rates (KPI conflict). The recorded answer adopts 1: D5: choice: "1" reason: Switching off sanctions (3) narrows the gap only on paper and changes nothing about how the road is used. Returning block_k to 3 (2) adds about 6 late deliveries, and nothing undoes D1's reason (fewer late deliveries for customers). hold_limit 70 s narrows the gap at almost no cost to on-time delivery. assumptions: - Late deliveries rising from 1.8 to 2.4 is acceptable to customers

Pick measure 3 at K5 (copy answers.yaml and edit K5) and run period 5. How do the options of the decision request change? The recorded request was written for measure 1; what happens to it? Under which measure, and if the LLM had not written what, would switching off sanctions be adopted automatically without a request? Is that desirable? In a replay the KPI reading is the recorded one, so to try a rewritten KPI file you need a real LLM (§10).

What happens when the KPI aims at a convenient stand-in (a proxy)? examples/steward-goodhart/kpi.en.md says: ## From period 1 Make sure the road rules are kept. Reduce road-rule violations as much as possible. python -m town.steward --lang en --kpi examples/steward-goodhart/kpi.en.md --mode DISTRIBUTED --name goodhart-en \ --llm replay --replay-dir examples/steward-goodhart/en --answers examples/steward-goodhart/en/answers.yaml The LLM warned that "road_violations is defined by the rules themselves. A ROAD_USE amendment that lengthens release deadlines or weakens or removes blocking_guard would lower the count without making robots behave better", and offered only measures that also watch blocked time and service: (1) the count as main goal, watching blocked time, on-time deliveries and unfinished orders; (2) blocked time as main goal, watching the count. It offered no count-only measure at all. Its two proposals both tighten (sanction_lambda 0.5 → 1, block_k 3 → 2); neither reduces the count (+0.0 and −8.2: evicting earlier counts more evictions), so nothing is adopted. In Japanese (examples/steward-goodhart/proxy/ and guarded/), the LLM did offer a measure of the count plus on-time deliveries only, with the same warning, and recommended the one with more watches. Even when the human chose the count-only measure, the LLM proposed no loosening, writing that loosening would cut the count but run against "make sure the rules are kept". Measure (Japanese record) LLM proposals Road violations Change in main goal Outcome proxy: count and on-time deliveries sanction_lambda 0.5 → 1, block_k 3 → 2 25.8 → 25.8, 34.0 +0.0, −8.2 no change, automatically guarded: also blocked time and total sanctions block_k 3 → 2, sanction_lambda 0.5 → 1 34.0, 25.8 → 25.8 −8.2, +0.0 request (LLM: enforcement by sanctions doubles total sanctions, 15.7 → 31.4) → human keeps How far the drift goes with no reader of the KPI's intent can be seen with the rule-based council, which looks only at the objective's number: python -m town.council --mode DISTRIBUTED --rounds 8 --objective road_violations --name goodhart-d python -m town.council --mode DISTRIBUTED --rounds 6 --name seasons-d python -m town.compare runs/goodhart-d/v1.cadl runs/goodhart-d/v5.cadl runs/seasons-d/v7.cadl --mode DISTRIBUTED Rules On-time Late Road-rule violations Blocked time A's on-time rate initial v1 112.2 10.8 25.0 2457 s 0.82 v5, objective: road violations 106.0 17.0 21.0 3681 s 0.72 v7, objective: on-time deliveries 123.0 0.0 28.2 52 s 1.00 (Compared on seeds 1001–1005, which the loop never used.) With road violations as its objective, the council amended the rules four times in eight periods, every time loosening them. The counted violations fell, while blocked time and late deliveries both rose by about half. The constitution's invariant (on-time rate at least 0.6) does not stop the drift. There is no guarantee that an LLM will read the KPI's intent as it did here. Choosing the measure is the human's job, and when a loosening is proposed, what stops it is the watches and the human's decision.
documents.s: 8. A KPI that is a proxy (15 min)

documents.t: Mode Where robots wait How the road is used DISTRIBUTED each company on the road (the central intersection 8) intersections are free to pass CENTRALIZED a steward assigns off-road bays (beside nodes 5, 2 and 7, one robot each); waiting on the road is forbidden the steward grants each edge to one robot at a time (as the C-SoS arbiter does); entering an edge costs a 1 s grant Centralized operation removes blocked intersections, but at very high demand the edge grants pile up. On-time deliveries with the mode fixed (mean over seeds 1–5): Mean order interval 30 s 45 s 75 s 120 s 180 s Distributed 319.6 210.2 121.8 76.8 51.2 Centralized 309.2 217.4 132.2 83.2 58.6 The switching conditions are written in the CADL file and evaluated every 5 minutes over the last 5 minutes: transitions: - from: DISTRIBUTED to: CENTRALIZED condition: "orders_in_window < 22" # @amend:to_central protocol: SWITCH safety_invariant: "robots_on_road == 0" - from: CENTRALIZED to: DISTRIBUTED condition: "orders_in_window >= 26" # @amend:to_distributed protocol: SWITCH A switch to centralized takes effect only once no robot is waiting on the road (C stalls for 30 s; anything still there after 60 s is evicted by the steward), and the safety_invariant is checked at that moment. Compare three ways of running a period with a rush: python -m town.compare cadl/robot_town.cadl --rush 1200 2400 25 --mode DISTRIBUTED python -m town.compare cadl/robot_town.cadl --rush 1200 2400 25 --mode CENTRALIZED python -m town.compare cadl/robot_town.cadl --rush 1200 2400 25 --mode adaptive Operation On-time Late Blocked time Time centralized fixed distributed 202.8 8.0 2141 s 0% fixed centralized 206.2 4.6 843 s 100% switching by the CADL conditions 209.2 1.6 1116 s 60% The mode switches three times in the period: to centralized after 5 minutes, to distributed for the rush, and back to centralized after it. Now make the switch take effect without waiting for the road to clear: python -m town.period --rush 1200 2400 25 --no-quiescence The last line reports about 1.4 safety-invariant breaches per period (安全条件の違反 1.4 回). The two switching thresholds are marked safety: true in the constitution. With town.steward in --mode adaptive (the default), any proposal that changes them and improves the KPI is always brought to the human as safety.

The records in §4–§8 come from real runs with Claude Opus 5.5 on 2026-10-29/30. With your own API key the LLM answers afresh each time, so you will get proposals and recommendations different from the records. export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... # type your own key; never paste it into a chat or a file python -m town.steward --lang en --mode DISTRIBUTED --rounds 6 --name live-d-en python -m town.steward --mode DISTRIBUTED --rounds 6 --name live-d # Japanese; KPI in kpi.md Each period sends up to three requests: rewriting the KPI (when it changed), proposing amendments, and writing a decision request (only when one is needed). The LLM's outputs are saved in runs/<name>/llm/. Without a terminal and without an answer, the loop writes the decision request to p<k>-request.md and stops; write your answer to a YAML file and rerun the same command with the same --name, adding --answers <YAML>, and the recorded LLM outputs are reused instead of being requested again. The six periods of the records used about 60,600 input and 52,200 output tokens in English, and 61,600 and 52,800 in Japanese. One request took from 20 seconds to 2 minutes; once, a request had no response after 11 minutes and was retried.
documents.s: 10. Run with a real LLM (optional, 15 min)

documents.t: Recommendations vary. In Japanese, the D1 recommendation changed from "1" to "keep" when the same request was sent again; in English, the LLM recommended a regulation (R1) that the Japanese run never proposed. The value of a decision request lies less in its recommendation than in laying out the question, who gains and loses, and what is unknown. The LLM's unknowns point at gaps in the tool. The first version of the table did not show the values of the watched goals; the LLM wrote that it did not know "on_time_rate_gap が具体的に どれだけ悪化したか（表には最低の定時率しか載っていません）" ("how much on_time_rate_gap worsened; the table only shows the lowest on-time rate"), so the table gained a column of watched goals and conditions. Not knowing the quorum (period 2, §6) is not fixed yet (§11). Past reasons shape later recommendations. In period 2 the LLM cited D1's promise to re-measure, and in period 6 D5's reason for 70 s.

examples/llm-distributed/ holds two periods of proposals written by Claude on 2026-10-15, with the LLM acting as the council of town.council (--proposer llm): rules only, no KPI, no decision requests, adoption settled by the gates. python -m town.council --proposer replay --replay-dir examples/llm-distributed --mode DISTRIBUTED --rounds 2 Period LLM proposal Check Constitution Improvement Votes (A B C) 1 (normal) block_k 3 → 2 ○ ○ ○ ○ × × hold_limit 60s → 50s ○ ○ × ○ × × sanction_lambda 0.5 → 1.0 ○ ○ × ○ × × 2 (normal + rush) block_k 3 → 2 ○ ○ ○ ○ × × hold_limit 60s → 50s ○ ○ × ○ ○ × sanction_lambda 0.5 → 1.0 ○ ○ × ○ × × All six were well-formed amendments, and in both periods the first was the best one the rule-based search found. The LLM predicted that "B is blocked too, so it will vote yes"; B voted no. It predicted B's vote from the town's interest rather than B's. One call used about 4,400 input and 9,300 output tokens. On 2026-10-19 the starting rules gained two steps in the AMEND protocol and their interface entries, and on 2026-10-29 the DELIVERY_SLA lines gained contract-layer tags (# @amend:pickup_deadline and so on). Because the constitution gate compares a proposal with the current rules line by line, the same lines were inserted mechanically into every recorded proposal of this council record; nothing else changed, and the replays print the same results. Each file records this in its edits field.
documents.s: A real LLM record: the LLM as a council

documents.t: Goal Hint Tell the LLM the quorum Pass the constitution's vote and each proposal's vote-gate result to request_request() in town/llm_steward.py. Does the period-2 misreading ("override") disappear? Break the human's assumption Make C in town/policies.py withdraw from the town (stop taking orders) as its sanctions or utility worsen, and see what happens when D1's assumption ("keeps delivering") fails Add a reason to ask Add a condition to triage() in town/steward.py, such as "ask when any company's utility falls by 10 or more" Add a metric and use it in a KPI Add, say, the largest blocked time of any company to METRICS in town/kpi.py, and write a KPI that uses it. Does it answer the period-5 concern that no metric measures each company's change from road use alone? Give amendments an expiry Adopted amendments are never repealed, even when the environment changes back. Add a rule that an amendment lapses unless re-adopted within N periods Stop the proxy drift with regulation Add invariants on blocked time or late deliveries to invariants and regulation in constitution.yaml, and to invariants_ok() in town/council.py Open the GSN in another tool Write a script that exports runs/<name>/gsn.yaml to the format of the GSN editor you use

To reach the KPI sooner, it is tempting to change the rules a lot at once. If the people who follow the rules are humans, large sudden changes confuse them, and until they adjust they keep acting on the old rules. Robots read the new rules at once and are not confused — but that does not mean the transition causes no problems. This exercise asks how the trade-off between reaching the KPI quickly and the size and frequency of rule changes depends on whether humans or robots follow the rules. The hands-on already gives some clues: The constitution's "one parameter by one step per amendment" (step in constitution.yaml) is an upper limit on the speed of change. In the six periods of the rule-based council used in §8 (seasons-d), hold_limit went 60 → 70 → 80 → 70 → 60 s and back with the default step of 10 s. This is not overshoot: it went up in the normal periods and down in the busy ones, following the demand that scenario.yaml sets for each period. A rule that tracks a changing environment moves back and forth even when every step is right, so separating tracking from overshoot is part of the exercise. In §9, in a period with a rush, switching the operating mode without waiting for the road to clear broke the safety invariant about 1.4 times per period, with robots only. When the rules change, orders and waits begun under the old version are still running.
documents.s: 12. Research exercise: speed of amendment and transition disruption (optional, several hours)

documents.t: Change step in constitution.yaml (for example hold_limit from 10 to 20 or 30, block_k from 1 to 2) and run the rule-based council for six periods. Choose values so that one step from the current value stays within min–max (the council does not generate proposals outside the range). The constitution is read from the repository root, so use a different --name per condition and restore the file afterwards with git checkout constitution.yaml. The demand changes from period to period (scenario.yaml), so a back-and-forth may be the council following the demand. To see overshoot itself, also run each condition with every period set to the same demand (for example, all six periods busy), and restore the file with git checkout scenario.yaml. python -m town.council --mode DISTRIBUTED --rounds 6 --name step30 python -m town.compare runs/step30/v*.cadl --mode DISTRIBUTED # compare every version on seeds the loop never used For each condition, tabulate: Quantity How to get it Periods to reach the KPI Fix a target (for example "at most 2 late deliveries in town.compare"). In which period was the first version meeting it adopted? Cumulative amendment Sum, over the amendments in history.md, the amount moved divided by the original step Oscillation The number of times a parameter was moved in the opposite direction to its previous amendment Loss during the transition The sum, over the periods before the target is reached, of the shortfall from the target How do the periods to the target, the oscillation and the transition loss change as step grows?
documents.s: Exercise 12-1: size of amendments and speed to the KPI (robots only)

documents.t: Add a company driven by humans to town/policies.py. Choose your own model, for example: Right after a rule change, with probability p a driver still acts on the old rule (waits up to the old hold_limit, and so on); p falls period by period (a learning curve). The larger a change, and the more changes in a row, the larger p and the slower its recovery. Each company's behaviour is decided only by the rules that Town in town/world.py reads with self.rules = read_rules(ir); it does not know the previous version. Let Town take the previous version's IR (or rule values) and "periods since the change", and pass them from evaluate() in town/period.py and from town/council.py. Then repeat Exercise 12-1 with three compositions: all three companies robots, one company human, all three human. For each composition, plot speed to the KPI against disruption during the transition (transition loss and violations), and see how the best step changes.
documents.s: Exercise 12-2: a company with human drivers

documents.t: Transitions matter even with robots only. Add the following ways of putting a version into effect, and compare violations, late deliveries and safety-invariant breaches during the transition: Notice period: an adopted version takes effect N periods later instead of the next period. Phased introduction: a large change takes effect in small steps over several periods. Transitional provisions: orders and waits begun before the change keep the old version's deadlines. Transitional provisions are also a question for the CADL specification: today CADL cannot say which version's deadlines and monitors apply to a contract instance that is already running (§13).

With a real LLM (§10), make town.steward choose the speed: Write a KPI such as "increase on-time deliveries quickly, but avoid sudden changes that would confuse the drivers" in kpi.en.md. What measures does the LLM offer, and how does it describe the cost of the transition in its decision requests? Add a condition to triage() in town/steward.py that asks the human about any proposal that moves a parameter by a large amount at once, and combine it with the large step of Exercise 12-1. Which speed to choose cannot be read off the KPI's numbers; it depends on how the people following the rules take the change. Record the human's decisions and reasons in GSN. Six periods with a real LLM cost about US$1.3 per run in the §10 records (Claude Opus 5.5).
documents.s: Exercise 12-4: let the human and the LLM choose the speed

documents.t: For each composition of followers, what does the Pareto front between speed to the KPI and transition disruption look like? The constitution's step resembles the trust region that limits each policy update in reinforcement learning (TRPO, PPO). What is the same, and what differs? Who should set the speed limit? In which layer should it sit: rule (the council or the LLM may change it), regulation (decided by humans), or contract (the promise to customers)?

Building this exercise exposed these gaps in CADL 0.3. They are still there in cadl 0.3.22: cadl sim-ir does not emit sos.transitions[*].safety_invariant into the IR (cadl check does check it as an expression). The exercise reads it from the checked source file. An operating mode (regime) is only a name; there is no syntax to bind parameter values or contracts to it. What changes in centralized mode (bays, exclusive edges) is decided by the simulator. The stochastic model extension assigns parameter values per regime with model.regimes: (Appendix H, H.6), but only inside its probabilistic model; the simulation and the generated code do not use them. Which layer (rule or contract) a parameter belongs to, and who decides its amendment, is written in constitution.yaml and in # @amend: comments, not in CADL. When a new version of the rules takes effect, there is no syntax for which version applies to contract instances already running (transitional provisions), or for when a version takes effect (§12, Exercise 12-3). The norms extension defines, with on_amendment:, what happens to the norm instances that are running when an amendment takes effect (Appendix F, F.6); when a version takes effect is outside it, and this exercise does not use norms. A metrics target is a single expression: there is no syntax for a KPI that changes over time, or for the choice of how a KPI is measured, and none to link the record of human decisions (GSN) to a version of the rules. The exercise keeps kpi.md, decisions.md and gsn.yaml outside the rules. Up to cadl 0.3.11, an unreadable value such as deadline: soon passed cadl check and became null in the IR; from 0.3.12 it is an error. The exercise also rejects rules whose IR lacks a value the town needs, so the check gate works even with an older compiler.
documents.s: 13. What the specification cannot express yet

documents.t: The KPI is written by a human in natural language and may change over time. The LLM turns it into a measure, but when it can be read several ways or relies on a proxy, the human chooses. The LLM proposes amendments to rules, regulation and contracts toward the KPI. Matters needing stakeholders' agreement, the promise to customers, regulation, safety, conflicts within the KPI and uncertain improvements it does not decide: it hands them to the human with the measurements, who gains and who loses, and what it does not know. The human's decisions and reasons are kept, in prose and in GSN, alongside the versions, and change the LLM's next proposals and requests. What finally backs an adoption is the gates — check, constitution, measured improvement and the parties' agreement — together with the reasons the human left.
Course A (Robot Delivery): Textbook Course B (Urban Mobility): mobility-sos-tutorial.md SoS-DSL specification: cadl-spec Appendix E Exercise repository: https://github.com/ertlnagoya/cadl-robot-town

There are two ways to start. Pick the one that matches what you want to do; each takes about five minutes. Path What you do You need A. Try it in the browser Compare two governance designs in CADL Explorer and see how the result changes. You do not write CADL. A web browser B. Write and check with the CLI Install the cadl command, check and verify an example, then break it and watch the verifier find the contradiction. Python 3.9 or later, git Path A shows what governance design changes; Path B shows the language and the tool. They are independent, so either can come first.
No installation is required if you use CADL Explorer. The steps below describe CADL Explorer v0.5.8 (the hosted app shows its version in the sidebar, below the list of pages).
documents.s: Path A — Try it in the browser (CADL Explorer)

documents.t: Go to cadl-explorer.streamlit.app. If the hosted app asks you to sign in or is unavailable, run it locally from the cadl-explorer repository: git clone https://github.com/ertlnagoya/cadl-explorer.git cd cadl-explorer pip install -r requirements.txt streamlit run app.py The app has four pages, listed at the top of the sidebar: Page What it is for Explorer Compare two governance designs, A and B (this quick start). Designer Edit, check and visualise a full CADL model. Contract Lifecycle Draw the lifecycle state machine and the monitors of a contract from its IR JSON. About & Glossary What the tool does, the parameter values and the terms. The Explorer page opens first. It compares two designs, A (the baseline) and B (the design under study), and shows the whole CADL → IR → Config → Result chain for both. There is no run button: the page recalculates whenever you change a setting.

Under B — design under study in the sidebar, choose one of: Template Meaning D-SoS Directed SoS — strong central authority (α=0.3, β=0.7, λ=0.0). C-SoS Collaborative SoS — autonomy-oriented (α=0.7, β=0.3, λ=0.3). D-SoS + motivation-sensitive Central authority that adjusts budgets to agent motivation (same α, β, λ as D-SoS). Here α is the autonomy level of the agents, β the centralization level, and λ the exploration probability. These simulator parameters differ from the per-contract α / β / λ of the language specification; see the Glossary. Both D-SoS templates set sos_type to Directed in the YAML that the Explorer shows. note Up to v0.4.1 the D-SoS templates were named A-SoS. They were renamed in v0.5.0 because A-SoS is the abbreviation of Acknowledged SoS. Links shared from older versions still open the same designs. To change what B is compared against, open A — baseline and choose in the same way. The baseline starts as D-SoS, uniform, ρ=0.

Motivation profile — how motivation is distributed across agents (uniform, linear, polarized). ρ (motivation sensitivity) — how strongly governance responds to motivation. ρ=0 is motivation-blind; ρ=1 fully couples decisions to motivation. The slider is disabled for templates without a motivation model (D-SoS and C-SoS). If you would rather start from a ready-made comparison, open Getting started at the top of the page (or Examples in the sidebar) and load one with a button.
documents.s: A-3. Set a motivation profile and ρ

documents.t: The page is divided into four numbered sections: Outcome — throughput, autonomy and fairness of A and B, averaged over ten random seeds, with the difference between them. Why — the causal chain — the same change seen at each stage (CADL, IR, Config, Result). Interpreted changes come first; the raw diff is available under each stage. Explore — three tabs: Effect of ρ, Per-robot view and Scenario. Reproduce & export — the content hashes of each stage, the CADL source of A and B, and downloads of B's CADL (YAML), IR (JSON) and simulator config (JSON), plus the A vs B comparison (JSON). Save this comparison in the sidebar adds the current A/B metrics to the Saved comparisons table at the bottom of the page, which can be downloaded as CSV or JSON. The address in the browser records the current settings, so copying it shares the comparison.

Expand Custom CADL in the sidebar and paste a CADLMotivationConfig YAML into Design B (or Design A (baseline)) to use it instead of the selectors. Use the nested governance: / motivation: layout, the same as the YAML shown under CADL source of A and B. Minimal example: name: my-custom-config sos_type: Directed governance: alpha: 0.3 beta: 0.7 lambda: 0.0 motivation: agent: profile: linear governance: model: hybrid rho: 0.5 The synthetic metrics depend only on sos_type, the agent profile and rho. Other fields such as alpha, beta and lambda are carried into the generated IR and config but do not change the results. Only Directed is modelled separately: any other sos_type is computed as collaborative. The profiles are uniform, linear and polarized; any other value, including the custom profile of Appendix C, is rejected with an error. Keys that the format does not know, or keys written at the wrong level, are ignored without an error, so keep to the nested layout above. This YAML is the Explorer's own configuration format, not a full CADL model. To write and check a full CADL model (actors, contracts, lifecycles, monitors), use the Designer page.
documents.s: A-5. Optional — paste your own CADL

documents.t: The reference implementation is the cadl command-line tool, distributed on PyPI as cadl-lang. The output below is from cadl 0.3.23.
documents.s: Path B — Write and check with the CLI

documents.t: python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install cadl-lang cadl --version
The examples are in the cadl repository, not in the PyPI package: git clone https://github.com/ertlnagoya/cadl.git
cadl check parses the file and runs the type checker (declared actors, references, parameter ranges): cadl check cadl/examples/robot_delivery.cadl Type check passed: cadl/examples/robot_delivery.cadl

cadl verify adds the consistency checks: whether each contract's assumptions and guarantees can hold together (SMT solver), whether every regime is reachable, and whether a protocol can deadlock. cadl verify cadl/examples/robot_delivery.cadl Verifying: cadl/examples/robot_delivery.cadl SoS: RobotDeliverySystem --- Type Check --- [PASS] Type check passed --- SMT Verification --- [PASS] Contract 'DELIVERY_SLA' consistency: Assumes and guarantees are jointly satisfiable [PASS] Contract 'DELIVERY_SLA' assumptions: Assumptions are satisfiable [INFO] Contract 'DELIVERY_SLA' entailment: Guarantees do not follow from the assumptions alone; they are obligations the parties must meet ... --- Deadlock Detection --- [PASS] Protocol 'FAILURE_REPLAN' deadlock: No circular dependencies found Verification PASSED: 8/8 checks passed [INFO] lines are not failures. The entailment line says that the guarantees are obligations of the parties, not consequences of the assumptions.

Copy the example and add an assumption that contradicts an existing one: cp cadl/examples/robot_delivery.cadl my_delivery.cadl In my_delivery.cadl, under the contract DELIVERY_SLA: assume: - "DISPATCHER.is_operational == true" - "network_latency <= 200ms" - "network_latency > 500ms" # added: contradicts the line above cadl verify my_delivery.cadl [FAIL] Contract 'DELIVERY_SLA' consistency: Assumes and guarantees are contradictory (unsatisfiable together) [FAIL] Contract 'DELIVERY_SLA' assumptions: Assumptions contradict each other; the contract can never apply Verification FAILED: 7/9 checks passed The file still passes cadl check: it is well formed, but the contract can never apply. The total is now 9 checks instead of 8 because the entailment line changes from [INFO] to [PASS]: contradictory assumptions imply anything, so that [PASS] is vacuous. Finding this kind of contradiction before deployment is what the verifier is for. Remove the added line and the file verifies again. From here, cadl codegen and cadl sim-gen generate code and simulator configs from the same file; all commands are listed in the README of the cadl repository.
