documents.t: To learn by doing → the Textbook (Course A), then the other courses of the Hands-on index, which gives the order in which to take them. Read the Specification Introduction for the language as a whole. Chapter 5. Language Specification covers the three-layer syntax. Chapter 7. Examples walks through larger worked examples.

A CADL file is a YAML 1.2 document [Ben-Kiki+, 2021]. This appendix gives the reference grammar of CADL v0.3 in two parts: the structure of the document (A.2–A.9), written as EBNF over YAML mappings and sequences, and the expression sub-language (A.1, A.10) that is written inside individual YAML string scalars. Chapter 5 and this appendix describe the same syntax. This appendix is normative for the concrete syntax; Chapter 5 is explanatory. The reference implementation (cadl) is expected to accept exactly this syntax; known deviations of cadl 0.3 are listed in A.12. To try the grammar, install the reference implementation (see Path B of the Quick Start) and run cadl parse or cadl check; runnable files are in the examples/ directory of the cadl repository. Notation. The grammar uses ISO/IEC 14977 EBNF [ISO/IEC 14977:1996] with the following conventions. A terminal ending in a colon, such as "name:", is a key of a YAML mapping, followed by its value. The entries of one mapping may appear in any order, each at most once. { "-" , x } is a YAML sequence whose items are x. Block style and flow style ([a, b]) are equivalent. k , ":" , v with a non-terminal k is a mapping whose keys are chosen by the author. text is any YAML string scalar, number any YAML integer or float, and scalar any YAML scalar. Their content is not interpreted further. any_char is any single character. The string rule (A.1) excludes the double quotation mark from it, so a string ends at the next ". Productions marked (* string *) describe the content of a single YAML string scalar. Indentation, comments, quoting, and the choice between block and flow style are governed by YAML and are not shown. A scalar that contains [, ], *, ->, or ": " — for example an actor reference such as "TAXI[*]" or a step such as "A -> B : msg" — SHOULD be quoted, and MUST be quoted inside a flow sequence, where YAML would otherwise read it differently. A sharing_entry (A.4) MUST be a quoted string wherever it is written. Keys that this appendix does not define are not part of CADL v0.3. A processor MUST NOT reject a file because of them; the reference implementation ignores them. The grammar covers the design and verification levels of Section 5.1.1. An overview-level description is informal input for AI-assisted refinement and need not conform to it.

These rules apply inside scalars. letter = "A" | … | "Z" | "a" | … | "z" ; digit = "0" | … | "9" ; identifier = ( letter | "_" ) , { letter | digit | "_" } ; hyphen_name = identifier , { "-" , name_part } ; name_part = ( letter | digit | "_" ) , { letter | digit | "_" } ; actor_ref = identifier , [ "[" , index , "]" ] ; (* string *) index = "*" | range_expr | int_literal | identifier ; range_expr = int_literal , ".." , ( int_literal | identifier ) ; string = '"' , { any_char - '"' } , '"' ; int_literal = digit , { digit } ; float_literal = int_literal , "." , [ int_literal ] , [ exponent ] | "." , int_literal , [ exponent ] | int_literal , exponent ; exponent = ( "e" | "E" ) , [ "+" | "-" ] , int_literal ; bool_literal = "true" | "false" ; duration_lit = int_literal , ( "ms" | "s" | "min" | "h" ) ; literal = string | int_literal | float_literal | bool_literal | duration_lit ; identifier names actors, contracts, protocols, regimes, and metrics. hyphen_name is used only for extension names and codegen target names (for example sos-dsl, unity-csharp). Numeric literals are unsigned. Identifiers are ASCII. Strings and comments may contain any Unicode character, which is what requirement NFR-7 (Chapter 4) asks for. From cadl 0.3.9 the reference implementation reports an id or regime name that violates the ASCII rule as an error (A.12).

cadl_file = "sos:" , sos_body ; sos_body = "name:" , text , [ "type:" , sos_type ] , [ "version:" , scalar ] , [ "description:" , text ] , [ "extensions:" , { "-" , extension_decl } ] , [ "context:" , context_block ] , [ "actors:" , { "-" , actor_def } ] , [ "contracts:" , { "-" , contract_def } ] , [ "protocols:" , { "-" , protocol_def } ] , [ "algorithms:" , { algorithm_def } ] , [ "transitions:" , { "-" , transition_def } ] , [ "metrics:" , { "-" , metric_def } ] , [ "verification:" , { "-" , verify_def } ] , [ "codegen:" , { "-" , codegen_def } ] , [ "motivation:" , motivation_block ] , [ "model:" , model_block ] ; (* Appendix H *) sos_type = "Directed" | "Acknowledged" | "Collaborative" | "Virtual" ; extension_decl = hyphen_name , ":" , scalar ; One file contains one SoS definition. version: is conventionally a semantic version string such as "1.0.0". Extension points. extensions: declares the language extensions a file relies on, each as a name and a version (for example - sos-dsl: 0.1). Seven extensions are defined; all but the last have a name that can be declared: the SoS-DSL extension (Appendix E), declared as sos-dsl with version 0.1, which adds the keys lifecycle: and monitors: to contract_def (A.4); the norms extension (Appendix F), declared as norms with version 0.1, which adds the keys norms: and counts_as: to contract_def (A.4) and bounded temporal operators to the predicates of a contract. A file that uses it MUST declare it; the agent governance extension (Appendix G), declared as agents with version 0.1, which requires norms and adds the key agent: to actor_def (A.3), the keys enforcement: and delegations: to contract_def (A.4), and on_denied: to a prohibition; the stochastic model extension (Appendix H), declared as stochastic with version 0.1, which adds the key model: to sos_body; the strategic model extension (Appendix I), declared as games with version 0.1, which requires stochastic and adds players, profiles, payoffs, and equilibrium queries to model:; the grounding extension (Appendix J), declared as grounding with version 0.1, which requires norms and adds the key grounding: to contract_def (A.4), the keys shares: and on_fulfilment: to a norm and magnitude: to its on_violation:, and, with games, the keys sanction_of: and reward_of: to a payoff term; the motivation extension (Appendix C), which defines motivation_block. It has no extensions: name in v0.3 and is used simply by writing a motivation: block.

context_block = [ "environment:" , { identifier , ":" , scalar } ] , [ "assumptions:" , { "-" , text } ] ; actor_def = "id:" , actor_ref , "role:" , text , [ "autonomy:" , autonomy_level ] , [ "capabilities:" , { "-" , text } ] , [ "interface:" , interface_def ] , [ "agent:" , agent_binding ] ; (* Appendix G *) autonomy_level = "low" | "medium" | "high" ; interface_def = [ "input:" , { "-" , text } ] , [ "output:" , { "-" , text } ] ; metric_def = "id:" , identifier , [ "formula:" , predicate ] , (* string *) [ "target:" , scalar ] ; autonomy: defaults to medium. In actor_def, the index of id: is normally a range ("ROBOT[1..N]") and declares a parameterised set of actors. The upper bound of a range_expr is an integer or an identifier. An identifier such as N is a symbolic size; v0.3 has no construct that binds it to a value (see A.12 for what the reference implementation does with it). A non-string value in environment: is read as a literal (A.1); a string value is kept verbatim.

The Institution layer consists of contracts:, defined here, together with actors: (A.3) and transitions: (A.7). contract_def = "id:" , identifier , "parties:" , { "-" , actor_ref } , [ "assume:" , { "-" , predicate } ] , [ "guarantee:" , { "-" , predicate } ] , [ "authority:" , authority_block ] , [ "information:" , information_block ] , [ "responsibilities:" , { actor_ref , ":" , { "-" , text } } ] , [ "incentives:" , incentive_block ] , [ "violation:" , violation_block ] , [ "duration:" , scalar ] , [ "lifecycle:" , lifecycle_block ] , (* Appendix E *) [ "monitors:" , { "-" , monitor_def } ] , (* Appendix E *) [ "norms:" , { "-" , norm_def } ] , (* Appendix F *) [ "counts_as:" , { "-" , counts_as_def } ] , (* Appendix F *) [ "enforcement:" , enforcement_block ] , (* Appendix G *) [ "delegations:" , { "-" , delegation_def } ] , (* Appendix G *) [ "grounding:" , grounding_block ] ; (* Appendix J *) authority_block = [ "decision_scope:" , text ] , [ "decision_holder:" , actor_ref ] , [ "beta:" , number ] , [ "mode:" , text ] ; information_block = [ "alpha:" , number ] , [ "views:" , { actor_ref , ":" , text } ] , [ "sharing:" , { "-" , sharing_entry } ] ; sharing_entry = actor_ref , "->" , actor_ref , ":" , identifier ; (* string *) incentive_block = [ "type:" , text ] , [ "lambda:" , number ] , [ "rules:" , { "-" , text } ] ; violation_block = [ "detect:" , text ] , [ "action:" , text ] , [ "escalation:" , text ] ; Each item of assume: and guarantee: is a string holding a predicate (A.10). alpha, beta, and lambda MUST lie in [0, 1]. parties: MUST name at least one declared actor, and every actor reference in a contract MUST refer to an actor declared in actors:. duration: is indefinite, a duration_lit, or an event description. A sharing_entry MUST be written as a quoted string (- "TAXI[*] -> CENTRAL : position"); unquoted, YAML reads it as a one-entry mapping and not as a string.

protocol_def = "id:" , identifier , "trigger:" , text , [ "precondition:" , text ] , "steps:" , { "-" , step } , [ "timing:" , { identifier , ":" , scalar } ] , [ "fallback:" , { identifier , ":" , text } ] , [ "rollback:" , rollback_block ] , [ "postcondition:" , text ] , [ "safety_invariant:" , text ] ; rollback_block = [ "condition:" , text ] , [ "action:" , text ] ; step = message_step | compute_step | conditional_step | parallel_step | barrier_step ; message_step = actor_ref , "->" , actor_ref , ":" , step_expr ; compute_step = actor_ref , ":" , step_expr ; conditional_step = "if" , predicate , ":" , { "-" , step } , [ "else:" , { "-" , step } ] ; parallel_step = "parallel:" , { "-" , step } ; barrier_step = "barrier:" , predicate ; step_expr = function_call | identifier ; A message_step or compute_step is one sequence item. It may be written as a quoted string (- "A -> B : msg(x)", recommended) or unquoted, in which case YAML reads it as a one-entry mapping; both forms are equivalent. conditional_step, parallel_step, and barrier_step are mappings whose key is if <predicate>, parallel, or barrier. Typical keys of timing: are max_response, max_total, and checkpoint_interval; typical keys of fallback: are on_timeout and on_failure.

algorithm_def = identifier , ":" , algorithm_body ; algorithm_body = [ "central:" , text ] , [ "local:" , text ] ; algorithms: is a mapping from a function name (for example pathfinding) to the algorithms used centrally and locally.

transition_def = "from:" , identifier , "to:" , identifier , [ "condition:" , predicate ] , (* string *) [ "protocol:" , identifier ] , [ "safety_invariant:" , predicate ] ; (* string *) from: and to: name regimes. A regime is introduced by its use in a transition; there is no separate declaration. protocol: SHOULD name a protocol declared in protocols:.

verify_def = "id:" , identifier , "type:" , text , [ "target:" , verify_target ] , [ "property:" , text ] , [ "method:" , verify_method ] , [ "expr:" , predicate ] , (* string *) [ "bound:" , int_literal ] ; verify_target = identifier | identifier , "->" , identifier ; (* FROM->TO *) verify_method = "smt" | "model_check" | "simulation" | "proof" ; type: names the kind of property, for example consistency, deadlock, safety, or liveness. target: names the contract, protocol, or transition concerned: the id of a contract or protocol, the name of a regime, or FROM->TO for the transition between two regimes. method: defaults to smt. A processor that does not implement a declared method MUST report the entry as not_supported rather than skip it silently, and MUST report an unknown method as an error. A target: that names nothing declared SHOULD be reported as an error.

codegen_def = [ "target:" , hyphen_name ] , [ "output:" , text ] , [ "mappings:" , { identifier , ":" , text } ] ; target: defaults to python. The target names are catalogued in Appendix D. output: is the output path and mappings: passes target-specific name mappings to the generator.

A predicate is written inside one YAML string scalar. predicate = or_expr ; or_expr = and_expr , { "OR" , and_expr } ; and_expr = not_expr , { "AND" , not_expr } ; not_expr = "NOT" , not_expr | comparison ; comparison = arith_expr , [ comp_op , arith_expr ] | quantified_expr ; comp_op = "==" | "!=" | "<=" | ">=" | "<" | ">" ; quantified_expr = ( "for all" | "exists" ) , identifier , "in" , arith_expr , ":" , predicate ; arith_expr = term , { ( "+" | "-" ) , term } ; term = factor , { ( "*" | "/" ) , factor } ; factor = "(" , predicate , ")" | "-" , factor | function_call | member_access | literal | indexed_ref ; function_call = identifier , "(" , [ arg_list ] , ")" ; arg_list = arg , { "," , arg } ; arg = predicate | comprehension ; comprehension = predicate , "for" , identifier , "in" , ( range_expr | arith_expr ) ; member_access = indexed_ref , "." , identifier , { "." , identifier } ; indexed_ref = identifier , [ "[" , ( "*" | range_expr | arith_expr ) , "]" ] ; Operators bind, from loosest to tightest: OR, AND, NOT, comparison, + -, * /, unary -. A unary - in front of a numeric literal gives a negative number (permit_state == -2); in front of any other factor, -x has the value of 0 - x. Binary operators of equal precedence associate to the left. A comparison is not associative (a < b < c is not a predicate). A quantifier extends as far to the right as possible. White space between tokens is ignored. A comprehension is the argument of an aggregate function and evaluates its predicate once for each value of the bound identifier, for example sum(ROBOT[i].goal_count for i in 1..N) or sum(r.load for r in ROBOT[*]). This appendix fixes the form of quantifiers and comprehensions, not the set of aggregate functions or the values of these expressions on observations. The norms extension defines them for its dynamic semantics: the domain of a quantifier or comprehension (a set of actors, possibly with a symbolic bound, or a range), the meaning of the bound identifier, the aggregate functions sum, count, min, max, and avg, and three-valued values over domains whose members are not all known (Appendix F, F.5, "Quantifiers and aggregates"). An indexed_ref with * or a range outside a domain, as in ROBOT[*].battery > 10, is accepted by the grammar but has no defined value in a predicate. An item of assume: or guarantee: that does not conform to this grammar is not a syntax error: it is retained as an opaque predicate, which a processor carries through unchanged and excludes from formal verification. This permits natural-language conditions at the design level. The same applies to step expressions and conditions in A.5.

Keywords of the expression sub-language. They MUST NOT be used as identifiers. AND OR NOT true false for all exists in for on its own (it introduces a comprehension) and all are not reserved. IN (upper case, set membership inside a monitor rule, Appendix E) and in (lower case, quantifier and comprehension domains) are distinct keywords. Keys of the structure, by the block in which they are recognised. Block Keys file sos sos name type version description extensions context actors contracts protocols algorithms transitions metrics verification codegen motivation model context environment assumptions actor id role autonomy capabilities interface (input output) contract id parties assume guarantee authority information responsibilities incentives violation duration lifecycle monitors norms counts_as enforcement delegations grounding norm (Appendix F) id kind bearer counterparty trigger until content deadline on_violation (severity sanction reparation transition) effects (activate suspend resume discharge) on_amendment (transform) counts-as rule (Appendix F) when creates if agent governance (Appendix G) actor agent (kind protocol tools); contract enforcement (default point), delegations (norm to grant revoke max_depth until); prohibition on_denied (escalate_to timeout fallback notify) stochastic model (Appendix H) model (kind parameters variables commands labels regimes rewards properties regime_maps); the keys of each entry are listed in H.2 strategic model (Appendix I) model (players profiles compliance payoffs equilibria); command owner; property and regime map profile; the keys of each entry are listed in I.2 grounding (Appendix J) contract grounding (items tolerance); norm shares, on_fulfilment (reward magnitude), on_violation (magnitude); payoff term sanction_of reward_of authority decision_scope decision_holder beta mode information alpha views sharing incentives type lambda rules violation detect action escalation protocol id trigger precondition steps timing fallback rollback (condition action) postcondition safety_invariant step if else parallel barrier algorithm central local transition from to condition protocol safety_invariant metric id formula target verification id type target property method expr bound codegen target output mappings Enumerated values: Directed Acknowledged Collaborative Virtual (SoS type); low medium high (autonomy); smt model_check simulation proof (verification method); ms s min h (duration units). The keys and values of the extensions are listed in Appendix C, Appendix E, Appendix F, Appendix G, Appendix H, Appendix I, and Appendix J.

The reference implementation reads the file with a YAML 1.1 loader and is lenient: only a missing sos: mapping, invalid YAML, an invalid type:, and an alpha, beta, or lambda that is not a number are rejected by the parser. cadl check additionally reports duplicate ids, undeclared actors, a party listed twice, a contract without parties, governance parameters outside [0, 1], a severity: other than Minor, Major, or Critical, an autonomy: other than low, medium, or high, an id or regime name that is not an identifier, a malformed sharing: entry, and a violation of rules L-1, L-2, L-3, L-5, M-1 (from cadl 0.3.11), or M-3 of Appendix E, and (from cadl 0.3.12) a deadline: or sampling: value that cannot be read, as errors. In an item of assume: or guarantee:, a name counts as an actor reference, and must be declared, when it is indexed (ROBOT[i]) or is the object of a member access (ROBOT.battery), including inside an index; a name standing alone is taken as a state variable and is not checked. The predicates of condition:, safety_invariant:, formula:, expr:, monitor rule:, lifecycle when:, and an on: that is not a message event are not checked for undeclared actors. Other missing required keys are replaced by an empty value. cadl 0.3 deviates from this appendix as follows (checked against cadl 0.3.23). Expressions. Expressions follow A.10 and A.11 in cadl 0.3.23; no deviation is known. Up to cadl 0.3.17 the unary - of factor was not accepted: an item that used it was kept as an opaque predicate, and for a lifecycle on: or when: or a monitor rule:, cadl check gave a warning. Identifiers. From cadl 0.3.9, cadl check reports as an error an actor, contract, protocol, or metric id, or a regime name, that is not an identifier of A.1 (for example one with non-ASCII characters or a hyphen) or that is a reserved word of A.11 or the IN of Appendix E. From cadl 0.3.10 the same check applies to the names of lifecycle states, the ids of lifecycle transitions and monitors, and the violation labels of monitors. The ids of verification entries are not checked. Up to cadl 0.3.12 an unquoted true or false used as such a name or as a regime name was read by YAML as a boolean, became True / False, and was accepted. Ranges. A range with a symbolic bound ("TAXI[1..N]") is kept as written. N is not looked up in environment:, and an index is not checked against the declared range. cadl sim-gen writes a count only when both bounds are integers. Types. The types of Section 5.2.1 are not checked. A value written with a type constructor (for example Range(1, 4)) is kept as text. Lenient forms. The parser also accepts parties: written as one string ("[A, B]"), a non-negative numeric deadline:, possibly fractional (read as seconds), a duration or period with a space before its unit (5 s, periodic( 500ms )), sampling: written as the mapping {kind: periodic, period_ms: <non-negative integer>} or {kind: event}, and a method: in any letter case. These forms are not part of this appendix. Steps. From cadl 0.3.10 the else: branch of a conditional_step and the condition of a barrier_step are retained, so actors named in an else: branch are checked and both reach the simulator IR; earlier releases discarded them. Contracts. From cadl 0.3.9, a sharing: entry that is not a string of the form "SOURCE -> TARGET : item", or whose item does not begin with an identifier, is an error in cadl check; earlier releases dropped an unquoted entry without a diagnostic. An entry whose item begins with an identifier and continues with other text, such as the arguments in "A -> B : report(period: 5s)", is accepted with a warning and only the leading name is kept; this form is not part of this appendix. From cadl 0.3.10 an autonomy: value other than low, medium, or high is an error in cadl check; earlier releases read it as medium without a diagnostic. Verification. method:, expr:, and bound: are read. Methods other than smt are reported as not_supported (shown as [SKIP] in text output), and an unknown method is an error. A target: that names nothing declared is an error for every method. For an smt entry an unsatisfiable expr: is an error, and an expr: that does not conform to A.10 is reported as unknown and not checked; expr is not proved against the model. The contract and transition checks of Section 6.3 run whether or not entries are present. Codegen. codegen: entries are parsed but not acted upon; the target is selected on the command line (Appendix D). From cadl 0.3.9, an entry whose target: the implementation cannot emit (for example target: ros2) gets a warning from cadl check, cadl verify, and cadl codegen, which is the diagnostic that Appendix D, Section D.4 requires; the file remains valid. On the command line -t ros2 is rejected. Extensions. lifecycle: and monitors: are recognised whether or not extensions: declares sos-dsl. From cadl 0.3.9, cadl check emits an informational diagnostic, which never makes a file invalid, for an extensions: name other than sos-dsl, for a version of sos-dsl other than 0.1, and for a motivation: block, as Appendix C asks of a processor that does not implement the extension. The motivation: block is not interpreted, but cadl sim-ir passes it on as written under the key motivation_block (Appendix C, Section C.6); the key is absent when the file has no such block. Where cadl falls short of Appendix E itself is stated in Section E.4. From cadl 0.3.19 the declared extension norms with version 0.1 is implemented and gets no such diagnostic; what cadl implements of Appendix F is stated in Section F.10. From cadl 0.3.20 the same holds for agents 0.1 (Appendix G, G.13) and stochastic 0.1 (Appendix H, H.14), and cadl sim-ir emits the key stochastic_model, which is null for a file without that extension. cadl 0.3.22 adds the certified regime maps of H.9, the runtime of G.5 to G.8 with the rules G-17 to G-19, and the online monitor of norms in the generated Python code; the three sections named above state what each covers. The extensions games 0.1 (Appendix I, I.14) and grounding 0.1 (Appendix J, J.11) are implemented from cadl 0.3.23 (cadl game-check, cadl norms-indices); the two sections named state what each covers. Up to 0.3.22 their names got the informational diagnostic for an unknown extension; for a model with kind: smg, cadl check 0.3.22 reports errors of S-1 and S-9 where H.10 and H.15 ask for one informational diagnostic, and it ignores the keys of Appendix J without a diagnostic. Releases of cadl before 0.3.7 differed in several of these points; the history is in the CHANGELOG of the cadl repository.

This appendix describes the motivation extension to CADL used in the CADL Explorer demonstrator and the D-SoS motivation-sensitive governance experiments. The core language (Chapter 5 and Appendix A) does not mandate this block; a conforming CADL processor that does not implement the extension MUST NOT reject a file because of the motivation: block. It SHOULD accept the block syntactically and emit an informational diagnostic. The extension is versioned independently from the core language; this document describes v0.1-ext, which is the version label of the extension text. In v0.3 the extension has no name to declare under extensions: (Appendix A.2); a file uses it simply by writing a motivation: block.

The extension adds two concepts on top of the Institution layer: Agent motivation — a per-actor scalar m ∈ [0, 1] describing intrinsic willingness to accept tasks. A profile selector names a distribution of motivation values across the actor set. Governance motivation interpretation — how the authority layer couples motivation into budget / wait-time decisions, via parameters ρ (sensitivity) and κ (scale). These parameters supplement the governance parameters (α, β, λ) of the contracts; they do not replace them. The block originated as the configuration schema of the simulator of CADL Explorer (cadl_sim). In a CADL file it is the optional motivation: key of the sos: mapping, i.e. the motivation_block of Appendix A.2.

The grammar uses the notation of Appendix A; number and int_literal are defined there. motivation_block = [ "agent:" , agent_motivation ] , [ "governance:" , governance_motivation ] ; agent_motivation = [ "profile:" , motivation_profile ] , [ "values:" , { "-" , number } ] ; motivation_profile = "uniform" | "linear" | "polarized" | "custom" ; governance_motivation = [ "model:" , motivation_model ] , [ "rho:" , number ] , [ "kappa:" , number ] , [ "budget_base:" , int_literal ] , [ "wait_scale:" , number ] ; motivation_model = "none" | "commitment_budget" | "hybrid" ; Defaults: profile: uniform, model: none, rho: 0.0, kappa: 5.0, budget_base: 3, wait_scale: 3.0.

Symbol Name Range Meaning m_i Motivation of actor i [0, 1] 0 = unwilling, 1 = fully willing ρ (rho) Motivation sensitivity [0, 1] 0 = ignore motivation; 1 = throttle over-budget actors at full strength κ (kappa) Budget scale ≥ 0 Multiplier from motivation to budget extension budget_base Baseline budget ℤ ≥ 0 Per-actor commitment budget before motivation wait_scale Overshoot→retry factor ≥ 0 Converts budget overshoot to retry wait time

For N actors: uniform — every actor gets m = 0.5. linear — motivations are linearly spaced over [0.2, 1.0] (m_i = 0.2 + 0.8 · i/(N−1) for i = 0 … N−1; for N = 1, m = 0.5). polarized — first ⌊N/2⌋ actors get m = 0.2, the rest m = 0.9. custom — explicit values list of length N MUST be provided.

model Effect none Baseline — motivation is ignored (equivalent to ρ = 0). commitment_budget Actor i gets the commitment budget B_i = budget_base + κ · m_i. An actor that exceeds its budget is throttled by an extra wait of ⌊ρ · overshoot · wait_scale⌋. hybrid Reserved. In v0.1-ext it has the same effect as commitment_budget (see below). The quantities in the table are defined as follows. used_i is the cumulative number of goals (commitments) actor i has taken on since the start of the run. overshoot = max(0, used_i − B_i) is the amount by which actor i exceeds its budget; it is 0 while the actor is within budget. The extra wait ⌊ρ · overshoot · wait_scale⌋ is counted in retry ticks of the runtime's dispatcher and is added to the wait the actor would have anyway before its next routing attempt. hybrid is reserved for a model that adds a preference-sensitive routing priority to the budget constraint. v0.1-ext defines no rule for that priority. A processor MUST accept model: hybrid and MUST treat it as commitment_budget; the reference simulator does so. A later version of the extension may define the priority rule, so a file that needs only the budget constraint SHOULD say commitment_budget. Effective sensitivity is ρ · 𝟙[model ≠ "none"]; when model = "none" the runtime MUST ignore rho.

In a CADL file the block is written under sos:. sos: name: "MotivationSensitiveDelivery" type: Directed # actors, contracts, ... as in Chapter 5 motivation: agent: profile: linear governance: model: commitment_budget rho: 0.6 kappa: 5.0 budget_base: 3 wait_scale: 3.0 CADL Explorer's simulator reads the same motivation: block from its own configuration file, next to simulator settings such as sos_type: and environment:. That file also has a top-level governance: mapping with keys alpha, beta, and lambda. These are simulator parameters — autonomy level, centralization level, and exploration probability — and are not the per-contract α (information sharing), β (decision centralization), and λ (incentive intensity) of Section 5.4.2. The simulator configuration file is not a CADL file in the sense of Appendix A.

A CADL processor is core-conforming if it accepts files without the motivation: block and fully implements Chapter 5 and Appendix A. A processor is motivation-conforming if it additionally: Parses the motivation: block per the EBNF in §C.2. Validates profile and model against the enumerations in §C.2. Resolves profiles to concrete per-actor motivation vectors per §C.3. Documents how it passes motivation parameters to downstream codegen targets (simulator config, policy code, etc.). A processor that does not support the extension SHOULD preserve the block verbatim so downstream tools can consume it.

CADL Explorer (demo): implements v0.1-ext in the configuration schema of its simulator (cadl_sim/schema/motivation_schema.py). The Explorer page accepts the profiles uniform, linear and polarized; it rejects custom. cadl (reference implementation): defines an optional MotivationBlock on SoSDefinition in its AST. From cadl 0.3.9 the parser reads the motivation: block: cadl check emits an informational diagnostic for it, and cadl sim-ir passes it on as written under the key motivation_block (C.6). Verification and code generation do not use it. The reference implementation implements the core language with the deviations listed in Appendix A §A.12 and does not implement the motivation extension: it does not validate the block, resolve profiles, or apply a governance model. Glossary — definitions of ρ, κ, profile terms.

This appendix enumerates the code-generation targets defined by CADL v0.3 and the mapping to the reference implementation's directory layout. Appendix A §A.9 defines the EBNF for codegen: entries; this appendix pairs each target name with its category, intended artifact, and implementation location in the reference implementation (cadl 0.3).

Target name Category Emitted artifact Reference-impl module Command python Runtime code Python package (actors, contract monitors, protocols, regime controller, metrics, runtime; for a file that declares norms: 0.1, also a monitor of the norms of Appendix F) cadl.codegen cadl codegen -t python solidity Institutional contract Solidity [Solidity Documentation] smart contracts, one per contract cadl.codegen.solidity cadl codegen -t solidity opa Institutional policy Rego / OPA [Open Policy Agent] policies, one per contract cadl.codegen.opa cadl codegen -t opa unity-csharp Runtime code Unity C# classes for the lifecycles and monitors of Appendix E cadl.codegen.unity_csharp cadl codegen -t unity-csharp unity Simulator config JSON for a Unity-based simulator cadl.sim.gen_unity cadl sim-gen -t unity go Simulator config JSON for a Go-based simulator cadl.sim.gen_go cadl sim-gen -t go python (simulator) Simulator config YAML for a Python-based simulator cadl.sim.gen_python cadl sim-gen -t python agent-rego Boundary policy Rego policy that returns the allow / deny / escalate decision of Appendix G for a message cadl.codegen cadl codegen -t agent-rego agent-cedar Boundary policy Cedar policies and a side table for the statically decidable part of Appendix G cadl.codegen cadl codegen -t agent-cedar ros2 Runtime node ROS 2 [Macenski+, 2022] node scaffolds not implemented in cadl 0.3 — other name (user-defined) Plugin Whatever the user plugin emits no plugin mechanism exists in cadl 0.3; other target names are rejected on the command line and get a warning in a codegen: entry — The name python denotes the runtime-code target in a codegen: entry; the simulator configuration of the same name is requested with cadl sim-gen. The Python simulator config therefore cannot be requested from a codegen: entry in v0.3; use cadl sim-gen -t python. In the reference implementation (cadl 0.3) the target is selected on the command line as shown in the last column; codegen: entries in the file are parsed but do not yet drive generation. From cadl 0.3.9, an entry that names a target the implementation cannot emit gets a warning (D.4). For a file that declares the norms extension (Appendix F), the python target also emits the module norms_monitor.py (from cadl 0.3.22). It monitors the norms: and counts_as: blocks and the assume: and guarantee: items of each contract, including the items with temporal operators, for one contract instance while the system runs: it is given one observation at a time and returns the norm instances and items whose state or verdict (pending, fulfilled, violated, excused) changed. Unlike the other modules of the package, it does not import cadl: it carries the declared actors and the contracts as data (one JSON text) and the evaluation code of cadl norms-eval, and uses only the standard library of Python. The generator checks the module before it writes it and writes nothing when the check fails. F.10 gives the details. The solidity, opa, and unity-csharp targets do not monitor norms; solidity and opa leave the items with temporal operators out of the generated checks, with a comment and a warning.

The reference implementation splits codegen into two tiers, reflecting whether the output is code that enforces or executes the contracts or a configuration for a simulator: src/cadl/ ├── codegen/ ← code tier (cadl codegen) │ ├── *_gen.py ← Python runtime package │ ├── solidity/ ← smart-contract enforcement of contracts │ ├── opa/ ← policy enforcement (Rego) of contracts │ └── unity_csharp/ ← Unity C# lifecycle / monitor runtime └── sim/ ← simulator tier (cadl sim-gen) ├── ir.py ← three-layer simulator IR ├── gen_unity.py ├── gen_go.py └── gen_python.py A single CADL source file MAY declare targets from both tiers in one codegen: block. The processor SHOULD dispatch each target to its tier independently.

Pick unity when the experiment is a multi-agent simulation with graphical inspection, and unity-csharp when contract lifecycles and monitors (Appendix E) are to run inside that simulation. Pick python when you want an executable runtime skeleton of the actors, contract monitors, and protocols, or when the norms of Appendix F are to be monitored while the system runs; ros2 is reserved for driving actual robots and is not implemented in cadl 0.3. Pick solidity when the Institution-layer contracts must be enforced on-chain (blockchain deployment). Pick opa when contracts should be enforced as policies at API / service boundaries (policy-as-code). Multiple targets in one file are permitted but the resulting artifacts are independent — the CADL toolchain does not guarantee runtime interoperability between, e.g., a Unity simulator config and a Solidity contract generated from the same source.

A processor is codegen-core-conforming if it supports at least one target from each tier (for example unity together with solidity or opa). A processor that cannot emit a requested target MUST report a clear diagnostic (for example, "codegen target ros2 is not supported by this processor") rather than silently skipping it.

This appendix specifies the SoS Contract DSL extension to CADL. It augments the contract_def production of Appendix A.4 with two keys, lifecycle: and monitors:, that promote contract execution state and runtime observation to first-class language constructs. The core language (Chapter 5, Appendix A) does not mandate these blocks; a conforming CADL processor that does not implement the extension MUST NOT reject a file because of the new keys. It SHOULD accept them syntactically and emit an informational diagnostic. This extension is versioned independently from the core language. Its name is sos-dsl and this appendix describes version 0.1 (the same revision is labelled v0.1-sos-ext in the source of the reference implementation). Files that rely on it SHOULD declare it with the extensions: key of Appendix A.2: sos: ... extensions: - sos-dsl: 0.1
documents.s: Appendix E — SoS Contract DSL Extension (sos-dsl 0.1)

documents.t: CADL contracts as defined today describe classes of normative agreements — they declare parties, A/G clauses, authority, information flows, incentive parameters, and an aggregate violation-detection predicate. This is sufficient to specify what must hold across the SoS, but it is intentionally silent on: Per-instance contract lifecycle. A "delivery contract" is instantiated once per DeliveryRequest and progresses through distinct states (Proposed → Assigned → Accepted → Delivering → Completed/Violated). The class-level contract spec cannot express this per-instance state machine. Declarative observation. violation.detect collapses observation sources, sampling strategy, and detection logic into a single string-encoded predicate. There is no first-class way to declare what is being observed and how often. Norm-bound deadlines. protocol.timing.max_response captures timing on a protocol step; it does not bind a deadline to a step of an individual contract instance as a normative constraint. Runtime event emission for visualization. Without an explicit lifecycle, downstream tools (CADL Explorer, runtimes) cannot subscribe to contract events at the level that operators reason about. The SoS-DSL extension addresses these four gaps additively, preserving backward compatibility with existing contract definitions.

Layer Existing CADL SoS-DSL Extension Class-level normative spec parties / assume / guarantee / authority / information / responsibilities / incentives / violation unchanged Per-instance lifecycle — lifecycle: Declarative observation one-shot violation.detect monitors: Norm-bound deadlines implicit via timing deadline: on lifecycle transitions The extension does not introduce a parallel contract namespace. lifecycle: and monitors: are keys of the same contract_def that already accepts assume:, guarantee:, and the other keys of Appendix A.4.

The grammar uses the notation of Appendix A: a terminal ending in a colon is a key of a YAML mapping, { "-" , x } is a YAML sequence, and a production marked (* string *) describes the content of one YAML string scalar. lifecycle_block and monitor_def are the two non-terminals that A.4 refers to. lifecycle_block = "states:" , state_list , "initial:" , identifier , "terminal:" , state_list , [ "transitions:" , { "-" , lifecycle_trans } ] ; state_list = { "-" , identifier } ; lifecycle_trans = "id:" , identifier , "from:" , ( identifier | state_list ) , "to:" , identifier , "on:" , event , [ "when:" , rule ] , [ "deadline:" , duration_lit ] , [ "on_violation:" , on_violation_body ] , [ "emit:" , { "-" , text } ] ; on_violation_body = "transition:" , identifier , [ "severity:" , severity ] ; severity = "Minor" | "Major" | "Critical" ; monitor_def = "id:" , identifier , "observe:" , ( observation | { "-" , observation } ) , [ "sampling:" , sampling_spec ] , "rule:" , rule , [ "on_match:" , on_match_body ] ; on_match_body = [ "violation:" , identifier ] , [ "transition:" , identifier ] , [ "severity:" , severity ] ; event = message_event | rule ; (* string *) message_event = actor_ref , "->" , actor_ref , ":" , step_expr ; rule = predicate ; (* string *) membership = arith_expr , "IN" , "[" , arith_expr , { "," , arith_expr } , "]" ; observation = member_access | identifier ; (* string *) sampling_spec = "event" | "periodic" , "(" , duration_lit , ")" ; (* string *) identifier, actor_ref, duration_lit, step_expr, predicate, arith_expr, and member_access are defined in Appendix A (A.1, A.5, A.10). Inside a rule, membership is an additional alternative of the comparison production of A.10, and IN is a reserved keyword; an example is state IN [Assigned, Accepted]. IN is distinct from the lower-case in of Appendix A, which introduces the domain of a quantifier or comprehension. sampling: defaults to event and severity: to Major. The values of on:, when:, rule:, and of observe: entries that contain [, ->, or ": " have to be quoted, as in the example of E.6. The key on SHOULD be written without quotation marks; a processor built on a YAML 1.1 loader, which reads an unquoted on as a boolean, MUST still recognise it as this key.

A SoS-DSL-aware processor MUST, in addition to existing checks: L-1. Every lifecycle.initial and lifecycle.terminal state MUST appear in lifecycle.states. L-2. Every lifecycle.transitions[*].from and .to MUST appear in lifecycle.states. L-3. lifecycle.terminal MUST list at least one state, and at least one terminal state MUST be reachable from the initial state. L-4. A deadline: on a transition implicitly introduces a Timeout event scoped to that transition's from state. Two transitions out of the same state MAY have deadlines; their semantics are independent. A transition with a deadline: SHOULD also have an on_violation: block. When a transition has a deadline: but no on_violation.transition, missing the deadline is still a violation (severity Major unless overridden) but causes no change of state. sos-dsl 0.1 defines no way to refer to the implicit Timeout event from on:. L-5. Every lifecycle.transitions[*].on_violation.transition MUST name a state that appears in lifecycle.states (the target state of the forced move, e.g. Violated). M-1. Every monitor.observe entry MUST be an attribute of a declared actor (e.g. ROBOT[i].battery), a message name, or one of the reserved identifiers time and state. M-2. on_match.violation is an identifier that labels the reported violation (the norm that was broken, e.g. collision). It need not be declared elsewhere; when it is omitted, the id of the monitor is used as the label. M-3. on_match.transition references MUST name a state that appears in lifecycle.states of the same contract. The value is the target state of the forced move (e.g. Violated), not the id of a declared transition. In both on_violation: and on_match:, the key transition: therefore always holds a target state name. This matches the examples in E.6, the IR fields on_violation_transition / on_match_transition (E.7), and the reference Unity C# generator, which records such a move as a <jump> from the current state to the named state. In a rule (and therefore in when: and in an on: event), three identifiers are reserved: state is the current lifecycle state of the instance, now is the current time, and request is the request that created the instance (e.g. request.deadline). A bare identifier that names a lifecycle state (e.g. Assigned) denotes that state. sos-dsl 0.1 has no syntax for the trigger that creates an instance or for the fields of request; the host application creates instances and supplies request (see E.8). In a monitor, observe: names the quantities the monitor reads and is carried into the IR; in sos-dsl 0.1 it does not restrict which names a rule may mention. time in observe: denotes the clock that now reads in a rule. The reference implementation (cadl 0.3) parses both blocks and lowers them to the IR (E.7). From cadl 0.3.10 cadl check applies the rules above: a violation of L-1, L-2, L-3, L-5, or M-3 is an error, as are a lifecycle without an initial state, a duplicate transition or monitor id, a monitor without a rule:, an undeclared actor in a message_event of on:, and a state name, transition id, monitor id, or violation label that is not an identifier. From cadl 0.3.11 a violation of M-1 is an error as well: an observe: entry whose object is not a declared actor, or that is neither an attribute of an actor nor a name. cadl 0.3.10 reported it as a warning, because the example of E.6 then observed OBSTACLES.positions although no actor OBSTACLES is declared; the example now observes DISPATCHER.obstacle_positions and passes without a diagnostic. Two findings are warnings and leave the file valid: a deadline: without an on_violation: block (the SHOULD of L-4), and an on:, when:, or rule: that is not a rule of E.3, which is then kept as text. An observe: entry that is a bare name is accepted, since it cannot be told from a message name, and the actors named inside a rule: or when: are not checked. From cadl 0.3.7 cadl check reports a severity: other than Minor, Major, or Critical as an error. From cadl 0.3.12 it also reports as an error a deadline: that is not a duration_lit (a non-negative number of seconds is accepted as a lenient form, Appendix A §A.12) and a sampling: that is not a sampling_spec (or the mapping form of A.12); earlier releases accepted such a deadline: and put no deadline in the IR or, for yes / no and negative numbers, a meaningless one (1000, 0 and -5000 ms for yes, no and -5), and read such a sampling: as event. Releases before 0.3.10 did not check rules L-1 to M-3.

A contract instance is created when its initial trigger fires (e.g., a DeliveryRequest arrives). sos-dsl 0.1 has no syntax for this trigger or for the fields of request; the host application creates instances and supplies request (see E.8). It advances through lifecycle.states driven by lifecycle.transitions[*].on events, deadline timers (which move the instance to on_violation.transition), and monitors[*].on_match.transition actions (which move it to the named state). A transition fires when the instance is in one of its from states, its on: event occurs, and its when: guard, if any, holds. A message_event occurs when that message is sent; a rule used as an event occurs when it becomes true. A transition's deadline: defines a normative time bound, measured from the moment the instance enters one of the transition's from states. If the transition has not fired by then, this is a violation whose severity is Major unless overridden in the on_violation: block, and the instance moves to the state named by on_violation.transition. When the transition has no on_violation.transition, missing the deadline is still a violation but causes no change of state. emit: lists the names of additional events to publish when the transition fires, for consumption by visualization and logging tools. The reference generators carry emit: into the IR but do not act on it in cadl 0.3; every transition is published as a lifecycle event regardless. monitors evaluate independently of the lifecycle state machine but can read state (current lifecycle state) in their rule:. A monitor with sampling: event is evaluated on every event delivered to the instance, one with periodic(d) every d. On match, a monitor reports a violation labelled by on_match.violation and, if on_match.transition is given, also moves the instance to that state. incentives.rules (existing) and monitor.on_match (extension) cooperate: rewards/penalties reference the violations and transitions that this extension makes addressable.

The contract below is taken from examples/sos_dsl_robot_delivery.cadl in the cadl repository. It is abridged: the authority, information, incentives, and violation blocks of the contract and the rest of the file (actors:, metrics:) are omitted. contracts: - id: DELIVERY_SLA parties: [DISPATCHER, "ROBOT[*]", "CUSTOMER[*]"] assume: - "ROBOT[i].battery > 20" guarantee: - "delivery_time <= 300s" # === SoS-DSL extension: per-instance lifecycle === lifecycle: states: [Proposed, Assigned, Accepted, Delivering, Completed, Violated, Terminated] initial: Proposed terminal: [Completed, Violated, Terminated] transitions: - id: assign from: Proposed to: Assigned on: "DISPATCHER -> ROBOT[i] : route_assignment" - id: accept from: Assigned to: Accepted on: "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : ack(accepted)" deadline: 5s on_violation: transition: Violated severity: Major - id: start_delivery from: Accepted to: Delivering on: "ROBOT[i].status == InTransit" - id: complete from: Delivering to: Completed on: "ROBOT[i].status == Delivered" when: "now <= request.deadline" - id: late_failure from: [Assigned, Accepted, Delivering] to: Violated on: "now > request.deadline" # === SoS-DSL extension: declarative monitors === monitors: - id: battery_guard observe: "ROBOT[i].battery" sampling: periodic(500ms) rule: "ROBOT[i].battery < 20 AND state == Assigned" on_match: transition: Violated severity: Major - id: collision_watch observe: ["ROBOT[i].position", "DISPATCHER.obstacle_positions"] sampling: periodic(100ms) rule: "min_dist(ROBOT[i].position, DISPATCHER.obstacle_positions) < 0.05" on_match: violation: collision severity: Critical - id: deadline_watch observe: time sampling: periodic(1s) rule: "now > request.deadline" on_match: transition: Violated severity: Critical No transition in this example leads to Terminated; the state is declared for completeness.

The CADL simulator IR (module cadl.sim.ir of the cadl repository) is extended with a lifecycle and a monitors field on each contract IR object under institution.contracts. The shape is a direct serialization of the IR dataclasses (asdict()), which applies normalizations to the surface syntax and denormalizes the nested on_violation / on_match / sampling blocks into flat fields prefixed with their parent (this keeps the JSON stable for generators that read it field-by-field): { "institution": { "actors": [...], "contracts": [ { "id": "DELIVERY_SLA", "parties": ["DISPATCHER", "ROBOT[*]", "CUSTOMER[*]"], "assume": [...], "guarantee": [...], "governance": {...}, "violation_detect": "...", "violation_action": "...", "lifecycle": { "states": ["Proposed", "Assigned", "Accepted", "Delivering", "Completed", "Violated", "Terminated"], "initial": "Proposed", "terminal": ["Completed", "Violated", "Terminated"], "transitions": [ { "id": "assign", "from_states": ["Proposed"], "to_state": "Assigned", "on": "DISPATCHER -> ROBOT[i] : route_assignment", "when": null, "deadline_ms": null, "on_violation_transition": null, "on_violation_severity": null, "emit": [] }, { "id": "accept", "from_states": ["Assigned"], "to_state": "Accepted", "on": "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : ack(accepted)", "when": null, "deadline_ms": 5000, "on_violation_transition": "Violated", "on_violation_severity": "Major", "emit": [] } ] }, "monitors": [ { "id": "battery_guard", "observe": ["ROBOT[i].battery"], "sampling_kind": "periodic", "sampling_period_ms": 500, "rule": "ROBOT[i].battery < 20 AND state == Assigned", "on_match_violation": null, "on_match_transition": "Violated", "on_match_severity": "Major" } ] } ] } } Normalizations applied during lowering: Surface syntax Normalized IR field(s) from: Assigned (single id) "from_states": ["Assigned"] from: [Assigned, Accepted] "from_states": ["Assigned", "Accepted"] to: Accepted "to_state": "Accepted" deadline: 5s "deadline_ms": 5000 on_violation: { transition: V, severity: Major } "on_violation_transition": "V", "on_violation_severity": "Major" sampling: periodic(500ms) "sampling_kind": "periodic", "sampling_period_ms": 500 sampling: event "sampling_kind": "event", "sampling_period_ms": null on_match: { violation, transition, severity } "on_match_violation", "on_match_transition", "on_match_severity" The IR does not fill in every default. When the violation label (on_match.violation) is omitted, the IR records null. The severity fields are null when the whole on_violation: or on_match: block is omitted; when the block is present without severity:, the IR records Major. Where the IR records null, applying the defaults (Major; the monitor's id as label) is left to the consumer of the IR. The cadl sim-ir <file> --format json command emits this shape (abridged above) for downstream tools such as the Contract Lifecycle page of CADL Explorer. The Unity C# generator (cadl codegen --target unity-csharp) works from the same parsed contract. A Python reference runtime also consumes this JSON; it is published in the cadl-raspimouse-simulator repository under cadl/runtime/.

Code generation targets MAY emit code from the lifecycle and monitors blocks. The reference generator for this extension is the unity-csharp target (Appendix D). For each contract that has a lifecycle: or monitors: block it produces: a state machine class per contract (states from lifecycle.states, transitions from lifecycle.transitions), a deadline timer per transition with a deadline_ms (in cadl 0.3 only when the transition also names a state in on_violation.transition; a deadline without one is not enforced by the generated code), a periodic / event-driven monitor task per monitor, a violation log entry per fired on_violation or on_match.violation. In cadl 0.3 the generated runtime matches an on: event by comparing its text with the name of the event posted by the host application, and it evaluates a rule without function calls: a rule that contains one, such as collision_watch in E.6, never matches. The generated evaluator does not support the arithmetic operators + - * / or duration literals (5s) in a rule either. The values of now, request, and the observed attributes are supplied by the host. Reward / sanction execution is out of scope for this revision; the runtime SHOULD record reward and sanction events but is not required to act on them.

Files written against unmodified CADL v0.3 remain valid. Files that use the SoS-DSL extension SHOULD declare sos-dsl: 0.1 under extensions: in the sos: mapping. Processors that do not implement the extension MUST NOT reject such files; they SHOULD emit a single informational diagnostic per file.

This appendix specifies the norms extension to CADL. It adds to the contract_def production of Appendix A.4 two keys, norms: and counts_as:, and adds bounded temporal operators to some predicates of a contract. With them, the obligations, permissions, prohibitions, and powers that the core language leaves in the text of assume:, guarantee:, and responsibilities: become objects with a bearer, a deadline, a state over time, and a defined consequence of violation. The core language (Chapter 5, Appendix A) does not mandate these blocks; a conforming CADL processor that does not implement the extension MUST NOT reject a file because of the new keys. It SHOULD accept them syntactically and emit an informational diagnostic. The extension is versioned independently from the core language. Its name is norms and this appendix describes version 0.1. Because the temporal operators of F.4 change how some predicates are read, a file that uses the extension MUST declare it with the extensions: key of Appendix A.2; F.11 says what a processor does with an undeclared use. sos: ... extensions: - norms: 0.1 The extension can be used with or without the SoS-DSL extension (Appendix E). Where a contract also has a lifecycle: block, a norm can move the contract instance to a lifecycle state on violation (F.3).

The research directions of Section 9.6 identify four gaps. Version 0.1 of this extension is a first step on each: Norms are not first-class. A guarantee such as "delivery_time <= 300s" says what must hold, but not who must make it hold, from when, until when, and what follows when it does not. Deontic contract languages such as Symboleo treat obligations and powers as objects with a lifecycle [Sharifi+, 2020]; CADL contracts did not. Predicates have no time. assume: and guarantee: are state predicates. Deadlines exist only on lifecycle transitions of the SoS-DSL extension. Protocols and contracts are not connected. Nothing says that a message of a protocol counts as an act in a contract, which is how institutions create institutional facts from other facts [Boella & van der Torre, KR 2004]. Amendments have no effect on running norms. When a contract is amended while the SoS runs (as in Course D of the hands-on materials), nothing says what happens to an obligation that is already active. Norms 0.1 deliberately stays small: it fixes the vocabulary and the static and dynamic semantics, so that design-time checking (by translation to a model checker) and runtime monitoring can be added by processors without changing the language. It does not give the institutional parameters α, β, and λ a formal meaning for norms (F.7); the grounding extension (Appendix J) takes a first step from the norms of a contract to the parameters.

Concept Meaning in norms 0.1 Norm An obligation, permission, prohibition, or power of one bearer, declared in a contract. Obligation The bearer must bring about its content (make a predicate true or make an event occur), by the deadline: if one is given. Prohibition The bearer must not bring about its content while the norm is active (and, if a deadline: is given, only within that window). Permission The bearer may bring about its content. A permission is never violated; it records what is allowed. Power The bearer can perform an institutional act (its content) that changes the state of other norms of the contract (effects:). A power is neither fulfilled nor violated. Institutional event A named event of a contract that is created by a counts_as: rule from a message or a condition, for example "this message counts as a reassignment". Contract instance One execution of a contract, as in Appendix E. F.5 says when it starts and ends. Norm instance The norm within one contract instance. Each norm has exactly one instance per contract instance in version 0.1. An index such as i in ROBOT[i] is bound by the contract instance. Verdict The value of a norm instance or of a temporal guarantee on the trace observed so far: pending, fulfilled, violated, or excused (F.5).

The grammar uses the notation of Appendix A. identifier, actor_ref, duration_lit, predicate, and text are defined in Appendix A; message_event and severity in Appendix E, E.3. contract_def gains two optional keys: contract_def = ... , [ "norms:" , { "-" , norm_def } ] , [ "counts_as:" , { "-" , counts_as_def } ] ; norm_def = "id:" , identifier , "kind:" , norm_kind , "bearer:" , actor_ref , [ "counterparty:" , actor_ref ] , [ "trigger:" , norm_event ] , [ "until:" , norm_event ] , "content:" , norm_content , [ "deadline:" , duration_lit ] , [ "on_violation:" , norm_violation ] , [ "effects:" , power_effects ] , [ "on_amendment:" , amendment_policy ] ; norm_kind = "obligation" | "permission" | "prohibition" | "power" ; norm_event = message_event | identifier | predicate ; (* string *) norm_content = message_event | identifier | tpredicate ; (* string *) norm_violation = [ "severity:" , severity ] , [ "sanction:" , text ] , [ "reparation:" , identifier ] , [ "transition:" , identifier ] ; power_effects = [ "activate:" , { "-" , identifier } ] , [ "suspend:" , { "-" , identifier } ] , [ "resume:" , { "-" , identifier } ] , [ "discharge:" , { "-" , identifier } ] ; amendment_policy = "carry_over" | "discharge" | ( "transform:" , identifier ) ; counts_as_def = "when:" , ( message_event | predicate ) , "creates:" , identifier , [ "if:" , predicate ] ; A norm_event or norm_content is read as follows. A string of the form A -> B : m is a message_event. A string that consists of a single identifier names the institutional event of that name when the contract declares one in counts_as:; otherwise it is a predicate (a state variable, N-8). Any other string is a predicate (norm_event) or a tpredicate (norm_content). An institutional event name inside a larger predicate (reassignment AND x > 0) is a state variable, not the event. Values that contain [, ], *, ->, or ": " SHOULD be quoted and MUST be quoted inside a flow sequence, as for every scalar of Appendix A. A message_event S -> R : m occurs at an observation that carries a message with the name m whose sender matches S and whose receiver matches R; when m is written with arguments, they must equal the arguments of the message. An actor reference matches a concrete actor of a message as follows, wherever a message_event stands: in a trigger:, an until:, a content:, and the when: of a counts_as: rule. Reference Matches A the actor A, declared without index; never an indexed member A[k] A[3] the member A[3] A[*] every member of the declared set A A[1..3] the members A[1] to A[3]; with a symbolic bound (A[1..N]), every member of the set A[i] the member A[v] when the contract instance binds i to v; every member of the set when it binds no value to i (a processor SHOULD warn) A[k] is a member of the set A when A is declared with a range and k lies within its integer bounds: a set declared as A[1..3] does not contain A[7]. When the declared upper bound is symbolic (A[1..N]), every index from the lower bound on is a member, and A[0] is not. An actor that is not declared, or that lies outside the bounds of its set, matches no reference. In these predicates the reserved identifiers of Appendix E, E.4 are available as in a rule: now, request, and, when the contract has a lifecycle: block, state; and so is the membership x IN [a, b] of E.3. In on_violation:, reparation: names another norm of the same contract that is activated when this norm is violated (a contrary-to-duty norm), sanction: describes the sanction in text, and transition: names a state of the contract's lifecycle: block (Appendix E), to which the contract instance moves as with on_violation.transition of a lifecycle transition. severity: defaults to Major and on_amendment: to carry_over. counterparty: names the party to whom the norm is owed; it is informative in version 0.1 and has no effect on the semantics. The key until: and the temporal operator until(...) of F.4 are different things and may appear in the same norm.

A tpredicate is a predicate of Appendix A.10 in which three bounded temporal operators may appear wherever a function_call may. They are written as function calls, so the expression grammar of A.10 is unchanged; the extension gives these three names a meaning: tpredicate = predicate ; (* in which the calls below have temporal meaning *) temporal_call = "within" , "(" , duration_lit , "," , tpredicate , ")" | "throughout" , "(" , duration_lit , "," , tpredicate , ")" | "until" , "(" , tpredicate , "," , tpredicate , "," , duration_lit , ")" ; Operator Holds at time t when Metric temporal logic within(d, p) p holds at some time in [t, t + d] F[0,d] p throughout(d, p) p holds at every time in [t, t + d] G[0,d] p until(p, q, d) q holds at some time t′ in [t, t + d], and p holds at every time in [t, t′) p U[0,d] q The operators are evaluated on a timed trace: a sequence of observations, each a snapshot of the observed quantities with a non-decreasing time stamp, as delivered to the monitors of Appendix E. "At some time" and "at every time" range over the observations whose time stamps fall in the interval (pointwise semantics); an interval that contains no observation makes within false and throughout true. d MUST be a duration_lit greater than zero; operators may be nested. Where they may appear. With the extension declared, temporal operators may appear only in the assume: and guarantee: items of a contract and in the content: of a norm. They MUST NOT appear in any other predicate or condition of the file in version 0.1 (N-10): among others the trigger: and until: of a norm, the when: and if: of a counts_as: rule, monitor rule:, lifecycle when: and on:, condition:, safety_invariant:, formula:, expr:, and protocol conditions. Events and conditions are evaluated at a single observation, and a future-time operator there would not be decided until later. When they are evaluated. A tpredicate in assume: or guarantee: is evaluated at the time the contract instance starts: within(300s, p) there means "p within 300 s of the start of the contract instance". To state an invariant, write it with throughout. A tpredicate in content: is evaluated at observation times after the norm's activation (F.5). A predicate without temporal operators keeps the meaning it has in the core language. When their value is known. The value of an operator at time t can depend on observations after t. It is decided at the first observation that determines it; before that it is not decided, and a decided value does not change. For an operator whose operands contain no temporal operator, the rule is as follows. within(d, p) is decided true, and throughout(d, p) false, at the observation in [t, t + d] that shows it; until(p, q, d) is decided true at the observation at which q holds, and false at an observation at which p fails before q has held. Otherwise the value is decided at the first observation whose time stamp is after t + d. The interval is then over: within and until are false and throughout is true, unless an operand was undefined (F.5) at an observation of the interval and a value of that operand could have decided it otherwise; in that case the value is undefined. For until(p, q, d) this is so only for an undefined q, or for an undefined p at an observation before one at which q held: an undefined p does not matter when q never held, and the value is then false. Likewise until is not decided false by a failing p at an observation before which q was undefined; its value is then undefined. The end of an interval is therefore not known at the time t + d itself but at the first observation after it; that observation need not change any quantity (F.5). An operator whose operand contains a temporal operator is decided once the values of the operand on which it depends are decided, each by the same rule at its own observation. This can be later than t + d. within(2s, throughout(5s, p)) at time t needs the value of throughout(5s, p) at the observations of [t, t + 2s], and that value, when p keeps holding, is decided only by an observation more than 5 s later: the operator can stay undecided until an observation after t + 7s. In general the value of a tpredicate at time t is decided at the latest by the first observation after t plus the largest sum of the durations of operators nested in one another. A file that does not declare norms: 0.1 reads within, throughout, and until as ordinary function names, as in the core language.

Norms are judged per contract instance. When the contract has a lifecycle: block, contract instances are those of Appendix E, E.5: the host application creates them, and an instance ends when it reaches a terminal state. When the contract has no lifecycle: block, the host application creates and ends contract instances in the same way, without states; with no host, a single instance starts at the first observation and ends at the last. A trace that stops while the contract instance is still running is a prefix: the instance has not ended, and nothing is settled. A processor that receives the observations one at a time, while the system runs, does not know that an observation is the last one when it processes it. For such a processor the end of the instance is signalled separately, after that observation, and the norms are then settled (item 6 below) at the last observation received, with its time stamp, as in step 6 of that observation. An observation that arrives after the contract instance has ended is not part of the instance and has no effect on it. An observation need not change anything. An observation that carries only a time stamp is an observation like any other: predicates are evaluated and deadlines are checked at it. A passed deadline and the end of an interval are detected at an observation and not between observations (items 2 and 3 below, F.4). A processor that monitors a running system SHOULD therefore make an observation soon after the deadline of an active norm passes; without one, the violation, and with it the decision between violated and excused, waits for the next observation. A predicate has one of three values at an observation: true, false, or undefined, when it refers to a quantity that has no value yet; AND, OR, and NOT follow Kleene's three-valued logic. An undefined predicate does not hold and does not fail: an event or condition does not occur on it, and an assumption or guarantee is not decided by it. "Becomes true" means: true at the current observation, and not true at the previous observation of the instance or no previous observation. In a contract with a lifecycle: block, state in a predicate is the lifecycle state before the transitions of the current observation. A name that stands alone in a predicate, such as load in load > 5 or Delivered in ROBOT[i].status == Delivered, is an observed quantity or a symbolic value. The set of names that are observed quantities is fixed for the contract instance: it is given to the processor when the instance starts, or, for a recorded trace, it is the set of names that have a value in some observation of the instance. A name of this set is a quantity at every observation of the instance, and is undefined, not a symbolic value, at the observations before its first value. Every other name that stands alone is a symbolic value. A symbolic value can only be compared with a text value, by ==, !=, or IN; a predicate that uses it in another way is undefined.

A quantified predicate exists x in D: p or for all x in D: p, and a comprehension f(e for x in D) as the argument of an aggregate function (Appendix A, A.10), are evaluated at an observation over a domain D. The domain names a declared set of actors: A, A[*], or A[lo..hi]. The domain of a comprehension may also be a range of integers lo..hi. A predicate with any other domain is not evaluated (F.10). The variable x takes the indices of the members of the domain. In p or e, an actor reference indexed by x (A[x], also inside an index expression such as A[x+1]) denotes the member with that index, and an index that is not a member of A (F.3) denotes no member, so a quantity of it is undefined, whatever the trace gives for it; x.q denotes the quantity q of that member (r.load in sum(r.load for r in ROBOT[*])); and x alone is the integer index, so j != k says that j and k are different members. Within p or e, x hides an index of the same name that the contract instance binds, an observed quantity of the same name, and the variable of an enclosing quantifier or comprehension. It never hides a symbolic bound of a set declaration: the bound N of a set declared as A[1..N] is read outside every quantifier and comprehension, also when one of them has a variable named N (N-14). Closed and open domains. The members of a set are those of F.3; a range A[lo..hi] keeps the members within its bounds. When every bound is an integer, the domain is closed: it is exactly those members. A symbolic bound (N in a set declared as A[1..N], in A[2..N], or in 1..N) has a value at an observation when the contract instance binds the name to an integer or the name is an observed quantity whose value at the observation is an integer. A domain with a symbolic bound is closed as well when every such bound has a value and, for the symbolic bound of the set declaration, no member with an index beyond its value has been named at or before the observation. F.3 makes every index from the lower bound on a member, whatever value the bound has, so a member named beyond the value keeps the domain open; a processor SHOULD warn when that happens. Otherwise the domain is open: the number of members is not known. The known members of an open domain at an observation are the members of the set, within the integer bounds, that the contract instance has named at that observation or before: in the name of a value (A[3].delivery), as the sender or receiver of a message, or by binding an index i to k where a norm or a counts_as: rule of the contract writes A[i]. Observations after the current one are never used, so an open domain is not closed by what is observed later. A processor MAY limit the number of members of a closed domain that it enumerates, since a bound that the trace gives can be arbitrarily large. A closed domain with more members than the limit is then evaluated as an open domain, with its known members; by the argument below this is sound, and only a value that the closed domain would decide may become undefined. A processor that does so SHOULD warn and name the set and the size. Values. Over a closed domain the quantifiers follow Kleene's three-valued logic: exists x in D: p is true when p is true for some member, false when p is false for every member, and undefined otherwise; for all x in D: p is false when p is false for some member, true when p is true for every member, and undefined otherwise. Over an empty domain exists is false and for all is true. Over an open domain only a known member decides: exists is true when p is true for some known member, for all is false when p is false for some known member, and the value is undefined otherwise, also when p has the same value for every known member and when no member is known. When p contains a temporal operator (F.4), the value is not decided while it is not decided for a member that could still decide it. The rule for open domains is sound. Let a closed domain contain the known members with the values they have at the observation, and any further members with any values, defined or not; such a domain is a possible completion of the open domain, whatever value the bound later takes, because it contains every member named so far. A member for which p is true makes exists true over that domain too, and a member for which p is false makes for all false, because in Kleene's logic a disjunction with a true operand is true and a conjunction with a false operand is false, whatever the other operands are. So a value that is true or false over the open domain is the value over every such closed domain. The rule is also the strongest one: when the known members do not decide, a further member for which p is true, or false, changes the value, and undefined is the value F.5 gives to a predicate that refers to quantities without values. In particular exists over an open domain is never false and for all never true: a prohibition whose content: is such an exists is violated when known members witness it, and otherwise, as for every undefined content, it is not. Aggregates. Of the aggregate functions of a comprehension, the norms extension evaluates sum, count, min, max, and avg. count(p for x in D) is the number of members for which p is true, where a value of p counts as true when it is true or a number other than 0, and a text value or a symbolic value makes the count undefined; the other functions take the values of e, which are numbers. sum and count of an empty domain are 0. An aggregate is undefined over an open domain, when e (for count, p) is undefined for a member, when a value of e is not a number, and for min, max, and avg over an empty domain. A predicate that compares such a value is undefined. Another function, and a temporal operator inside a comprehension, are not evaluated (F.10). A wildcard or range reference outside a domain, as in ROBOT[*].battery > 10 or count(ROBOT[*].status == Collision), has no value that Appendix A defines in a predicate, and a predicate that contains one is not evaluated (F.10). The quantified form states the meaning: for all j in ROBOT: ROBOT[j].battery > 10 and count(ROBOT[j].status == Collision for j in ROBOT). The domain and its known members at an observation depend only on the observations up to it. The values of quantified predicates and aggregates therefore keep the property of the verdicts below: the verdicts after an observation are those of the trace up to it. A predicate that is undefined at an observation because its domain is open may have a value at a later observation, when a member is named or the bound gets a value; its value at the earlier observation stays undefined.

A norm instance is in one of six states: State Meaning inactive Not yet in force. active In force; an obligation or prohibition is being judged. suspended Temporarily not in force (by a power). Its deadline and window clocks stop. fulfilled An obligation whose content was brought about in time, or a prohibition whose window closed without the content occurring. violated An obligation whose deadline passed without the content, or a prohibition whose content occurred. discharged Ended without being fulfilled or violated: by until:, by a power, by the end of the contract instance, or by an amendment (F.6). fulfilled, violated, and discharged are final: in version 0.1 a norm instance is judged at most once per contract instance. A trigger that occurs while the norm instance is not inactive is ignored, and a prohibition reports only its first violation. Activation. A norm instance starts inactive. It becomes active: when its trigger: occurs (a message is sent, an institutional event is created, or a predicate becomes true); when the contract instance starts, if the norm has no trigger: and is neither named as the reparation: of another norm nor in the activate: effect of a power; when the norm it repairs is violated (reparation:), or when a power activates it (activate:). The activation time is the time stamp of the observation at which the norm becomes active. Obligation. An active obligation becomes fulfilled at the first observation, at or after its activation, at which its content occurs (a message or an institutional event) or holds (a tpredicate evaluated at that observation). It becomes violated when its deadline:, measured from the activation time without the time spent suspended, has passed without that happening; content at exactly the deadline is in time, and content while the obligation is suspended does not count. The violation takes place at the first observation after the deadline. When the content is a tpredicate with temporal operators, its value at an observation may be known only later; the obligation stays pending until it is decided, and only observations up to the deadline count. Prohibition. An active prohibition becomes violated at the first observation at which its content occurs or holds. It becomes fulfilled when its deadline: window, measured from the activation time without the time spent suspended, has closed; content at exactly the end of the window is a violation. A suspended prohibition is not judged. Permission and power. They stay active until they are discharged. Discharge. A norm instance that is active or suspended becomes discharged when its until: occurs, whatever its deadline, or when a power discharges it. End of the contract instance. When the contract instance ends, every norm instance that is not final is settled: an active or suspended obligation without deadline: becomes violated; an obligation whose deadline has not yet passed becomes discharged; a prohibition becomes fulfilled; every other norm instance, including an inactive one, becomes discharged. Two exceptions: a norm instance that became active at the observation at which the instance ends, and that step 4 of that observation did not make final, becomes discharged, since no observation followed its activation; and an obligation or prohibition whose tpredicate content is still undecided stays as it is, with the verdict pending. A violation that arises from this settlement is reported with its severity, but its reparation: and transition: do not apply, since the instance has ended. Powers.
