An institutional event created from a message is performed by the sender of that message; one created from a predicate has no performer. When the bearer of an active power performs its content (an institutional event, or a message the bearer sends), the effects: apply to the norm instances of the same contract instance: activate makes an inactive norm active, suspend makes an active norm suspended, resume makes a suspended norm active, and discharge makes an active or suspended norm discharged. An effect on a norm in another state does nothing. When the act is performed while no matching power of the performer is active, the effects do not apply (the institutional event itself still exists for other norms); a processor that monitors norms SHOULD record the act as unauthorised. Violation. When a norm instance becomes violated, its on_violation: applies: a violation with the given severity: (default Major) and the norm id as label is reported, the reparation: norm is activated, and the contract instance moves to the transition: state if one is given and the instance is not already in a terminal state.

A counts_as: rule creates its institutional event in a contract instance when its when: occurs (a message is sent, or a predicate becomes true) and its if: condition, if any, holds at that observation. Institutional events are local to the contract instance. They exist only as events: they can trigger, end, or fulfil norms, and they are the content of powers.

One observation can carry a message that creates an institutional event, triggers a norm, fulfils another, and fires a lifecycle transition. A processor applies the steps in this order, each to the state left by the previous one. Before step 1 it evaluates the assume: items and then the guarantee: items of the contract, so an assumption that fails at an observation excuses the violations of that observation; and at the first observation of the instance it first activates the norms that become active when the instance starts. create the institutional events of the counts_as: rules; apply the effects of powers (item 7), power by power in the order of declaration and, within one power, in the order activate, suspend, resume, discharge; whether a power is active is decided at the beginning of this step; activate norms whose triggers occurred (item 1); judge the active norms, for each norm in this order: a deadline that has passed, then the content, then until: (items 2, 3, 5); so a violation by a passed deadline comes before a discharge at the same observation, and content before until:. A norm activated in step 3 is judged in this step too, so content at its activation time counts; apply on_violation: (item 8); a reparation norm activated here is first judged at the next observation; fire the lifecycle transitions of Appendix E, and, if the contract instance has ended, settle its norms (item 6).

The verdict of a norm instance, or of a guarantee with temporal operators, on the finite trace observed so far is one of four values: Verdict Norm instance Guarantee of a contract pending inactive, active, or suspended not yet decided on the observed prefix fulfilled fulfilled, or discharged holds on every continuation of the prefix violated violated while no assumption of the contract had failed fails on every continuation, while no assumption had failed excused violated at or after the observation at which an assumption of the contract failed fails at or after the observation at which an assumption failed An assumption fails at the first observation at which its value becomes false (for an item with temporal operators, the observation at which its value is decided false, F.4); an assumption whose value is not yet decided, or is undefined, has not failed. An assume: or guarantee: item without temporal operators is a state predicate and is evaluated at every observation: it fails at the first observation at which it is false, and a guarantee that has not failed when the contract instance ends is fulfilled. An item that mixes a state predicate with temporal operators is a tpredicate and is evaluated once, at the start of the instance. Once an assumption has failed, every later violation in the same contract instance is excused; a guarantee or norm becomes excused only when it itself fails, not when the assumption fails. A discharged permission or power has the verdict fulfilled, although it is not fulfilled in the sense of F.2. A violation by a passed deadline is judged violated or excused at the observation at which it takes place, not at the time of the deadline. When a trace ends, pending verdicts stay pending: a trace that stops before a deadline or the end of an interval does not decide it, and neither does the end of the contract instance for a temporal item whose interval is not over. With the set of observed quantities fixed for the contract instance (see "Contract instances" above), the verdicts after an observation are those of the trace up to that observation, read as a prefix with the same set. They do not depend on later observations, and a verdict other than pending does not change afterwards. A processor MAY therefore compute the verdicts while the system runs, observation by observation; given the same set of quantities, it gives the verdicts that a processor reading the recorded trace gives. A processor that is not given the names of the quantities and learns them from the observations reads a name as a symbolic value until its first value arrives. For a predicate that uses such a name before its first value, it MAY give a verdict that differs from the one above. This is the only permitted difference. Such a processor SHOULD be given the names; the difference arises only where the name is compared with a text value, since any other use of a symbolic value is undefined, as is the quantity without a value. excused separates "the bearer failed" from "the bearer was not given what the contract assumes", which is the basis of assigning blame in deontic runtime verification [Kharraz+, ICTAC 2023]; taking the assumption into account also makes more properties monitorable [Henzinger & Saraç, RV 2020]. Version 0.1 uses this weak reading of assumptions. The strong reading of Section 5.4.1, under which the guarantee must still hold for a short time after an assumption stops holding, is not expressed by verdicts in version 0.1. An excused norm still triggers its on_violation:, because the consequence for the contract instance does not depend on blame; the reported violation carries the verdict excused.

An amendment replaces the definition of a contract by a new version with the same contract id while contract instances are running. How versions are made, approved, and put into effect is outside norms 0.1; the Course D hands-on materials show one procedure. The new version takes effect at an observation, before anything else is evaluated at that observation (before the assumptions and guarantees and before step 1 of F.5); a norm that the amendment makes active is therefore judged at that same observation. Norm instances are treated as follows. An active or suspended norm instance follows the on_amendment: of its norm in the old version: on_amendment: Effect carry_over (default) The instance continues under the norm with the same id in the new version, keeping its state and the time already elapsed against its deadline. It is discharged instead when the new version has no norm with that id or when that norm has a different kind. If the content changes, the instance is judged on the new content from this observation on. If the elapsed time already exceeds the new deadline (elapsed time equal to it does not), an obligation, also a suspended one, becomes violated when the new version takes effect, and the window of a prohibition has closed, so it becomes fulfilled. discharge The instance is discharged. transform: X The instance is discharged, and the norm X of the new version is activated if it is inactive, with the time already elapsed counted against its deadline (for an obligation or prohibition; for a permission or power the time has no effect). If X is not inactive, nothing more happens. The entries of the table are applied in the order in which the old version declares the norms, and before new norms are activated. When the target X of transform: does not exist in the new version, the instance is only discharged. An inactive norm instance takes the definition of the norm with the same id in the new version, and is removed when the new version has no such norm; it is not activated by the amendment, even if its new definition has no trigger:. A norm is new when the old version has no norm with its id; it starts inactive, and becomes active at once if it has no trigger: and is not a reparation or activation target (F.5, item 1). Final instances (fulfilled, violated, discharged) are not affected and their ids are not used again in the contract instance: a norm of the new version with the id of a final instance gets no new instance. In particular, a violation stays a violation of the version under which it occurred, while a violation that occurs after the amendment uses the on_violation: of the new version. The counts_as: rules of the new version apply from the time it takes effect. An assume: or guarantee: item whose text is the same in both versions continues with its value; an item that is new is evaluated from this observation on (a tpredicate at this observation); an item that is removed keeps the verdict it had. An assumption that failed before the amendment still excuses later violations. When the contract has a lifecycle: block, the current state of the instance MUST be a state of the new version; otherwise the amendment cannot be applied to that instance. A regime transition (A.7) does not affect norm instances in version 0.1. A processor that applies amendments SHOULD report, before the new version takes effect, every carried-over norm whose content or deadline: changes.

A norms-aware processor MUST, in addition to existing checks: N-1. Every norm id MUST be an identifier, MUST NOT be a reserved word (including the IN of Appendix E), and MUST be unique within its contract. The name in creates: MUST be an identifier and MUST NOT equal the id of a norm of the same contract. (Under a YAML 1.1 loader an unquoted yes, no, on, or off is a boolean, not a name; see A.12.) N-2. kind: MUST be one of obligation, permission, prohibition, power. N-3. bearer: and counterparty: MUST name single declared actors: without an index, with an integer index (ROBOT[1]), or with an index that the contract instance binds (ROBOT[i]); a wildcard or a range (ROBOT[*], ROBOT[1..3]) is not allowed. They SHOULD name parties of the contract. N-4. deadline: MUST be a duration_lit and is allowed only for an obligation or a prohibition. on_violation: is allowed only for an obligation or a prohibition. N-5. effects: is allowed only for a power, and a power MUST have at least one effect. Every name in effects: MUST be the id of a norm of the same contract other than the power itself. N-6. on_violation.reparation MUST name an obligation or a prohibition of the same contract that has no trigger:. Following reparation: from any norm MUST NOT lead back to that norm. N-7. on_violation.transition MUST name a state in lifecycle.states of the same contract; the contract MUST therefore have a lifecycle: block (Appendix E). N-8. A processor SHOULD warn when an identifier used as a whole trigger:, until:, or content: is not an institutional event of the contract but is the id of a norm, which is likely a mistake. N-9. In a message_event of a norm or a counts_as: rule, the sender and the receiver MUST name declared actors. The content of a power MUST be an institutional event that every counts_as: rule creating it creates from a message_event, or a message_event whose sender is the bearer. For an obligation or a prohibition whose content is a message_event, the sender SHOULD be the bearer. N-10. A temporal operator MUST have the arguments of F.4, its duration MUST be a duration_lit greater than zero, and it MUST NOT appear outside the places F.4 allows. N-11. on_amendment: MUST be carry_over, discharge, or { transform: X } with an identifier X. (Whether X exists in the new version can only be checked against that version.) N-12. A processor SHOULD warn when a permission and a prohibition of the same contract have the same bearer: and textually identical content:, since the two conflict. N-13. A processor SHOULD warn when the trigger: of a prohibition is a message_event and every occurrence of the trigger is an occurrence of the content: the content is a message_event with the same message name, with the same argument values when the content has arguments, and with actor references that match every actor that those of the trigger match (D -> R[i] : go and D -> R[1..3] : go for a set declared as R[1..3]); or the content is an institutional event that a counts_as: rule without if: creates from such a message. The check is a best effort and does not detect every such prohibition (for example, one whose content is a predicate that the trigger message makes true). Such a prohibition is violated at the observation that activates it (F.5, step 4), which is rarely what is meant: a prohibition of a second occurrence is a quantified predicate over the state (F.5, "Quantifiers and aggregates") or an until:-bounded prohibition triggered by an earlier event. N-14. A processor SHOULD warn when the variable of a quantifier or a comprehension has the name of a symbolic bound of a declared set (for all N in S: ... with S[1..N]). The bound keeps its own value inside the quantifier (F.5), which a reader may not expect.

The consistency checks of Section 6.3 (satisfiability of assume: and guarantee: with an SMT solver) apply to state predicates. An assume: or guarantee: item that contains a temporal operator is not a state predicate. A norms-aware processor that does not translate temporal predicates MUST leave such an item out of the SMT checks and report that it did so; it MUST NOT treat the operator as an uninterpreted function.

The parameters of Section 5.4.2 are not given a formal meaning for norms in version 0.1. The intended reading, to be made precise in a later version (RD-6.1 in Section 9.6), is: β, the degree of centralisation of decision-making, describes who holds the powers of a contract; α, the degree of information sharing, describes which triggers and contents the other parties can observe; and λ, the incentive intensity, scales the sanctions of violated norms. The grounding extension (Appendix J, grounding 0.1) defines indices related to this reading without changing this appendix: for β, the concentration of the powers of a contract; for α, the sharing of declared information items (not the observability of triggers and contents); and, for λ, a numeric magnitude of a sanction that a strategic model multiplies by λ, together with a count of the norms that carry a sanction or a reward.

The contract below is a simplified variant of the delivery contract of Appendix E, E.6 with norms added. It is taken from examples/norms_robot_delivery.cadl in the cadl repository and abridged. sos: name: "RobotDeliveryNorms" extensions: - sos-dsl: 0.1 - norms: 0.1 # actors DISPATCHER, ROBOT[1..N], CUSTOMER[1..M] as in Appendix E contracts: - id: DELIVERY_SLA parties: [DISPATCHER, "ROBOT[*]", "CUSTOMER[*]"] assume: - "throughout(300s, DISPATCHER.is_operational == true)" guarantee: - "within(300s, ROBOT[i].status == Delivered)" lifecycle: states: [Proposed, Assigned, Delivering, Completed, Violated] initial: Proposed terminal: [Completed, Violated] transitions: - { id: assign, from: Proposed, to: Assigned, on: "DISPATCHER -> ROBOT[i] : route_assignment" } - { id: start, from: Assigned, to: Delivering, on: "ROBOT[i].status == InTransit" } - { id: complete, from: Delivering, to: Completed, on: "ROBOT[i].status == Delivered" } counts_as: - when: "DISPATCHER -> ROBOT[i] : replan_command" creates: reassignment norms: - id: acknowledge kind: obligation bearer: "ROBOT[i]" counterparty: DISPATCHER trigger: "DISPATCHER -> ROBOT[i] : route_assignment" content: "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : ack(accepted)" deadline: 5s on_violation: severity: Major reparation: report_failure - id: report_failure kind: obligation bearer: "ROBOT[i]" counterparty: DISPATCHER content: "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : failure_report" deadline: 2s on_violation: severity: Critical transition: Violated - id: no_low_battery_driving kind: prohibition bearer: "ROBOT[i]" content: "ROBOT[i].battery < 10 AND ROBOT[i].status == InTransit" on_violation: severity: Critical sanction: "removed from the dispatch pool for one period" - id: may_return_to_charge kind: permission bearer: "ROBOT[i]" content: "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : charging_request" - id: reassign kind: power bearer: DISPATCHER content: reassignment effects: discharge: [acknowledge, report_failure] on_amendment: discharge acknowledge is triggered by the route assignment and must be met within 5 s. If it is violated, the robot must report a failure within 2 s (report_failure, a contrary-to-duty obligation, which stays inactive until then); failing that too moves the contract instance to Violated. no_low_battery_driving, may_return_to_charge, and reassign have no trigger and are active from the start of the contract instance. The dispatcher's replan_command counts as a reassignment performed by the dispatcher, which discharges both obligations while the power reassign is active; since each norm is judged once per contract instance, a later route assignment in the same instance creates no new obligation. The guarantee says that the robot delivers within 300 s of the start of the contract instance; if the dispatcher stops operating before a late delivery, the delivery is excused rather than violated.

The simulator IR (E.7) is extended with two fields on each contract under institution.contracts: norms and counts_as. As in E.7, the IR is a direct serialization of dataclasses and flattens nested blocks: { "norms": [ { "id": "acknowledge", "kind": "obligation", "bearer": "ROBOT[i]", "counterparty": "DISPATCHER", "trigger": "DISPATCHER -> ROBOT[i] : route_assignment", "until": null, "content": "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : ack(accepted)", "deadline_ms": 5000, "on_violation_severity": "Major", "on_violation_sanction": null, "on_violation_reparation": "report_failure", "on_violation_transition": null, "effects_activate": [], "effects_suspend": [], "effects_resume": [], "effects_discharge": [], "on_amendment": "carry_over", "transform_to": null } ], "counts_as": [ { "when": "DISPATCHER -> ROBOT[i] : replan_command", "creates": "reassignment", "if": null } ] } trigger, until, content, when, and if are kept as text, like the rules of E.7. The key if is written as if in the serialized IR, although a dataclass field cannot have that name in every host language. on_violation_severity is null when the whole on_violation: block is omitted and Major when the block is present without severity:. on_amendment is always filled in: carry_over, discharge, or transform; transform_to is the target of transform: and null otherwise. norms and counts_as are empty lists for a contract without them.

The reference implementation (cadl 0.3) implements norms 0.1 from cadl 0.3.19 as follows: cadl parses norms: and counts_as: and the temporal operators of F.4, applies rules N-1 to N-14 in cadl check (N-8, N-12, N-13, N-14, and the SHOULDs of N-3 and N-9 as warnings; N-13 and N-14 from cadl 0.3.23), and lowers both blocks to the IR of F.9. The SMT checks of cadl verify leave out assume: and guarantee: items that contain temporal operators and report each one as not checked (F.7). cadl codegen leaves the same items out of the contract code of every target, with a comment in the code and a warning; it does not translate temporal operators into the target languages. The Python target monitors them in a separate module (see below). A numeric deadline: of a norm is read as seconds, the lenient form that A.12 describes for lifecycle deadlines. cadl check looks for temporal operators in the places listed in F.4; it does not look inside violation.detect, incentives.rules, a protocol trigger:, or context.assumptions, which are text. From cadl 0.3.20, cadl norms-eval computes the norm states, verdicts, violations, institutional events, and unauthorised acts of F.5 for one contract instance from a recorded trace (JSON Lines, one observation per line; the format is described in the README of the cadl repository), and applies the amendments of F.6 that the trace names. It takes the lifecycle state from the trace and does not run the lifecycle state machine: a transition: requested by a violation is reported, not applied. Up to cadl 0.3.21 it matched the actor references of message events too widely: a range such as A[1..2] matched every actor named A[k], and A[*] and an unbound A[i] also matched actors outside the declared set. cadl 0.3.22 matches them by the table of F.3; verdicts computed for a file that uses such references in a trigger:, an until:, a content:, or a counts_as: rule SHOULD be computed again. It also tests the lower bound of a set with a symbolic upper bound. The time of a trace is a finite number of at most 253 in absolute value, so epoch seconds and epoch milliseconds are accepted. The actors and the name of a message of a trace are read as written: ROBOT[ 2 ], which 0.3.21 read as ROBOT[2], is a trace error. This is deliberate, because two spellings of one actor in a recorded trace defeat a check that compares names. It also ignores the observations after the end of the contract instance entirely: up to 0.3.21 it took the names of the observed quantities (F.5) also from them, so that such an observation could change a verdict. Up to cadl 0.3.22 a norm or item that contains a quantifier or an aggregate was not evaluated. From cadl 0.3.23 it evaluates them as F.5 defines ("Quantifiers and aggregates"); it enumerates at most 10 000 members of a closed domain and evaluates a larger one as an open domain, with a warning. A norm or item that contains a function call other than a temporal operator or sum, count, min, max, or avg of a comprehension, a wildcard or range reference outside the domain of a quantifier or a comprehension (ROBOT[*].battery), a quantifier or comprehension whose domain is not a set of actors or a range, x.q for a variable x over a range of integers, or a temporal operator inside a comprehension is not evaluated and stays pending, with the reason in the report. cadl norms-diff compares two versions of a file and reports what F.6 does to the norms of each contract, including every carried-over norm whose content or deadline: changes and a transform: target that the new version lacks. From cadl 0.3.22, cadl codegen -t python writes, for a file that declares norms: 0.1, a module norms_monitor.py into the generated package (Appendix D, D.1). It monitors one contract instance while the system runs: the host makes a monitor for the instance, passes it one observation at a time, and gets back the norm instances, guarantees, and assumptions whose state or verdict changed at that observation, with time and reason; it signals the end of the instance, and can ask for the current verdicts. The module contains the evaluation code of cadl norms-eval, copied verbatim, and the contracts of the file as data; it does not need cadl at run time, and for a recorded trace it gives the result of cadl norms-eval. As that command, it takes the lifecycle state from the observations and reports a transition: without applying it. It reads the points that F.4 and F.5 state for a processor that receives the observations one at a time as follows. A passed deadline and the end of an interval are detected at the next observation; the monitor tells the host the earliest time stamp at which an observation is certain to decide something that only waits for time (a little after the deadline or the end of the interval, since content at the deadline itself is in time; times are compared with a tolerance of 10-9 s). The host names the quantities that are written without an actor; a name it does not name is read as a symbolic value until its first value, which is the difference F.5 permits (cadl norms-eval takes the names from the observations of the instance in the trace). An observation after the end of the instance has no effect and is counted in a warning. An observation that is malformed, or whose amendment cannot be applied, is refused and leaves the monitor as it was. The monitor keeps the observations of the instance until it is dropped. An amendment (F.6) is applied when the host supplies the data of the monitor generated from the new version; the monitor cannot read a CADL file. Before cadl codegen writes the module it checks that the module compiles and that every name it uses is defined in it, and it refuses to generate otherwise. The Solidity, OPA, and Unity C# targets do not monitor norms, and translation of norms to a model checker for design-time checking is not implemented.

Files written against CADL v0.3 without this extension remain valid and are read the same way. A file that uses norms:, counts_as:, or the temporal operators without declaring norms: 0.1 does not conform to this appendix. A norms-aware processor reads within, throughout, and until in such a file as ordinary function names, does not interpret its norms: and counts_as: blocks (they are not checked and not lowered to the IR), and SHOULD report them as undeclared extension keys. Processors that do not implement the extension MUST NOT reject such files; they SHOULD emit a single informational diagnostic per file.

This appendix specifies the agent governance extension to CADL. It builds on the norms extension (Appendix F) and adds the key agent: to actor_def (A.3), the keys enforcement: and delegations: to contract_def (A.4), and the key on_denied: to norm_def (F.3). With them, the permissions and prohibitions of a contract determine, for every message that arrives at an enforcement point, one of three decisions: allow, deny, or escalate. The decision is made before the message takes effect, and it is a function of the message and of the state of the norm instances; no part of it is left to the judgement of an agent. The core language does not mandate these blocks; a conforming CADL processor that does not implement the extension MUST NOT reject a file because of the new keys. It SHOULD accept them syntactically and emit an informational diagnostic. The extension is named agents and this appendix describes version 0.1. It requires norms: 0.1: the norms are what is enforced. A file that uses it MUST declare both under extensions: (A.2); G.14 says what a processor does with an undeclared use. sos: ... extensions: - norms: 0.1 - agents: 0.1

LLM-based agents are becoming constituent systems of SoS, and the protocols that connect them are being standardised [MCP, 2026-07-28] [Linux Foundation, A2A 2025]. Enforcement is converging on deterministic checks at the tool-call boundary; for example, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Policy authorises tool calls with Cedar policies and denies by default [AWS, AgentCore Policy]. What is missing is the step from an organisational contract (who is allowed to do what, on whose authority) to such a check. Version 0.1 is a first step on four research directions of Section 9.8: RD-8.1, compiling contracts to boundary policies. Nothing in a CADL file says which actor is an agent, which message is a tool call, and what a generated policy has to decide (G.4, G.5, G.10). RD-8.2, provenance of delegated authority. A check that sees only the local state cannot tell whether an action reached the caller through delegations that its originator was not entitled to make. G.7 gives delegated permissions a provenance chain. RD-8.3, recovery after a blocked action. A preprint review reports a study in which blocking 94% of unsafe actions still left fewer than 5% of tasks completed safely and correctly [Dantas+, arXiv 2026]. G.6 defines escalation to a named actor and a fallback message. Part of RD-8.4, audit. Community governance has been found to be a layer missing above the protocols [Kang & Diponegoro, arXiv 2026], and a governance graph enforced with an append-only audit log constrained LLM agents where a prompt-only "constitution" did not [Bracale Syrnikov+, arXiv 2026]. G.8 fixes the format of an audit record. Scope of version 0.1. The extension is small on purpose. It has no primitives for membership, voting, or the preservation of dissent (RD-8.4 otherwise remains open, for a later version); it does not verify plans or the interaction of several agents (RD-8.5), since every decision concerns one message; it maps no article of any regulation to CADL; and it does not cover authentication: the sender and the receiver of a message are taken as given. At the boundary it considers only norms whose content is a message, and only the sender, the receiver, and the name of a message, not its arguments.

Concept Meaning in agents 0.1 Tool call A message whose receiver is an actor of kind tool_server and whose name is one of the tools: of that actor. Enforced contract A contract that has the key enforcement:. Only enforced contracts take part in decisions. Enforcement point The one logical place where the decision for a message is made, over all enforced contracts of the file. Decision allow, deny, or escalate, computed for one message by the decision function of G.5 before the message takes effect. Ground A prohibition that applies to a message in the decision function. For a hold, grounds are counted per contract instance: a ground of a hold is a prohibition in one contract instance in which it applies (G.6). Hold The record of a message whose decision is escalate; the message is kept back until the hold reaches a final state (G.6). Derived instance A permission held by a delegate (G.7), with its provenance chain: the actors from the bearer of the original permission to the holder, one link per delegation. Audit record What an enforcement point records for one decision (G.8). Norm, norm instance, contract instance, institutional event, and observation have the meaning of Appendix F.

The grammar uses the notation of Appendix A, which defines identifier, hyphen_name, actor_ref, int_literal, and duration_lit; message_event is defined in E.3 and norm_event in F.3. actor_def = ... , [ "agent:" , agent_binding ] ; agent_binding = "kind:" , agent_kind , [ "protocol:" , hyphen_name ] , [ "tools:" , { "-" , identifier } ] ; agent_kind = "llm_agent" | "tool_server" | "human" | "service" ; contract_def = ... , [ "enforcement:" , enforcement_block ] , [ "delegations:" , { "-" , delegation_def } ] ; enforcement_block = [ "default:" , ( "deny" | "allow" ) ] , [ "point:" , ( "caller" | "receiver" | "gateway" ) ] ; norm_def = ... , [ "on_denied:" , denial_recovery ] ; denial_recovery = [ "escalate_to:" , actor_ref ] , [ "timeout:" , duration_lit ] , [ "fallback:" , message_event ] , (* string *) [ "notify:" , actor_ref ] ; delegation_def = "norm:" , identifier , "to:" , { "-" , actor_ref } , "grant:" , identifier , [ "revoke:" , identifier ] , [ "max_depth:" , int_literal ] , [ "until:" , norm_event ] ; (* string *) An actor without agent: has no agent kind. The kind tool_server defines tool calls (G.4); llm_agent, human, and service have no meaning beyond the static rule that names one of them (G-8) and the use generators make of them. protocol: (mcp, a2a, or another name) has no default and no effect on decisions. An agent: on an actor declared with a range applies to every actor of the set. A tool name is an identifier, because it is the message name of a message_event. Where the protocol-level name is not an identifier, the mappings: of a codegen: entry (A.9) relates the two. A contract is enforced when it has the key enforcement:; an empty mapping or a null value (enforcement: {}, or the bare key) means "enforced with all defaults". When default: is omitted, the default decision is deny for a tool call and allow for every other message; when given, it applies to both (G.5). point: (default gateway) is a deployment hint for generators and has no effect on the decision. Whatever the deployment, there is one logical enforcement point: every governed message is decided once, over all enforced contracts, on one state. on_denied: is allowed only on a prohibition. timeout: has no default. fallback: and notify: are data: they are copied into the result of the decision (G.10) and have no other effect. max_depth: defaults to 1. Without revoke: a delegation cannot be revoked by a message; without until: it has no end of its own. Keys added, by block: actor — agent (kind protocol tools); contract — enforcement (default point), delegations (norm to grant revoke max_depth until); norm — on_denied (escalate_to timeout fallback notify). In an enforced contract the names approval and rejection are reserved for the institutional events of G.6.
documents.s: G.3 Syntax (EBNF additions to A.3, A.4, and F.3)

documents.t: A message has a sender and a receiver, each one concrete actor, a name, and arguments. It is a tool call when its receiver has agent.kind: tool_server and its name is one of that actor's tools:; a message to a tool server with any other name is a call of an undeclared tool; every other message is an ordinary message. The result that a tool server returns is not a separate message in version 0.1. At the boundary, a message_event S -> R : e is matched against a message on three components: the sender, the receiver, and the message name (the identifier of e, or the name of the call). Arguments written in e are not considered in version 0.1: delete_file and delete_file(path) match the same messages. Each component is true, false, or unknown, and the match is their Kleene conjunction: false when any component is false, otherwise unknown when any is unknown, otherwise true. An actor reference matches a concrete actor as follows: Reference Matches A the actor A, declared without index; never an indexed member A[k] A[3], A[*], A[1..3] A[3]; every member of the set A; A[1] to A[3] A[1..N] (symbolic bound) every member of the set A; the bounds are not compared A[i] false when the concrete actor is not a member of A. Otherwise: exactly A[v] when the contract instance binds i to v, and unknown when it binds no value to i. The table is that of F.3, which the norms engine uses for the events of a trace, with two differences. First, F.3 compares the arguments written in a message event with those of the message, and the boundary does not consider arguments. Second, where the contract instance binds no value to i, F.3 lets A[i] match every member of the set, and at the boundary the match is unknown and is resolved fail-closed (G.5). The second difference also holds for the events of an enforced contract that the norms engine evaluates, and for the performer of a power (G.5, "Unknown occurrences"). A[k] is a member of the set A when A is declared with a range and k lies within its integer bounds (a set declared as A[1..3] does not contain A[7]); when the declared upper bound is symbolic, every index from the lower bound on is a member.

For an enforced contract without host-created instances, the single instance of F.5 exists from the start of the enforcement point, not from the first observation; this addition to F.5 lets the first message be decided. When a host application creates and ends the instances, the running instances are those it has created and not ended. Whether an enforced contract governs a message m is decided before any instance is considered, so no binding is applied to parties:: a party A[i] or A[*] matches every member of A. A message whose receiver is a tool server (a tool call or a call of an undeclared tool) is governed by every enforced contract of which that tool server is a party, whatever its sender: a party, a declared actor that is not a party, or an undeclared actor. Steps 2 to 4 below therefore apply to outsiders too. When a tool server is a party of several enforced contracts, each of them governs every call to it, and a call that one of them does not allow is denied (step 4): contracts that share a tool server each have to permit the calls they intend. An ordinary message is governed by an enforced contract when its sender and its receiver each match a party. A norm still applies only to its bearer or to a valid holder (below). The enforcement point decides the messages one at a time, in the order in which they arrive, each on the state left by all earlier observations, and the decision MUST be deterministic. A decision never depends on a later observation. This holds also for the reading of a bare name in a predicate as a quantity or as a symbolic value (F.5): an enforcement point that is given the quantity names uses them from the start, and one that is not takes a name as a quantity from the first observation on that gives it a value, never earlier. Only a permission or a prohibition whose content: is a message_event takes part in a decision. One whose content is a predicate, a tpredicate with temporal operators, or an institutional event has no effect at the boundary in version 0.1 and is monitored under Appendix F only. Obligations and powers do not take part: the message that an obligation requires, or by which a power is exercised, is decided like any other, and F.5, item 7 is unchanged. A norm instance takes part while it is in force at the boundary. The flag is an addition to F.5; the states and verdicts of F.5 are unchanged. A permission is in force while its instance is active. A prohibition is in force while its instance is active. When the instance becomes violated, the prohibition stays in force: the violation is reported once (F.5) but does not lift the prohibition. It then stays in force until the first of: the time at which its deadline: window would have closed; the occurrence of its until:; a discharge effect of a power that names it; an amendment under which it is not carried over (F.6); the end of the contract instance. suspend and resume effects that name it put it out of force and back, also after a violation. A norm instance in force applies to m when its content matches m (G.4) and the sender of m is its bearer. A derived instance of a permission (G.7) applies when it is valid and the content matches with the holder as sender. The result is unknown when the match is unknown or the enforcement point does not have the flag. Unknown is resolved fail-closed: an unknown prohibition applies, an unknown permission does not. Missing data. The enforcement point also does not have the flag when it cannot determine it because a quantity has no value yet. This concerns the trigger: of a prohibition that is inactive and the until: of a permission that is active, in two forms. Directly: while that trigger: or until: is a predicate that is undefined (F.5), the flag is unknown. Through an institutional event: while it is an event that a counts_as: rule creates from a predicate when:, and the when: or the if: of such a rule is undefined, the flag is unknown; with several rules for the event, as long as one of them is undefined. A quantified predicate or aggregate over an open domain (F.5, "Quantifiers and aggregates") that the known members do not decide is undefined in this sense: the members not yet named are the missing data. While its domain is open, a prohibition whose trigger: is exists x in A: p therefore always applies: as missing data until a known member makes p true, and from then on as long as it is in force, which ends by its until: or otherwise as G.5 describes above. A permission whose until: is for all x in A: p applies only while a known member makes p false. Where such a predicate governs the boundary, the contract instance SHOULD give the bound of the set a value (F.5). An unknown prohibition applies and an unknown permission does not. Nothing is latched: the state of the norm instance and its verdict are those of F.5, where an undefined predicate does not occur; as soon as the predicates have values, the flag is the one of the state again. Two cases need no rule, because F.5 already blocks: an undefined trigger: does not activate a permission, and an undefined until: does not end a prohibition. A processor SHOULD warn when it decides a message on a flag that is unknown for this reason. The consequence at the start is intended: a message that arrives before the quantities of such a predicate have their first values is denied or escalated. One case is not covered. A rule with a message when: and an if: creates its event at the moment of that message or never. When the message arrives while the if: is undefined, no event is created (F.5); that blocks where the event would let a message through, but where the event would bring a prohibition into force or end a permission, the boundary does not block, and there is no later moment at which the flag could be corrected without inventing a state that F.5 does not have. G-19 warns about such a contract, and a processor SHOULD warn when it observes such a message. Unknown occurrences. G-18 requires every index variable of an enforced contract to be the index of a party, and a contract instance binds the indices of its parties (F.2). A processor that creates the instances itself MUST refuse an instance of an enforced contract that does not bind every index variable of its parties:. So no index is unbound in a conforming run. The following rule is a second line of defence for a processor that is handed such an instance all the same. Where the occurrence of an event of an enforced contract, the value of one of its predicates, or the identity of the performer of an act depends on an index that the contract instance does not bind, it is unknown, and unknown is resolved fail-closed by what the occurrence would do: an unknown occurrence never has an effect that lets a message through (it does not activate or resume a permission, end, suspend, or discharge a prohibition, create an institutional event, exercise a power, or fulfil an obligation), and it always has the effects that block (it activates a prohibition and ends a permission or a derived instance). There is one exception to "always blocks": a power is the act of a determined party, so a performer who is unknown exercises no power, also when the effects of the power would block (activate a prohibition, suspend or discharge a permission). The exception cannot arise in a processor that refuses instances without bindings. A processor SHOULD warn. Grant and revoke messages name no index variable (G-11, G-12) and are never unknown. The requirement to refuse an instance is on a processor that creates contract instances. The policy input of G.10 is a description of instances that a caller supplies, and it may describe an instance that binds nothing, as it does when the field instances is absent; the decision function then takes every match that depends on the index as unknown (G.4) and resolves it fail-closed as above. The two do not conflict: the decision for such an input is defined, and a conforming runtime does not produce such an input.
documents.s: Instances, governed messages, and norms that take part

documents.t: For a message m, the following steps give a result (fields in G.10), in this order. Ungoverned. If no enforced contract governs m: allow, reason ungoverned. This appendix does not restrict such a message. Undeclared tool. If m is a call of an undeclared tool: deny, reason undeclared_tool. Per contract. Each governing contract C decides, over all its running instances: If C has no running instance: deny, reason no_instance, when m is a tool call; otherwise as in step 3.4. If prohibitions of C apply to m, they are the grounds and the reason is prohibition. C decides escalate when every ground has an on_denied.escalate_to, all name the same actor, and that actor is not the sender of m; otherwise deny. An escalate_to: A[i] is resolved with the bindings of each instance in which the ground applies; an unbound index, or different actors in different instances, gives deny. Otherwise, if a permission of C, original or derived, applies to m: allow, reason permission. Otherwise the default: of C or, when it is omitted, deny if m is a tool call and allow if not; reason default. Combination (deny overrides). If some contract decides deny, the decision is deny. Otherwise, if some contract decides escalate, the decision is escalate when all escalating contracts name the same actor and deny when they do not (a hold has a single approver). Otherwise it is allow. The determining contracts are those that decided deny; if none, those that decided escalate; if none, all governing contracts. The reason of the result is, for deny and escalate, the first of no_instance, prohibition, default that a determining contract has; for allow, permission if a contract has it, else default. The result lists the grounds or applying permissions of the determining contracts and, whenever the reason is prohibition (for deny as well as for escalate), the fallback and notify of those grounds and the smallest timeout: among them. It follows that within a contract a prohibition overrides a permission (N-12 still warns), that a message governed by two enforced contracts has to be allowed by both, that a prohibition without escalate_to: is never escalated, and that an actor cannot approve its own message. The default differs by kind of message for a reason. Tools are enumerated and a tool call acts outside the contract, so a closed policy can be reviewed tool by tool; it is also the default of the enforcement cited in G.1. Ordinary messages include the coordination messages on which protocols, lifecycles, and triggers rely; a contract written for norms 0.1 has no permissions for them, and deny would stop them all. default: deny closes the policy for them too.

allow. The message takes effect and becomes an observation, with the time of the decision as its time stamp, for the instances of the enforced contracts that govern it. An instance of an enforced contract observes a message only when its contract governs the message: a message that no enforced contract governs (step 1) is an observation for no enforced contract, and a message that one enforced contract governs is no observation for another that does not. So a message cannot trigger, end, or fulfil a norm of an enforced contract, or create an institutional event in it, without having been decided by that contract. It follows that a message event of an enforced contract whose sender or receiver is not a party could never occur: a prohibition with such a trigger: would never come into force, and a permission with such an until: would never end. G-17 therefore makes such an event an error. Contracts that are not enforced keep F.5 unchanged. deny. The message does not take effect and is not an observation: it triggers no norm, creates no institutional event, fires no lifecycle transition, fulfils no obligation, and violates no prohibition. The enforcement point SHOULD return the result to the sender. escalate. The message is held (G.6); while held it is not an observation. The deadlines of Appendix F keep running while a message is denied or held. Before a message is decided, the enforcement point observes the time of the decision: an observation that carries no message, at which F.5 settles every deadline and every window that has passed. A decision therefore never rests on a prohibition whose window closed, or on an obligation whose deadline passed, before the time of the decision. A denied trigger: message does not activate its norm. As an addition to the verdicts of F.5, a violated obligation has the verdict excused when, between its activation and the violation, a message of its bearer that matches its content was denied with the obligation's own contract among the determining contracts, or was held on a ground of that contract and not released before the violation: the contract itself prevented the fulfilment. Its on_violation: still applies, as for every excused norm.
documents.s: Effect of a decision on the trace

documents.t: on_denied: on a prohibition says what follows when that prohibition is a ground. fallback: names a message the sender could send instead and notify: an actor to be informed; both are only copied into the result. A fallback gives no permission: when sent, it is decided like any other message. escalate_to: and timeout: define holds. When the decision is escalate, the enforcement point creates a hold with a hold_id unique within the enforcement point, the message, the time of the decision, the grounds, the approver, and a deadline (the time of the decision plus the timeout of the result, or none). A ground of a hold is a prohibition in one contract instance in which it applies to the message. The grounds of a hold are all of them, over all governing contracts, and their contract instances are the contract instances of the grounds. A prohibition that applies in two contract instances is two grounds. A hold without deadline in a contract instance that never ends is held for ever. How the hold id reaches the approver depends on the protocol. State Entered when Closing record (G.8) held the hold is created; the only state that is not final — approved the approver approves; the message is released allow, reason approved (or the denial of the release) rejected the approver rejects deny, reason rejected expired the deadline has passed deny, reason expired, with the deadline as time cancelled a contract instance of a ground ends, or a contract of a ground is amended deny, reason cancelled The approver acts through two institutional events, approval and rejection, each created by a counts_as: rule from a message of the approver (G-9), for example when: "OPERATOR -> PLANNER : approve", creates: approval. As an extension of F.5, where institutional events "exist only as events", these two carry one value, the hold id: the first argument of the message that created them. This is the only use of a message argument in version 0.1. The approver's message is itself governed and decided by G.5. The order of steps within one observation (F.5) is extended: After step 1: an approval (rejection) whose hold id names a held hold, whose performer (F.5, item 7) is the approver of that hold, and which was created in a contract instance of a ground of the hold makes it approved (rejected). When the hold has several contract instances of grounds, one such event is enough; an event that one message creates in several contract instances is one event. Any other approval or rejection changes no hold and SHOULD be recorded as unauthorised. Then the grants, revocations, and until: events of G.7 are applied. In step 6: when a contract instance ends, the held holds with a ground in it become cancelled, before its norms are settled. After step 6: each hold that became approved at this observation is released, in the order of creation. Release. The message is decided again, on the current state and at the time of the approving observation. The approval stands in for the permission and for the grounds, and for nothing else: If the message is now a call of an undeclared tool: deny, reason undeclared_tool. A governing contract that has a ground of the hold denies with the reason no_instance when a contract instance of one of its grounds is no longer running, and with the reason prohibition when one of its prohibitions applies in a contract instance in which it is not a ground of the hold (norms lists these prohibitions). This includes a prohibition of the grounds that now applies in another contract instance, for example one created after the hold. Otherwise the contract allows: it tests neither a permission nor its default. This is so also when a prohibition of the grounds is no longer in force at the time of the approval, for example after its until:: the approval stands in for the permission in that contract, and the message is released. The reason no_instance arises only when the approving observation itself ends that contract instance (step 6); an instance that ended earlier has cancelled the hold. The reference runtime does not reach it, because there the end of an instance is an observation of its own (G.13). Every other governing contract decides in full by step 3 of G.5 and has to allow, by a permission, original or derived and valid now, or by its default. A contract that would decide escalate denies, with the reason prohibition. If no contract denies, the message is released. Otherwise the release is denied; the result is formed as in step 4 of G.5 from the contracts that deny: contracts lists them, the reason is the first of no_instance, prohibition, default among them, and for prohibition the norms, timeout, fallback, and notify are those of G.10. escalate_to is null. A denial of the release is final: it creates no hold, and the hold stays approved. With these rules a release keeps what G.5 and G.7 state for every other message: a message governed by two enforced contracts is allowed by both, and no actor acts on an authority that its originator no longer has. A delegation revoked, a contract instance ended, or a contract amended between the hold and the approval in a contract without a ground therefore denies the release. If the message is released, it takes effect as the immediately following observation, with the time stamp of the approving observation, before any other message is decided. As an addition to F.5, item 3, it is not an occurrence of the content of a prohibition in a contract instance in which that prohibition is a ground of the hold: an approved exception does not violate its grounds. An approval releases one message; a later message with the same sender, receiver, and name is decided again. Hold identifiers. An approval or a rejection names a hold by its identifier and by nothing else. An identifier need not be unpredictable: what protects a hold is that only its approver can close it, through a message that the contract governs, and not the secrecy of the identifier. An approver's message that is itself held and released later applies to the hold that has the identifier when that message is released; if that hold is no longer held, it changes nothing and is recorded as unauthorised. Expiry. Before each decision and each observation whose time is later than the deadline of a held hold, that hold becomes expired. Holds that expire together do so in the order of their deadlines, and of their creation when the deadlines are equal. An approval at exactly the deadline is in time.

An entry of delegations: makes one permission delegable: norm: names it, to: lists the actors that may hold a derived instance at any depth, grant: and revoke: name the messages that delegate and revoke, max_depth: is the largest number of links in a chain, and until: is an event that ends every derived instance of the entry. Only a permission whose content is a message_event can be delegated in version 0.1; a power cannot. A derived instance is a permission with the same content, read with its holder as sender, in one contract instance. Its provenance chain is a0, …, an: a0 is the bearer of the original permission, an the holder, and each pair of neighbours a link made by one grant; the chain of the bearer is a0 alone. A derived instance is active or discharged (final). Derived instances are an addition to Appendix F, which has one instance per norm; there is at most one active derived instance per norm, holder, and contract instance, so every holder has one chain. A derived instance is valid when the original permission is in force (G.5), the derived instance is active, its chain has at most max_depth links, and every actor of the chain after the first matches a reference in to:. While the original is suspended, its derived instances are not valid. Grant. A message X -> Y : g, where g is the grant: name of an entry of a contract that governs it, is decided by G.5 like any other message. When it is observed, these conditions are tested in each running instance of the contract: X is the bearer and the permission is in force, or X holds a valid derived instance; Y matches a reference in to:; Y does not occur in the chain of X; the chain of X has fewer than max_depth links; Y holds no active derived instance of the permission. If all hold, a derived instance is created for Y, with the chain of X followed by Y. If 1 to 4 hold and 5 fails, the grant is a no-op. If one of 1 to 4 fails, the grant has no effect and SHOULD be recorded as unauthorised. The granter keeps its instance: delegation shares authority and does not transfer it. End. A derived instance becomes discharged when (a) a message X -> Y : r with the revoke: name of the entry is observed and X occurs before Y in the chain of Y: the instance of Y and every derived instance in whose chain Y occurs are discharged; (b) the until: of the entry occurs, as for the until: of a norm: the derived instances that are active at that observation are discharged, and the entry stays delegable; (c) the original permission becomes discharged or the contract instance ends. A revoke message that does not satisfy (a) has no effect. A discharged instance is not revived; a new grant creates a new one. Because validity is computed from the whole chain, an actor cannot obtain through intermediaries an authority that its originator did not have or no longer has: a grant by an actor without a valid instance creates nothing, a chain is never longer than the contract allows, and revoking one link ends everything derived through it. Amendments. F.6 governs the norm instances of an amended contract. This appendix adds two rules: when a new version of an enforced contract takes effect, (1) every held hold with a ground in that contract becomes cancelled, and (2) the validity of every derived instance is tested against the new version; an instance whose permission has no delegations: entry there, or whose original was discharged by the amendment, is discharged.

An enforcement point SHOULD record every decision and SHOULD keep the records append-only. Recording is a recommendation; the format is normative. An audit record is the result of the decision (G.10) with five more fields: Field Content time The time of the decision, on the clock of the trace. message from, to, and name, as in the policy input. instances The running instances of the governing contracts: contract id and an identifier of the instance. In a closing record: the contract instances of the grounds of the hold, whether they are still running or not. hold_id For an escalate decision and for the record that closes the hold; otherwise null. The identifier is unique within the enforcement point and need not be unpredictable (G.6). outcome In the record that closes a hold, its final state; otherwise null. An escalate decision gives two records with the same hold_id: one when the hold is created and a closing record when it reaches a final state (table of G.6). The closing record keeps the contracts, norms, and escalate_to of the hold; when its reason is rejected, expired, or cancelled, it also keeps the fallback and notify of the hold, so that the sender finds them in the denial. Its timeout is null. When the release is denied (G.6), the closing record has the result of that denial instead, and its outcome is approved. The time of a closing record is the time of the observation that closed the hold, except for expired, where it is the deadline; such a record is written when the expiry is found, before the next decision or observation, so the times of a log never decrease. A denial or an escalation that rests on a flag that is unknown (G.5) has the reason prohibition and lists the norm in norms, like any other. What distinguishes it is in the policy input of the decision, where the flag is absent from in_force, and in the warning of the processor. The remedy of the sender differs: for missing data it is to wait for the data, not to ask the approver. Grants, revocations, and acts recorded as unauthorised SHOULD be written to the same log, as event records, and so SHOULD every other change of the state on which later decisions rest: the end of a derived instance for any cause, the start and the end of a contract instance, and an amendment. An event record has no result; it has the field event in place of decision, and these fields: Field Content time, message As in an audit record: the observation and the message that the event comes from; message is null when there is none. event grant, revoke, delegation_end (a derived instance ended for another cause than a revoke message; one record per derived instance), instance_start, instance_end, amendment, unauthorised_grant, unauthorised_approval, unauthorised_rejection, or unauthorised_act (an act that F.5, item 7 records as unauthorised). instances The contract instance or instances in which the event took place; for amendment, the running instances of the amended contracts. norm For a grant, a revocation, or a delegation_end, the delegable permission as <contract id>.<norm id>; otherwise null. chain For a grant, the chain of the derived instance of the receiver; for a revoke that has an effect, the chain of the revoked instance; for a delegation_end, the chain of the instance that ended; otherwise null. holders The holders whose derived instance the event created or discharged, in the order of creation; otherwise empty. hold_id For an unauthorised approval or rejection, the hold id it carried, if any; otherwise null. reason null for a grant or a revocation that has an effect; holder_exists for a grant that is a no-op (condition 5 of G.7); no_effect for a revoke message that does not satisfy (a); for unauthorised_grant the first condition that fails: no_authority (1), not_in_to (2), in_chain (3), max_depth (4); for an unauthorised approval or rejection unknown_hold, not_held, not_approver, or other_instance (not created in a contract instance of a ground); for unauthorised_act, no_power; for delegation_end the cause: until, original_discharged, instance_end, or amendment; for instance_end, end or terminal_state; for amendment, the name of the new version; for instance_start, null. Records are written in the order in which the enforcement point produces them: the record of a decision, then the event records of the observation that the message becomes, then the closing records of the holds that this observation approved or rejected. A change of the in-force flag of a norm has no record of its own: it follows from the recorded messages, from the times, and from the values that the predicates of the contract read. This appendix defines no integrity protection for the log, such as a hash chain or a signature; a deployment that needs one adds it outside the record.

An agents-aware processor MUST, in addition to the checks of Appendix F: G-1. A file that declares agents: 0.1 MUST also declare norms: 0.1; otherwise the processor reports an error and does not interpret the keys of this extension. G-2. An agent: mapping MUST have kind:, one of llm_agent, tool_server, human, service; protocol: MUST be a hyphen_name. G-3. tools: is allowed only for a tool_server, which MUST list at least one tool. A tool name MUST be an identifier, not a reserved word, and unique within its actor. (Under a YAML 1.1 loader an unquoted yes, no, on, off, true, false, or null is not a name; see A.12.) G-4. When the receiver of a message_event is a tool server, the message name MUST be one of its tools:. This applies to the trigger:, until:, and content: of a norm, the when: of a counts_as: rule, the on: of a lifecycle transition, and a fallback:. A processor SHOULD warn about a message step of a protocol (A.5) that does not satisfy it. G-5. enforcement.default MUST be deny or allow, and enforcement.point one of caller, receiver, gateway. A null or empty enforcement: is valid. G-6. In an enforced contract, the sender of the message_event content of a permission or a prohibition MUST be textually equal to its bearer:. G-7. on_denied: is allowed only on a prohibition whose content is a message_event, in an enforced contract, and MUST have at least one key. timeout: MUST be a duration_lit greater than zero and requires escalate_to:. A processor SHOULD warn about an escalate_to: without timeout:. G-8. escalate_to: and notify: MUST name single declared actors (as N-3). escalate_to: MUST name a party of the contract, so that its messages are governed, MUST NOT be textually equal to the bearer: of its prohibition, and SHOULD have agent.kind: human. G-9. A contract with an escalate_to: A MUST have a counts_as: rule that creates approval from a message_event whose sender is A, and SHOULD have one for rejection. In an enforced contract, every rule that creates approval or rejection MUST have as when: a message_event whose sender is the escalate_to: of a prohibition of the contract, and no norm id may equal either name; these are the only uses that are errors. By G-17 the sender and the receiver of that message_event are parties of the contract, so the contract governs the approver's message and its instances observe it. A reference to the two events in a trigger:, until:, or content: is allowed. G-10. A fallback: MUST be a message_event whose sender is textually equal to the bearer: of its prohibition and whose receiver is a declared actor, and MUST differ from the content of the prohibition in receiver or message name. G-11. delegations: is allowed only in an enforced contract. norm: MUST be the id of a permission of the contract whose content is a message_event; at most one entry may name a norm. The bearer: of that permission MUST NOT have an index bound by the contract instance (ROBOT[i]), so that the first actor of every chain can be read from the file. G-12. to: MUST list at least one reference, each naming declared actors; a wildcard or a range is allowed, an index bound by the contract instance is not. to: MUST NOT name a tool server and SHOULD NOT include the bearer. max_depth: MUST be an integer of at least 1. until: MUST satisfy the rules of Appendix F for the until: of a norm (N-9, N-10). G-13. grant: and revoke: MUST be identifiers and not reserved words. Within a contract, all grant: and revoke: names MUST differ from each other and from approval and rejection, and none may be a tool of a tool server that is a party. (The YAML 1.1 note of G-3 applies.) G-14. A processor SHOULD warn, in an enforced contract, about a permission or prohibition (a) whose content is not a message_event, because it has no effect at the boundary, or (b) whose message_event content has arguments, because they are not considered. G-15. A processor SHOULD warn about (a) a tool of a party of an enforced contract with default: allow that no permission or prohibition of the contract covers, and (b) a tool server that is a party of no enforced contract, whose tool calls are ungoverned. A norm covers a message when its message_event content has that receiver and message name. G-16. A processor SHOULD warn about a message that a contract needs and would itself deny: (a) the content of an obligation, or a fallback:, that a prohibition without trigger: whose bearer is the sender of that message covers, or that is a tool call covered by no permission of its sender while the default for tool calls is deny; a message that the sender could send only through a derived permission still gets the warning, because delegations are runtime state; (b) under default: deny, a grant: or revoke: name, or the when: message of a rule that creates approval or rejection, that no permission covers. G-17. In an enforced contract, the sender and the receiver of every message_event of the contract MUST be covered by the parties and MUST name declared members only: the trigger:, until:, and content: of its norms, the when: of its counts_as: rules, and the until: of its delegations. A reference is covered when one reference in parties: matches every actor that it can name (G.5): A by a party A; A[3] by a party A[3], A[i], A[*], or a range that contains 3; A[1..3] by a party A[i], A[*], or a range that contains it; A[*] and A[i] by a party A[i] or A[*], or by a party range that contains the whole declared set. Two party references are not combined: the parties A[1..2] and A[3] do not cover A[1..3]. A literal index or a range MUST lie within the declared set: for a set declared as A[1..3], A[7] and A[2..5] are errors. An instance of an enforced contract observes only the messages that the contract governs (G.5), so an event that is not covered, or that names no declared member, could never occur for some or all of the actors it names. The receiver of a tool call is included: G-4 requires the tool, and this rule that the tool server is a party. So is its sender: a contract cannot make the tool call of an actor that is not a party the content or the event of a norm. Such a call to a tool server that is a party is governed all the same (G.5); it is decided by the default of the contract and by the norms written for parties, and that is intended. A fallback: is not included: it is data for the sender and no event of the contract, G-10 requires its receiver only to be declared, and a fallback sent to an actor that is not a party is not governed by this contract. G-18. In an enforced contract, every index variable MUST be bound. An index variable is a name that is used as an index or inside an index expression (j in ROBOT[j], in ROBOT[j+1], and in ROBOT[SLOT[j].next]). There are three binders: a reference in parties: binds its index variable for the whole contract (i for a party ROBOT[i]); a quantifier binds its variable within its predicate (exists j in ROBOT: ROBOT[j].battery < 20, A.10); and a comprehension binds its variable within its element (sum(ROBOT[j].load for j in ROBOT), A.10). Every other index variable is an error, wherever an expression of the contract can stand: in the bearer: and the counterparty: of a norm; in escalate_to:, notify:, and the sender and receiver of a fallback:; in the sender, the receiver, and the arguments of every message_event that G-17 names, including the content: of a norm of any kind; and in every predicate of the contract, which are the trigger:, until:, and content: of its norms, the when: and if: of its counts_as: rules, the until: of its delegations, and its assume: and guarantee: items. The contract instance binds the index variables of its parties (F.2) and no others; a variable without a binder has no value that the file accounts for: by F.3 an event or a power with such a variable would hold for every member of the set, and a predicate with it would read a quantity that no actor has. That a quantifier binds its variable makes the predicate valid; whether a processor can evaluate it is a separate matter (G.13). G-19. A processor SHOULD warn, in an enforced contract, about an institutional event that a counts_as: rule creates under an if: and that is the trigger: of a prohibition or the until: of a permission. When the when: of the rule is a message that arrives while the if: is undefined, the event is not created and the boundary does not block (G.5, "Missing data"). The MUST rules are errors; the SHOULD rules are warnings and leave the file valid. N-1 to N-12 of Appendix F apply unchanged.

Two code targets generate a boundary policy from the enforced contracts of a file. They are listed in Appendix D in the category Boundary policy: agent-rego emits Rego [Open Policy Agent] and is independent of the opa target, which emits one policy per contract from other parts of the contract; agent-cedar emits Cedar policies [AWS, AgentCore Policy]. The syntax of the policies and the layout of the files belong to the targets. // policy input { "message": { "from": "SUMMARIZER", "to": "FILES", "name": "read_file" }, "now": "2026-11-10T09:00:05Z", "instances": [ { "contract": "ASSISTED_REPORTING", "instance": "default", "bindings": {}, "in_force": {}, "derived": [ { "norm": "may_read", "holder": "SUMMARIZER", "chain": ["OPERATOR", "PLANNER", "SUMMARIZER"] } ] } ] } // result { "decision": "allow", "reason": "permission", "contracts": ["ASSISTED_REPORTING"], "norms": ["ASSISTED_REPORTING.may_read"], "provenance": [["OPERATOR", "PLANNER", "SUMMARIZER"]], "escalate_to": null, "timeout": null, "fallback": [], "notify": [] } Input: message (required): from and to are concrete actors written as in the file (PLANNER, ROBOT[2]); name is the message name. Arguments are not part of the input. now (optional): the time of the decision; it does not influence the decision. instances (optional): every running instance of every enforced contract; a contract without an entry has no running instance. When the field is absent, the policy assumes one running instance of each enforced contract, with no index bound and no derived instance; a match that depends on an index is then unknown (G.4, and G.5 for the relation to the instances a runtime creates). Per instance: bindings maps index names to integers; in_force maps the id of each norm that is not static (below) to true or false, and a missing entry is unknown; derived lists the derived instances that the runtime found valid by G.7, with their chains. A derived entry is re-checked fail-closed. It applies only if its norm is a delegable permission of that contract, the holder is the sender of the message and the last element of the chain, the chain has at most max_depth links, its first element matches the bearer and every later one a reference in to:, and the original permission is in force (static, or flag true; a missing flag does not count). Any other entry is ignored. For an input that does not have this form no decision is defined: a processor reports an error, and a generated policy denies. Result: decision: allow, deny, or escalate. reason: one of ungoverned, undeclared_tool, no_instance, prohibition, permission, default; in a closing record (G.6) also approved, rejected, expired, cancelled. contracts: the ids of the determining contracts (G.5); empty for ungoverned and undeclared_tool. norms: the grounds (reason prohibition) or the applying permissions (reason permission) of the determining contracts, each as <contract id>.<norm id>, each once, in the order of declaration; empty for the other reasons. provenance: the chains of the applying derived instances, in the order of their norms and then of the input, without duplicates; empty when only original permissions applied. escalate_to: the approver for escalate and in a closing record that keeps it (G.8), as a concrete actor; otherwise null. timeout (milliseconds), fallback (message events as text), and notify (actor references) are filled whenever the reason is prohibition, for deny as well as for escalate, from the grounds, without duplicates, in the order of declaration; for every other reason they are null, [], and [], except that a closing record with the reason rejected, expired, or cancelled keeps the fallback and notify of its hold (G.8). A norm is static when it is a permission or a prohibition whose content is a message_event, it has no trigger:, until:, or deadline:, no power names it in effects:, no norm names it as reparation:, and no actor reference of the norm has an index bound by the contract instance: its bearer, counterparty, and content, its escalate_to and notify, and the sender and receiver of its fallback. By G.5 a static norm is in force in every running instance from its start to its end, so the input carries no flag for it. A policy is generated for one version of the contracts; an amendment requires a new policy. A generated policy MUST return, for every input, the same decision as the decision function of G.5, with static norms taken as in force, the other flags and the derived instances taken from the input, and everything the input does not supply taken as unknown. A target whose policy language has only two outcomes returns deny where G.5 gives escalate. The other result fields MAY be produced by the policy or by the runtime, from a table that the generator emits beside the policy (per prohibition: escalate_to, timeout, fallback, notify). A generator MUST list in the generated artifact, as needing runtime state, each permission or prohibition with a message content that is not static, and separately, as having no effect at the boundary, each permission or prohibition with another content; norms of other kinds are not listed. Holds, release, and the bookkeeping of delegations (G.6, G.7) belong to the runtime, not to the policy. For the example of G.12 with only message in the input (informative): message Result PLANNER -> TICKETS : search_tickets allow, permission, may_search (static permission) PLANNER -> FILES : delete_file escalate to OPERATOR, prohibition, no_delete PLANNER -> FILES : format_disk deny, undeclared_tool SUMMARIZER -> FILES : read_file deny, default; with the derived entry shown above, allow, permission Cedar mapping (informative). In Cedar [Cutler+, OOPSLA 2024] a request is denied unless a permit policy is satisfied, a satisfied forbid policy overrides every permit, and a policy whose evaluation raises an error is skipped. Undeclared tools and prohibitions therefore become forbid policies, permissions permit policies, and the default for tool calls is the default denial of the language; escalate is returned as a denial and resolved by the runtime from the emitted table. Because an erroring forbid policy would be skipped and so would not deny, a generated policy must not raise an error on any input of the schema above: it tests the presence of every optional attribute before reading it. Messages that G.5 allows without a permission (ungoverned messages, a contract whose default is allow) need explicit permit policies, and with more than one enforced contract, deny-overrides across contracts needs an additional forbid policy per contract for what that contract does not allow. From the Cedar answer alone, a denial by such a policy or by the language default cannot be told apart from "a non-static or derived permission might allow"; the Cedar target therefore covers static norms only, and the runtime decides the rest.

The decision function does not depend on a protocol. The table gives the intended correspondence; nothing normative depends on it. CADL (agents 0.1) MCP [MCP, 2026-07-28] A2A [Linux Foundation, A2A 2025] (to be confirmed) kind: tool_server; tool; tool call An MCP server; a tool of it; a request to call the tool — kind: llm_agent An MCP client, when it calls tools An A2A agent Ordinary message between agents — A message from one agent to another point: gateway A gateway in front of the server; the specification requires the headers Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name so that gateways can route and meter requests without parsing their bodies An intermediary between the agents escalate_to:, hold id Outside the protocol Outside the protocol

A human operator asks an LLM planner to prepare a report. The planner calls the tools of two tool servers and uses a sub-agent to summarise files.
