The file satisfies every rule of this appendix and N-1 to N-12 of Appendix F. sos: name: "AssistedReporting" extensions: - norms: 0.1 - agents: 0.1 actors: - id: OPERATOR role: "Human operator who owns the task and the files" agent: { kind: human } - id: PLANNER role: "LLM agent that plans the report and calls tools" agent: { kind: llm_agent, protocol: a2a } - id: SUMMARIZER role: "LLM sub-agent that summarises files for the planner" agent: { kind: llm_agent, protocol: a2a } - id: FILES role: "File store" agent: { kind: tool_server, protocol: mcp, tools: [read_file, delete_file] } - id: TICKETS role: "Issue tracker" agent: { kind: tool_server, protocol: mcp, tools: [search_tickets, create_ticket] } contracts: - id: ASSISTED_REPORTING parties: [OPERATOR, PLANNER, SUMMARIZER, FILES, TICKETS] enforcement: point: gateway # default: omitted -> deny tool calls, allow other messages counts_as: - { when: "OPERATOR -> PLANNER : approve", creates: approval } - { when: "OPERATOR -> PLANNER : reject", creates: rejection } norms: - id: may_read kind: permission bearer: OPERATOR content: "OPERATOR -> FILES : read_file" - id: may_search kind: permission bearer: PLANNER content: "PLANNER -> TICKETS : search_tickets" - id: may_file_ticket kind: permission bearer: PLANNER content: "PLANNER -> TICKETS : create_ticket" - id: no_delete kind: prohibition bearer: PLANNER content: "PLANNER -> FILES : delete_file" on_denied: escalate_to: OPERATOR timeout: 10min fallback: "PLANNER -> TICKETS : create_ticket" notify: OPERATOR delegations: - norm: may_read to: [PLANNER, SUMMARIZER] grant: grant_read revoke: revoke_read max_depth: 2 The contract has no lifecycle: block and no host creates instances, so its single instance, here called default, exists from the start of the enforcement point. The four norms have no trigger: they are in force from the start, and all four are static (G.10). The permission to read belongs to the operator; the planner and the sub-agent read only through a delegation, over at most two links. At 09:00:00 the operator sends OPERATOR -> PLANNER : grant_read, and at 09:00:02 the planner sends PLANNER -> SUMMARIZER : grant_read. Both are ordinary messages to which no norm applies, so the default allows them. The first creates a derived instance of may_read for PLANNER with the chain OPERATOR → PLANNER, the second one for SUMMARIZER with the chain OPERATOR → PLANNER → SUMMARIZER. A further SUMMARIZER -> PLANNER : grant_read would be recorded as unauthorised: PLANNER occurs in the chain of SUMMARIZER (condition 3), which already has two links (condition 4). Call 1 — allowed through a chain. At 09:00:05 the sub-agent sends SUMMARIZER -> FILES : read_file. The message is governed and the tool is declared. No prohibition applies: the sender is not the bearer of no_delete. The derived instance of SUMMARIZER is valid (may_read is in force, the chain has two links, its actors are in to:), and its content, read with the holder as sender, matches: allow. Call 2 — escalated and approved. At 09:03:00 the planner sends PLANNER -> FILES : delete_file. no_delete is in force and applies; it is the only ground and its escalate_to: is not the sender, so the decision is escalate. The hold h-1 is created with the approver OPERATOR and the deadline 09:13:00. At 09:03:40 the operator sends OPERATOR -> PLANNER : approve("h-1"), an ordinary message that the default allows. After step 1 of that observation the event approval, performed by OPERATOR, carries the hold id h-1, and the hold becomes approved. After step 6 the message is decided again: the tool is declared, the instance of the ground is running, no prohibition applies outside the grounds, and no other enforced contract governs the call, so the held message becomes the next observation, with the time stamp 09:03:40. It is not an occurrence of the content of no_delete, which stays active. Had the operator sent reject("h-1"), or nothing until 09:13:00, the closing record would be a deny with the reason rejected, or expired with the time 09:13:00; the planner would find the fallback in the result, and may_file_ticket allows that call. Call 3 — denied after a revocation. At 09:10:00 the operator sends OPERATOR -> PLANNER : revoke_read. OPERATOR occurs before PLANNER in the chain of PLANNER, so the instance of PLANNER is discharged, and with it the instance of SUMMARIZER, in whose chain PLANNER occurs. At 09:10:30 the sub-agent sends SUMMARIZER -> FILES : read_file. No prohibition applies; SUMMARIZER holds no valid permission, and the original may_read does not apply because the sender is not its bearer; the message is a tool call and default: is omitted, so the contract denies. The sub-agent cannot keep an authority that the planner no longer has. The audit records of the three calls (the two of call 2 share the hold h-1). In all four, instances is the instance default of ASSISTED_REPORTING and contracts is ["ASSISTED_REPORTING"]; the first record of call 2 is written out below the table. time message decision reason norms provenance hold_id outcome 09:00:05 SUMMARIZER, FILES, read_file allow permission may_read OPERATOR, PLANNER, SUMMARIZER null null 09:03:00 PLANNER, FILES, delete_file escalate prohibition no_delete — h-1 null 09:03:40 PLANNER, FILES, delete_file allow approved no_delete — h-1 approved 09:10:30 SUMMARIZER, FILES, read_file deny default — — null null { "time": "2026-11-10T09:03:00Z", "message": { "from": "PLANNER", "to": "FILES", "name": "delete_file" }, "instances": [ { "contract": "ASSISTED_REPORTING", "instance": "default" } ], "decision": "escalate", "reason": "prohibition", "contracts": ["ASSISTED_REPORTING"], "norms": ["ASSISTED_REPORTING.no_delete"], "provenance": [], "escalate_to": "OPERATOR", "timeout": 600000, "fallback": ["PLANNER -> TICKETS : create_ticket"], "notify": ["OPERATOR"], "hold_id": "h-1", "outcome": null }

The simulator IR (E.7, F.9) is extended in three places; as there, it is a direct serialization of dataclasses and flattens nested blocks. // each actor under institution.actors { "id": "FILES", "agent_kind": "tool_server", // null for an actor without agent: "agent_protocol": "mcp", "agent_tools": ["read_file", "delete_file"] } // each contract under institution.contracts { "enforced": true, "enforcement_default": null, "enforcement_point": "gateway", "norms": [ { "id": "no_delete", // ... and the fields of F.9 "on_denied_escalate_to": "OPERATOR", "on_denied_timeout_ms": 600000, "on_denied_fallback": "PLANNER -> TICKETS : create_ticket", "on_denied_notify": "OPERATOR" } ], "delegations": [ { "norm": "may_read", "to": ["PLANNER", "SUMMARIZER"], "grant": "grant_read", "revoke": "revoke_read", "max_depth": 2, "until": null } ] } enforced is true when the contract has the key enforcement:, also with a null or empty value. enforcement_default is null when default: is omitted, because the default then depends on the kind of message; applying it is left to the consumer. enforcement_point is filled in for an enforced contract (gateway) and null otherwise; max_depth is always filled in (1). fallback and until are kept as text. agent_tools and delegations are empty lists when there is nothing to list, and the four on_denied_* fields are null for a norm without on_denied:. All fields shown here (agent_*, enforced, enforcement_*, delegations, on_denied_*) are present only when the file declares agents: 0.1; a file that declares only norms: 0.1 has exactly the IR of F.9. Reference implementation. cadl 0.3.20 implements agents 0.1 as follows. It parses the four new keys, applies G-1 to G-16 in cadl check (the SHOULDs as warnings; G-17 to G-19 from cadl 0.3.22), and lowers the blocks to the IR above; a timeout: given as a bare number is read as seconds, the lenient form that A.12 describes for deadlines. cadl agents-decide implements the decision function of G.5 over the policy input of G.10. It is stateless: the in-force flags and the valid derived instances come in through the input. cadl codegen -t agent-rego emits a Rego policy that returns the full result, and -t agent-cedar emits Cedar policies for the static norms with a side table. Runtime. cadl 0.3.22 adds cadl agents-run FILE --trace TRACE [--audit OUT.jsonl], a reference runtime for G.5 to G.8. It is deterministic and offline: it replays a recorded sequence of messages through one enforcement point over all enforced contracts of the file, and its only clock is the time of the trace. For each message it takes the in-force flags from the verdict engine of cadl norms-eval (F.10), the valid derived instances from the grants and revocations observed so far, and the running contract instances from the trace; it builds the policy input of G.10 from them and calls the decision function of cadl agents-decide. It then applies the decision as G.5 says, keeps the holds and the derived instances (G.6, G.7), decides an approved message again before it releases it, and writes the audit records and event records of G.8, as JSON Lines when --audit is given. Hold ids are h-1, h-2, and so on, in the order of creation. The trace is that of cadl norms-eval (JSON Lines with t, bindings, request, values, messages, state, amend, end), read for the whole enforcement point, with two more keys: epoch, the time of t = 0 as an ISO 8601 time stamp, which makes the times of the records time stamps; and instances, the contract instances that a host creates and ends, with their bindings. Every instance has to bind the index variables of the parties of its contract, the single instance of a contract without host through the bindings of the first line, and each value has to be the index of a member of the set that the party names; otherwise the trace is rejected, with the contract, the instance, the variable, and the value in the message. A binding of a variable that no party has is ignored, with a warning. A value has to be the index of a member of every declared set that the variable indexes in the contract, not only of the party's set. The key quantities of the first line gives the quantity names of the run (F.5); then exactly these names are quantities, from the start and for every instance. Without it the runtime takes a name as a quantity from the first line on that gives it a value, so that no decision depends on a later line (G.5); a bare name without a value so far is a symbolic value. This can differ from the verdicts of cadl norms-eval on the same lines for a name before its first value, and the runtime warns when a name that a predicate uses gets its first value after a message was decided. Nothing after the end of an instance has an effect on it. Which contracts have host-created instances is likewise fixed on the first line: a contract that the first line names in instances, or lists under the key host_instances when its first instance is created later, has the instances that the trace creates, and none before; every other enforced contract has its single instance from the start, and a later line that creates an instance of it is a trace error. When a message is decided while a flag is unknown for missing data (G.5), the runtime warns once per norm and names the quantity without a value. Messages sent before the first values of such quantities are therefore denied or escalated; a trace gives the initial values on its first line to avoid that. A grant that is sent while the until: of the delegable permission is undefined is recorded as unauthorised_grant with the reason no_authority, because the permission is not known to be in force, and has to be sent again. Two limits remain for missing data. A message that would create a blocking event under an if: that is undefined creates nothing (G.5, G-19); the runtime warns and names the rule, the event, and the quantity. And the rule does not reach through an obligation: while the predicate trigger: of an obligation is undefined, the obligation is not activated, so it is not violated, and a prohibition that is its reparation: does not arise. One line is processed in this order: holds whose deadline lies before its time expire; instances are created; the time and the values of the line are observed without message (G.5), together with an amendment; each message is decided, and an allowed one is one observation; a change of lifecycle state and the end of instances are a last observation. Messages after the end of an instance are still decided and recorded. Three points are readings of the implementation and not rules of this appendix. An amendment applies to the enforced contracts whose definition differs between the two versions, and it may not add or remove an enforced contract. After a violation, the window clock of a prohibition stops while the prohibition is suspended, as it does before (F.5). A message matches the content of an obligation, for the verdict excused, as at the boundary: on sender, receiver, and name. Known limits. The runtime is not connected to a protocol: it replays a trace and does not run agents or tools. It does not protect the log against later changes. The log has no record for a change of the in-force flag of a norm (G.8). A holder whose derived instance is active but no longer valid after an amendment of to: cannot be granted the permission again: the grant is the no-op of condition 5 (holder_exists). A trace gives time as a finite number of at most 253 in absolute value; with an epoch, every time and every deadline of a hold has to be an instant that an ISO 8601 time stamp can express. A trace error on a later line is raised before anything is printed or written, but after the earlier lines have been decided in memory; the audit file is written only when the whole trace was replayed. The functions of the runtime refuse a file with errors of cadl check and an instance without the bindings of its parties; a switch for tests turns both off, and only then is the resolution of unknown occurrences (G.5) reached. The decision function cadl agents-decide still takes instances without bindings and treats the match as unknown (G.4). Up to cadl 0.3.22 the runtime, like cadl norms-eval, did not evaluate a predicate with a quantifier or an aggregate. From cadl 0.3.23 it evaluates them as F.5 defines; a quantified predicate that is undefined because its domain is open is missing data (G.5). The runtime still does not evaluate the predicates that F.10 lists as not evaluated, among them a wildcard or range reference outside the domain of a quantifier (A[*].x > 0); a norm whose trigger:, until:, or content: is such a predicate is not judged, and its in-force flag is unknown for the whole run. By G.5 a prohibition of that kind then always applies and a permission never does: fail-closed, but perhaps not what the author expects. Writing the reference as a quantifier (for all j in A: A[j].x > 0) avoids this. The tests replay each step of the runtime through the decision function with the state the runtime computed, and through the generated Rego policy under OPA 1.22.3: 81 decisions of nine hand-written scenarios (the three calls of G.12, rejection, timeout, a prohibition between a trigger and an until:, delegation with a depth limit, two contracts with bound indices and host-created instances) and 7 800 decisions of 26 generated traces over eleven files gave the same result in both. The generated traces have host-created instances with different bindings, senders outside the declared sets and undeclared senders, a hold with a ground in one of two contracts, and revocations, ends of instances, and amendments between a hold and its approval. Every release in them, 176 with 15 denied, and 13 more with 8 denied under random amendments, was checked from its recorded policy input against the rules of G.6. A second model of G.4 to G.7 and F.3, written by the reviewer from the text of the appendices without code of the reference implementation, gave the same 8 102 decision and closing records on 108 further traces over seven files: 60 traces with every index bound, run as cadl agents-run runs them, and 48 with instances that bind nothing or with two files that cadl check rejects by G-17 and G-18, run with the switch for tests. That model has no powers and no obligations. For them, 60 generated traces of 200 messages over two files check that without a binding no power is exercised, no institutional event is created, and no obligation is fulfilled, and that with a binding only the bound member does these things. The expected records of the scenario tests were derived from the text of this appendix before the runtime was run, and the runtime produced them. An independent review of the first version of the runtime found defects that these tests had not shown, in the implementation and in the text. All of them let a message take effect that should not have, and all are corrected. The grounds of a hold were kept per contract and not per contract instance, so an approval also covered the same prohibition in an instance created later (G.6). The re-check of a released message tested only new prohibitions, so a message was released although another governing contract no longer allowed it, for example after a revocation (G.6; the text said "nothing else is re-checked"). An actor reference with a range in a trigger:, an until:, or a counts_as: rule matched every actor of that name, and A[*] matched actors outside the declared set; this was a defect of cadl norms-eval since 0.3.20 (F.3, F.10). An instance observed messages that its contract does not govern (G.5). The generated traces had also shown one defect: holds that expired together were closed in the order of creation, not of their deadlines. A second review confirmed these corrections and found what the rule of governed observations had opened. A message event of an enforced contract that names an actor who is not a party could never occur, so a prohibition triggered by such an actor never came into force; G-17 now makes that an error. An index variable that the contract instance does not bind matched every member of the set in a trigger:, an until:, or a counts_as: rule, so any member could activate a permission or lift a prohibition; G-18 excludes it, and the runtime resolves the unknown occurrence fail-closed (G.5). A set with a symbolic upper bound took an index below its lower bound as a member, in the decision function, the Rego policy, and cadl norms-eval. A third review found that the unbound index was still a way through for powers and obligations, which the second model does not have: with a bearer SUP[k] and no binding for k, any member of SUP exercised a power that suspends a prohibition or activates a permission, and a message to any member fulfilled an obligation whose reparation is a prohibition. The cause was the same in every case, a contract instance that runs with an index unbound, and it is now removed at the root: G-18 covers every index variable of an enforced contract, the runtime refuses an instance that does not bind the indices of its parties, and its functions refuse a file with errors. The fail-closed resolution of G.5 is complete and remains as a second line. G-17 also rejects a literal index outside the declared set, and says that coverage is by one party reference. A fourth review found the same cause once more, in a place the rule did not yet name: an index variable in a predicate. A prohibition with the trigger: W[j].alarm == true and no party W[j] passed the check and never came into force. G-18 now covers every predicate of an enforced contract, with the exception of a variable that a quantifier binds, and the runtime resolves such a predicate as an unknown occurrence. The review also found that the runtime took the quantity names of an instance from the whole trace, so a value given after the end of an instance could change its verdict from violated to fulfilled, and that it accepted a binding outside the declared set, so a prohibition of W[i] applied to nobody; both are corrected. A fifth review found that decisions depended on later lines of the trace. The runtime had taken the quantity names from the whole trace since its first version, and the correction after the fourth review had only narrowed that to the lines of the instance: a value that a later line gave to a name changed how an earlier predicate read that name, and with it an earlier decision from deny to allow. The runtime now decides causally (G.5): the names are given with the trace, or a name becomes a quantity with its first value. The tests check, for every prefix of generated traces, that the decisions on the prefix are the first decisions on the whole trace; that invariant was missing. G-18 also missed an index variable inside an index expression and inside the arguments of a message event; it is now stated by its binders, and the checker walks every expression of the contract. A sixth review found one more look-ahead of the same kind: whether a contract has host-created instances was read from the whole trace, so an instances entry on a later line removed the single instance from the start and changed an earlier denial into an allowance. It is now fixed on the first line. The review also led to the rule for missing data in G.5: a prohibition whose trigger: could not be evaluated for want of a value was not in force, and a message was allowed on data that the enforcement point did not have. A seventh review found that this rule looked only at the predicate of the norm itself: a prohibition whose trigger: is an institutional event that a rule creates from a predicate was not in force while that predicate had no value. The rule of G.5 now reaches through such an event, and G-19 and the two limits above state what it does not reach. Writing and reviewing the runtime showed these gaps in the text of agents 0.1, which this revision of the appendix closes: the state on which a message is decided did not include deadlines that had passed since the last observation, and it was not said which contract instances observe an allowed message (G.5); the grounds of a hold, the contract instance in which an approval has to be created, the decision at a release, and the order of holds that expire together were not stated or were stated too weakly (G.6); whether the until: of a delegation ends the entry or its instances was open (G.7); the fallback that G.12 lets the sender find in a closing record was excluded by G.10; the records of grants, revocations, unauthorised acts, and other changes of state had no format (G.8); and nothing required the contract to govern the messages its events name, or to bind the indices they use (G-17 and G-18, added at the end of G.9; no earlier rule changes). The generated policies have been run with OPA 1.22.3 and the Cedar CLI 4.14.1 and compared with cadl agents-decide. Under OPA the full result was equal for 20 400 inputs (three variants of a file with two enforced contracts, actor sets, contract instances, in-force flags, and delegation chains). Under Cedar the outcome was equal for 5 640 requests, where Deny stands for deny and escalate, except for the case that G.10 names: a prohibition that is not static is not enforced by the Cedar policies. The tests of the reference implementation repeat both comparisons when opa or cedar is installed. This run found a defect in the Rego policy of cadl 0.3.20: a reference A[i] whose index the contract instance does not bind was treated as no match instead of unknown (G.4), so a prohibition with such a bearer did not apply, and a contract with default: allow allowed the message. cadl 0.3.21 corrects it; a policy generated by 0.3.20 SHOULD be generated again.

documents.t: Files written against CADL v0.3 without this extension remain valid and are read the same way; so are files that declare only norms: 0.1. A contract without the key enforcement: is not enforced, and its norms keep exactly the meaning of Appendix F. For an enforced contract this appendix makes these additions to F.5 and no other change: the instance of a contract without host exists from the start of the enforcement point; a denied or held message is not an observation; an instance of an enforced contract observes only the messages that its contract governs, and an occurrence that depends on an unbound index is unknown; the in-force flag is unknown while a quantity that it depends on has no value, without a change to the states of F.5; the time of a decision is observed before the message is decided; permissions and prohibitions have an in-force flag; an obligation whose content the contract itself denied or held is excused (all G.5); approval and rejection carry a hold id, the order of steps is extended, and a released message does not violate its grounds (G.6); permissions have derived instances (G.7). A file that uses agent:, enforcement:, delegations:, or on_denied: without declaring agents: 0.1 does not conform to this appendix. An agents-aware processor does not interpret these keys in such a file (they are not checked and not lowered to the IR) and SHOULD emit one warning per file that names the keys used. A file that declares agents: 0.1 without norms: 0.1 gets the error of G-1. Processors that do not implement the extension MUST NOT reject files that use it; they SHOULD emit a single informational diagnostic per file.

This appendix specifies the stochastic model extension to CADL. It adds one key, model:, to the sos_body production of Appendix A.2. With it, a file can carry an explicit stochastic model in which the institutional parameters α, β, and λ appear, state properties of that model, and ask the question of a regime map: which regime is best in which region of the parameter space. The core language does not mandate this block; a conforming CADL processor that does not implement the extension MUST NOT reject a file because of the new key. It SHOULD accept it syntactically and emit an informational diagnostic. The extension is versioned independently from the core language: its name is stochastic and this appendix describes version 0.1. A file that uses it MUST declare it with the entry - stochastic: 0.1 under extensions: (H.15 says what a processor does with an undeclared use). The extension changes the meaning of no construct of the core language or of the other extensions; in particular the verification: block of Appendix A.8 is unchanged.

Section 5.4.2 says that the institutional parameters "form the basis for regime map construction", but nothing in the core language connects a parameter to behaviour, and the cadl regime-map command reports the graph of regime names, not a map of the parameter space. RD-1.3 of Section 9.1 asks for that connection. Parameter synthesis for parametric Markov models partitions a parameter space into regions certified to satisfy or to violate a property [Junges+, FMSD 2024], and Storm implements it and reads the PRISM modelling language [Hensel+, STTT 2022] [Kwiatkowska+, CAV 2011]; CADL has no model to give to such a tool. Stochastic 0.1 is a small first step: The author writes the model: state variables and probabilistic commands that refer to parameters. Nothing is derived from contracts, protocols, or norms. What the extension fixes is the link: a parameter can be bound to alpha, beta, or lambda of a contract, so that contract and model use the same number. The semantics is a translation. A model and a regime define a parametric discrete-time Markov chain (H.7), which a processor exports to the PRISM modelling language by fixed rules (H.11). The regime map question is defined, not solved. H.9 defines what a query asks and what a correct answer is, not how to compute it. H.14 describes the method of the reference implementation. Scope of version 0.1. Time is discrete: one step is one transition, unrelated to a duration_lit. No continuous-time or timed models; finite state. Every regime model is a Markov chain: no nondeterminism (S-9), no synchronisation of commands. A switch between regimes (A.7) is not part of the model: each regime is analysed as a model of its own. Monotonicity claims ("raising α does not lower the success probability") are deferred; monotonicity checking exists for parametric Markov chains [Spel+, ATVA 2019], but that work concerns reachability probabilities. There is no game semantics in this appendix. Reading the model as a game among the actors, to ask whether compliance is an equilibrium (RD-7.1, RD-7.2 of Section 9.7; rational verification [Gutierrez+, AI 2020], correlated equilibria of concurrent stochastic games [Kwiatkowska+, TACAS 2022]), is the subject of the strategic model extension (Appendix I, games 0.1). Reserved for it, and not to be used with another meaning: the keys owner: (of a variable or a command) and sync: (of a command); players:, payoffs:, and equilibria: of model:; the value mdp of kind:; and the parameter sources motivation.rho and motivation.kappa. In a file that declares games: 0.1, Appendix I defines players:, payoffs:, equilibria:, and owner: of a command, adds the value smg of kind:, and replaces S-9 for a model of that kind; sync:, owner: of a variable, mdp, and the two parameter sources remain reserved there too. In a file that does not declare it, all of them remain reserved.

The grammar uses the notation of Appendix A. identifier, int_literal, bool_literal, string, number, scalar, and comp_op are defined there. sos_body gains one optional key: sos_body = ... , [ "model:" , model_block ] ; model_block = [ "kind:" , "dtmc" ] , [ "parameters:" , { "-" , param_def } ] , "variables:" , { "-" , var_def } , "commands:" , { "-" , command_def } , [ "labels:" , { identifier , ":" , state_pred } ] , [ "regimes:" , { identifier , ":" , regime_def } ] , [ "rewards:" , { "-" , reward_def } ] , [ "properties:" , { "-" , property_def } ] , [ "regime_maps:" , { "-" , regime_map_def } ] ; param_def = "id:" , identifier , ( "from:" , param_source , [ "range:" , interval ] | "range:" , interval , [ "value:" , number ] ) ; param_source = identifier , "." , ( "alpha" | "beta" | "lambda" ) | "environment" , "." , identifier ; (* string *) interval = "-" , number , "-" , number ; (* a sequence of exactly two numbers: [lo, hi] *) var_def = "id:" , identifier , "type:" , var_type , "init:" , scalar ; var_type = "bool" | int_range | enum_type ; (* string *) int_range = "[" , int_const , ".." , int_const , "]" ; enum_type = "{" , identifier , { "," , identifier } , "}" ; int_const = [ "-" ] , int_literal ; command_def = [ "action:" , identifier ] , [ "when:" , { "-" , identifier } ] , [ "guard:" , state_pred ] , (* string *) "updates:" , { "-" , update_def } ; update_def = [ "prob:" , ( param_expr | "rest" ) ] , (* string or number *) [ "set:" , { identifier , ":" , state_pred } ] ; regime_def = [ "parameters:" , { identifier , ":" , number } ] ; reward_def = "id:" , identifier , "items:" , { "-" , reward_item } ; reward_item = [ "action:" , identifier ] , [ "guard:" , state_pred ] , (* string *) "value:" , param_expr ; (* string or number *) property_def = "id:" , identifier , [ "regimes:" , { "-" , identifier } ] , "expr:" , property ; (* string *) regime_map_def = "id:" , identifier , "over:" , { identifier , ":" , interval } , [ "regimes:" , { "-" , identifier } ] , "objective:" , objective , [ "constraint:" , threshold_prop ] , (* string *) [ "resolution:" , number ] ; objective = "maximize:" , query_prop (* string *) | "minimize:" , query_prop ; (* string *) Three small expression languages are written inside string scalars. state_pred and param_expr are subsets of the predicate and arith_expr of Appendix A.10, with the same precedence and associativity; property is new (H.8). state_pred = s_and , { "OR" , s_and } ; s_and = s_not , { "AND" , s_not } ; s_not = "NOT" , s_not | s_cmp ; s_cmp = s_sum , [ comp_op , s_sum ] ; s_sum = s_term , { ( "+" | "-" ) , s_term } ; s_term = s_factor , { "*" , s_factor } ; s_factor = "(" , state_pred , ")" | "-" , s_factor | int_literal | bool_literal | identifier ; param_expr = p_term , { ( "+" | "-" ) , p_term } ; p_term = p_factor , { "*" , p_factor } ; p_factor = "(" , param_expr , ")" | "-" , p_factor | decimal | identifier ; decimal = int_literal , [ "." , int_literal ] ; property = query_prop | threshold_prop ; query_prop = quantity , "=?" , "[" , path , "]" ; threshold_prop = quantity , threshold_op , decimal , "[" , path , "]" ; quantity = "P" | "R" , "{" , string , "}" ; threshold_op = ">=" | ">" | "<=" | "<" ; path = "F" , [ step_bound ] , state_pred | state_pred , "U" , [ step_bound ] , state_pred ; step_bound = "<=" , int_literal ; With R{"…"} the path MUST be F φ without a step bound (S-13). A state_pred has no quantifiers, function calls, member accesses, indexed references, strings, durations, floating-point literals, or division. A param_expr is a polynomial: no division, no comparison, no function call. A number in the three sub-languages is digits with an optional fractional part (decimal); there is no exponent form. Writing the values in YAML. A var_type other than bool, a from:, an expr:, and the values of maximize:, minimize:, and constraint: MUST be quoted strings; a property with a reward name is written in a single-quoted scalar ('R{"delay"}<=1.5 [ F done ]'). A prob:, a reward value:, an init:, and the right-hand side of a set: entry may be a YAML number or boolean instead of a string (prob: 0.5, init: false), and a guard: may be the YAML boolean true or false. Under a YAML 1.1 loader the unquoted scalars ON, No, Off, Yes, null, and ~ are booleans or null, not names: such a name MUST be quoted where it is a mapping key (model.regimes:, over:, set:) or an init: value (see A.12). Such a loader also reads 1e-3 as a string; numbers SHOULD be written without an exponent (range: [0, 0.001]). Numbers are real numbers and are treated exactly. A numeric literal inside a string is the decimal fraction that is written. A numeric YAML scalar is read as the shortest decimal that round-trips the floating-point value the loader produced; an author MUST NOT write more than 15 significant digits, so that this decimal is the one written. Defaults. kind: is dtmc. guard: is "true". An omitted prob: is rest; an omitted set: changes no variable; an omitted when: means every design. The range: of an institutional parameter is [0, 1]. The regimes: of a property is all designs, that of a regime map all regimes of the file. resolution: is 0.05.

model.parameters: declares the parameters. A parameter without from: is free. With from: it is bound: from: Bound to Declared value "C.alpha" information.alpha of the contract with id: C the number written there, if any "C.beta" authority.beta of the contract C the number written there, if any "C.lambda" incentives.lambda of the contract C the number written there, if any "environment.X" the entry X of context.environment the entry, which MUST be a YAML number The word environment before the dot always denotes context.environment; any other name MUST be the id of a contract. A parameter bound to a contract is an institutional parameter. A bound parameter has no value:; the declared value of a free parameter is its value:, if present. range: [lo, hi] is the closed interval lo ≤ x ≤ hi with finite numbers lo ≤ hi, the declared range. For an institutional parameter it defaults to [0, 1] and, when given, MUST lie within [0, 1]; for every other parameter it is REQUIRED. Every value the parameter is given anywhere in the file, including the number of the contract it is bound to, MUST lie in the declared range (S-4). Under a design D (H.6) the fixed value of a parameter is the value the regime of D assigns to it, if it assigns one, and otherwise the declared value. Every parameter MUST have a fixed value under every design (S-11). A parameter is open in a regime map query when the query lists it in over:; there it ranges over an interval and its fixed value is not used. Everywhere else, in particular in every property of model.properties:, every parameter has its fixed value.

model.variables: declares at least one state variable: type: Domain Values are written as bool false, true true, false "[lo..hi]" the integers lo, …, hi, with lo ≤ hi integer literals "{A, B, C}" the listed enumeration literals, at least one, all different the literal names init: is REQUIRED and MUST be a value of the domain; the single initial state gives every variable its init: value. An enumeration is not ordered. Two enumeration types are the same when they list the same literals in the same order; a literal may occur in several types. A state_pred is evaluated in a state. An identifier in it is a variable, an enumeration literal, or, in a property only, a label; a parameter MUST NOT appear in it. It is integer (integer literals and variables with +, -, *), boolean (true, false, boolean variables, labels, comparisons, and AND, OR, NOT), or of an enumeration type (a literal or a variable). <, <=, >, >= compare two integers; == and != compare two integers, two booleans, or two values of the same enumeration type, of which at least one is a variable (two literals are not compared with each other). A guard, a label, a reward guard, and each state_pred of a property MUST be boolean. Integer arithmetic is exact and is not confined to a variable's range; only a value assigned by an update must lie in the domain (H.5). model.labels: names boolean state predicates (delivered: "task == Delivered"). A label may be used in the state_pred of a property wherever a boolean variable may, and nowhere else; its own predicate refers to variables only.
documents.s: H.4 Variables, labels, and state expressions

documents.t: model.commands: is a list of guarded probabilistic commands; H.12 has an example. Enabledness. A command exists in a design when it has no when: or its when: lists the regime of the design. It is enabled in a state when it exists in the design and its guard is true in the state. In every state at most one command may be enabled (S-9). Updates. Taking an update in a state s gives the state in which each variable named in set: has the value of its right-hand side evaluated in s (all right-hand sides before any assignment), and every other variable keeps its value. The value MUST lie in the domain whenever the command is enabled (S-7); it is never wrapped or clamped. Probabilities. prob: is a param_expr over numeric literals and parameters. At most one update of a command has the probability rest, written or by omission: one minus the sum of the other probabilities of the command. A command without rest MUST have only probabilities without parameters, and they MUST sum to exactly 1 (S-8). A command in which a parameter occurs therefore always has exactly one rest, and its probabilities sum to one by construction. Well-definedness. A design is well-defined at an assignment of numbers to all parameters when every probability of every command that exists in the design, including the value of rest, lies in [0, 1] and every reward value (H.8) is not negative. H.7 to H.9 are defined only there; S-11 requires it at the fixed values and S-14 on the region of a regime map. Graph preservation. A region is graph-preserving for a design when no probability of its commands is zero at a valuation of the region unless it is zero at all of them. Where a probability becomes zero, a solution function (H.7) need not be continuous: a probability of reaching a state can drop to zero, and an expected reward can become +∞. A processor MAY decline to certify cells that are not graph-preserving; they are then undecided (H.9). A processor that certifies such a cell MUST use a method that is sound without the assumption; a method that assumes graph preservation MUST NOT be applied to it. Action labels. action: names a command; several commands may share a name. Commands do not synchronise on it. Transition rewards refer to it (H.8), and it appears in the exported model (H.11). Deadlock. A state in which no command is enabled stays where it is with probability 1. This is not an error; absorbing states such as "delivered" are written by enabling nothing.

A.7 introduces regimes only through transitions:: the regimes of a file are the names used in from: and to: there. Comparing designs therefore requires a transitions: block. model.regimes: assigns parameter values per regime, and when: on a command (H.5) says in which regimes it exists: regimes: CENTRALIZED: { parameters: { beta: 0.9 } } DISTRIBUTED: { parameters: { beta: 0.1 } } An assigned value replaces the declared value under that regime and MUST lie in the declared range. For a bound parameter, the contract gives the value of the design as declared, and a regime that assigns it describes the operating mode in which it has another value. A regime without an entry assigns nothing. A design is a regime together with its parameter assignment and the set of commands that exist in it; "the model under regime R", "the design R", and "the institution R" all mean this. A file with regimes has one design per regime, named after it; wherever designs are listed or exported, their order is that of first appearance in transitions: (the from: of an entry before its to:). A file without transitions: has exactly one design, named base, with no assignment and every command; in such a file model.regimes:, when:, and model.regime_maps: MUST NOT appear (S-10). The condition: of a transition_def is the operational rule for switching; this appendix does not compare it with a regime map.

For a command c with k updates, write f(c, j) for the probability expression of its j-th update (for rest: one minus the sum of the others) and u(c, j)(s) for the state that the j-th update gives in state s. Fix a design D, and let θ assign a number to every parameter such that D is well-defined at θ (H.5); f[θ] is the value of f under θ. The regime model of D at θ is the discrete-time Markov chain M(D, θ) = (S, s₀, P): States. S is the set of all assignments of a domain value to every variable. It is finite and depends on neither θ nor D. Initial state. s₀ is the state given by the init: values. Transition function. If a command c is enabled in s under D (it is unique by S-9), P(s, s′) is the sum of f(c, j)[θ] over the updates j with u(c, j)(s) = s′. If no command is enabled in s, P(s, s) = 1 and P(s, s′) = 0 for every other s′. P(s, ·) is a probability distribution for every s. A path is an infinite sequence of states s₀ s₁ s₂ … in which every P(sᵢ, sᵢ₊₁) is positive; each transition is one step. M(D, θ) induces a probability measure on paths in the standard way. For a property (H.8), θ gives every parameter its fixed value under D. For a regime map query with region B (H.9), each valuation v ∈ B gives the θ that agrees with v on the open parameters and has the fixed values elsewhere; the value of a query is then a function J_D of v, from B to the real numbers extended with +∞, the solution function of the design.
documents.s: H.7 Semantics: the induced parametric Markov chain

documents.t: Rewards. model.rewards: declares named reward structures. Each item has a value:, a param_expr (it may depend on parameters, not on the state). An item without action: is a state reward, earned at each step taken from a state in which its guard is true, including the self-loop of a deadlock state. An item with action: is a transition reward, earned at each step in which a command with that action label is taken from a state in which its guard is true. The reward of a step is the sum of the values of all items of the structure that apply to it. The property language. A property (H.2) is written as in the PRISM property language [Kwiatkowska+, CAV 2011] and is a small fragment of the probabilistic temporal logic PCTL [Hansson & Jonsson, 1994] with an expected-reward operator, with the standard meaning. Operators cannot be nested. Let s₀ s₁ s₂ … be a path and φ, φ₁, φ₂ state predicates. Path formula The path satisfies it when F φ φ holds in sᵢ for some i ≥ 0 F<=k φ φ holds in sᵢ for some 0 ≤ i ≤ k φ₁ U φ₂ φ₂ holds in sᵢ for some i ≥ 0, and φ₁ holds in every sⱼ with j < i φ₁ U<=k φ₂ the same with 0 ≤ i ≤ k A step bound counts steps from the initial state. An F or U whose next token is <= has a step bound, whatever the white space between them (F x <= 3 is the unbounded F of the predicate x <= 3). Property Meaning in M(D, θ) P=? [ ψ ] the probability of the paths that satisfy ψ P⋈b [ ψ ] that probability ⋈ b, for ⋈ one of >=, >, <=, < R{"r"}=? [ F φ ] the expected reward of structure r accumulated until φ first holds R{"r"}⋈c [ F φ ] that expectation ⋈ c For R, let i be the first position of a path at which φ holds; the accumulated reward of the path is the sum of the rewards of the steps 0, …, i − 1. The expected reward is the expectation of this sum when φ is reached with probability 1, and +∞ otherwise; +∞ is greater than every number. A property with =? is a query; one with a threshold is a threshold property. model.properties:. Each entry states a property of the designs listed in regimes: (default: all designs), at the fixed values of all parameters. The result, per design, is the value of a query, or satisfied or violated for a threshold property. A processor that reports results MUST compute them with exact arithmetic or with numerics that have a sound error bound, or mark the result as approximate; a threshold that the error bound does not decide is inconclusive. The operators F and U are not the within, throughout, and until of Appendix F: those are evaluated on one timed trace of the running system and give a verdict, these on all paths of the model, in steps, and give a probability or an expectation. The two cannot be mixed, and version 0.1 defines no translation between a norm and a property of the model.

model.regime_maps: lists regime map queries (an example is in H.12). The keys of a query: over: gives the open parameters, at least one and at most four, each with a closed interval [lo, hi], lo < hi, within the declared range. The region B is the box of these intervals. A parameter in over: MUST NOT be assigned by any regime in model.regimes:. Institutional parameters may be opened like any other, which is how a map over α or λ is asked for. regimes: lists the regimes to compare, at least two, each once. objective: has exactly one key, maximize: or minimize:, with a query. J_R(v) is the value of the query in the design of regime R at valuation v (H.7). Write x ⪰ y for "x is at least as good as y": x ≥ y under maximize: and x ≤ y under minimize:. constraint: is an optional threshold property. Write sat_R(v) for: the design of R satisfies the constraint at v (true when there is none) and, under minimize:, J_R(v) is finite. Under maximize: the value +∞ is admitted and is at least as good as every value. resolution: is a number r with 0 < r < 1: the fraction of the volume of B that may remain undecided. Every compared design MUST be well-defined at every valuation of B (S-14). What is asked. At a valuation v, a regime is optimal when it satisfies the constraint and is at least as good as every regime that satisfies it: R ∈ opt(v) iff sat_R(v), and J_R(v) ⪰ J_R'(v) for every compared regime R' with sat_R'(v) opt(v) is empty exactly when no regime satisfies the constraint at v (under minimize:, also when every regime has the value +∞), and has several members when regimes tie. A cell is a closed box contained in B. A regime R is optimal on a cell C when R ∈ opt(v) for every v ∈ C; C is infeasible when opt(v) is empty for every v ∈ C. Deciding that a regime is optimal on a cell is the comparative region verification problem of RD-1.3. Region verification in parameter synthesis asks whether one model satisfies a threshold on a region [Junges+, FMSD 2024]; here the solution functions of several models are compared with each other. The result. The answer, the regime map, is a finite set of cells that cover B and whose interiors are pairwise disjoint, each with a status and a set best, together with the undecided fraction (the volume of the undecided cells divided by the volume of B) and whether it is at most resolution:. status Claim best decided every regime in best is optimal on the cell a non-empty set of regimes infeasible the cell is infeasible empty undecided none: the best regime changes inside the cell, or the processor could not decide empty best need not contain every regime that is optimal on the cell; where regimes tie on a whole cell it SHOULD list them all. Because ⪰ is not strict, adjacent cells with different best sets are consistent: on their common boundary the regimes of both are optimal. The points at which the optimal regime changes pass through the interior of cells, so some cells stay undecided however fine the partition, which is why resolution: is greater than zero. Certified. decided and infeasible are claims about every valuation of the cell. A processor MUST NOT make them unless it has established them by a method that is sound for the whole cell, with exact arithmetic or numerics with a sound error bound; this holds also for a claim about a single point. Region verification by parameter lifting and exact reasoning on the solution functions are such methods; evaluation at sample points, however many, is not. Only such certified cells count toward resolution:. A processor that cannot reach the requested resolution still reports the map and says so. A processor SHOULD name the method together with the map. The claims presuppose that H.7 is defined on the cell. A processor MUST NOT claim decided or infeasible for a cell unless every compared design is well-defined (H.5) at every valuation of the cell. The corner check of S-14 establishes this for a design whose probabilities are multi-affine in the open parameters. For any other design the processor has to establish it for the cell, or leave the cell undecided. Deciding a cell from bounds. Suppose a method gives, for each compared regime R, a lower bound l_R and an upper bound u_R of J_R that hold at every valuation of a cell C (a bound may be +∞), and likewise bounds of the quantity of the constraint. Say that R is in on C when the bounds show sat_R(v) for every v ∈ C, and out on C when they show that sat_R(v) fails for every v ∈ C. Then: C is infeasible when every compared regime is out on C; R is optimal on C when R is in on C and, for every other compared regime R′, either R′ is out on C or l_R ≥ u_R′ under maximize: (u_R ≤ l_R′ under minimize:). These conditions are sufficient, not necessary. They compare a bound of one solution function with a bound of another, not the two functions at the same valuation. A cell near a point where two regimes tie can therefore stay undecided although one regime is optimal on it, and regimes that tie on a whole cell are both found only when their bounds coincide, or when the processor knows that the two solution functions are the same. Estimates. A processor MAY additionally report estimates of the objective at sample points, for example from simulation, with their confidence. It reports them separately from the cells: they are claims about those points only, never change the status of a cell, and never count toward resolution:.

A processor that implements the extension MUST, in a file that declares stochastic: 0.1, in addition to existing checks: S-1. model: MUST have variables: with at least one variable and commands:, which may be an empty list. kind:, if present, MUST be dtmc. One case is not an error of this rule: in a file that declares the extension games, in any version (Appendix I), a processor that does not implement that extension does not interpret a model whose kind: is present and is not dtmc. It emits one informational diagnostic, applies none of S-2 to S-15 to the block, and MUST NOT evaluate, lower, or export the block as a Markov chain (H.15). In a file that does not declare games, such a kind: is an error. S-2. The id of a parameter, variable, reward structure, property, and regime map, every label name, every enumeration literal, and every action label MUST be an identifier and MUST NOT be a keyword of the expression sub-language of A.11 (AND, OR, NOT, true, false, in, exists), IN, or a keyword of the sub-languages of this appendix (rest, F, U, P, R). The structure keys of A.11 (alpha, beta, …) are not reserved here. Parameters, variables, labels, and enumeration literals share one namespace in which every name is declared once, except that a literal may occur in several enumeration types. For an enumeration variable x with literal L, the generated name x_L (H.11) MUST be distinct from every name declared in that namespace and from every other generated name. A label MUST NOT be named init or deadlock, which are built-in labels of PRISM. Reward structures, properties together with regime maps, and action labels each have a namespace of their own; an action label may be used by several commands. S-3. from: MUST be a string of the form C.alpha, C.beta, C.lambda, or environment.X, where C is the id of a declared contract and X a key of context.environment whose value is a YAML number. A parameter with from: MUST NOT have value:. A processor SHOULD warn when two parameters have the same source. S-4. range: MUST be a sequence of two finite numbers [lo, hi] with lo ≤ hi. It is REQUIRED except for an institutional parameter, where it MUST lie within [0, 1]. A value:, the number given by a source, and every value assigned by a regime MUST lie in the declared range. S-5. type: MUST be bool, an int_range with lo ≤ hi, or an enum_type with at least one literal and no literal twice. init: MUST be a value of the domain. S-6. Every state_pred MUST conform to the grammar of H.2 and be well typed (H.4): its identifiers are declared variables, enumeration literals of the right type, or, in a property only, labels, and never parameters. A string that does not conform is an error; it is not kept as an opaque predicate. For the right-hand side of a set: entry, a syntax error falls under this rule and a type or domain error under S-7. S-7. Every key of set: MUST be a declared variable, and its right-hand side MUST have the type of the variable. For every design in which the command exists and every state of S in which its guard is true, the value of the right-hand side MUST lie in the domain. (This is decided by enumerating S, as is S-9.) S-8. prob: MUST be rest, a number, or a param_expr whose identifiers are declared parameters. A command MUST have at least one update and at most one update with rest (written or by omission). In a command without rest, no probability may contain a parameter, and the probabilities MUST sum to exactly 1. A probability without parameters MUST lie in [0, 1]. S-9. For every design and every state of S (reachable or not), at most one command that exists in the design may have a true guard. S-10. Every key of model.regimes: and every name in a when: MUST be a regime of the file; every key of a regime's parameters: MUST be a declared parameter and its value a number. In a file without transitions:, model.regimes:, when:, and model.regime_maps: MUST NOT appear. A processor SHOULD warn about a regime that has no entry in model.regimes: when the block is present. S-11. Every parameter MUST have a fixed value under every design, and every design MUST be well-defined at its fixed values (H.5). S-12. A reward structure MUST have at least one item. In an item, action: MUST be the action label of at least one command, and value: a number or a param_expr over declared parameters. A value: MUST NOT mention a parameter that occurs in the over: of a regime map: in PRISM a parameter of parametric model checking can only be used in probabilities [Kwiatkowska+, CAV 2011]. S-13. Every property MUST conform to the grammar of H.2. With R, the name MUST be a declared reward structure and the path MUST be F φ without a step bound. A probability threshold MUST lie in [0, 1]. The regimes: of a property MUST name designs of the file, each once. S-14. In a regime map: over: MUST have one to four declared parameters, each with lo < hi within the declared range and none assigned by any regime in model.regimes:; regimes: MUST name at least two regimes of the file, each once (so the default, all regimes, is an error in a file with fewer than two); objective: MUST have exactly one of maximize: and minimize:, with a query; constraint: MUST be a threshold property; resolution: MUST satisfy 0 < r < 1. Every compared design MUST be well-defined on the whole region; a processor MUST check this at least at the corner points of the region, which decide the whole box when no open parameter occurs with a power above one (the expressions are then multi-affine in the open parameters). S-15. A processor SHOULD emit an informational diagnostic for a key or value reserved in H.1 and MUST NOT give it a meaning. A reserved value (kind: mdp, a motivation. source) gets this diagnostic in addition to the error of S-1 or S-3. The checks of Section 6.3 do not read model:. The rule of A.4 that alpha, beta, and lambda lie in [0, 1] is unchanged. This appendix does not change Section 5.4.2: α, β, and λ acquire behaviour only through the expressions an author writes. What is guaranteed is that the number a model uses for a bound parameter is the number of the contract, unless a regime assigns another in model.regimes:, where the difference is visible.

This section is normative for a processor that exports. It exports, per design, one model file in the PRISM modelling language and one companion properties file, for tools that do model checking, region verification, and parameter synthesis. The files are named <name>_<design>.prism and <name>_<design>.props, where <name> is the SoS name with every character outside [A-Za-z0-9_.-] replaced by _. The listings of H.12 show the canonical layout (indentation, one blank line between parts, single spaces around binary operators, source parentheses kept); two exports that differ only in white space and blank lines are equal. tr(e) below is the translation of an expression: AND, OR, NOT, == become &, |, !, =; an enumeration literal L that is compared with, or assigned to, the variable x becomes x_L; everything else, including parentheses, is kept as written. Model file, in this order: The line dtmc. One constant per parameter, in declaration order. A parameter that occurs in the over: of at least one regime map of the file is open and is written without a value, const double p;. Every other parameter is written with its fixed value under the design, const double p = 0.9;. (An over: parameter is assigned by no regime, S-14, so the two cases do not conflict.) For each enumeration variable x, in declaration order, and each literal L of its type at position i (from 0), const int x_L = i;. module main, then the variables in declaration order: x : bool init true; or x : bool init false;, x : [lo..hi] init v;, and for an enumeration with k literals x : [0..k-1] init i; with i the position of the init: literal. The commands that exist in the design, in declaration order, each as [a] tr(guard) -> (p1) : upd1 + (p2) : upd2 + … ; where a is the action label (empty when there is none); each probability expression is written in parentheses; rest is written as (1 - ((p1) + (p2) + …)) over the other probabilities of the command, in their order; the probability of a single update with rest is (1). An update is (x'=tr(e)) for each entry of set:, in the order of variable declaration, joined by &; an update without set: is true. One deadlock command, [] !((g1) | (g2) | …) -> true;, where g1, g2, … are the translated guards of the commands of step 5, in order ([] true -> true; when the design has no command). It is always written, so that the model does not depend on how a tool treats deadlock states. Then endmodule. For each label, in declaration order, label "name" = (tr(pred));. For each reward structure, rewards "id", then its items in order, a state reward as tr(guard) : (value); and a transition reward as [a] tr(guard) : (value);, then endrewards. A transition reward whose action label no command of the design has is not written: it is never earned in that design, and PRISM and Storm reject an item that names an action the model does not have. When no item of a structure is written, the single item true : (0); is written instead, because Storm rejects an empty reward structure. Numbers are written as the shortest decimal that round-trips, without an exponent (0.9, 1, 0.001). Identifiers. Parameter, variable, and action names, and the generated names x_L, are written unchanged, except that a name equal to a keyword of the PRISM language, or to one of its built-in function names floor, ceil, round, pow, mod, log, gets one trailing underscore; an exporter MUST report an error when the result collides with another name. Label and reward names are written in quotation marks and are renamed by the same rule: PRISM and Storm accept only an identifier that is no keyword between the quotation marks (label "max" is a syntax error in both), and Storm also rejects the built-in function names there. Labels and reward structures each have a namespace of their own in PRISM, so a collision is reported only between two labels or between two reward structures. The reserved keywords are those of the PRISM manual [Kwiatkowska+, CAV 2011], which are case-sensitive: A, bool, clock, const, ctmc, C, double, dtmc, E, endinit, endinvariant, endmodule, endobservables, endrewards, endsystem, false, formula, filter, func, F, global, G, init, invariant, I, int, label, max, mdp, min, module, X, nondeterministic, observable, observables, of, Pmax, Pmin, P, pomdp, popta, probabilistic, prob, pta, rate, rewards, Rmax, Rmin, R, S, stochastic, system, true, U, W. Properties file, in this order: for each open parameter, a comment line // const p = v with its declared value; then each property of model.properties: that concerns the design, preceded by a comment line // id; then, for each regime map that compares the design, its objective and its constraint, preceded by // id objective and // id constraint. A property is written as in the file, with every state_pred translated by tr, every label in quotation marks, and an operand of F or U in parentheses unless it is a single identifier, a quoted label, or already one parenthesised expression: P=? [ F<=3 "delivered" ]. Regions, the regimes compared, and resolution: are arguments of an analysis and are not exported. Parameter lifting [Quatmann+, ATVA 2016] in its classic form assumes probabilities that are multi-affine in the parameters and regions that are graph-preserving (H.5) [Heck+, ATVA 2025]. Regime maps are not a function of existing tools: a processor builds them from several analyses of several regime models.
documents.s: H.11 Export to the PRISM modelling language

documents.t: A dispatcher and robots deliver parcels. In the centralised regime most delivery decisions are taken by the dispatcher, whose plan is good when information is shared (α) but reaches the robot only when the dispatcher is up and the message is not lost. In the distributed regime most decisions are taken by the robot from local information, with a fixed quality. β is the probability that a decision is taken centrally. A robot makes at most three attempts. sos: name: "RobotDeliveryStochastic" type: Acknowledged extensions: - stochastic: 0.1 actors: - { id: DISPATCHER, role: "Assigns and replans routes" } - { id: "ROBOT[1..N]", role: "Delivers parcels" } contracts: - id: DELIVERY parties: [DISPATCHER, "ROBOT[*]"] information: { alpha: 0.9 } authority: { decision_holder: DISPATCHER, beta: 0.9 } transitions: - { from: CENTRALIZED, to: DISTRIBUTED, condition: "loss_rate > 0.3" } - { from: DISTRIBUTED, to: CENTRALIZED, condition: "loss_rate <= 0.2" } model: kind: dtmc parameters: - { id: p_fail, range: [0, 0.5], value: 0.05 } # dispatcher out of service during an attempt - { id: p_loss, range: [0, 0.5], value: 0.1 } # message from the dispatcher lost - { id: alpha, from: "DELIVERY.alpha" } # 0.9, range [0, 1] - { id: beta, from: "DELIVERY.beta" } # assigned by the regimes - { id: q_local, range: [0, 1], value: 0.6 } # success of a local decision variables: - { id: task, type: "{Pending, Delivered}", init: Pending } - { id: attempts, type: "[0..3]", init: 0 } labels: delivered: "task == Delivered" given_up: "task == Pending AND attempts == 3" commands: - action: attempt guard: "task == Pending AND attempts < 3" updates: - prob: "beta * alpha * (1 - p_fail) * (1 - p_loss) + (1 - beta) * q_local" set: { task: Delivered, attempts: "attempts + 1" } - prob: rest set: { attempts: "attempts + 1" } regimes: CENTRALIZED: { parameters: { beta: 0.9 } } DISTRIBUTED: { parameters: { beta: 0.1 } } rewards: - { id: delay, items: [ { action: attempt, value: 1 } ] } properties: - { id: P_DELIVERY, expr: "P>=0.95 [ F<=3 delivered ]" } - { id: P_EVENTUAL, expr: "P=? [ F delivered ]" } - { id: P_DELAY, regimes: [CENTRALIZED], expr: 'R{"delay"}<=1.5 [ F delivered OR given_up ]' } regime_maps: - id: best_for_delivery over: { p_fail: [0, 0.5], p_loss: [0, 0.5] } regimes: [CENTRALIZED, DISTRIBUTED] objective: { maximize: "P=? [ F<=3 delivered ]" } constraint: "P>=0.9 [ F<=3 delivered ]" resolution: 0.05 The condition: of the two transitions (thresholds on loss_rate) is the operational switching rule; it is independent of the certified boundary computed below. The model has eight states, seven of them reachable. The single command satisfies S-9, and its update attempts + 1 stays in [0..3] because the guard requires attempts < 3 (S-7). The states with task == Delivered and the state given_up enable nothing and loop on themselves. The two designs differ only in β. Write x = (1 − p_fail)(1 − p_loss), and s for the probability that one attempt succeeds. With α = 0.9 and q_local = 0.6: Regime β s = β·α·x + (1 − β)·q_local CENTRALIZED 0.9 s_C = 0.81·x + 0.06 DISTRIBUTED 0.1 s_D = 0.09·x + 0.54 On the region of the query, 0.25 ≤ x ≤ 1, so 0.2625 ≤ s_C ≤ 0.87 and 0.5625 ≤ s_D ≤ 0.63: both designs are well-defined on the region, the region is graph-preserving, and the probability is multi-affine in p_fail and p_loss. Each attempt succeeds independently, so for either regime: P=? [ F<=3 delivered ] has the value 1 − (1 − s)³, and P=? [ F delivered ] has the same value, because the model is acyclic and every path is absorbed within three steps; R{"delay"}=? [ F delivered OR given_up ] has the value 1 + (1 − s) + (1 − s)², the expected number of attempts. The value of R{"delay"}=? [ F delivered ] is +∞, because delivered is not reached with probability 1. The properties. At the fixed values p_fail = 0.05 and p_loss = 0.1, x = 0.855, s_C = 0.75255, and s_D = 0.61695. Computed values in this section are rounded to six decimals. Property Design Value Result P_DELIVERY CENTRALIZED 1 − 0.24745³ = 0.984848 satisfied P_DELIVERY DISTRIBUTED 1 − 0.38305³ = 0.943796 violated P_EVENTUAL CENTRALIZED / DISTRIBUTED 0.984848 / 0.943796 (query) P_DELAY CENTRALIZED 1 + 0.24745 + 0.24745² = 1.308682 satisfied P_DELAY is restricted to CENTRALIZED; on DISTRIBUTED the value would be 1.529777, above the bound of 1.5. The regime map. 1 − (1 − s)³ grows with s, so CENTRALIZED is at least as good as DISTRIBUTED exactly when s_C ≥ s_D, that is, when 0.72·x ≥ 0.48: CENTRALIZED is optimal where (1 − p_fail)(1 − p_loss) ≥ 2/3; DISTRIBUTED is optimal where (1 − p_fail)(1 − p_loss) ≤ 2/3; on the curve p_loss = 1 − 2 / (3·(1 − p_fail)), which runs from (p_fail, p_loss) = (0, 1/3) to (1/3, 0), both are optimal, with s = 0.6 and probability 1 − 0.4³ = 0.936. The constraint holds where s ≥ 1 − 0.1^(1/3) = 0.535841. DISTRIBUTED satisfies it on the whole region (s_D ≥ 0.5625). CENTRALIZED satisfies it where x ≥ 0.587458 and violates it below, which lies inside the part where DISTRIBUTED is optimal, so the constraint removes CENTRALIZED from the candidates there but does not change best. Low failure and low loss favour the centralised regime, high failure or high loss the distributed one. Values at some points, for checking an implementation: p_fail p_loss x P, CENTRALIZED P, DISTRIBUTED best 0 0 1 0.997803 0.949347 CENTRALIZED 0.1 0.1 0.81 0.977118 0.941994 CENTRALIZED 0.2 1/6 2/3 0.936 0.936 both 0.3 0.3 0.49 0.839809 0.928061 DISTRIBUTED (CENTRALIZED violates the constraint) 0.5 0.5 0.25 0.598869 0.916260 DISTRIBUTED (CENTRALIZED violates the constraint) Because x decreases in both parameters, a cell [f₁, f₂] × [l₁, l₂] is certified by its corners: CENTRALIZED is optimal on it when (1 − f₂)(1 − l₂) ≥ 2/3, DISTRIBUTED when (1 − f₁)(1 − l₁) ≤ 2/3, and otherwise the curve crosses the cell and it is undecided. A method that decides a cell from bounds of the two designs (H.9) decides fewer cells. Write x_min = (1 − f₂)(1 − l₂) and x_max = (1 − f₁)(1 − l₁) for the least and the greatest x on the cell. The value of either design on the cell ranges exactly over 1 − (1 − s)³ for x between x_min and x_max. Comparing these ranges decides CENTRALIZED when s_C at x_min is at least s_D at x_max, that is when 0.81·x_min − 0.09·x_max ≥ 0.48, and DISTRIBUTED when 0.81·x_max − 0.09·x_min ≤ 0.48. A cell that satisfies neither is undecided, also when the curve does not cross it. Export. By H.11, the model file of the design CENTRALIZED is the following; p_fail and p_loss are open because the regime map lists them in over:. The file of DISTRIBUTED differs only in const double beta = 0.1;. dtmc const double p_fail; const double p_loss; const double alpha = 0.9; const double beta = 0.9; const double q_local = 0.6; const int task_Pending = 0; const int task_Delivered = 1; module main task : [0..1] init 0; attempts : [0..3] init 0; [attempt] task = task_Pending & attempts < 3 -> (beta * alpha * (1 - p_fail) * (1 - p_loss) + (1 - beta) * q_local) : (task'=task_Delivered) & (attempts'=attempts + 1) + (1 - ((beta * alpha * (1 - p_fail) * (1 - p_loss) + (1 - beta) * q_local))) : (attempts'=attempts + 1); [] !((task = task_Pending & attempts < 3)) -> true; endmodule label "delivered" = (task = task_Delivered); label "given_up" = (task = task_Pending & attempts = 3); rewards "delay" [attempt] true : (1); endrewards Its properties file: // const p_fail = 0.05 // const p_loss = 0.1 // P_DELIVERY P>=0.95 [ F<=3 "delivered" ] // P_EVENTUAL P=? [ F "delivered" ] // P_DELAY R{"delay"}<=1.5 [ F ("delivered" | "given_up") ] // best_for_delivery objective P=? [ F<=3 "delivered" ] // best_for_delivery constraint P>=0.9 [ F<=3 "delivered" ]

The IR gains one top-level field, stochastic_model, next to the three layers; it is null when the extension is not declared, when there is no model:, or when the block has a check error. As in Appendix E, E.7, expressions are kept as text. The sample is abridged where marked: { "stochastic_model": { "kind": "dtmc", "parameters": [ { "id": "p_fail", "source": null, "range": [0, 0.5], "value": 0.05, "open": true }, { "id": "alpha", "source": "DELIVERY.alpha", "range": [0, 1], "value": 0.9, "open": false } // ... p_loss, beta, q_local ], "designs": [ { "name": "CENTRALIZED", "parameters": { "beta": 0.9 } } ], // ... DISTRIBUTED "properties": [ // ... P_EVENTUAL, P_DELAY { "id": "P_DELIVERY", "regimes": ["CENTRALIZED", "DISTRIBUTED"], "expr": "P>=0.95 [ F<=3 delivered ]" } ], // ... "variables", "labels", "commands", "rewards": the fields of H.2 under the same names; // a variable has "kind" (bool | int | enum), "lo", "hi", "literals", "init"; // a command has "index", "action", "when", "guard", "updates" (each with "prob", "set") "regime_maps": [ { "id": "best_for_delivery", "over": { "p_fail": [0, 0.5], "p_loss": [0, 0.5] }, "regimes": ["CENTRALIZED", "DISTRIBUTED"], "direction": "maximize", "objective": "P=? [ F<=3 delivered ]", "constraint": "P>=0.9 [ F<=3 delivered ]", "resolution": 0.05 } ] } } The keys are in the order kind, parameters, designs, properties, variables, labels, commands, rewards, regime_maps. labels maps each name to its text; prob is text ("rest" or the expression or decimal as text); set maps each variable to text; a reward item is {action, guard, value} with value as text; an unused lo or hi is null and unused literals is []. The defaults of H.2 are filled in (when: [] means every design). value is the declared value of H.3, or null; open is true for a parameter that some regime map lists in over:. designs lists every design with the values its regime assigns (the single entry base for a file without transitions:). index is the position of the command in model.commands:, from 1. Results of analyses are not in the IR.

The reference implementation implements stochastic 0.1 from cadl 0.3.20 as follows: cadl parses model:, applies rules S-1 to S-15 in cadl check (the SHOULDs as warnings; S-7 and S-9 by enumerating the state space, which is refused above 200 000 states), and lowers the block to the IR of H.13. cadl model-export writes the files of H.11. cadl model-check is a small reference evaluator with exact rational arithmetic for one design at fixed parameter values. It evaluates the properties of H.8, up to 2 000 unknowns. With --regime-map ID it evaluates the objective of a regime map at the points of a grid; these are reported as estimates at sample points (H.9), never as decided cells. cadl model-check --regime-map ID --certify computes the regime map of H.9, from cadl 0.3.22. It runs no external model checker. The method is parameter lifting [Quatmann+, ATVA 2016] with exact rational arithmetic. On a cell, a design is relaxed to a Markov decision process in which every state chooses, independently of the other states, a corner of the cell for the open parameters that occur in its outgoing probabilities. When those probabilities are multi-affine, the chain at any valuation of the cell is this process under one randomised policy, so the minimal and the maximal value of the process bound the solution function on the whole cell. Bounded properties are solved by backward induction, unbounded ones by policy iteration with exact linear solves. A cell is decided from these bounds by the conditions of H.9. An undecided cell is bisected along the parameter whose interval is widest relative to the region, the largest undecided cell first, until the undecided fraction is at most resolution: or a budget is exhausted (--max-depth, by default 24 bisections of one cell; --max-cells, by default 20 000 cells). In the second case the map is reported with the statement that the resolution is not reached, and the exit status is 1. Two halves with the same claim are reported as one cell. The command reports the method, the cells, their numbers per status, and the undecided fraction as an exact number; estimates (--grid) and the certified map (--certify) are separate outputs and cannot be combined. Limits of the certified map: The bounds of two designs are compared, not their difference, so cells next to a boundary stay undecided (H.9, H.12). Regimes that tie on a cell are listed together only when their bounds coincide or their designs have the same model. A probability that is not multi-affine in the open parameters is enclosed by exact interval arithmetic on its monomials, and the state chooses a vertex of the set of distributions within these intervals. This is sound but coarser. Such a design counts as well-defined on a cell only when the intervals lie within [0, 1]; otherwise the cell is undecided and the report gives this reason. Interval arithmetic overestimates, so near a valuation where such a probability is 0 or 1 it may fail to establish this however small the cell is. Cells that are not graph-preserving are analysed, not declined. The bounds of a probability are those of the decision process. An expected reward gets a finite upper bound only when every policy of the process reaches the target with probability 1; it is +∞ on the whole cell when no policy does; its lower bound is the least expected reward that any policy accumulates. The cost grows with the number of cells, which grows with the number of open parameters, and with the number of states: every policy is evaluated by an exact linear system, of at most 2 000 unknowns. S-14 is checked by cadl check at the corners of the region. A probability that is not multi-affine can leave [0, 1] in the interior only; the certified mode reports that as an error (exit status 2) when the centre or a corner of a cell shows it, and otherwise leaves the cell undecided. A YAML number with more than 15 significant digits, which H.2 forbids, is rounded when the file is loaded and is not reported; the claims are then about the rounded model. For the example of H.12 (resolution: 0.05) the certified map has 95 cells, 60 decided and 35 undecided, after joining a partition of 121 cells; 241 cells were analysed, with at most 10 bisections of a cell. CENTRALIZED is certified on 235/1024 of the region (it is optimal on 0.2521 of it), DISTRIBUTED on 738/1024 (optimal on 0.7479), and the undecided fraction is 51/1024 = 0.0498. The curve crosses 31 of the 35 undecided cells; the other 4 lie next to it. The computation takes about 0.1 s on a laptop; with resolution: 0.01 it takes 0.8 s (726 cells before joining) and with resolution: 0.002 3.8 s (3 632 cells). The certified maps were checked in two ways. The tests of the reference implementation repeat both; the second needs stormpy. The eight maps are that of H.12 and seven maps of a second model with three regimes, cycles, minimize: with an expected reward that is +∞ for one regime everywhere and for the others at one face of the region, constraints that make part of the region infeasible, a probability that is not multi-affine, cells that are not graph-preserving, a tie on a whole cell, and three open parameters. Every decided and infeasible cell of the eight maps, 212 cells, was evaluated with the exact reference evaluator at its corners, its centre, and six random rational points: 2 512 point evaluations. At each of them every regime in best is optimal, or no regime satisfies the constraint, as claimed. The bounds were compared with Storm (stormpy 2.0.0, exact parameter lifting engine) on the exported files, for 134 pairs of a design and a cell that is graph-preserving for it. For the designs with multi-affine probabilities, the lower and upper bounds of cadl are equal, as rational numbers, to those of Storm (159 pairs of bounds). The extrema that Storm finds on the cell by refinement lie within the bounds of cadl (213 pairs). Storm's verdict on the constraint for the cell (all valuations satisfy it, all violate it, or neither) is the claim of cadl in 79 of 79 cases. Storm's parameter lifting assumes a graph-preserving region. stormpy's verify refuses a region that is not, and its extremum computation returned the minimum 1 for P=? [ F done ] on 0 ≤ p ≤ 1/2 for a design that reaches done with probability p in each step, where the value at p = 0 is 0. Cells that are not graph-preserving were therefore checked with the reference evaluator only. An independent review tried to break the certified mode and found no wrong claim: 3 290 random models, 56 782 decided or infeasible cells tested at 1 731 349 exact points, among them cells that are not graph-preserving and designs that are not multi-affine; the solvers of the decision process agreed with a brute-force search over all memoryless policies on 60 000 random processes; and four soundness errors injected into the code were each detected by the harness. cadl regime-map still reports the graph of regime names and transitions. Deviation: cadl 0.3.22 does not know the extension games (Appendix I). For a model with kind: smg in a file that declares games: 0.1 it reports an error of S-1 and, where two commands of one player are enabled in a state, an error of S-9, where S-1 and H.15 ask for one informational diagnostic and no further check.
