It does not evaluate or export the model. The exported files have been run through PRISM 4.11 and Storm (stormpy 2.0.0) for the example of H.12, for a second model that uses when:, updates with three branches, guarded state and transition rewards, U, U<=k, and keyword names, and for the model of the certified maps above: 39 properties in 7 designs. The state counts agree, and every value agrees with cadl model-check as a rational number under Storm and under the exact engine of PRISM. That engine does not support a step bound (F<=k, U<=k); those properties were compared with PRISM in floating point. The tests of the reference implementation repeat the comparison when prism or stormpy is installed. These runs found two defects of the export. cadl 0.3.20 wrote a label or reward structure named like a keyword unchanged, which neither tool loads; 0.3.21 renames it as H.11 now says. cadl up to 0.3.21 wrote a transition reward for an action that no command of the design has, which neither tool loads; 0.3.22 omits it as H.11 now says.

Files written against CADL v0.3 without this extension remain valid and are read the same way: the extension adds one key and changes the meaning of nothing that exists. A file that uses model: without declaring stochastic: 0.1 does not conform to this appendix. A processor that implements the extension does not interpret the model: block of such a file (it is not checked, not lowered to the IR, and not exported) and SHOULD report it as an undeclared extension key. Processors that do not implement the extension MUST NOT reject a file because of model:; they SHOULD emit a single informational diagnostic per file. A file may declare the extension games, in any version (Appendix I), and carry a model with kind: smg, which is a game and not a Markov chain. A processor that implements this appendix and not Appendix I skips such a model (S-1): it reports it with one informational diagnostic, stochastic_model is null, and it MUST NOT check, evaluate, or export the model by the rules of this appendix, since H.7 would give it a meaning it does not have. A model with kind: dtmc, or without kind:, in such a file is a model of this appendix and is read as before.

This appendix specifies the strategic model extension to CADL. It builds on the stochastic model extension (Appendix H) and adds to the model: block the keys players:, profiles:, compliance:, payoffs:, and equilibria:, the key owner: to a command, the key profile: to a property and to a regime map, and the value smg of kind:. With them, a file says which party chooses which command of the model and what each party gains, names the behaviour that the contract asks for, and asks whether that behaviour is an equilibrium against unilateral deviations: at the fixed values of the parameters, or as a map over a region of parameters. The core language does not mandate these keys; a conforming CADL processor that does not implement the extension MUST NOT reject a file because of them. It SHOULD accept them syntactically and emit an informational diagnostic. The extension is named games and this appendix describes version 0.1. It requires stochastic: 0.1: the game is played on the model of Appendix H. A file that uses it MUST declare both under extensions: (A.2); I.15 says what a processor does with an undeclared use. sos: ... extensions: - stochastic: 0.1 - games: 0.1 The extension does not depend on the norms extension (Appendix F). Appendix J relates the payoffs of a strategic model to the sanctions of norms.

Constituent systems keep their operational and managerial independence, so a constituent complies with a contract only when compliance pays (Section 9.7). The model of Appendix H has no party that chooses: every regime model is a Markov chain. Rational verification asks whether a property holds on the equilibria of a multi-agent system [Gutierrez+, AI 2020], also for probabilistic systems [Gutierrez+, KR 2021]; PRISM-games verifies turn-based stochastic games [Chen+, FMSD 2013] and computes equilibria of concurrent ones [Kwiatkowska+, TACAS 2022]; and Nash equilibria have been computed for games in which each player chooses the value of a parameter of a parametric Markov chain [Mu, QEST 2019]. Parameter lifting analyses a parametric Markov decision process through a stochastic game of two players [Quatmann+, ATVA 2016]; it bounds what a controller can achieve and does not decide whether a profile is an equilibrium. RD-7.2 asks for a map: the region of λ, and of other parameters, in which compliance is an equilibrium. We searched for tools and methods that compute such a region for a stochastic game whose transition probabilities are parametric (search terms: parametric stochastic games, Nash equilibrium, parameter synthesis, equilibrium region) and found none. Games 0.1 is a small first step on RD-7.1 and RD-7.2: The author writes the game. players: declares the players, owner: on a command says who chooses it, and payoffs: says what each player gains, built from the reward structures of H.8. Nothing is derived from contracts or norms. Compliance is a named profile. profiles: names profiles of memoryless deterministic strategies, and compliance: names the one that stands for the behaviour the contract asks for (I.4). The question is defined exactly. I.7 defines when a named profile is a Nash equilibrium of a design at a valuation, that is, when no player gains by deviating from it alone, and the deviation gain of each player. I.9 defines the equilibrium map: cells of a region of parameters, each certified in the sense of H.9 as equilibrium or not_equilibrium, or left undecided. The appendix defines what a correct answer is and gives sufficient conditions that a processor can compute; it prescribes no algorithm. Scope of version 0.1. The game is turn-based: in every state at most one player chooses (I-5). There are no concurrent moves and no synchronisation of commands. Strategies named in a file are memoryless and deterministic: a choice of one command per state. There are no mixed strategies, so an equilibrium in mixed strategies cannot be named or found. Every player observes the whole state. Equilibria under partial observation, which is what α controls (RD-7.3), remain open. A player is one representative of the actors it stands for, and an actor set has at most one player (I-3). Two members of one actor set, for example two robots that compete, cannot be two players. A payoff is a weighted sum of expected rewards accumulated until a target, for a profile from which no single player can keep the game away from its target (I.6). Discounted, mean-payoff, and step-bounded payoffs are not defined; a bounded horizon is written with a counter variable, as attempts in I.12. The equilibrium notion is the Nash equilibrium of a named profile and its ε-relaxation. I.7 also defines when a profile is an equilibrium from every reachable state, which a result may state. Subgame-perfect equilibria as a query, dominant strategies, the set of all equilibria of a game, and whether a property holds on every equilibrium (the question of RD-7.1 in full) are not defined. A centralised mediator, modelled as a correlated equilibrium, and the value of centralisation of RD-7.2 are out of scope. An equilibrium is asked for per design; a switch between regimes is not part of the game (H.1). Reserved, and not to be used with another meaning: the key sync: of a command and owner: of a variable; the keys mediator: and observations: of model:; the key concept: of an entry of equilibria:; the value mdp of kind:; and the parameter sources motivation.rho and motivation.kappa. Of the names that H.1 reserves, this appendix defines players:, payoffs:, equilibria:, and owner: of a command.

The grammar uses the notation of Appendix A. identifier, actor_ref, and number are defined there; state_pred, param_expr, and interval in H.2. model_block = ... , [ "kind:" , ( "dtmc" | "smg" ) ] , [ "players:" , { "-" , player_def } ] , [ "profiles:" , { identifier , ":" , { "-" , profile_rule } } ] , [ "compliance:" , identifier ] , [ "payoffs:" , { "-" , payoff_def } ] , [ "equilibria:" , { "-" , equilibrium_def } ] ; player_def = "id:" , identifier , "actors:" , { "-" , actor_ref } ; command_def = ... , [ "owner:" , identifier ] ; profile_rule = [ "guard:" , state_pred ] , (* string *) "choose:" , identifier ; payoff_def = "player:" , identifier , "until:" , state_pred , (* string *) "terms:" , { "-" , payoff_term } ; payoff_term = "reward:" , identifier , [ "weight:" , param_expr ] ; (* string or number *) property_def = ... , [ "profile:" , identifier ] ; regime_map_def = ... , [ "profile:" , identifier ] ; equilibrium_def = "id:" , identifier , [ "profile:" , identifier ] , [ "regimes:" , { "-" , identifier } ] , [ "epsilon:" , number ] , [ "over:" , { identifier , ":" , interval } ] , [ "resolution:" , number ] ; Writing the values in YAML. The rules of H.2 apply: until: and a guard: are quoted strings (a guard: may be the YAML boolean true or false), and a weight: may be a YAML number or a quoted string (weight: -1, weight: "-2 * lambda"). The value of a profile may be the empty sequence (comply: []). The names that a YAML 1.1 loader reads as booleans or null (H.2) MUST be quoted where they are a key of profiles: or over:. Defaults. The guard: of a profile rule is "true". weight: is 1. The profile: of a property, of a regime map, and of an entry of equilibria: is the compliance profile. The regimes: of an entry of equilibria: is all designs. epsilon: is 0. resolution: is 0.05.

A model with kind: smg is a strategic model. A model with kind: dtmc, or without kind:, is a model of Appendix H and MUST NOT use the keys of this appendix (I-2). model.players: declares the players. Each has an id and a list actors: of declared actors for which it stands; an actor stands behind at most one player (I-3). A player stands for one decision maker of the model, also when its actor is a set: "ROBOT[*]" in I.12 is one robot that represents any member of the set. The mapping to actors has no effect on the semantics of this appendix; Appendix J uses it to relate a payoff to the bearer of a norm. owner: on a command names the player who chooses it. A command with owner: is owned; one without is unowned and belongs to no player: it is a step of chance or of the environment, as every command of Appendix H. An owned command MUST have an action:, and all commands with one action label have the same owner or are all unowned (I-4), so an action label identifies its owner. Fix a design D (H.6). Write En(s) for the set of commands that are enabled in state s under D (H.5). Rule S-9 of H.10 is replaced, for a strategic model, by I-5: in every state of S, En(s) is empty: s is a deadlock state and stays where it is with probability 1 (H.5); or one unowned command: s is a chance state; or one or more commands that are all owned by the same player p, with pairwise different action labels: s is a state of p, and p chooses one of them. No other case is allowed. A state of p in which one command is enabled is a state of p with a single choice.

A strategy of a player p in a design D is a function that gives, for every state of p, one command of En(s). Unless said otherwise, a strategy in this appendix is of this kind: memoryless (it depends on the current state only) and deterministic (it chooses one command with certainty). A profile in D is one strategy for every player. For a profile σ, a player p, and a strategy τ of p, σ[p↦τ] is the profile that agrees with σ except that p plays τ. model.profiles: names profiles in a form that is finite to write. A named profile is an ordered list of rules, each with an action label (choose:) and a state predicate (guard:, by default true). A rule applies in a state s when its guard is true in s and a command of En(s) has its action label. The profile selects, in a state s of a player: the command of En(s) that has the action label of the first rule of the list that applies in s; or, when no rule applies and En(s) has one command, that command. When no rule applies in a state in which two or more commands are enabled, the file is in error (I-6). The rules of all players are written in one list; a rule concerns the player who owns its action label. A named profile therefore defines, in every design, one strategy for every player, on all states of S, reachable or not. model.compliance: names the compliance profile: the profile that, by the author's declaration, is the behaviour the contracts of the file ask of the players. It is REQUIRED in a strategic model. This appendix gives the declaration no other meaning than that of a default: properties, regime maps, and entries of equilibria: that name no profile refer to it. The appendix does not check that the compliance profile complies with any norm; version 0.1 defines no translation between a norm and a model (H.8). Appendix J, J.7 states what a processor can check when the file also declares norms with sanctions.
documents.s: I.4 Strategies, profiles, and the compliance profile

documents.t: Fix a design D and an assignment θ of a number to every parameter such that D is well-defined at θ (H.5). With f(c, j) and u(c, j) as in H.7, write P(s, c, s′) for the sum of f(c, j)[θ] over the updates j of the command c with u(c, j)(s) = s′. The game G(D, θ) has the states S and the initial state s₀ of H.7. In a state of a player p, p chooses a command c of En(s), and the next state is s′ with probability P(s, c, s′). In a chance state the single enabled command is taken. A deadlock state stays where it is. The model under a profile. For a profile σ, M(D, θ, σ) is the discrete-time Markov chain (S, s₀, P_σ) in which P_σ(s, s′) is P(s, c, s′) for the command c that σ selects in a state s of a player, or for the single enabled command of a chance state, and P_σ(s, s) = 1 in a deadlock state. M(D, θ, σ) is a regime model in the sense of H.7, and a step from a state of a player takes the selected command, with its action label. Everything that H.7 to H.9 define for M(D, θ) is defined for M(D, θ, σ) in the same way: paths, the reward of a step, the value of a property, solution functions, and regime maps. Properties and regime maps of a strategic model. In a strategic model, an entry of model.properties: or model.regime_maps: is evaluated in M(D, θ, σ), where σ is the profile named by its profile: key, by default the compliance profile. Its meaning, its results, and the certification requirement are those of H.8 and H.9. A regime map of a strategic model therefore compares the regimes under one fixed profile; it does not ask whether that profile is an equilibrium. General strategies. The definitions of I.7 quantify over more strategies than a file can name. A general strategy of p gives, for every finite sequence of states and commands that starts in s₀ and ends in a state s of p, a probability distribution over En(s). A strategy in the sense of I.4 is the special case that depends on s only and gives probability 1 to one command. One general strategy per player, together with θ, induces a probability measure on the infinite sequences of states and commands in the standard way [Puterman, 1994].

model.payoffs: gives every player exactly one payoff (I-7). A payoff has a target until: φ, a state predicate in which labels may be used as in a property (H.4), and one or more terms. A term names a reward structure r of model.rewards: (H.8) and has a weight: w, a param_expr over numeric literals and parameters. A weight may be negative and may contain a parameter that is open in an equilibrium map; a reward value: remains not negative (H.5) and MUST NOT contain such a parameter (I-9). Gains and costs are therefore written as terms with weights of opposite sign, and an incentive term carries λ in its weight (weight: "-2 * lambda"). For a path, the accumulated reward of r until φ is the sum of the rewards of the steps before the first position at which φ holds (H.8); what happens after that position does not count. Write φ_p for the target of the payoff of p. Under one general strategy per player, the payoff of p is u_p = Σ_k w_k[θ] · E[ accumulated reward of r_k until φ_p ] over the terms k of p's payoff, where E is the expectation under the induced measure. For a profile σ, the expectation of the k-th term is the value of the query R{"r_k"}=? [ F φ_p ] in M(D, θ, σ); write u_p(D, θ, σ) for the payoff. The game of one player against a profile. The question of I.7 lets one player deviate while the others follow a profile σ. For a player p, a command is allowed in a state s when s is a state of p and the command is in En(s), when s is a state of another player and σ selects the command, or when s is a chance state and the command is its enabled command. Reach_p(D, θ, σ), written Reach_p, is the set of states s for which there is a sequence s₀, …, s_n = s such that φ_p holds in none of s₀, …, s_(n−1) and each s_(i+1) has a positive probability P(s_i, c, s_(i+1)) for a command c allowed in s_i. These are the states that p can reach while its payoff is still accumulating; a state in which φ_p holds belongs to Reach_p when it is reached in this way, and nothing beyond it does. Admissible profiles. The definition needs every expectation to be finite, and a player must not be able to make its payoff infinite or undefined by keeping the game away from its target. A profile σ is admissible for p at θ when, for every strategy τ of p, the probability of F φ_p in M(D, θ, σ[p↦τ]) is 1. It is admissible at θ when it is admissible for every player. Admissibility depends only on which probabilities P(s, c, s′) are positive, and it has a graph characterisation: σ is admissible for p exactly when there is no non-empty set E of states of Reach_p in which φ_p does not hold such that every state of E either is a deadlock state or has an allowed command all of whose successors of positive probability lie in E. (Such a set is a deadlock in which the target does not hold, or an end component that avoids the target.) A processor decides it on the graph of Reach_p: starting from the states of Reach_p in which φ_p does not hold, it removes, as long as there is one, a state that is not a deadlock state and has no allowed command all of whose successors of positive probability remain; σ is admissible for p exactly when no state remains. When σ is admissible for p, φ_p is reached with probability 1 also under every general strategy of p against σ, from every state of Reach_p, and the expected number of steps until then is finite, because the minimal probability of reaching a set of states in a finite Markov decision process is attained by a memoryless deterministic policy [Baier & Katoen, 2008] (Chapter 10). The payoff of p is then a real number whatever p does. The statement concerns Reach_p only: a state that is reachable only after φ_p has held may be a deadlock state or lie on a cycle, and this does no harm. I.7 to I.9 are defined for a profile at the valuations at which the design is well-defined (H.5) and the profile is admissible. A profile that is not admissible at θ has no equilibrium status there. I-8 requires admissibility at the fixed values; I-9 and I.9 say what is required on the region of an equilibrium map. Admissibility is weaker than requiring that the game end under all profiles: it concerns the deviations of one player at a time from the profile that is asked about.

Fix a design D that is well-defined at θ and a profile σ that is admissible at θ. Nash equilibrium. σ is a Nash equilibrium of D at θ when no player gains by deviating alone: for every player p and every general strategy τ of p, the payoff of p when p plays τ and every other player plays as in σ is at most u_p(D, θ, σ). The notion concerns unilateral deviations only, from a profile that is named in the file. Memoryless deterministic deviations suffice. When the other players play as in σ, what remains is a finite Markov decision process on Reach_p in which p alone chooses, with the reward ρ_p(s, c) = Σ_k w_k[θ] · (reward of r_k for taking c in s) per step, of either sign, accumulated until φ_p. The stochastic shortest path problem of [Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis, 1991] is this problem with costs −ρ_p and the states of φ_p as the destination. Its two assumptions are that a proper stationary policy exists (one that reaches the destination with probability 1 from every state) and that every improper stationary policy has an infinite cost from some state; costs may have either sign. Under them, the optimal cost is the unique solution of Bellman's equation and is attained by a stationary deterministic policy. Here every stationary policy is proper, because σ is admissible for p, so the first assumption holds and the second holds vacuously. A policy that depends on the history or randomises attains no more: for every such policy and initial state there is a randomised policy that depends on the step and the current state only and has the same probability of every pair of a state and a command at every step ([Puterman, 1994], Section 5.5), hence the same expected total reward, and a randomised choice in a state attains at most the maximum over the commands in Bellman's equation. Hence the best-response value BR_p(D, θ, σ) = max over the strategies τ of p of u_p(D, θ, σ[p↦τ]) a maximum over finitely many strategies in the sense of I.4, is the supremum over all general strategies of p, and σ is a Nash equilibrium of D at θ exactly when BR_p(D, θ, σ) = u_p(D, θ, σ) for every player p. The claim "σ is a Nash equilibrium" thus covers deviations by all general strategies, although the profile itself is memoryless and deterministic. It says nothing about equilibria in which the players themselves randomise or use memory. Deviation gain. The deviation gain of p is gain_p(D, θ, σ) = BR_p(D, θ, σ) − u_p(D, θ, σ) It is never negative, since σ's own strategy of p is among the candidates. A strategy τ of p with u_p(D, θ, σ[p↦τ]) = BR_p(D, θ, σ) is a best response of p to σ. ε-equilibrium. For a number ε ≥ 0, σ is an ε-equilibrium of D at θ when gain_p(D, θ, σ) ≤ ε for every player p. A Nash equilibrium is a 0-equilibrium. ε is compared with the payoff of each player in that payoff's own unit; the appendix does not relate the units of different players. Deciding it at a valuation. Checking σ at θ consists of one best-response problem per player: evaluate u_p in the Markov chain M(D, θ, σ), and solve the Markov decision process of p on Reach_p for BR_p. Both are solved exactly by linear equations and policy iteration over the rational numbers when the parameters are rational. Values from a state. For a state s of Reach_p, write V_p(s) for the payoff of p under σ, and V*_p(s) for the best-response value of p, in the game started in s instead of s₀; both are 0 when φ_p holds in s. For a state s of Reach_p in which φ_p does not hold and a command c allowed in s, write Q_p(s, c) = ρ_p(s, c) + Σ_s′ P(s, c, s′) · V_p(s′) Q*_p(s, c) = ρ_p(s, c) + Σ_s′ P(s, c, s′) · V*_p(s′) Q_p(s, c) is the payoff of p when c is taken once in s and σ is followed afterwards. V*_p is the unique solution of V*_p(s) = max over the allowed commands c of Q*_p(s, c), and BR_p = V*_p(s₀). Equilibrium from every reachable state. σ is an equilibrium from every reachable state at θ when V*_p(s) = V_p(s) for every player p and every state s of Reach_p: no player gains by deviating alone, wherever in Reach_p it starts to deviate. This implies that σ is a Nash equilibrium. The converse does not hold: σ can be a Nash equilibrium although p could gain in a state that is reached only when p itself deviates. Version 0.1 does not offer this stronger notion, or subgame perfection, as a query (concept: is reserved); it is defined because the following test establishes exactly it, and a result says so when it was obtained that way (I.8, I.9). The one-step test. V*_p(s) = V_p(s) for every state s of Reach_p exactly when Q_p(s, c) ≤ V_p(s) for every state s of p in Reach_p in which φ_p does not hold and every command c of En(s). If the inequalities hold, V_p solves Bellman's equation, whose solution is unique; if one fails in s, taking c once in s gains from s. The test is therefore necessary and sufficient for "no gain of p from any state of Reach_p", and sufficient, not necessary, for gain_p = 0. The reported best response. Among the best responses of p, the canonical best response is the strategy that selects, in a state s of p in Reach_p in which φ_p does not hold, the command that σ selects when Q*_p(s, c) = V*_p(s) for it, and otherwise the first command c of En(s), in the order of model.commands:, with Q*_p(s, c) = V*_p(s); in every other state it selects what σ selects. It is a best response, it is determined by the file, and it differs from σ only where the command of σ is not optimal.

model.equilibria: lists equilibrium queries. An entry without over: is an equilibrium check: it asks, for each design listed in regimes: (default: all designs), whether the profile named by profile: (default: the compliance profile) is an ε-equilibrium of the design at the fixed values of all parameters (H.3), with ε given by epsilon: (default 0). In a file without transitions: the only design is base (H.6); regimes: is then omitted or is [base]. The result, per design, consists of: for every player p: the payoff u_p, the best-response value BR_p, and the deviation gain; the status: equilibrium when every gain is at most ε, and not_equilibrium otherwise; for not_equilibrium: the non-empty set deviators of the players whose gain exceeds ε, and for each of them the canonical best response (I.7), as the list of the states that are reachable from the initial state under σ[p↦τ] before φ_p holds and in which it selects another command than the profile, in the order of S (variables in declaration order, values in the order of their domains), each with the action label selected; from_every_state: true when the processor has established that the profile is an equilibrium from every reachable state (I.7), false when it has established that it is not, and absent or null when it has not examined the question. It is reported only with the status equilibrium and ε = 0. By I-8 the profile is admissible at the fixed values. A processor that evaluates a check at other values (I.13) first establishes that the design is well-defined and the profile admissible there, and reports an error otherwise. A processor that reports results MUST compute them with exact arithmetic or with numerics that have a sound error bound, or mark the result as approximate; a status that the error bound does not decide is inconclusive (as in H.8).
documents.s: I.8 Equilibrium checks at the fixed values

documents.t: An entry of model.equilibria: with over: is an equilibrium map query. Its keys: over: gives the open parameters, at least one and at most four, each with a closed interval [lo, hi], lo < hi, within the declared range, as in H.9. The region B is the box of these intervals. A parameter in over: MUST NOT be assigned by any regime in model.regimes: and MUST NOT occur in a reward value:; it may occur in probabilities and in weights. Institutional parameters may be opened like any other: a map over λ is asked for by opening the parameter bound to lambda. profile:, regimes:, epsilon: as in I.8. resolution: is a number r with 0 < r < 1: the fraction of the volume of B that may remain undecided, per design. For a design D and a valuation v ∈ B, θ(v) agrees with v on the open parameters and has the fixed values of D elsewhere (H.7). Write U_p(v), BR_p(v), and gain_p(v) for the payoff, the best-response value, and the deviation gain of p in D at θ(v) for the profile of the query; they are defined where D is well-defined and the profile admissible at θ(v). What is asked. For each listed design: at which valuations of B is the profile an ε-equilibrium? A cell is a closed box contained in B (H.9). The profile is an equilibrium on a cell C when, at every v ∈ C, D is well-defined and the profile admissible at θ(v), and gain_p(v) ≤ ε for every player p. A player p is a deviator on a cell C when, at every v ∈ C, D is well-defined and the profile admissible at θ(v), and gain_p(v) > ε. The result. The answer consists of one equilibrium map per listed design. An equilibrium map is a finite set of cells that cover B and whose interiors are pairwise disjoint, each with a status, together with the undecided fraction (the volume of the undecided cells divided by the volume of B) and whether it is at most resolution:. status Claim Reported with it equilibrium the profile is an equilibrium on the cell from_every_state (see below) not_equilibrium every player in deviators is a deviator on the cell deviators, a non-empty set of players undecided none reason deviators contains only players who gain at every valuation of the cell; a processor SHOULD list every player for whom it has established this. A cell that lies across the surface on which the deviator changes, so that at every valuation some player gains but no single player does everywhere, stays undecided until a refinement separates the parts. For a not_equilibrium cell a processor SHOULD also report, for each deviator, a strategy that gains more than ε at every valuation of the cell, when its method provides one (as condition N below does), and for every decided cell the bounds of the gains it established. from_every_state is true for an equilibrium cell when the processor has established that the profile is an equilibrium from every reachable state (I.7) at every valuation of the cell, and absent or null otherwise. For a cell the field does not depend on ε: it is a statement about gains of zero and is stronger than the claim of an ε-equilibrium, so it may be true also when ε > 0. An undecided cell SHOULD carry a reason: not_well_defined (the processor has not established that the design is well-defined on the cell), not_admissible (it has not established that the profile is admissible on the cell, or has found a valuation at which it is not), or bounds (its bounds do not decide the cell, or the budget is exhausted). A cell that contains both a valuation at which the profile is an ε-equilibrium and one at which it is not can have neither status. Where the two kinds of valuations meet, as at λ* in I.12, such cells remain however fine the partition, which is why resolution: is greater than zero. A processor MAY report the union of cells as one cell when the union is a box and the claim holds on each part: the same status; for not_equilibrium, deviators a non-empty subset of the deviators of every part, with a deviation only where the same strategy was reported for that deviator in every part; from_every_state: true only when every part carries it; gain_bounds the hull. Maps of several designs over the same region answer "in which regimes, and where, is the profile an equilibrium". The cells of two designs need not coincide; a processor MAY report the maps on a common refinement. Certified. equilibrium and not_equilibrium are claims about every valuation of the cell, and the certification requirement of H.9 applies to them: a processor MUST NOT make them unless it has established them by a method that is sound for the whole cell, with exact arithmetic or numerics with a sound error bound. Evaluation at sample points is not such a method on its own. Only certified cells count toward resolution:. A processor that cannot reach the requested resolution still reports the map and says so, and it SHOULD name its method. Estimates at sample points MAY be reported separately, as in H.9; they never change the status of a cell. Well-definedness and admissibility on the region. The claims presuppose that I.7 is defined on the cell. A processor MUST NOT claim equilibrium or not_equilibrium for a cell unless it has established that the design is well-defined (H.5) and the profile admissible (I.6) at every valuation of the cell. Checking the corners of a box is not enough for admissibility. A probability can be positive inside a box and zero at a corner, so the corners have the smallest graphs and the interior the largest. For a design whose probabilities are all multi-affine in the open parameters (no open parameter occurs with a power above one in a probability, the value of rest included) the following holds. Call a face of the box B a set obtained by fixing some of the open parameters, possibly none, at an end of their intervals and letting each of the others range over the open interval between its ends; B has 3ⁿ faces for n open parameters, and every valuation of B lies in exactly one of them. If the design is well-defined at the corners of B, a probability is a positive combination of its values at the corners of a face at every valuation of that face, so it is zero at one valuation of a face only if it is zero on the whole face. The graph of the game is therefore the same at all valuations of one face, and since admissibility depends on the graph only: For a design whose probabilities are multi-affine in the open parameters and that is well-defined at the corners of B, a profile is admissible at every valuation of B exactly when it is admissible at the centre of each of the 3ⁿ faces of B (the valuations in which every open parameter is at the lower end, the middle, or the upper end of its interval). I-9 requires this check. For such a design, a failure at the centre of a face means that the profile is not admissible at any valuation of that face. A region that touches a degenerate end, for example a retry loop whose success probability is 0 at lo, is therefore an error of the file, and the author shrinks the interval. When the check succeeds for such a design, the profile is admissible on every cell, and nothing remains to be established per cell for admissibility; a bounding method may still fail on a cell, for example the relaxation on a cell that touches such a face; that cell is undecided with the reason bounds. The reason not_admissible of an undecided cell can therefore occur only for a design that is not multi-affine. For a design with a probability that is not multi-affine, the processor establishes admissibility for each cell, for example by the relaxation below, or leaves the cell undecided with the reason not_admissible. Deciding a cell from bounds. For a player p and a cell C, let R_C(p) be a set of states that contains s₀ and, with a state s in which φ_p does not hold, every state s′ such that P(s, c, s′) is positive at some valuation of C for some command c allowed in s for p (I.6); it contains Reach_p at every valuation of C. Suppose a method gives, for each player p, numbers that hold at every valuation v of C: l_p ≤ U_p(v) ≤ u_p, bounds of the payoff under the profile; b_p ≥ BR_p(v), an upper bound of the best-response value; for one or more strategies τ of p, d_p(τ) ≤ U_p(τ, v), a lower bound of the payoff of p under the profile in which p plays τ; for every state s of R_C(p), numbers l_p(s) and u_p(s) with l_p(s) ≤ V_p(s, v) ≤ u_p(s) for every v in C and every state s of Reach_p at θ(v) (both 0 when φ_p holds in s), and, for every state s of p in R_C(p) in which φ_p does not hold and every command c of En(s), a number q_p(s, c) with q_p(s, c) ≥ Q_p(s, c, v) for every v in C at which s is a state of Reach_p at θ(v). Nothing is required at a valuation at which s is not reachable, where V_p(s, v) need not exist. Such a number is obtained from an upper bound of the step payoff ρ_p(s, c) on C and the upper bounds u_p(s′) of the successors: q_p(s, c) is at least ρ_p(s, c) + Σ_s′ μ(s′) · u_p(s′) for every distribution μ that the command can have on C. Then: N. p is a deviator on C when d_p(τ) − u_p > ε for some strategy τ of p. E1. gain_p(v) ≤ ε on C when b_p − l_p ≤ ε. E2. V*_p(s, v) = V_p(s, v) for every state s of Reach_p at every valuation of C, and in particular gain_p(v) = 0 on C, when q_p(s, c) ≤ l_p(s) for every state s of p in R_C(p) in which φ_p does not hold and every command c of En(s) other than the one the profile selects (the one-step test of I.7, with the upper bound of the deviating command against the lower bound of the profile in the same state). The profile is an equilibrium on C when every player satisfies E1 or E2. It is an equilibrium from every reachable state at every valuation of C (from_every_state: true) when every player satisfies E2. These conditions are sufficient, not necessary. E1 compares a bound of one function with a bound of another, as the conditions of H.9 do, and here the two functions touch: BR_p(v) ≥ U_p(v) everywhere, with equality wherever p does not gain. With ε = 0, E1 therefore holds only when U_p is constant on the cell and both bounds are exact. That is the case when the open parameters occur only in weights of terms that are zero under the profile, as λ does in I.12; it is not the case as soon as an open parameter changes the payoff under the profile. E2 does not have this defect: it compares the payoff of a one-step deviation with the payoff of the profile in the same state, and these differ at the valuations where the deviation strictly loses. E2 establishes more than is asked, so it fails on a cell of Nash equilibria in which p could gain in a state that only its own deviation reaches. A cell next to the boundary stays undecided under all three conditions. Bounds by parameter lifting (informative). The relaxation of H.14 extends to the game of one player against the profile. On a cell, every state chooses, independently of the other states, a distribution for each of its allowed commands; a state of the player under study chooses a command as well, and every other state of a player takes the command the profile selects. When the probabilities of a command are multi-affine in the open parameters, the distributions to choose from are those at the corners of the cell, and the distribution at any valuation of the cell is a mixture of them. When they are not, corners do not suffice: each probability is enclosed by an interval on the cell, as H.14 describes, and the state chooses a vertex of the set of distributions within these intervals. The step payoff ρ_p(s, c) is enclosed by its extreme values on the cell (at the corners when the weights are multi-affine in the open parameters, by interval arithmetic otherwise). The states reachable in the relaxed process form a set R_C(p). When every policy of the relaxed process reaches φ_p with probability 1, the profile is admissible for p on the cell; the maximal value of the process with the upper step payoffs is a number b_p, and the minimal and maximal values with the player's commands fixed by τ or by the profile, with the lower and the upper step payoffs, are numbers d_p(τ), l_p, and u_p, and with each state of R_C(p) as the initial state, l_p(s) and u_p(s). For condition N, a strategy τ can be chosen, for example, as the canonical best response of p (I.7) at the centre of the cell, restricted to the states that are reachable under it there; it decides how much of a region gets not_equilibrium. Other sound methods are admissible, for example exact reasoning on the rational functions U_p and BR_p, or a proof that a gain is convex or monotone in a parameter (J.7).

A processor that implements the extension MUST, in a file that declares games: 0.1, apply the rules of H.10 with the changes stated here, and in addition: I-1. A file that declares games: 0.1 MUST also declare stochastic: 0.1; otherwise the processor reports an error and does not interpret the keys of this extension. I-2. kind:, if present, MUST be dtmc or smg (this replaces the last sentence of S-1). A model with kind: smg MUST have players: with at least one player, profiles:, compliance:, and payoffs:. A model whose kind: is dtmc or absent MUST NOT have players:, profiles:, compliance:, payoffs:, or equilibria:, an owner: on a command, or a profile: on a property or regime map; it is a model of Appendix H, and S-9 applies to it. I-3. The id of a player MUST be an identifier, MUST NOT be a keyword of A.11, IN, or rest, and MUST be unique among the players. The keywords F, U, P, and R of the property sub-language are admitted, since a player id occurs in no expression. actors: MUST list at least one actor reference, each naming a declared actor. Two players MUST NOT list references with the same actor name, and neither may one player. I-4. owner: MUST name a declared player. An owned command MUST have an action:. The commands with one action label MUST all have the same owner or all be unowned. I-5. (Replaces S-9 for a strategic model.) For every design and every state of S, reachable or not, the commands that exist in the design and have a true guard MUST be at most one command, or commands that are all owned by the same player and have pairwise different action labels. This is decided by enumerating S. I-6. The name of a profile MUST be an identifier, MUST NOT be one of the keywords that S-2 excludes, and MUST be unique among the profiles. In a rule, choose: MUST be the action label of an owned command, and guard: MUST be a boolean state_pred over variables and enumeration literals (S-6), without labels. For every design and every state of S in which two or more commands are enabled, some rule of every profile MUST apply (I.4). compliance: MUST name a profile. A processor SHOULD warn about a rule that is the first applicable rule in no state of any design. (profiles: is a YAML mapping: a processor that reads the file through a YAML loader cannot detect two profiles with the same name, since the loader keeps one of them; the same holds for the labels of H.4.) I-7. model.payoffs: MUST have exactly one entry for every player, and player: MUST name a declared player. until: MUST be a boolean state_pred in which labels may be used as in a property (S-6). terms: MUST have at least one term; reward: MUST name a declared reward structure, at most once per payoff; weight: MUST be a number or a param_expr whose identifiers are declared parameters. A processor SHOULD warn when the target of a payoff holds in the initial state: the payoff is then 0 under every profile. The keys sanction_of: and reward_of: of a term are defined by Appendix J. In a file that does not declare grounding: 0.1, a term that has one of them is an error. In a file that declares it, a processor that does not implement Appendix J MUST NOT evaluate a payoff that has such a term, nor a query that needs that payoff: it reports the query as not evaluated, with a diagnostic that names the term. Every entry of equilibria: needs the payoffs of all players and is then not evaluated; properties and regime maps need no payoff and are evaluated, and I-8 and I-9 need only the targets of the payoffs. Such a term is never read as a term with the default weight. I-8. Every design MUST be well-defined at its fixed values (S-11), and every profile of the file MUST be admissible (I.6) in every design at the fixed values. This is weaker than requiring that every play of the game end. I-9. The id of an entry of equilibria: MUST be an identifier that S-2 admits and MUST be unique in the namespace of properties and regime maps. profile: MUST name a profile. regimes: MUST name designs of the file, at least one, each once. epsilon: MUST be a finite number that is not negative. over: and resolution: MUST satisfy the conditions that S-14 states for a regime map (over: has one to four declared parameters, each with lo < hi within the declared range and none assigned by any regime; 0 < r < 1); resolution: MUST NOT appear without over:. Unlike a regime map (S-10), an entry with over: is allowed in a file without transitions:, where it concerns the design base. A parameter in the over: of an entry of equilibria: MUST NOT occur in the value: of a reward item. For every listed design, a processor MUST check that the design is well-defined at the corner points of the region (as S-14) and at the centre of every face, and that the profile is admissible at the centre of every face of the region (I.9: every open parameter at the lower end, the middle, or the upper end of its interval, 3ⁿ valuations); a failure at one of these valuations is an error of the file (for a multi-affine design the profile is then inadmissible on the whole face, I.9). For a design whose probabilities are multi-affine in the open parameters these checks decide both properties on the whole region (S-14, I.9). For any other design they do not; the processor then establishes both for each cell or leaves the cell undecided, and it MUST NOT certify a cell on which it has not established them. I-10. The profile: of a property or of a regime map MUST name a profile. S-12 to S-14 apply to a strategic model unchanged, with M(D, θ, σ) in the place of the regime model. I-11. A processor SHOULD emit an informational diagnostic for a key or value reserved in I.1 and MUST NOT give it a meaning (this replaces the list of S-15 for a file that declares games: 0.1). A reserved value (kind: mdp, a motivation. source) gets this diagnostic in addition to the error of I-2 or S-3. The rules S-2 to S-8 and S-10 to S-14 apply to a strategic model as written. A weight is not a probability and not a reward value: no rule restricts its sign or its range.

PRISM-games reads turn-based stochastic multi-player games in an extension of the PRISM modelling language: the model type is smg, and each player is declared by a player … endplayer construct that lists the action labels, in square brackets, and the modules that the player controls. A state in which all available transitions belong to one player is controlled by that player; actions and modules need not be allocated to a player as long as no state has several such transitions; a state whose transitions are owned by several players is an error [Kwiatkowska+, CAV 2020]. These are the conditions of I-4 and I-5. PRISM-games computes expected total rewards only for a stopping game, one in which terminal states with zero reward are reached with probability 1 under all strategies, which is more than the admissibility of I.6. Storm (stormpy 2.0.0) parses an exported smg file but refuses to build it unless every command is owned by a player; the export targets PRISM-games. H.11 does not apply to a strategic model as written: a design of a strategic model is not a Markov chain, and a processor MUST NOT export it as a dtmc file. Version 0.1 defines no export of the Markov chain M(D, θ, σ) of a profile either. A processor MAY export a design of a strategic model as the model file of H.11 with two changes: the first line is smg instead of dtmc; after it, for each player that owns a command of the design, in declaration order, one construct that lists the action labels of the commands of the design that the player owns, in the order of their first declaration: smg player R_ [careful], [careless] endplayer A player that owns no command of the design is not written. All commands of the design are written, whatever a profile selects; unowned commands and the deadlock command are allocated to no player. A player name is renamed by the rule of H.11 when it equals a keyword (R is one, hence player R_). For a strategic model the list of keywords of H.11 is extended by player, endplayer, smg, csg, and tptg, the keywords that the PRISM-games manual adds to the PRISM language; every name of the exported model is renamed by this extended list. This appendix does not determine whether PRISM-games accepts a player whose name equals another identifier of the model; an exporter SHOULD report such a name. A parameter that is open only in an equilibrium map is written with its fixed value (I.13). Version 0.1 defines no properties file for a strategic model. A payoff is a sum of expected rewards with weights of either sign, and the question of I.7 is a best response to a fixed profile. The property language of PRISM-games states what a coalition can guarantee against the other players, as in <<p1>> R{"r"}max=? [ F "success" ] [Chen+, FMSD 2013], and equilibria of its own choosing; neither is the question of this appendix, and a translation is left to a later version. The syntax above was checked against the PRISM-games manual (accessed Nov. 2026); files exported in this form have not been run through PRISM-games (I.14).

The first example extends that of H.12 by one choice; the second, at the end of the section, adds a choice of the dispatcher. Before each attempt the robot decides whether to follow the handling procedure. A careful attempt costs the robot an effort of 1 and succeeds with the probability s of H.12. A careless attempt costs no effort and succeeds with probability s/2. The dispatcher pays a fee of 10 for a delivered parcel, and a careless attempt is sanctioned: the robot loses 2·λ, where 2 is the size of the sanction at full intensity and λ is the incentive intensity of the contract. One more variable, settled, and one chance command, settle, close the task, so that the fee is the reward of a step. sos: name: "RobotDeliveryGame" type: Acknowledged extensions: - stochastic: 0.1 - games: 0.1 actors: - { id: DISPATCHER, role: "Assigns and replans routes" } - { id: "ROBOT[1..N]", role: "Delivers parcels" } contracts: - id: DELIVERY parties: [DISPATCHER, "ROBOT[*]"] information: { alpha: 0.9 } authority: { decision_holder: DISPATCHER, beta: 0.9 } incentives: { lambda: 0.1 } transitions: - { from: CENTRALIZED, to: DISTRIBUTED, condition: "loss_rate > 0.3" } - { from: DISTRIBUTED, to: CENTRALIZED, condition: "loss_rate <= 0.2" } model: kind: smg parameters: - { id: p_fail, range: [0, 0.5], value: 0.05 } - { id: p_loss, range: [0, 0.5], value: 0.1 } - { id: alpha, from: "DELIVERY.alpha" } - { id: beta, from: "DELIVERY.beta" } - { id: lambda, from: "DELIVERY.lambda" } # 0.1, range [0, 1] - { id: q_local, range: [0, 1], value: 0.6 } variables: - { id: task, type: "{Pending, Delivered}", init: Pending } - { id: attempts, type: "[0..3]", init: 0 } - { id: settled, type: bool, init: false } labels: delivered: "task == Delivered" players: - { id: R, actors: ["ROBOT[*]"] } - { id: D, actors: [DISPATCHER] } commands: - action: careful owner: R guard: "task == Pending AND attempts < 3" updates: - prob: "beta * alpha * (1 - p_fail) * (1 - p_loss) + (1 - beta) * q_local" set: { task: Delivered, attempts: "attempts + 1" } - prob: rest set: { attempts: "attempts + 1" } - action: careless owner: R guard: "task == Pending AND attempts < 3" updates: - prob: "0.5 * (beta * alpha * (1 - p_fail) * (1 - p_loss) + (1 - beta) * q_local)" set: { task: Delivered, attempts: "attempts + 1" } - prob: rest set: { attempts: "attempts + 1" } - action: settle guard: "(task == Delivered OR attempts == 3) AND NOT settled" updates: - set: { settled: true } regimes: CENTRALIZED: { parameters: { beta: 0.9 } } DISTRIBUTED: { parameters: { beta: 0.1 } } rewards: - { id: fee, items: [ { action: settle, guard: "task == Delivered", value: 1 } ] } - { id: effort, items: [ { action: careful, value: 1 } ] } - { id: shortcuts, items: [ { action: careless, value: 1 } ] } profiles: comply: - { choose: careful } shortcut_first: - { guard: "attempts == 0", choose: careless } - { choose: careful } compliance: comply payoffs: - player: R until: "settled" terms: - { reward: fee, weight: 10 } - { reward: effort, weight: -1 } - { reward: shortcuts, weight: "-2 * lambda" } - player: D until: "settled" terms: - { reward: fee, weight: 5 } properties: - { id: P_DELIVERY, expr: "P>=0.95 [ F<=3 delivered ]" } - { id: P_DELIVERY_SHORTCUT, profile: shortcut_first, expr: "P=? [ F<=3 delivered ]" } equilibria: - { id: comply_nash } - { id: shortcut_nash, profile: shortcut_first } - { id: comply_by_lambda, over: { lambda: [0, 1] }, resolution: 0.05 } - id: comply_by_lambda_and_failure regimes: [CENTRALIZED, DISTRIBUTED] over: { lambda: [0, 0.4], p_fail: [0, 0.5] } resolution: 0.05 The game. The model has 16 states, 11 of them reachable. In the states with task == Pending AND attempts < 3 the two commands of R are enabled: these are the states of R (I-5). In the states with task == Delivered OR attempts == 3 that are not yet settled, the unowned command settle is enabled: these are chance states. The settled states are deadlock states. The player D owns no command and has no choice; it is declared so that the fee has a receiver. Every path reaches settled within four steps whatever R does, so every profile is admissible at every valuation, and all probabilities lie in [0, 1] on the regions of the two maps. The profile comply selects careful in every state of R. The profile shortcut_first selects careless before the first attempt, by its first rule, and careful afterwards. Under comply the model is that of H.12 with one more step, so P_DELIVERY has the values of H.12: 0.984848 (satisfied) in CENTRALIZED and 0.943796 (violated) in DISTRIBUTED. Under shortcut_first, P_DELIVERY_SHORTCUT is 1 − (1 − s/2)(1 − s)²: 0.961808 and 0.898534. Computed values in this section are rounded to six decimals. The closed form. Write g = 10 for the fee, c = 1 for the cost of effort, m = 2 for the size of the sanction, and s for the probability that a careful attempt succeeds (s_C = 0.75255 and s_D = 0.61695 at the fixed values, H.12). Let V_k be the payoff of R under comply from a state in which k attempts remain: V_0 = 0, V_k = s·g − c + (1 − s)·V_(k−1) V_1 = s·g − c, V_2 = (s·g − c)(2 − s), V_3 = (s·g − c)(1 + (1 − s) + (1 − s)²) V_3 is the payoff of R under comply; λ does not occur in it, because comply takes no careless attempt. A single careless attempt with k attempts remaining, followed by comply, gives −m·λ + (s/2)·g + (1 − s/2)·V_(k−1). It is at most V_k exactly when λ ≥ T_k, where T_k = ( c − (s/2)·(g − V_(k−1)) ) / m Being careless saves the effort c and loses, with probability s/2, the difference between delivering now and continuing. Let λ* = max(0, T_1, T_2, T_3) T_1 = ( c − (s/2)·g ) / m T_2 = ( c − (s/2)·(g − (s·g − c)) ) / m T_3 = ( c − (s/2)·( g·(1 − s)² + c·(2 − s) ) ) / m (for T_3, g − V_2 = g·(1 − s)² + c·(2 − s)). For 0 ≤ s < 1, comply is a Nash equilibrium of a design at θ exactly when λ ≥ λ*. Under comply each of the three states of R is reached with positive probability, since an attempt fails with probability 1 − s > 0. So R has no gain exactly when the one-step test of I.7 holds in the three states, that is, when λ ≥ T_k for k = 1, 2, 3; D has no choice and no gain. The condition s < 1 is needed for "exactly": at s = 1 the later states are reached only when R deviates. When s·g ≥ c, that is for s ≥ 0.1, V_0 ≤ V_1 ≤ V_2 and therefore T_1 ≤ T_2 ≤ T_3, so λ* = max(0, T_3): the temptation is greatest before the first attempt, when a failure can still be repaired. This is the case at the fixed values and on the regions of the two maps below, where s ≥ 0.4245. It is not the case for small s: at s = 0.07695 (DISTRIBUTED with q_local = 0), T_1 = 0.307625 is the largest of the three. By the same computation, for 0 ≤ s < 1, shortcut_first is a Nash equilibrium exactly when max(0, T_1, T_2) ≤ λ ≤ T_3: R must prefer the shortcut before the first attempt and care afterwards. In both designs T_1 and T_2 are negative at the fixed values (T_2 is −0.153684 and −0.245044) and T_3 is positive. There, for every λ ≥ 0, a careless attempt later than the first one loses, shortcut_first is the best response for λ < λ*, it is a Nash equilibrium exactly when λ ≤ λ*, both profiles are equilibria at λ = λ*, and gain_R = max(0, m·(λ* − λ)) = max(0, 2·(λ* − λ)) The checks. At the fixed values, with λ = 0.1: CENTRALIZED DISTRIBUTED s 0.75255 0.61695 λ* = T_3 480347064349/3200000000000 = 0.150108 193194567781/3200000000000 = 0.060373 under comply: expected fee, effort, shortcuts 0.984848, 1.308682, 0 0.943796, 1.529777, 0 u_R under comply 6831840915651/800000000000 = 8.539801 6326547012219/800000000000 = 7.908184 under shortcut_first: expected fee, effort, shortcuts 0.961808, 0.778066, 1 0.898534, 0.956414, 1 u_R under shortcut_first 8.840018 − 2·λ = 8.640018 8.028930 − 2·λ = 7.828930 u_D under comply / shortcut_first 4.924241 / 4.809042 4.718981 / 4.492672 comply_nash: BR_R, gain_R 8.640018, 160347064349/1600000000000 = 0.100217 7.908184, 0 comply_nash: status not_equilibrium, deviators: R, canonical best response: careless in the state with attempts == 0 equilibrium, from_every_state: true shortcut_nash: gain_R, status 0, equilibrium, from_every_state: true 126805432219/1600000000000 = 0.079253, not_equilibrium, deviators: R With the declared λ = 0.1, compliance is an equilibrium in the distributed regime and not in the centralised one. The gain of D is 0 in every check. When R takes the shortcut, D loses: the fee is paid less often. The map over λ. comply_by_lambda opens λ on [0, 1] in both designs. A cell [a, b] is an equilibrium cell exactly when a ≥ λ*, and R is a deviator on it exactly when b < λ*; the cell that contains λ* in its interior is undecided. Conditions E1 and N of I.9 decide all other cells, with exact bounds: U_R is constant in λ, the largest best-response value on the cell is the one at λ = a, and the payoff of shortcut_first is least at λ = b. A processor that bisects the largest undecided cell until the resolution of 0.05 is reached, and joins cells with the same claim (I.9), reports: Design not_equilibrium (deviators: R) undecided (reason: bounds) equilibrium Undecided fraction CENTRALIZED [0, 1/8] [1/8, 5/32] [5/32, 1] 1/32 DISTRIBUTED [0, 1/32] [1/32, 1/16] [1/16, 1] 1/32 For 0.060373 ≤ λ < 0.150108, compliance is an equilibrium in DISTRIBUTED only; from 0.150108 on, in both. The map over λ and the failure probability. comply_by_lambda_and_failure also opens p_fail. With the other parameters fixed, s_C = 0.729·(1 − p_fail) + 0.06 and s_D = 0.081·(1 − p_fail) + 0.54, and in each design comply is an equilibrium exactly where λ ≥ λ*(s). T_3 increases with s on the range of s that occurs, so the region in which compliance is not an equilibrium lies below a curve that falls as p_fail grows. Values of λ* for checking an implementation: p_fail s_C λ*, CENTRALIZED s_D λ*, DISTRIBUTED 0 0.789 0.173313 0.621 0.062908 0.05 0.75255 0.150108 0.61695 0.060373 0.1 0.7161 0.125857 0.6129 0.057859 0.2 0.6432 0.077118 0.6048 0.052897 0.3 0.5703 0.032907 0.5967 0.048028 0.4 0.4974 0 0.5886 0.043261 0.5 0.4245 0 0.5805 0.038604 In CENTRALIZED, T_3 = 0 at s = 1/2, that is at p_fail = 289/729 = 0.396433: when the dispatcher fails that often, a failed attempt costs the robot so much that it is careful without any sanction. Up to p_fail = 0.2 the centralised regime needs the stronger incentive; at p_fail = 0.3 the distributed one does. On this map U_R varies with p_fail, so E1 decides no equilibrium cell (I.9); the cells away from the curve are decided by E2 and N.

In the first example only the robot chooses, so the check of each player is an optimisation of one player. In the second, the dispatcher chooses too: before the first attempt it decides whether to monitor the robot, at a cost κ, or to trust it. A careless attempt is sanctioned only when the dispatcher monitors. The file is that of the first example with the following changes (the commands careful and careless keep their updates): model: kind: smg parameters: # ... as above, and: - { id: kappa, range: [0, 1], value: 0.05 } # cost of monitoring variables: - { id: watch, type: "{Open, On, Off}", init: Open } # ... task, attempts, settled as above commands: - action: monitor owner: D guard: "watch == Open AND task == Pending AND attempts == 0" updates: - set: { watch: "On" } - action: trust owner: D guard: "watch == Open AND task == Pending AND attempts == 0" updates: - set: { watch: "Off" } - action: careful owner: R guard: "watch != Open AND task == Pending AND attempts < 3" # updates as above - action: careless owner: R guard: "watch != Open AND task == Pending AND attempts < 3" # updates as above - action: settle guard: "watch != Open AND (task == Delivered OR attempts == 3) AND NOT settled" updates: - set: { settled: true } rewards: - { id: fee, items: [ { action: settle, guard: "task == Delivered", value: 1 } ] } - { id: effort, items: [ { action: careful, value: 1 } ] } - { id: shortcuts, items: [ { action: careless, guard: "watch == On", value: 1 } ] } - { id: monitoring, items: [ { action: monitor, value: 1 } ] } profiles: comply: - { choose: monitor } - { choose: careful } comply_if_watched: - { choose: monitor } - { guard: "watch == Off AND attempts == 0", choose: careless } - { choose: careful } compliance: comply payoffs: - player: R until: "settled" terms: - { reward: fee, weight: 10 } - { reward: effort, weight: -1 } - { reward: shortcuts, weight: "-2 * lambda" } - player: D until: "settled" terms: - { reward: fee, weight: 5 } - { reward: monitoring, weight: "-kappa" } equilibria: - { id: comply_nash } - { id: watched_nash, profile: comply_if_watched } - id: watched_map profile: comply_if_watched regimes: [CENTRALIZED] over: { lambda: [0, 0.4], kappa: [0, 0.4] } resolution: 0.25 The model has 48 states. The initial state is a state of D; the states with watch != Open AND task == Pending AND attempts < 3 are states of R; the guards are written so that I-5 holds in the unreachable states too. Every path reaches settled within five steps, so every profile is admissible at every valuation. Both profiles let D monitor and R be careful along the path that is played, so they give the same payoffs: u_R is V_3 as before, and u_D = 5·(1 − (1 − s)³) − κ. They differ in what R would do if D did not monitor: under comply, R is careful all the same; under comply_if_watched, R takes the shortcut before the first attempt. R. While D monitors, the game of R against either profile is the first example, so gain_R = max(0, 2·(λ* − λ)) at the fixed values, with the λ* of the first example. The states with watch == Off are not in Reach_R, and what the profile selects there does not matter for R. D. Against comply, trusting saves κ and changes nothing else, so gain_D = κ: for every κ > 0, D is a deviator and comply is not a Nash equilibrium, whatever λ is. Against comply_if_watched, trusting saves κ and lets R take the shortcut, which lowers the probability of delivery from 1 − (1 − s)³ to 1 − (1 − s/2)(1 − s)². With κ* = 5 · (s/2) · (1 − s)² D loses 5·(s/2)(1 − s)² − κ by trusting, and gain_D = max(0, κ − κ*). comply_if_watched is a Nash equilibrium of a design, at the fixed values of the other parameters, exactly when λ ≥ λ* and κ ≤ κ*. The behaviour that is played is the one of comply; it is an equilibrium only together with what the robot would do when it is not watched, which is what makes monitoring worth its cost. CENTRALIZED DISTRIBUTED λ* 0.150108 0.060373 κ* 368638137651/3200000000000 = 0.115199 724187274219/3200000000000 = 0.226309 u_R, u_D under both profiles (λ = 0.1, κ = 0.05) 8.539801, 7798786117651/1600000000000 = 4.874241 7.908184, 7470368854219/1600000000000 = 4.668981 u_D when D trusts, against comply / comply_if_watched 4.924241 / 4.809042 4.718981 / 4.492672 comply_nash: gain_R, gain_D 0.100217, 1/20 0, 1/20 comply_nash: status not_equilibrium, deviators R and D not_equilibrium, deviator D watched_nash: gain_R, gain_D 0.100217, 0 0, 0 watched_nash: status not_equilibrium, deviator R equilibrium In comply_nash the canonical best response of D is trust in the initial state. In watched_nash for DISTRIBUTED the one-step test holds for both players, so the result carries from_every_state: true. The map. watched_map opens λ and κ in CENTRALIZED. R is a deviator where λ < 0.150108 and D where κ > 0.115199. On the uniform partition of the region into 4 × 4 cells (not the cells of a bisection), the conditions of I.9 give the following; the columns are the intervals of λ, the rows those of κ: κ \ λ [0, 0.1] [0.1, 0.2] [0.2, 0.3] [0.3, 0.4] [0.3, 0.4] not_equilibrium, R and D not_equilibrium, D not_equilibrium, D not_equilibrium, D [0.2, 0.3] not_equilibrium, R and D not_equilibrium, D not_equilibrium, D not_equilibrium, D [0.1, 0.2] not_equilibrium, R undecided undecided undecided [0, 0.1] not_equilibrium, R undecided equilibrium equilibrium A bisection decides λ ∈ [0, 0.4] × κ ∈ [0.2, 0.4] as one cell with deviators: [D]; a coarser cell can list fewer deviators. Four of the 16 cells are undecided, with the reason bounds: the undecided fraction is 1/4, which is the resolution: of the query. N decides the deviators: for R with the strategy that is careless before the first attempt while watched, whose payoff is least at the upper end of λ; for D with trust, against the payoff of the profile at the lower end of κ. In the cells of the second column and the two upper rows, D is a deviator and R is not established as one, because λ* lies inside the column; deviators lists what is established. In the two equilibrium cells, E2 holds for both players (for D: the payoff of trust, 4.809042, is at most the lower bound 4.824241 of the payoff of the profile at κ = 0.1), so they carry from_every_state: true. E1 holds for R, whose payoff under the profile is constant, and fails for D, whose payoff under the profile falls with κ.

documents.t: The field stochastic_model of H.13 is extended for a strategic model. kind is "smg". Every command has a field owner (a player id, or null), after action. Every property has a field profile after regimes, and every regime map a field profile after regimes, with the default filled in. Every parameter has a field open_in_equilibria after open: true when some entry of equilibria: lists the parameter in over:. The open field keeps its meaning of H.13 (open in some regime map), and only open decides how a parameter is written by H.11: a parameter that is open in an equilibrium map only is exported with its fixed value. Five fields are added after regime_maps, in this order: { "stochastic_model": { "kind": "smg", // ... the fields of H.13 "players": [ { "id": "R", "actors": ["ROBOT[*]"] }, { "id": "D", "actors": ["DISPATCHER"] } ], "profiles": [ { "id": "comply", "rules": [ { "guard": "true", "choose": "careful" } ] }, { "id": "shortcut_first", "rules": [ { "guard": "attempts == 0", "choose": "careless" }, { "guard": "true", "choose": "careful" } ] } ], "compliance": "comply", "payoffs": [ { "player": "R", "until": "settled", "terms": [ { "reward": "fee", "weight": "10" }, { "reward": "effort", "weight": "-1" }, { "reward": "shortcuts", "weight": "-2 * lambda" } ] } // ... D ], "equilibria": [ { "id": "comply_nash", "profile": "comply", "regimes": ["CENTRALIZED", "DISTRIBUTED"], "epsilon": 0, "over": null, "resolution": null }, { "id": "comply_by_lambda", "profile": "comply", "regimes": ["CENTRALIZED", "DISTRIBUTED"], "epsilon": 0, "over": { "lambda": [0, 1] }, "resolution": 0.05 } // ... shortcut_nash, comply_by_lambda_and_failure ] } } Guards, targets, and weights are kept as text, like the expressions of H.13; the defaults of I.2 are filled in. profiles is a list in the order of the file. For a model of Appendix H the five fields are absent and owner, profile, and open_in_equilibria are not written, so the IR of a file that does not use the extension is unchanged. Results of analyses are not in the IR. Results (informative, but a processor that emits JSON SHOULD use this shape). Exact numbers are strings: an integer, or a fraction "n/d" in lowest terms. The result of an equilibrium check (abridged): { "id": "comply_nash", "profile": "comply", "epsilon": "0", "designs": [ { "design": "CENTRALIZED", "parameters": { "p_fail": "1/20", "lambda": "1/10" /* ... every parameter */ }, "status": "not_equilibrium", // equilibrium | not_equilibrium | inconclusive | not_evaluated "deviators": ["R"], // [] unless not_equilibrium "from_every_state": null, // true | false | null "players": [ { "player": "R", "payoff": "6831840915651/800000000000", "best_response_value": "13824028895651/1600000000000", "gain": "160347064349/1600000000000", "best_response": [ { "state": { "task": "Pending", "attempts": 0, "settled": false }, "action": "careless" } ] }, { "player": "D", "payoff": "7878786117651/1600000000000", "best_response_value": "7878786117651/1600000000000", "gain": "0", "best_response": [] } ] } // ... DISTRIBUTED ] } The result of an equilibrium map query: { "id": "comply_by_lambda", "profile": "comply", "epsilon": "0", "over": { "lambda": ["0", "1"] }, "resolution": "1/20", "designs": [ { "design": "CENTRALIZED", "method": "...", "parameters": { "p_fail": "1/20" /* ... every parameter that is not open */ }, "cells": [ { "box": { "lambda": ["0", "1/8"] }, "status": "not_equilibrium", "deviators": ["R"] }, { "box": { "lambda": ["1/8", "5/32"] }, "status": "undecided", "reason": "bounds" }, { "box": { "lambda": ["5/32", "1"] }, "status": "equilibrium", "from_every_state": true } ], "undecided_fraction": "1/32", "resolution_reached": true } // ... DISTRIBUTED ] } When a processor does not evaluate a query because a payoff has a sanction_of: or reward_of: term that it does not implement (I-7), the result of each design, in a check and in a map, is { "design": "...", "status": "not_evaluated", "reason": "..." }, where reason names the term, and has no other field. A map result carries, per design, a field parameters like that of a check, with the fixed values of the parameters that are not open. players is in the order of declaration, and cells in the lexicographic order of their lower corners, with the parameters in the order of over:; best_response is the canonical best response of I.7, with the values of all variables in declaration order, and is empty for a player without a gain above ε. A cell may also carry deviations (for each deviator, a strategy in the form of best_response) and gain_bounds (for each player, a pair of a lower and an upper bound). Processor behaviour. A processor that offers the checks and maps as a command MUST distinguish three outcomes by its exit status: Exit status Meaning 0 every requested result was computed, whatever the answers (equilibrium or not_equilibrium, any number of undecided cells within the resolution) 1 some result is inconclusive or not_evaluated, or some map did not reach its resolution: 2 nothing can be claimed: a static error of the file, a usage error of the command, or a design that is not well-defined or a profile that is not admissible at the values at which the command was asked to evaluate When the command lets the user give a parameter another value than its fixed value (as --set of cadl model-check does), the value MUST lie in the declared range, giving a value to a parameter that the evaluated query lists in over: is a usage error (exit status 2), and the processor MUST check, for every design and profile of the evaluated queries, that the design is well-defined and the profile admissible at the values it uses (for a map, the checks of I-9) before it evaluates. When the command lets the user restrict the evaluation to one design (as --regime), a query whose regimes: does not list that design is reported with "the query does not concern this design", which is not an error (exit status 0). A command MAY offer to start a map from the uniform partition of the region into N intervals per open parameter and to report the cells as analysed, without joining them (I.9); in cadl game-check these are --partition N and --no-merge.
documents.s: I.13 Intermediate Representation (IR) addition and results

documents.t: The reference implementation implements games 0.1 from cadl 0.3.23 as follows. Up to 0.3.22, cadl check reported the extension name games as unknown and a strategic model as errors of S-1 and S-9 (see H.14). cadl check applies the rules I-1 to I-11 (the SHOULDs as warnings), including the corner and face-centre checks of I-9, and lowers the strategic model to the IR of I.13. A player id may be F, U, P, or R (I-3). Two profiles with the same name cannot be detected (I-6), because the file is read through a YAML loader. An undeclared use of the keys of this appendix gets one informational diagnostic (I.15). cadl game-check evaluates the equilibrium checks of I.8 with exact rational arithmetic (explicit enumeration, policy iteration), and, with --certify, the equilibrium maps of I.9 by the relaxation of I.9 on top of the solvers of the certified regime maps (H.14). Options: --equilibrium ID (repeatable), --regime, --set, --certify, --max-depth, --max-cells, --partition N, --no-merge, --format text|json. Without --certify the maps are listed as not computed; naming a map with --equilibrium without --certify is a usage error. The results and exit statuses are those of I.13; inconclusive does not occur, since the arithmetic is exact. For condition N it uses the canonical best response at the centre of the cell (I.9) and tries N only for a player for whom E1 and E2 fail. Cells with the same claim are joined (I.9) unless --no-merge is given. cadl model-export writes the file of I.11 (smg and the player constructs, with the renaming of H.11 and of the keywords that I.11 adds for a strategic model, and a check that two players do not collide). A payoff with a sanction_of: or reward_of: term gets the weight of J.7, and J-14 is used in --certify (J.11); the status not_evaluated of I.13 remains for a processor without Appendix J. Every number of I.12 is reproduced by cadl game-check: payoffs, best-response values, and gains as the fractions printed; λ* and κ* through the gains, and the table of λ* by --set; statuses, deviators, and from_every_state. The maps of the first example have 3 cells per design after joining for comply_by_lambda (11 cells analysed, about 0.4 s for both designs), and 257 and 17 cells after joining (3 849 and 271 analysed, about 6.3 s) for comply_by_lambda_and_failure, with the fractions given in I.12 (CENTRALIZED: 0.808838 equilibrium, 0.141235 not_equilibrium, 409/8192 undecided). For watched_map a bisection gives 5 cells after joining (17 analysed); --partition 4 --no-merge gives the table of I.12. Times are wall-clock on a laptop. Verification by the implementer, with an oracle that shares no code with cadl and enumerates every memoryless deterministic strategy: 2 500 random parametric games with 2 or 3 players, cycles, signed weights with parameters, parameters in probabilities (also not multi-affine), regions that touch probability 0 or 1, and ε ∈ 1. Every decided cell (1 933 equilibrium, 2 504 not_equilibrium) was evaluated at the corners, face centres, and centre and at random rational points: 69 195 point evaluations, no wrong claim. The checks at the fixed values agreed with the oracle on all 2 500 models. Five soundness errors injected into the code were each detected. The payoff under the profile and the best-response value were compared with Storm (stormpy 2.0.0, exact) on the game of one player against the profile, written as an MDP: 90 values, all equal as rational numbers. An independent review ran 860 generated models through the command line (cadl check, cadl game-check --certify): 76 921 exact point evaluations of decided cells, no wrong claim. It compared 244 best-response values with Storm, all equal, and found no regression against cadl 0.3.22. Not exercised: the export of I.11 was not run through PRISM-games. Games with three or more players occur only in the implementer's fuzzing. Maps with more than two open parameters were not measured.

Files written against CADL v0.3 without this extension remain valid and are read the same way. A file that declares stochastic: 0.1 and not games: 0.1 is read by Appendix H unchanged: the names that H.1 reserves stay reserved for it, and S-1, S-9, and S-15 apply. A file that uses kind: smg or the keys of this appendix without declaring games: 0.1 does not conform to this appendix. A processor that implements the extension reads the model: block of such a file by Appendix H and SHOULD report the keys as an undeclared extension, with an informational diagnostic. A file that declares games: 0.1 without stochastic: 0.1 gets the error of I-1. A processor that implements Appendix H and not this appendix cannot read a strategic model as a Markov chain. H.10 (S-1) and H.15 say what it does with a file that declares games: 0.1 and has a model whose kind: is not dtmc: it skips the model with one informational diagnostic and MUST NOT evaluate it as a Markov chain; the block is not checked by S-2 to S-15, not lowered to the IR, and not exported. Processors that implement neither extension MUST NOT reject a file because of model:; they SHOULD emit a single informational diagnostic per file.

This appendix specifies the grounding extension to CADL. It builds on the norms extension (Appendix F) and adds the key grounding: to contract_def (A.4), the keys shares: and on_fulfilment: to norm_def and the key magnitude: to on_violation: (F.3), and, in a file that also uses the strategic model extension (Appendix I), the keys sanction_of: and reward_of: to a payoff term (I.2). With them, a processor computes from the norms of a contract two derived indices, α̂ and β̂, and the incentive coverage χ, all in [0, 1], and compares the declared alpha and beta with the indices. The extension also defines the weight of a payoff term that is declared to stand for the sanction of a norm in a strategic model: the size the norm declares, multiplied by λ. The core language does not mandate these keys; a conforming CADL processor that does not implement the extension MUST NOT reject a file because of them. It SHOULD accept them syntactically and emit an informational diagnostic. The extension is named grounding and this appendix describes version 0.1. It requires norms: 0.1. A file that uses it MUST declare both under extensions: (A.2); J.12 says what a processor does with an undeclared use. The keys sanction_of: and reward_of: additionally require stochastic: 0.1 and games: 0.1. sos: ... extensions: - norms: 0.1 - grounding: 0.1
documents.s: Appendix J — Grounding of the Institutional Parameters in Norms (grounding 0.1)

documents.t: Section 5.4.2 defines the institutional parameters α, β, and λ as numbers in [0, 1] with qualitative end points, and nothing else in the language says what an intermediate value means. A designer writes beta: 0.7, and no rule relates that number to the contract in which it stands. Appendix F states an intended reading (β describes who holds the powers of a contract, α which triggers and contents the other parties can observe, and λ scales the sanctions of violated norms) and leaves it informative; Section 9.6 lists the formal link between norms and the parameters as open, and RD-1.5 asks for λ to be treated as a parameter of the contracts. The classification of institutional rules by what they affect, among them information rules, aggregation rules, and payoff rules [Ostrom, 2005], suggests that the three parameters summarise three kinds of norms. Grounding 0.1 is a first step. It does not give α, β, and λ a formal meaning in terms of norms; that remains open beyond what follows. Two indices and a coverage are computed from the file. J.4 defines α̂, β̂, and χ as ratios of counts over finite sets that are read from one contract. They are reproducible in the sense that two processors compute the same numbers from the same file. For α̂ both counts rest on annotations of the author (the items and the shares: lists), so the index is as good as the annotation. Indices are evidence, not meaning. The indices do not replace the declared parameters and do not change Section 5.4.2. They are structural facts about the norms of a contract with which a declared value can agree or disagree. J.4 says what they cannot capture. Declared values are compared with them. A disagreement between a declared α or β and its index is a warning that names the construct concerned (J.5).
