ID Description C-1 Be able to map to the five-layer framework [Shimoyama & Matsubara, 2026]; the mapping is given in Section 2.2. C-2 Be able to describe SoS classifications (D/A/C/V-SoS) from [ISO/IEC/IEEE 21841:2019]. C-3 Be able to integrate with IEC 62853 [IEC 62853:2018] process views (consensus-building, accountability, fault response, change management). C-4 Have a formal foundation based on assume-guarantee contract semantics.

Based on use case analysis in Chapter 8 and a survey of existing research, we organize research directions toward CADL realization and development. For each direction, we state what the current state of the art already provides (named tools and results), what remains open for CADL, and the concrete research challenges that CADL should address. Where an existing tool already solves part of a problem, we say which part CADL would hand to that tool and which question the tool cannot answer. The starting point is this specification (Version 0.3) and the reference implementation cadl 0.3.23. It checks the satisfiability of contracts with Z3 [de Moura & Bjørner, 2008], detects protocol deadlocks by structural analysis, supports the SoS-DSL extension (Appendix E: lifecycle:, monitors:, deadline:), generates Python, Solidity, OPA/Rego, and Unity C# code, drafts CADL from natural language with cadl ai (a parse / type-check / retry loop, and with --verify the checks of cadl verify), and reports a mapping to IEC 62853 (Chapter 10). Statements below that no work addresses a given problem are based on a limited literature search (mainly 2023–2026). They mean that we did not find such work, not that none exists.

Establishment of an algebraic foundation for safely composing and decomposing multiple institutional descriptions is necessary. Benveniste et al. [Foundations and Trends in EDA, 2018] theorized parallel composition of contracts C₁ ⊗ C₂ in component design. Since then the algebra of assume-guarantee contracts has been largely completed: hypercontracts give closed forms for composition and quotient (the specification of a missing component) over hyperproperties [Incer+, NFM 2022], and Pacti computes the algebraic operations of contract theory efficiently [Incer+, arXiv 2023]. OCRA checks the refinement of contracts written in LTL, including metric real-time constraints [Cimatti+, ASE 2013]; Kind 2 checks that the modes of a contract cover its assumptions [Champion+, CAV 2016]; and contracts have been composed across agents with quantitative temporal requirements [Dewes & Dimitrova, AAAI 2025]. SysML v2 [OMG, 2025] gives requirements an assume constraint and a require constraint, and SAWS² connects a fragment of SysML v2 to OCRA, nuXmv, and xSAP [FBK, SAWS²]. What remains open for CADL is the institutional interpretation of these operators. The parties of a CADL contract are autonomous organisations whose compliance depends on incentives rather than on the designer's authority; composition must therefore be indexed by institutional parameters and its guarantees must hold in equilibrium. Switching between whole operating modes (regimes), including the transitional phase, must be safe, and the algebra must stay open to constituents joining and leaving. For example, when composing household chore-sharing institution with shared resource usage institution, a theory that algebraically guarantees absence of obligation conflicts and incentive interference is required. Mode-aware contracts address components, and the evolution of SoS configurations has been checked without a contract algebra [Etzien+, ISORC 2013]. We found no work that models normative concepts (obligation, permission, sanction) in SysML v2. The structure of the institutional parameter space (α, β, λ) is a second open area. Parameter synthesis for parametric Markov chains and MDPs already partitions a parameter space into regions certified to satisfy or to violate a property [Junges+, FMSD 2024]; Storm implements it and can be called from Python [Hensel+, STTT 2022], and monotonicity checking proves, region by region, that a probability increases or decreases with a parameter [Spel+, ATVA 2019]. These tools answer whether one design satisfies a threshold on a region. They do not answer which design is best where, which is the question of a regime map. The stochastic model extension (Appendix H, stochastic 0.1) is a first step on RD-1.3: it lets a file state a parametric Markov model in which α, β, and λ appear, defines the regime map as a query whose result is a set of certified cells, and fixes an export to the PRISM language. The reference implementation computes certified cells by parameter lifting (H.14). The strategic model extension (Appendix I) adds the game reading of Section 9.7 to that model, and the grounding extension (Appendix J) lets a payoff term take the size of a sanction from a norm and multiply it by λ, a first step on RD-1.5 in which λ is a parameter of a model, not yet of a composition. Deriving the model from contracts and scaling beyond small models remain open. ID Challenge Content RD-1.1 Institutional Composition Algebra Build parallel composition and merging on the existing hypercontract results [Incer+, NFM 2022], and concentrate CADL's own contribution on sequential and choice composition and on the institutional interpretation of the three layers (Institution, Protocol, Algorithm), with soundness proofs. RD-1.2 Institutional Refinement Relations Formal proofs that overview level → design level → verification level refinements preserve institutional properties. Use OCRA's temporal refinement [Cimatti+, ASE 2013] and Pacti's refinement check [Incer+, arXiv 2023] as the means of checking refinement between description levels. RD-1.3 Certified Regime Maps by Parameter Synthesis Translate CADL descriptions into parametric MDPs (PRISM/JANI) in which α, β, and λ appear in transition probabilities and rewards; generate certified regions per regime with Storm [Hensel+, STTT 2022]; prove qualitative design laws (for example, that raising α does not lower the mission success probability in a region) by monotonicity checking [Spel+, ATVA 2019]; and define comparative region verification ("which regime is best where") as a new problem. Exact partitioning is practical only for a few parameters [Junges+, FMSD 2024], so the scale of this approach is an open question. RD-1.4 Safety of Regime Transitions Lift mode exhaustiveness (as checked by Kind 2 [Champion+, CAV 2016]) and proof obligations before and after a mode transition to switches between centralised and decentralised regimes, with an explicit contract for the transitional phase. Course D of the hands-on materials shows that switching without waiting for the shared road to clear breaks the safety invariant. RD-1.5 Incentive-parameterised Composition Treat λ as a parameter of the contracts and compute, through the quotient, the range of λ under which the composition of constituent contracts refines the system contract. Related to the equilibrium analysis of RD-7.2. RD-1.6 Interoperability with SysML v2 Map actors to part def and contracts to requirement def with assume constraint and require constraint [OMG, 2025]; delegate the algebraic computation to SAWS²/OCRA [FBK, SAWS²] or Pacti; add normative concepts and regimes as a CADL model library, since SysML v2 does not define them.

Establishment of technology to explicitly formalize institutional knowledge implicitly shared in household rules and community customs as CADL descriptions is required. IndoorWorld [Wu+, Findings of EMNLP 2025] realizes behavior simulation of LLM agents in indoor environments, but the inverse problem of extracting institutional rules from observed behavior patterns (institutional reverse engineering) remains unaddressed. For timed properties, procedures that mine signal temporal logic specifications from traces have been surveyed [Bartocci+, Inf. Comput. 2022]. LLM-based translation into formal specifications is accurate only for simple targets. A fine-tuned model reached more than 95% accuracy in translating natural language into temporal logic with abstracted propositions, while GPT-4 with few-shot prompting reached 77.7% [Chen+, EMNLP 2023]. For TLA+, the best of thirty LLMs produced semantically correct specifications in 8.6% of the cases [Bisharat+, ICSOFT 2026]. The LLM-based generation of Symboleo [Zitouni+, 2025] assessed 38 prompt configurations against 16 error types and found the results promising but with many remaining errors. cadl ai already loops over parsing, type checking, and retries, and with --verify runs the SMT and deadlock checks; this assures syntactic validity and consistency, not that the description is faithful to the source text. We found no benchmark for translating deontic content (obligation, permission, remedy). ID Challenge Content RD-2.1 Institutional Inference from Behavioral Observation Algorithm to infer potential institutional rules (implicit authority structures, information sharing patterns, incentive structures) from IoT sensor data and behavior logs. Includes estimating candidate deadline values and guarantee thresholds from simulation and monitor logs by specification mining [Bartocci+, Inf. Comput. 2022]. RD-2.2 LLM-based Institutional Description Generation and Faithfulness Checking Technology to generate CADL descriptions from natural language interview records and meeting minutes, extending LLM-based Symboleo generation [Zitouni+, 2025] to general institutional descriptions. Beyond the syntactic checks of cadl ai, check faithfulness: compare round-trip translations (NL → CADL → NL), validate the generated contracts against scenario traces in the CADL simulator, and show the reviewer the clauses with low confidence. RD-2.3 Tacit Knowledge Ontology for Institutions Build ontology systematically classifying and structuring implicit institutional knowledge. Map Ostrom [1990] IAD framework [Ostrom, 2005] to CADL vocabulary. RD-2.4 NL→CADL Benchmark A benchmark of natural-language institutional descriptions paired with reference CADL descriptions and scenario traces, including deontic content, to measure the accuracy and faithfulness of RD-2.2 and of other translators [Bisharat+, ICSOFT 2026].
documents.s: 9.2 Extraction and Institutionalization of Tacit Knowledge

documents.t: Developing the concept of Digital Twins of Organization [Lyytinen+, J. Organization Design, 2024], establishment of technology to build and simulate institutions themselves as digital twins is the next-generation research direction. Lyytinen et al. argue that a full twin of an organization may not be feasible because organizations involve agency, conflict, and emergence; a reply argues that a twin built for a narrow purpose from digital trace data is feasible [Winkler & Kremser, J. Organization Design, 2024]. A CADL description can serve as the normative layer of such a narrow twin: it mirrors the agreed rules, not the whole organization. vCity [BSC] and Social Digital Twin [Fujitsu] advance twinning of physical and social aspects, but twinning of institutions (governance structures, rules, incentives) is, to our knowledge, not their main target. Dynamic assurance cases connect a model to runtime evidence. Starting from dynamic safety cases [Denney+, ICSE 2015], ACCESS evaluates an assurance case both at design time and at runtime, where the validity of the case depends on runtime data checked by a monitor [Wei+, JSS 2024], and Trusta checks LLM-drafted assurance cases against formal constraints [Chen+, SCP 2025]. The notations are GSN Community Standard Version 3 [SCSC-141C, 2021] and OMG SACM 2.3 [OMG SACM, 2023]. The divergence between a model and the running system is studied as models@run.time [Bencomo+, SoSyM 2019]. Three problems remain open for CADL. First, the dynamic assurance cases we found assure a single technical system; we found none whose claims are the obligations, permissions, and amendment procedures of several organizations and whose evidence comes from monitors owned by different parties. Second, research on twin synchronization assumes that reality corrects the model. For an institution the model is normative: a divergence is either a violation by a participant (evidence against an assurance claim) or a drift in which the rules actually in force changed without an amendment of the CADL description (the twin is stale), and observation alone does not tell them apart. Updating the model automatically to fit observed practice would ratify violations. Third, statistical evaluation of institutions on a simulator needs confidence bounds, and experiments on institutions change the behaviour of the people who take part in them. ID Challenge Content RD-3.1 Institutional Simulator Technology to automatically generate institutional simulation models from CADL descriptions and what-if analyze impacts of institutional parameter changes. MAPF simulator integration is initial target. Wrap the simulator as a black-box oracle for statistical model checking, attach a confidence interval to each parameter point, and mark boundaries where the intervals of competing regimes overlap as statistically indistinguishable; export to JANI to reach both exact tools (RD-1.3) and statistical model checkers such as modes [Budde+, TACAS 2018]. RD-3.2 Divergence Classification and Connection to Amendment Detect divergence between institutional operation and the CADL description by checking monitor traces against it, and classify each divergence as a violation or as a drift. A violation is handled by the contract (violation handling and sanctions) and counts as evidence against the assurance case. A drift is not corrected by updating the description automatically: it goes through the amendment procedure (in Course D, a constitution gate and a versioned record of amendments) and from there into the change management process of IEC 62853 [IEC 62853:2018]. RD-3.3 Verified Institutional A/B Testing Technology to operate different institutional designs in parallel and compare their performance. Institutional parameters proposed by reinforcement learning, as in AI Economist [Zheng+, 2022], or by LLM agents are certified with the methods of RD-1.3 and RD-7.1 before they are deployed. The "rationality" of LLM agents is not the rationality assumed by game theory, and this must be stated as a precondition of any claim. Because experiments on institutions affect their participants, they need a framework of ethics and consent. RD-3.4 Assurance Cases Generated from CADL Derive the claims of an assurance case deterministically from contract elements, use design-time static checks and operation-time monitor verdicts as evidence, output the case in GSN [SCSC-141C, 2021] or SACM [OMG SACM, 2023], and use it as the dependability case of IEC 62853. Re-evaluate the case when monitors report, as ACCESS does for technical systems [Wei+, JSS 2024]. Open points: argument patterns for institutional claims (fairness, accountability, amendability), aggregating confidence over monitors owned by different organizations, and referring to the constituents' own assurance cases as away goals.

Scalability of formal verification and code generation of institutions is one of the most critical challenges toward practical deployment. To complete verification of SoS descriptions containing 100+ actors and 50+ contracts within practical time, theoretical analysis of computational complexity of verification methods and development of efficient algorithms are necessary. Some bounds are already known for the strategic questions of Section 9.7: checking LTL properties on the equilibria of probabilistic systems is 2EXPTIME-complete [Gutierrez+, KR 2021]; designing incentives so that a property holds on equilibria is in PSPACE for LTL and in NP or Σ₂ᴾ for GR(1) goals [Gutierrez+, LMCS 2024]; and verifying incentives with quantitative goals is 2EXPTIME-complete [Hyland+, KR 2024]. Practical tools will therefore need restricted fragments such as GR(1) [Piterman+, VMCAI 2006], finite traces, or bounded horizons. ID Challenge Content RD-4.1 Computational Complexity of Institutional Verification Determine computational complexity classes for consistency verification, deadlock detection, safety verification, realizability of temporal contract sets, and equilibrium properties of CADL descriptions respectively, starting from the known results above. Identify decidability boundary conditions and the fragments (for example GR(1) [Piterman+, VMCAI 2006]) that keep them tractable. RD-4.2 Abstraction-based Scalable Verification Methods to efficiently verify large-scale SoS through hierarchical abstraction of institutional descriptions. Application of counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR) [Clarke+, 2000] to institutional verification, and compositional assume-guarantee reasoning per constituent for the equilibrium checks of Section 9.7. RD-4.3 Incremental Verification Confirm consistency through differential verification rather than full re-verification when actors join or leave or institutions change. Formulate leaving as the quotient C_sys / C_rest (the specification that a replacement must satisfy given the remaining constituents) and joining as re-checking the refinement of the new composition, computable with Pacti [Incer+, arXiv 2023] for the fragments it supports. We found no work that formulates join and leave this way; earlier work on evolving SoS checks the reachability of critical configurations without a contract algebra [Etzien+, ISORC 2013].

For CADL to be applied to international SoS, support for different legal systems, cultural norms, and language environments is necessary. The EU Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854) sets essential requirements for smart contracts used for the automated execution of data sharing agreements, but institutional compatibility with other jurisdictions (Japan, US, China, etc.) remains an unresolved challenge. For data usage, ODRL is used as the policy layer of data spaces [Iannella+, W3C Blog 2025], and the draft ODRL Formal Semantics of the W3C Community Group defines deontic states for permissions, prohibitions, and duties and separates access control from monitoring; it leaves remedies unformalized and the handling of conflicts pending [W3C ODRL CG, Formal Semantics]. We found no reliable source that maps the obligations of the EU Data Act to ODRL policies, and CADL does not assume such a mapping. ID Challenge Content RD-5.1 Cross-jurisdictional Institutional Compatibility Verification Technology to detect legal contradictions when composing CADL descriptions from different jurisdictions (e.g., differences between EU GDPR [Regulation (EU) 2016/679] and Japanese Personal Information Protection Act [Act No. 57 of 2003]). For data-sharing norms, refer to the conflict semantics of ODRL as it is formalized [W3C ODRL CG, Formal Semantics]. RD-5.2 Parameterization of Cultural Norms Technology to model cultural dimensions (collectivism/individualism, power distance, uncertainty avoidance, etc.) as institutional parameters and handle cross-cultural governance differences quantitatively. RD-5.3 Multilingual Institutional Description Enable CADL overview-level descriptions in multiple languages with AI verifying institutional equivalence across languages. This goes beyond NFR-7 (internationalization), which only requires that human-readable text can be written in any language.

CADL contracts describe normative agreements, but norms are not yet first-class objects with their own state over time. Symboleo [Sharifi+, 2020] treats obligations and powers as objects with lifecycles (creation, activation, suspension, resumption, fulfilment, violation, termination), SymboleoPC translates Symboleo to nuXmv and checks LTL and CTL properties [Parvizimosaed+, SoSyM 2025], and Symboleo specifications have been translated into smart contracts [Rasti+, MODELS 2022]. The normative programming language NPL handles obligations with deadlines and sanctions in multi-agent organisations [Hübner+, AMAI 2011], and constitutive norms (counts-as) create institutional facts from other facts, as distinct from regulative norms [Boella & van der Torre, KR 2004]. Norms can also be synthesized automatically for multi-agent systems [Alechina+, KR 2022]. On the side of time and monitoring, RTAMT computes the robustness of signal temporal logic online, and its interface-aware variant separates input signals from output signals, which matches CADL's split between assume and guarantee [Ničković & Yamaguchi, ATVA 2020] [Yamaguchi+, STTT 2024]. R2U2 compiles temporal specifications into hardware or software observers [Johannsen+, CAV 2023]. An assumption can make more properties monitorable by restricting the traces a monitor must handle [Henzinger & Saraç, RV 2020]. Deontic runtime verification identifies the party to blame [Kharraz+, ICTAC 2023] and distinguishes where a violation is detected from where it occurred [Colombo+, ISoLA 2024]. Monitoring has been decentralized [Francalanza+, 2018], and shields synthesized from temporal safety specifications block unsafe actions [Alshiekh+, AAAI 2018], also per agent without communication [Melcer+, NeurIPS 2022]. In the core language, assume and guarantee are state predicates without temporal operators, deadlines exist only on lifecycle transitions (deadline:), monitors are hand-written rule: predicates, and Z3 is used only for satisfiability. The norms extension (Appendix F, norms 0.1) is a first step on RD-6.1, RD-6.2, RD-6.3, and RD-6.5: it defines first-class norms, bounded temporal operators with four-valued verdicts, counts-as rules, and what happens to running norms on an amendment. The generated Python code monitors norms at run time (F.10). The grounding extension (Appendix J, grounding 0.1) is a first step towards the link to α, β, and λ: it derives from the norms of a contract an index of information sharing over declared items and an index of the concentration of powers, compares the declared α and β with them, measures how many norms carry a sanction or a reward, and gives sanctions a numeric magnitude that λ scales. The indices are counts and are evidence about a contract, not the meaning of the parameters. The formal meaning of α, β, and λ in terms of norms, design-time checking by a model checker, monitoring in the other generated runtimes, indices that are weighted or aggregated over the contracts of an SoS, norms per regime, and the derivation of model probabilities from norms remain open. We found no work that handles first-class norm objects together with the institutional parameters α, β, and λ, the composition of many contracts in an SoS, and amendment during operation. We also found no tool that connects deontic blame semantics with efficient monitoring engines, or that lets several organizations, each observing only its own interface with unsynchronized clocks, agree on a verdict and on the responsible party. ID Challenge Content RD-6.1 First-class Norm Objects A candidate norms: block whose norms have a kind (obligation, permission, prohibition, power), a bearer, a counterparty, a trigger, a deadline, and the handling of violation (a contrary-to-duty obligation or a sanction), with the lifecycle of Symboleo [Sharifi+, 2020]. Check norms at design time by translation to nuXmv, as SymboleoPC does [Parvizimosaed+, SoSyM 2025], and export data-sharing norms to ODRL. The holder of a power corresponds to β, the observability of trigger and fulfilment to α, and the size of a sanction to λ; whether the probability of compliance can be analysed as a function of λ and α is an open question. RD-6.2 Temporal Assume-Guarantee and Four-valued Verdicts Allow bounded MTL/STL in contracts and give four verdicts: pending (open and within its deadline), fulfilled, violated, and assumption violated (the provider is not to blame) [Henzinger & Saraç, RV 2020]. Translate them to RTAMT for the Python backend [Yamaguchi+, STTT 2024] and to generated observers in the style of R2U2 for the Unity C# backend [Johannsen+, CAV 2023]. RD-6.3 Counts-as Bridge to Protocols Rules of the form "message m in protocol P counts as institutional event e in contract C" [Boella & van der Torre, KR 2004], so that protocol traces change the state of norms. RD-6.4 Cross-organizational Monitoring and Blame Placement of monitors (provider, consumer, neutral third party) [Francalanza+, 2018], uncertainty of clocks, tamper-evident records, and tracing the cause of a violation upstream along the graph of delegated contracts, using the blame semantics of deontic runtime verification [Kharraz+, ICTAC 2023] [Colombo+, ISoLA 2024]. RD-6.5 Continuity of Norms across Amendments Define what happens to obligations that are active, suspended, or violated when a regime transition or an amendment takes effect: carried over, discharged, or transformed, together with transitional provisions and the time a version takes effect. To our knowledge Symboleo, ODRL, and NPL do not define this. Course D of the hands-on materials amends rules while the system runs and lists the missing syntax for transitional provisions; its research exercise on the speed of amendment is a first experiment. RD-6.6 From Monitoring to Enforcement Synthesize per-party shields [Alshiekh+, AAAI 2018] [Melcer+, NeurIPS 2022] or Simplex-style fallback behaviour from CADL contracts, using the lifecycle state machines as the finite abstraction. The shields we found act on physical actions; we found none for institutional acts.

CADL assumes that constituent systems keep their operational and managerial independence, so they may not comply with a contract when compliance does not pay. Rational verification checks whether a temporal property holds on the Nash equilibria of a multi-agent system: EVE takes modules with LTL goals and reduces the problem to parity games [Gutierrez+, AI 2020], and the problem has been extended to probabilistic systems [Gutierrez+, KR 2021]. Recent work moved from checking to design: equilibrium design chooses incentives within a budget so that a property holds on equilibria [Gutierrez+, LMCS 2024], incentive design handles static and dynamic incentives with quantitative goals [Hyland+, KR 2024], and norms can be synthesized against strategic objectives [Alechina+, KR 2022]. PRISM-games verifies Nash and correlated equilibria of concurrent stochastic games with social-welfare and fairness criteria [Kwiatkowska+, TACAS 2022] and has been extended to psychological games, whose payoffs depend on beliefs [Kwiatkowska+, 2024]. Bayesian incentive compatibility of mechanisms has been reduced to model checking [Mittelmann+, AAAI 2023]. Learning-based institution design such as AI Economist [Zheng+, 2022] gives no formal guarantee. What remains open for CADL is a map rather than a point. Equilibrium design finds one incentive scheme; CADL needs the range of λ (and of the motivation parameters ρ and κ, Appendix C) in which compliance is an equilibrium. We found no tool that combines parametric transition probabilities with equilibrium computation, and little work on equilibria when constituents observe only part of the state, which is what α controls. The strategic model extension (Appendix I, games 0.1) is a first step on RD-7.1 and RD-7.2. It reads the model of Appendix H as a turn-based stochastic game and defines when a named memoryless deterministic profile, in particular the compliance profile, is an equilibrium against unilateral deviations, and the equilibrium map: the cells of a region of parameters, λ among them, on which the profile is certified to be such an equilibrium or not to be one. It does not compute the equilibria of a game. With the grounding extension (Appendix J) the sanction term of a payoff is, by definition, the magnitude of a norm multiplied by λ, and under the conditions of J.7 the set of λ at which compliance is an equilibrium is empty or an upper interval. The extension is implemented from cadl 0.3.23 (I.14). Concurrent moves, mixed strategies, properties that must hold on every equilibrium, the mediator and the value of centralisation of RD-7.2, the motivation parameters ρ and κ, and partial observation (RD-7.3) remain open. ID Challenge Content RD-7.1 Verifying that Compliance is Rational Translate CADL constituent systems and their goals into the input of EVE [Gutierrez+, AI 2020] or into concurrent stochastic games for PRISM-games [Kwiatkowska+, TACAS 2022], and check whether the compliance properties hold on every equilibrium. Use restricted fragments (Section 9.4) to keep the checks tractable. RD-7.2 Parametric Equilibrium Analysis Compute the region of λ, ρ, and κ in which compliance is an equilibrium. Model a centralized mediator as a correlated equilibrium and decentralized operation as a Nash equilibrium, and measure the difference between their values at each parameter point as the value of centralization (β). Relates to RD-1.3 and RD-1.5. RD-7.3 Equilibria under Partial Observation Equilibrium analysis when each constituent observes only what the information sharing degree α allows, with compositional reasoning per constituent for scale.

LLM-based agents are becoming constituent systems of SoS, and the protocols that connect them are being standardized. The current specification of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) has a stateless core, requires Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers so that gateways can route and meter requests without parsing their bodies, and adds a framework for extensions [MCP, 2026-07-28]. MCP is a project of the Agentic AI Foundation of the Linux Foundation [Linux Foundation, AAIF 2025], and the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol was contributed to the Linux Foundation [Linux Foundation, A2A 2025]. A preprint that compares MCP, A2A, and three other protocols finds that none of them supports voting or preserving dissent, and concludes that community governance is a layer missing above them [Kang & Diponegoro, arXiv 2026]. Enforcement is converging on deterministic checks at the tool-call boundary; for example, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Policy authorizes tool calls with Cedar policies and denies by default [AWS, AgentCore Policy]. A preprint review of 38 studies finds that writing the specification is the bottleneck, that runtime monitoring is the most mature approach but gives guarantees for single steps, and reports a study in which blocking 94% of unsafe actions still left fewer than 5% of tasks completed safely and correctly [Dantas+, arXiv 2026]. From the side of institutional design, a preprint enforced a public governance graph with an append-only audit log and reduced severe collusion among LLM agents from 50% to 5.6% of runs, while a prompt-only "constitution" showed no reliable improvement [Bracale Syrnikov+, arXiv 2026]. Regulation such as the EU AI Act, with its requirements on record-keeping and human oversight, is a further motivation for executable governance; this chapter does not claim a mapping from its articles to CADL. What remains open for CADL is the step from organizational contracts (roles, obligations, the provenance of authority, incentives) to deterministic enforcement at the protocol level; we found no work that takes this step. The institutional designs above are built by hand for each case, and cadl ai assures only the syntactic validity and consistency of what it generates (Section 9.2). The agent governance extension (Appendix G, agents 0.1) is a first step on RD-8.1, RD-8.2, and RD-8.3: it defines the decision that the norms of a contract give for a message at the boundary, delegation with a provenance chain, and escalation after a denial. Governance elements such as voting and dissent (RD-8.4) and plan-level verification (RD-8.5) remain open. ID Challenge Content RD-8.1 Compiling Contracts to Boundary Policies Map actors to MCP clients and servers or to A2A agents, and compile contracts and authority into Rego [Open Policy Agent] (already generated), Cedar [AWS, AgentCore Policy], and Datalog policies, with the Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers [MCP, 2026-07-28] as the point of enforcement. RD-8.2 Provenance of Delegated Authority Authority parameters that carry the chain of delegation, so that a guard checks where an authority came from and not only the local state, which cannot show whether an action was passed on through delegations its originator was not entitled to make. RD-8.3 Recovery after a Blocked Action Protocols that define the path after a guard blocks an action (escalation to a human, an alternative provider, renegotiation of the contract), in response to the low task completion reported after blocking [Dantas+, arXiv 2026]. RD-8.4 Governance Elements Missing from Protocols Describe membership, voting, dissent, escalation to humans, and audit records as CADL protocols, and distribute them as MCP or A2A extensions [Kang & Diponegoro, arXiv 2026]. Course D of the hands-on materials already combines a vote of the companies with a recorded human decision. RD-8.5 Plan-level and Multi-agent Verification Verify properties of plans and of the interaction of several agents, not of single steps, using the strategic methods of Section 9.7, and evaluate the generated guards on public agent-security benchmarks against existing guards.

We organize the above research directions along a time axis and present a short-, medium-, and long-term research roadmap. The order follows the current implementation: items that extend what cadl 0.3.23 already provides come first. Period Key Challenges Content Short-term (2026-2027) RD-1.1, RD-1.2, RD-2.2, RD-4.1, RD-4.3, RD-6.1, RD-6.2, RD-8.1 Basic theory of institutional composition (RD-1.1) and of refinement between description levels (RD-1.2), faithfulness checking for CADL generation via LLM (RD-2.2), computational complexity analysis of verification (RD-4.1), incremental verification when actors join or leave (RD-4.3), first-class norms and temporal contracts with four-valued verdicts as extensions of the existing deadline: and monitors (RD-6.1, RD-6.2), and compilation of contracts to boundary policies as an extension of Rego generation (RD-8.1). Medium-term (2027-2028) RD-1.3, RD-1.4, RD-1.6, RD-2.1, RD-2.4, RD-3.1, RD-3.2, RD-4.2, RD-6.3-6.5, RD-7.1, RD-8.2, RD-8.3 Certified regime maps by parameter synthesis (RD-1.3), safety of regime transitions (RD-1.4), SysML v2 interoperability (RD-1.6), institutional inference including specification mining (RD-2.1), an NL→CADL benchmark (RD-2.4), institutional simulator with statistical model checking, starting with integrated experiments with a MAPF simulator (RD-3.1), classification of divergences connected to the amendment procedure (RD-3.2), scalable verification methods (RD-4.2), counts-as, cross-organizational monitoring, and continuity of norms across amendments (RD-6.3 to RD-6.5), verification that compliance is rational (RD-7.1), provenance of delegated authority and recovery after blocked actions (RD-8.2, RD-8.3). Long-term (2028-2030) RD-1.5, RD-2.3, RD-3.3, RD-3.4, RD-5.1-5.3, RD-6.6, RD-7.2, RD-7.3, RD-8.4, RD-8.5 Incentive-parameterised composition (RD-1.5), tacit knowledge ontology (RD-2.3), verified institutional A/B testing (RD-3.3), assurance cases generated from CADL (RD-3.4), multicultural and multi-jurisdictional support (RD-5.1 to RD-5.3), enforcement by shields (RD-6.6), parametric equilibrium analysis and equilibria under partial observation (RD-7.2, RD-7.3), governance elements for agent protocols and plan-level verification (RD-8.4, RD-8.5).

Below is a roadmap for CADL implementation and practical deployment, considering the research directions in Chapter 9. The periods are the originally planned ones; the status column records what the public reference implementation (cadl 0.3.23, as of November 2026) provides. For the up-to-date status, see the status table in the README of the cadl repository. The README lists features, not phases, so the two tables do not correspond row by row. Phase (planned period) Goal Content Status Phase 1 (2026 Q2-Q3) Language Core Design and Parser Implementation EBNF finalization, parser implementation, type checker implementation. Initial evaluation via MAPF simulator integration. Done. Parser, type checker, and simulator IR / config generation (Python, Unity, Go) are available. Phase 2 (2026 Q3-Q4) Verification Engine (Basic) SMT-based consistency verification, protocol deadlock detection. Verification experiments on robot delivery scenarios. Done. Z3-based consistency checks and protocol deadlock detection are available. The model_check, simulation, and proof methods are not supported yet. Phase 3 (2027 Q1-Q2) Runtime and Code Generation Python/TypeScript runtime generation, contract monitoring implementation. Demonstration on IoT data sharing scenarios. Partly available. Python runtime generation including contract monitor classes is available. TypeScript generation is planned. Phase 4 (2027 Q2-Q3) AI Integration NL→CADL conversion via LLM, regime recommendation engine. Evaluation on household rule design scenarios. Partly available. NL→CADL generation via an LLM with a parse / type-check / retry loop is available; with --verify, the generated definition also goes through the SMT and deadlock checks of cadl verify. The regime recommendation engine is planned. Phase 5 (2027 Q3-Q4) Institutional Transition and Regime Maps Safety verification of dynamic institutional switching, regime map construction support tool. Integrated experiments across domains. Partly available. Graph analysis of regime transitions (reachability, dead states, cycles) and a satisfiability check of safety invariants are available. Safety verification of dynamic switching and the construction support tool are planned. Phase 6 (2028 Q1-) IEC 62853 Integration and Practical Deployment Assurance case integration, smart contract generation. Real-world pilot projects. Partly available. An IEC 62853 mapping report and Solidity / OPA-Rego generation are available. Assurance case integration and pilot projects are planned. The status column covers the tooling only; the evaluation experiments and demonstrations listed for each phase are outside its scope. The reference implementation also provides the SoS-DSL extension (Appendix E: lifecycle: / monitors:) with Unity C# generation, which the original phase plan did not list. Five further extensions follow the research directions of Chapter 9 and are likewise outside the original phase plan. Each is specified in an appendix that states what the reference implementation provides: Extension Research challenges Reference implementation (cadl 0.3.23) Norms (Appendix F) RD-6.1, RD-6.2, RD-6.3, RD-6.5 Static rules; verdicts and amendments computed from a recorded trace (cadl norms-eval, cadl norms-diff); an online monitor in the generated Python code (norms_monitor.py). Not provided: monitoring in the other generated runtimes, translation to a model checker. Agent governance (Appendix G) RD-8.1, RD-8.2, RD-8.3 Static rules; the decision function for one message (cadl agents-decide); Rego and Cedar boundary policies; a reference runtime that replays a recorded trace with holds, delegation and audit records (cadl agents-run). Not provided: an adapter to an agent protocol, integrity protection of the audit log. Stochastic model (Appendix H) RD-1.3 Static rules; export to the PRISM language (cadl model-export); a reference evaluator at fixed parameter values (cadl model-check); certified regime maps by parameter lifting (--certify). Not provided: derivation of the model from contracts. Strategic model (Appendix I) RD-7.1, RD-7.2 From cadl 0.3.23: static rules; checks that a named memoryless deterministic profile is an equilibrium against unilateral deviations, with deviation gains, and certified equilibrium maps (cadl game-check); export to PRISM-games. Not provided: equilibria under partial observation, concurrent moves. Grounding of the institutional parameters (Appendix J) RD-6.1, RD-1.5 From cadl 0.3.23: static rules; indices for α and β and a coverage measure for incentives (cadl norms-indices); the payoff term of a sanction in a strategic model. Not provided: the formal meaning of α, β, and λ in terms of norms.

Based on the description examples of Chapter 7, we concretely examine feasible use cases of CADL. For each use case, we outline CADL's novelty through comparison with existing technologies and research. The comparisons reflect the scope of the authors' survey, and some use cases are still at the concept stage.

The description example in household rule design (Section 7.1) demonstrates the possibility of fundamentally extending the scope of application of traditional formal methods. IndoorWorld by Wu et al. (2025) enables LLM-driven agents to simulate physical tasks and social interactions in indoor environments, but does not target describing and verifying governance structure (authority, responsibility, incentives) itself. Furthermore, according to the OECD's overview page on innovative public participation [OECD, "Innovative public participation"], institutionalized deliberative citizen participation cases increased rapidly from 22 cases in 2020 to 41 cases in 2023, yet, to our knowledge, there are no tools for citizens to directly "write" governance rules. Use Case Overview Limitations of Existing Technologies CADL's Novelty Household Chore-Sharing Optimization AI analyzes chore-sharing rules written in CADL and optimizes fairness (Gini coefficient) and efficiency. AI refines design level descriptions from overview-level natural language. Existing chore-sharing apps focus on task management; rule formalization, verification, and optimization are not their main target. Quantitative household governance design via institutional parameters (β, λ). Enables formalization of implicit rules and contradiction detection. Condominium Bylaw Design Formalize management bylaws in CADL and automatically detect resident rights conflicts and obligation contradictions. Describe maintenance fund sharing rules with incentive models. Existing condominium management software focuses on accounting and minutes management; formal verification of bylaws is not in its scope. Formal verifiability of legal bylaws. Symboleo [Sharifi+, 2020] leads legal contract formalization, but three-layer integrated organizational governance description is a distinguishing feature of CADL. Local Community Autonomy Rules Describe neighborhood association rules in CADL, with AI detecting contradictions and proposing improvements. Municipal staff grasp the overall picture via visualization. Deliberative citizen participation as surveyed by the OECD [OECD, 2020] focuses on aggregating opinions and deliberation; rule formalization is not its target. Citizen participation platforms such as OpenStad [OpenStad] likewise do not target formal description of institutions. To our knowledge, there is little prior work on citizen-participatory formal institutional design. Through overview-level description + AI support, CADL aims to enable non-expert participation in institutional design.
documents.s: 8.1 Democratization of Institutional Design for Daily Life

documents.t: The robot delivery system (Section 7.2) provides an experimental platform that fuses MAPF research and institutional design. Friedrich et al. (IJCAI 2024) proposed Payment-CBS (PCBS) introducing VCG mechanisms to MAPF and realized strategyproof route assignment, but formal description of overall governance structure (who decides what, under what conditions rules change) is outside the scope. CADL adds "institutional layer" to MAPF research, making decision structures above the algorithm manipulable as experimental variables. Use Case Overview Limitations of Existing Technologies CADL's Novelty Institutional Parameter Experimentation Platform Systematically vary CADL institutional parameters (α, β, λ) on MAPF simulator, measure impacts on throughput, fairness, and resilience (cf. the game-theoretic resilience analysis of SoS by Zhang & Matsubara [2026]). Automatically construct regime maps. Payment-CBS [Friedrich+, IJCAI 2024]: Mechanism design for route assignment but does not address institutional design variables overall. Distributed MAPF research (e.g., PRIMAL [Sartoretti+, 2019]): Only computation distribution, governance distribution not considered. Systematic exploration of institutional parameter space and automatic regime map construction. Its distinguishing feature is treating governance structure itself as a MAPF experimental variable. Safety Verification of Dynamic Institutional Transitions Formally verify transitions between a centralized and a distributed regime (Section 7.2) responding to changes in failure rate and latency. Model checking verifies safety invariants during transitions (collision avoidance, order loss prevention). Adaptive governance research [Folke+, 2005]: Theoretical framework only, no formal transition condition description. AADL/HAMR [Hatcliff+, 2021]: Can generate code for architecture transitions, but not institutional transitions. To our knowledge, there is little prior work on formal verification of institutional transitions. CADL describes verifiable dynamic institutional switching via its transitions block and safety_invariant specification. Multi-Domain Delivery Coordination Institutional design for SoS with multiple delivery providers (drones, ground robots, human couriers). Describe competition and collaboration between providers with incentive models. Last-mile delivery research [Boysen+, 2021]: Individual optimization dominates. Multi-provider governance structure formalization remains unaddressed. Describe institutional design among heterogeneous actors in a single CADL file. Experimental verification platform for Shimoyama & Matsubara [2026] performance-autonomy value space.
documents.s: 8.2 Institutional Experimentation Platform for Robotics SoS

documents.t: The IoT data sharing system (Section 7.3) supports data sharing from upstream institutional design, in light of the requirements that the EU Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854) places on smart contracts used for the automated execution of data sharing agreements. IoT-Gov [Computing, 2022] and Policy-Based Smart Contracts [Future Internet, 2024] focus on the execution layer on blockchain, but do not address the entire lifecycle of institutional design, verification, and evolution. CADL integrates the complete pipeline: "institutional design → formal verification → code generation → runtime monitoring" for data sharing. Use Case Overview Limitations of Existing Technologies CADL's Novelty Smart City Data Coordination Describe data sharing rules for municipal, private sensors, and citizen data in CADL. Automatically detect contradictions between privacy constraints and open data requirements. IoT-Gov [2022]: Access control on Ethereum but no formal verification of privacy constraints. vCity [BSC]: Urban digital twin; institutional description is not its main target. Formal contradiction detection between privacy constraints and data publication requirements. Institutional simulation platform integrated with digital twins. Industrial Data Marketplace Institutionalize supply chain data sharing in manufacturing with CADL. Automatically generate Solidity/Python code from SLA contracts. Symboleo2SC [Rasti+, MODELS 2022]: Generates smart contract code from legal contract specifications. However, institutional parametrization and SLA contradiction detection are outside scope. Verify SLA constraint satisfiability with linear programming. Simultaneous verification of combined bandwidth, latency, and privacy constraints is novel. Healthcare Data Sharing Governance Describe inter-hospital patient data sharing rules in CADL. Formal verification of consent management, anonymization levels, and access rights. HL7 FHIR [HL7, 2023]: Data exchange standard but governance rule formal verification out of scope. Smart contract research for healthcare data sharing is in early stages. Check conformance to healthcare-specific strict privacy requirements via CADL's information flow verification (this does not by itself guarantee legal compliance). Detect consent management contradictions using deontic logic.
documents.s: 8.3 Trust Foundation for IoT Data Economy

documents.t: AI integration (Section 7.4) applies CADL to the field of AI governance whose social importance is rapidly increasing. As of 2026, AI governance has become a core issue for enterprises as "AI risk and compliance," but formal description and automatic verification of governance policies remain unestablished. CADL aims to formally describe AI safety contracts, authority boundaries, and human oversight requirements, and to automate contradiction detection and policy code generation. Use Case Overview Limitations of Existing Technologies CADL's Novelty LLM Governance Policy Describe LLM usage rules (access control, content filters, logging obligations) in CADL. Automatically generate policy code in OPA/Rego [Open Policy Agent] format. Procedural and ad-hoc policy management is currently mainstream in AI governance; to our knowledge, no formally verifiable governance description language is established. CADL as formal specification language for AI governance policy. AI safety contract verification via assume-guarantee semantics. Autonomous System Safety Certification Describe safety contracts for autonomous systems (autonomous vehicles, drones, etc.) in CADL. Automatically generate safe controllers via reactive synthesis (GR(1) [Piterman+, 2006]). Nuzzo+ [ACM TECS, 2019]: Probabilistic assume-guarantee contracts but CPS design only. Saoud+ [Automatica, 2021]: Continuous-time contracts but institutional layer excluded. Unified safety verification for institutional (governance) and control (algorithm) layers. Automatic safe controller generation via reactive synthesis from contract specifications. AI-Assisted Institutional Design Workflow Automated pipeline: Natural language → CADL conversion → formal verification → deployment. LLM generates and refines CADL descriptions in dialogue with institutional designers. LLM-based Symboleo generation [Zitouni+, 2025]: Natural language to legal contract specification conversion. CURRANTE [Rosa+, SANER 2026 registered report]: Human-in-the-loop specification → testing → code. End-to-end pipeline: NL → institutional specification → verification → code generation. While Symboleo is limited to legal contracts, CADL covers entire institutions. Demonstrations. Working minimal demonstrations for this section have been built in the cadl-ai-governance repository (not publicly available at present). The case numbers are those of the repository; the table shows what each case corresponds to in this specification. Case What it demonstrates Aspect of Section 7.4 Use case in the table above Case 1 Behavioural contracts on an LLM agent team are enforced at runtime (approval gate, review deadline, API budget). Third aspect: AI agents take part as constituent systems (AI_GOVERNANCE, AI_SAFETY_CONTRACT). LLM Governance Policy (enforcement at runtime) Case 2 Propose–verify–repair loop: an LLM's CADL drafts take effect only once they pass cadl check. First aspect: natural language to CADL (NL_TO_CADL_WORKFLOW). AI-Assisted Institutional Design Workflow Case 3 AI operation policies (72-hour human oversight, no PII egress) are audited after the fact by replaying gateway logs. Third aspect, checked from logs rather than at runtime. LLM Governance Policy (audit) The second aspect of Section 7.4 (regime recommendation by an AI advisor) and the use case "Autonomous System Safety Certification" (reactive synthesis) have no demonstration yet. The three cases share one IR-driven runtime with swappable bridges — itself a demonstration that the contract description is independent of the execution environment.
documents.s: 8.4 Formalization and Automation of AI Governance

documents.t: Based on the above use case analysis, we summarize CADL's novelty in five key points: ID Novelty Description and Differences from Existing Research N-1 Democratization of Institutional Design Overview-level description + AI support enables students, citizens, and municipal staff to participate in institutional design. Existing formal methods (Symboleo, MOISE+) mainly assume expert users. Deliberative citizen participation focuses on aggregating opinions and deliberation, and does not target institutional "description". N-2 Governance as an Experimental Science Systematic manipulation of institutional parameters (α, β, λ) and regime map construction aim to make institutional design an experimental science. Adds governance layer to MAPF research, enabling quantitative exploration of Shimoyama & Matsubara [2026] value space. N-3 Formal Verification of Dynamic Institutional Transitions Formally implements theory from adaptive governance [Folke+, 2005]. Verifiable description of transition conditions, safety invariants, and rollback has, to our knowledge, received little study. N-4 Unified Institutional Lifecycle Management Manage all stages design → verification → code generation → runtime monitoring in a single language. Symboleo2SC focuses on code generation and IoT-Gov [2022] on the execution layer; CADL differs in aiming at lifecycle integration. N-5 Institutional Integration with Digital Twins Provide institutional design layer to urban digital twins like vCity [BSC]. Aims to enable not only physical simulation but also "institutional simulation".

Audience: Undergraduates and beginning graduate students who have just been introduced to System of Systems (SoS) thinking. No CADL experience required. Duration: about 95 minutes — a 5-minute setup plus six 15-minute steps. What you take home: A working CADL specification you wrote yourself, a generated Unity C# implementation, and a running 5-robot delivery simulation in which missed deadlines and battery-rule violations are detected and the affected contract instances are moved to Violated. First time here? Read from Chapter 1 in order. The textbook explains everything it uses, so you do not need to read other pages first.

This textbook is Course A of the CADL hands-on materials. It walks once through the whole toolchain on a robot-delivery system and adds, at the end of Chapters 4–9, the exercises of a five-session class on the same system. Part Chapters I. Foundations 1. What is an SoS? · 2. The toolchain and setup · 3. Essentials of CADL II. Practice 4. Writing the structure · 5. Writing the norms · 6. Visualising the lifecycle · 7. Generating code and running the reference runtime · 8. Running the simulation in Unity · 9. Improving the specification III. Going further 10. Generating contracts with an LLM · 11. Where to go next Appendices A. Glossary · B. Notation quick reference · C. Using this textbook in a class · D. References There are two ways to use it: Self-study (about 95 minutes): follow Chapters 1–8 and skip the exercises at the end of each chapter. A class (five sessions, or three): Chapters 4–9 make up the five sessions; the exercises at the end of each chapter are done in class and as homework. See Appendix C.

The terms used in this textbook, grouped by topic. The right-hand column gives the sections of this textbook that explain each term. The Glossary of the specification also covers terms this textbook does not use.

Term Meaning Sections SoS (System of Systems) A set of systems, each operated independently, that together achieve a goal none of them can achieve alone 1.1, 1.2 Maier's five criteria Five criteria for deciding whether something is an SoS: operational independence, managerial independence, geographic distribution, emergent behaviour, evolutionary development [1] 1.3 Operational independence Each part works on its own when the SoS as a whole is off. Maier's criterion (1) 1.3 Managerial independence Each part has its own owner or decision-maker. Maier's criterion (2) 1.3 Emergent behaviour The whole does something no part can do alone. Maier's criterion (4) 1.3 SoS type One of four classes by the strength of the central authority (Directed, Acknowledged, Collaborative, Virtual) [2] [3]. Written as type: in a CADL file 1.4, 3.3 Directed An SoS managed centrally, with strong top-down authority 1.4 Acknowledged An SoS with an authority for the whole, whose constituents keep their ownership and their own management. The robot delivery of this textbook is modelled as this type 1.4 Collaborative An SoS with no single authority, whose parts cooperate voluntarily through shared agreements 1.4 Virtual An SoS with neither central management nor an agreed purpose, in which coordination arises on its own 1.4 Dispatcher (DISPATCHER) In the robot delivery of this textbook, the central coordinator that assigns deliveries to robots 1.1, 3.4

Term Meaning Sections CADL (Contract Architecture Description Language) A description language for writing the rules several systems must follow in one file, apart from their implementation code. Written in YAML 1.6 Structure layer The part that says what exists in the SoS: actors:, contracts:, protocols: 1.6, 3.2 Actor (actors:) A participant of the SoS. A range such as ROBOT[1..N] makes it a set of actors of the same kind 3.4 ROBOT[*] / ROBOT[i] The notation for a whole set of actors and for one member of it. ROBOT[i].battery is an attribute of that member 3.4 Autonomy (autonomy) How autonomous an actor is (low / medium / high). A descriptive label the tools do not check 3.4 Contract (contracts:) An agreement between actors: a class, "this is the kind of agreement we make" 3.5 Parties (parties) The actors that take part in a contract 3.5 Assume-guarantee form The way a contract is written: as long as the assumptions (assume) hold, the parties keep the guarantees (guarantee). If an assumption fails, the guarantees do not bind 3.5 Incentives (incentives:) Rewards and penalties. lambda (λ) is their strength; rules says who gets what and when 3.5 authority: / beta (β) Who decides, and how centralised decisions are. Not used by the subject of this textbook 3.5 information: / alpha (α) How much information is shared. Not used by the subject of this textbook 3.5 Protocol (protocols:) The procedure of an interaction between actors, written with trigger, precondition, steps and postcondition 3.6 Step One step of a protocol. A -> B : m sends a message; A : f(x) is a computation by A itself 3.6 Operating mode (regime) A way of operating the SoS that can be switched (for example, centralised or distributed). The switching conditions go in the top-level transitions:. Not used in this textbook 3.3
documents.s: A.2 The structure layer of CADL

documents.t: Term Meaning Sections Norms layer The part that says what should happen in the SoS: lifecycle: and monitors: inside a contract 1.6, 3.2 SoS-DSL extension The extension that adds lifecycle: and monitors: to CADL. A file that uses it declares sos-dsl: 0.1 under extensions: 1.6, 3.3 Contract instance One individual realisation of a contract, created for each order. It moves between states following the lifecycle. The application that runs the contracts creates it 3.7 Lifecycle (lifecycle:) The state machine a contract instance goes through 3.7, 5.3 Initial / final states (initial / terminal) The state of an instance when it is created, and the states it never leaves 3.7 Transition (transitions) A rule: when the instance is in a from state, the on: event occurs and when: holds, it moves to the to state 3.7 Event (on:) What triggers a transition. The form "A -> B : m" occurs when the message is sent; a condition occurs when it becomes true 3.7 Deadline (deadline:) A time bound measured from the moment the instance enters a from state, written as an integer with a unit, as in 5s 3.7 on_violation: What happens when a deadline is missed. transition: is the name of the target state (not a transition id); severity: is how serious the violation is 3.7 Violation A missed deadline, or a monitor whose condition holds. It is recorded and, if so specified, forces the instance to another state 3.7, 3.8 Severity (severity) How serious a violation is: Minor, Major or Critical; Major when omitted 3.7 Monitor (monitors:) A rule watched while a contract instance is running 3.8, 5.3 observe What a monitor reads: an attribute of a declared actor, a message name, time or state 3.8 sampling When a monitor is evaluated: periodic(500ms) at a fixed interval, event whenever an event arrives (the default) 3.8 rule The condition that counts as a violation, written as a string 3.8 on_match: What happens when a monitor's condition holds. violation: is the name the violation is recorded under, transition: the target state 3.8 Reserved names state / now / request In conditions: the current state of the instance, the current time, and the request that created the instance 3.8

Term Meaning Sections Toolchain The tools that produce check results, the IR, diagrams, code and executions from a CADL file 2.1 cadl check The command that checks syntax, types and the static rules of the SoS-DSL extension. Mistakes are reported as errors, discouraged forms as warnings 3.9 cadl verify The command that does what cadl check does and, with an SMT solver, also looks for contradictions between assumptions and guarantees and for deadlocks in protocols 3.9 SMT solver / Z3 A program that decides whether logical formulas can hold together. cadl verify uses Z3 [8] 2.1, 3.9 IR (intermediate representation, Sim-IR) The content of a CADL file as JSON in three layers (institution / protocol / algorithm). cadl sim-ir writes it, and the other tools read it 2.1, 7.6 Code generation (cadl codegen) Producing executable code from the IR. --target selects the target (python, solidity, opa, unity-csharp) 7.3, 7.6 e2e script cadl_repo/scripts/sos_dsl_handson_e2e.sh, which checks the file, writes the IR, generates the C# and copies it into the Unity project in one go 7.3 Python reference runtime A hand-written interpreter (engine.py) that reads the IR directly and replays how contract instances move between states. Used to cross-check the generated C# 7.5, 7.6 multi_robot_demo A demo that runs five robots through fixed scripts on the reference runtime. --summary prints a table of final states, --log writes an NDJSON trace, --ir uses your own IR 7.2, 7.9 NDJSON trace A record of events with one JSON object per line 7.9 cadl-explorer A Streamlit app that edits and checks CADL and draws state machines 6.3 Lifecycle View The diagram of a lifecycle drawn by the Contract Lifecycle page of cadl-explorer 6.2, 6.4

Term Meaning Sections cadl-raspimouse-simulator The simulator repository: Unity project, Go arbitrator and Python reference runtime 2.2 ContractRuntime The generated C# contract runtime: registers instances, delivers events, evaluates deadlines and monitors 7.6 ContractRuntimeHost One per scene. Holds the runtime, has it evaluate every frame, and prints events to the Console 8.2, 8.4 Bridge (PilotContractBridge) One per robot (a Unity MonoBehaviour). Observes changes of the robot state and turns them into contract events 8.2, 8.4 Pilot_CSoS The robot controller: follows paths, claims deliveries, delivers. It knows nothing about contracts 2.1, 8.4 Arbitrator The delivery dispatcher written in Go. It distributes deliveries over NATS and gives each to the robot that claims it first 8.2, 8.4 NATS The message broker that carries messages between the robots and the arbitrator 8.2 C-SoS The name of the simulator's operating mode (short for Collaborative SoS). Unrelated to the type: of a CADL file 2.2 cadl_config.json The road network (11 nodes, 17 edges), the robot count and the NATS settings. Read by both the arbitrator and Unity 8.4 Numbered references are listed in Appendix D.

The CADL notation, the commands and the file locations used in this textbook, on one page. Chapter 3 explains what each construct means. The CADL listings of this appendix fit together into one file, which passes cadl check and cadl verify of cadl 0.3.22.

sos: name: "MyDelivery" type: Acknowledged # Directed / Acknowledged / Collaborative / Virtual version: "0.1.0" extensions: # declare when you use lifecycle: and monitors: - sos-dsl: 0.1 context: environment: num_robots: 3 # values passed to simulators and others actors: [...] # B.2 contracts: [...] # B.2, B.3 protocols: [...] # B.2
documents.s: B.1 The skeleton of a file

documents.t: actors: - id: DISPATCHER role: "central_coordinator" autonomy: low # low / medium / high (medium when omitted) capabilities: [assign_tasks] interface: input: [position_report, ack] output: [route_assignment] - id: "ROBOT[1..N]" # a set of actors of the same kind role: "delivery_agent" autonomy: high contracts: - id: DELIVERY_SLA parties: [DISPATCHER, "ROBOT[*]"] assume: # assumptions - "ROBOT[i].battery > 20" guarantee: # guarantees - "delivery_time <= 300s" incentives: type: task_completion lambda: 0.5 # strength (λ) rules: - "reward(ROBOT[i], 10) when on_time_delivery" protocols: - id: DeliveryProposal trigger: "new_delivery_request(ROBOT[i])" precondition: "ROBOT[i].battery > 20" steps: - "DISPATCHER -> ROBOT[i] : route_assignment" # send a message - "DISPATCHER : log(route_assignment)" # a computation of its own - "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : ack" postcondition: "ROBOT[i].status == Delivered"

lifecycle: states: [Proposed, Assigned, Accepted, Completed, Violated] initial: Proposed terminal: [Completed, Violated] transitions: - id: assign from: Proposed to: Assigned on: "DISPATCHER -> ROBOT[i] : route_assignment" # a message event - id: accept from: Assigned # one state, or several as in [A, B] to: Accepted on: "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : ack(accepted)" when: "ROBOT[i].battery > 20" # optional: a condition that must also hold deadline: 5s # optional: bound from entering the from state on_violation: # write it whenever you write deadline: transition: Violated # the name of the target state (not a transition id) severity: Major # Minor / Major / Critical (Major when omitted) emit: [accepted] # optional: names of extra events to publish - id: complete from: [Accepted] to: Completed on: "ROBOT[i].status == Delivered" # a condition event (occurs when it becomes true) monitors: - id: battery_guard observe: "ROBOT[i].battery" # one entry, or several as in ["A.x", "B.y"] sampling: periodic(500ms) # event (the default) or periodic(<duration>) rule: "ROBOT[i].battery < 20 AND state IN [Assigned, Accepted]" on_match: violation: low_battery # optional: name to record (the id when omitted) transition: Violated # optional: the name of the target state severity: Major
documents.s: B.3 The norms layer (inside a contract)

documents.t: Conditions (assume, guarantee, on:, when:, rule: and others) are written inside quoted strings. Notation Meaning Example OR, AND, NOT Or, and, not (binding more tightly in this order) a > 1 AND NOT b ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= Comparison; cannot be chained as in a < b < c ROBOT[i].battery < 20 IN [ ... ] Equal to one of the listed values state IN [Assigned, Accepted] +, -, *, / Arithmetic deadline - now X[i].attr An attribute of an actor ROBOT[i].battery X[*], X[i], X[1..N] A whole set, one member, a range "ROBOT[*]" for all x in S: P, exists x in S: P P holds for every / some x for all t in TAXI[*]: has_capability(t, local_navigation) f(x, y) A function call min_dist(ROBOT[i].position, DISPATCHER.obstacle_positions) state, now, request Reserved: the current state, the current time, the request that created the instance state == Assigned Value How to write it Durations (deadline:, periodic(...)) An integer with the unit ms, s, min or h: 5s, 500ms, 2min. Decimals such as 0.5s are not accepted Severities Minor, Major, Critical Values that need quotes The values of on:, when: and rule:, and values containing [, -> or ": " (such as "ROBOT[*]")

Command What it does Sections cadl check <file> Checks syntax, types and the static rules of the SoS-DSL extension 3.9, 4.3 cadl verify <file> Does what cadl check does and also looks for contradictions between assumptions and guarantees and for deadlocks in protocols 3.9 cadl sim-ir <file> --format json Writes the IR as JSON 4.3, 5.3 cadl codegen --target unity-csharp -o <dir> <file> Generates Unity C# from the IR (--target is python, solidity, opa or unity-csharp; agent-rego and agent-cedar generate the boundary policies of the agent governance extension) 7.6 ./scripts/sos_dsl_handson_e2e.sh <file> --unity <dir> Checks the file, writes the IR, generates the C# and copies it into the Unity project in one go; --unity "" skips the copy 7.3 python3 -m cadl.runtime.multi_robot_demo [--summary] [--log <file>] [--ir <file>] Runs the five-robot demo on the reference runtime: --summary prints a table of final states, --log writes an NDJSON trace, --ir uses your own IR 7.5, 7.9 streamlit run app.py (in cadl-explorer) Starts cadl-explorer 6.3 nats-server -p 4222 Starts NATS 8.2 go run . (in arbitrator/C-SoS/main) Starts the arbitrator 8.2

documents.t: This appendix shows how to teach Chapters 4–9 as a five-session class (or a three-session one). Students who have read Chapters 1–3 and done the setup of Section 2.4 can start with Session 1.
documents.s: Appendix C — Using this textbook in a class

documents.t: Session Chapter Title Theme Deliverable 1 4 CADL Modelling Structure of an SoS my_delivery_v1.cadl (structure only) 2 5 DSL Design Norms: lifecycle and monitors my_delivery_v2.cadl (with lifecycle + monitors) 3 6 Visualisation Reading and comparing specs visually A/B comparison report with screenshots 4 7 (and 8) Simulation Executing the spec, reading traces Baseline trace + parameter sweep 5 9 Improvement Using observations to refine the spec my_delivery_v3.cadl + before/after report Chapter 8 (Unity) is optional in a class: its only exercise, 8.1 (★★★), belongs to Session 4. Each session is ~90 minutes in class plus ~3 hours of homework. The final deliverable across all five sessions is a 3-page report (initial model / simulation comparison / reflection). Repository availability Sessions 1–3 need only cadl and cadl-explorer (except the ★★★ Exercise 6.3, which takes a log from the simulator repository). Sessions 4–5 run the Python reference runtime that lives in cadl-raspimouse-simulator (see Section 2.4 for how to get it).

If you only have three sessions (e.g., a short module, an intensive weekend), use this mapping: 3-session Combines Session A Sessions 1 + 2 (Modelling + DSL design) Session B Sessions 3 + 4 (Visualisation + Simulation) Session C Session 5 (Improvement) The exercises stay the same; you simply move the optional / "stretch" exercises to homework.

Every session has the same shape, and each part is found in the same place of its chapter: Learning objectives — what you should be able to do by the end (Section N.1, "What you'll learn"). Prerequisites — deliverables from the previous session, plus reading ("Before the session" at the end of the chapter). Concept introduction (~30 min) — the small amount of theory you need (the subsection of "Background"). Exercises (~50 min) — graded ★ (basic) → ★★ (intermediate) → ★★★ (stretch) (the "Exercises" section). Wrap-up + homework (~10 min) — what to bring to next session ("Wrap-up and homework" at the end of the chapter). The procedure of each chapter (the former Course A steps, about 15 minutes each) can be done before the session as preparation or at its start.

The instructor can use this for grading; the student can self-check. Criterion Weight All ★ and ★★ exercises completed for every session 40% cadl check passes on every submitted CADL file 20% Final 3-page report demonstrates understanding (not just steps) 30% At least one ★★★ stretch exercise attempted 10%

By the end of Session 5, every student should have: Artefact From session Exercise my_delivery_v1.cadl (structure only) 1 4.1 my_delivery_v2.cadl (with lifecycle + monitors) 2 5.1–5.2 session3_comparison.md + 2 screenshots 3 6.2 session4_baseline.ndjson + parameter-sweep table 4 7.1–7.3 my_delivery_v3.cadl (improved) + 3-page final report 5 9.2, 9.4 (Optional) test_rewards.py + reward execution code 5 9.3 (Optional) violation_trace_view.py Streamlit page 3 6.3 All five (or seven, with optionals) live in a single course-deliverables repository.
