This chapter explains how to write the CADL files of Chapter 4 onwards, limited to what this textbook uses. The specification defines the whole language, but you do not need to read it to follow this textbook. Each section ends with the sections of the specification to read if you want the details. Reading the chapter takes about 15 minutes.

A CADL file consists of a structure layer (actors / contracts / protocols) and a norms layer (lifecycle / monitors). By which rules an individual agreement (a contract instance) moves between states, and when it becomes a violation. What cadl check and cadl verify check.

A specification of an SoS has two jobs: Descriptive — what exists: the participants, how they are connected, the messages they exchange. Normative — what should happen: obligations, deadlines, violations. CADL covers (1) in the core language. The SoS-DSL extension adds (2) on top of (1). The extension adds only two keys, lifecycle: and monitors:, placed inside a contract and written in the same way as the core.
documents.s: 3.2 Background: the structure layer and the norms layer

documents.t: A CADL file is written in YAML and has a single sos: at the top level. The keys used in this textbook are: sos: name: "MyDelivery" # name of the SoS type: Acknowledged # SoS type (Directed / Acknowledged / Collaborative / Virtual) version: "0.1.0" extensions: # declared by files that use the SoS-DSL extension (from Chapter 5) - sos-dsl: 0.1 context: # environment parameters (values passed to simulators and others) environment: num_robots: 3 actors: [...] # who exists contracts: [...] # who promises what to whom (the norms layer goes here too) protocols: [...] # in which order they interact type: takes one of the four types of Chapter 1, Section 1.4. It is a descriptive label; the tools do not check it against anything else in the file. The top level has other keys too, such as transitions:, which states the conditions for switching between operating modes (regimes); this textbook does not use them. Details: Chapter 5, Section 5.1, and Appendix A, Section A.2, of the specification.

An actor is a participant of the SoS. actors: - id: DISPATCHER role: "central_coordinator" autonomy: low capabilities: [assign_tasks] interface: input: [position_report, task_completion, ack] output: [route_assignment] - id: "ROBOT[1..N]" # N actors of the same kind role: "delivery_agent" autonomy: high Key What it says id Name of the actor. A range such as ROBOT[1..N] makes it a set of actors of the same kind role A string naming its role autonomy How autonomous it is (low / medium / high; medium when omitted). A descriptive label, like type: capabilities What the actor can do interface What it receives (input) and sends out (output) Elsewhere in the file, ROBOT[*] refers to the whole set and ROBOT[i] to one member of it. ROBOT[i].battery is the attribute battery of that robot. The upper bound N of a range is a symbol meaning "any number"; there is no syntax that gives it a value (a range can also be written with numbers, as in [1..3]). Details: Chapter 5, Section 5.2.2, of the specification.

A contract is an agreement between actors. A CADL contract is written in the form as long as the assumptions (assume) hold, the parties keep the guarantees (guarantee) (assume-guarantee form). If an assumption fails, the parties are not bound by the guarantees. contracts: - id: DELIVERY_SLA parties: [DISPATCHER, "ROBOT[*]", "CUSTOMER[*]"] assume: - "ROBOT[i].battery > 20" # assumption: the battery is above 20% guarantee: - "delivery_time <= 300s" # guarantee: delivered within 300 s incentives: type: task_completion lambda: 0.5 rules: - "reward(ROBOT[i], 10) when on_time_delivery" Key What it says id Name of the contract parties The parties to the contract (actor ids) assume Assumptions, as a list of expressions written as strings guarantee Guarantees, as a list of expressions written as strings incentives Rewards and penalties. type is the kind, lambda (λ) a number for their strength, and rules says who gets what and when Contracts have other keys as well, such as who decides (authority:, with the decision holder decision_holder and beta (β), how centralised decisions are) and how much information is shared (alpha (α) in information:). The subject of this textbook uses keys up to incentives:. A contract so far describes a class: "this is the kind of agreement we make". How each individual delivery goes through that agreement is written in the norms layer below. Details: Chapter 5, Sections 5.2.3 and 5.4.1, of the specification.

A protocol is the procedure of an interaction between actors. protocols: - id: DeliveryProposal trigger: "new_delivery_request(CUSTOMER[i])" # what starts it precondition: "ROBOT[i].battery > 20" # when it may start steps: - "DISPATCHER -> ROBOT[i] : route_assignment" # DISPATCHER sends route_assignment to ROBOT[i] - "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : ack" - "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : task_completion" postcondition: "ROBOT[i].status == Delivered" # what holds when it has finished Each line of steps is one step. A -> B : m means "A sends the message m to B", and A : f(x) means "A performs the computation f(x) itself". Steps can also branch on a condition (if / else), run without a fixed order (parallel:), or wait until a condition holds (barrier:). Details: Chapter 5, Section 5.2.4, of the specification.

The basic idea of the norms layer is the contract instance. Every time a delivery order arrives, one instance of the DELIVERY_SLA contract is created, and that instance moves from state to state. Instances are created by the application that runs the contracts (in this textbook, the simulator). The state machine an instance goes through is written in lifecycle:. lifecycle: states: [Proposed, Assigned, Accepted, Delivering, Completed, Violated, Terminated] initial: Proposed # the state when it is created terminal: [Completed, Violated, Terminated] # the final states transitions: - id: accept from: Assigned # when in this state to: Accepted # move to this state on: "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : ack(accepted)" # when this event occurs deadline: 5s # within 5 s of entering Assigned on_violation: # if that deadline is missed transition: Violated # force the instance to Violated severity: Major # how serious the violation is A transition (one item of transitions) works as follows. When the instance is in one of the from states, the on: event occurs and the when: condition (if written) holds, the transition fires and the instance moves to the to state. from may list several states, as in [Holding, Overstay]. An on: event is one of two kinds. The form "A -> B : m" occurs when that message is sent. A condition such as "ROBOT[i].status == Delivered" occurs when the condition becomes true. deadline: is a time bound measured from the moment the instance enters a from state. If the transition has not fired by then, this is a violation, and the instance moves to the state named in on_violation.transition. What transition: holds is the name of the target state, not the id of a transition. The severity of a violation, severity, is Minor, Major or Critical; it is Major when omitted. If on_violation: has no transition:, a missed deadline is recorded as a violation but the state does not change. A deadline is an integer with a unit: 5s, 500ms, 2min, 1h. Details: Appendix E, Sections E.3 and E.5, of the specification.
documents.s: 3.7 The norms layer (1): contract instances and the lifecycle

documents.t: monitors: holds rules that are watched while a contract instance is running. monitors: - id: battery_guard observe: "ROBOT[i].battery" # the value it reads sampling: periodic(500ms) # evaluate every 500 ms rule: "ROBOT[i].battery < 20 AND state == Assigned" # a violation when this holds on_match: transition: Violated # force the instance to Violated severity: Major Key What it says observe The values the monitor reads: an attribute of a declared actor (ROBOT[i].battery), a message name, or one of the reserved names time and state sampling When it is evaluated: periodic(500ms) at a fixed interval, event whenever an event reaches the instance. event when omitted rule The condition that counts as a violation on_match What happens when the condition holds: violation: is the name the violation is recorded under (the monitor's id when omitted), transition: the target state, severity: the severity (Major when omitted) Monitors are evaluated separately from the lifecycle, but a rule can read state, the current state of the instance. IN says "in one of these states", as in state IN [Assigned, Accepted]. Besides state, the names now (the current time) and request (the request that created the instance) are reserved in conditions. The values of on:, when: and rule:, and of observe: entries that contain [, -> or ": ", must be quoted as strings; otherwise YAML reads them as other constructs. Details: Appendix E, Sections E.3–E.5, of the specification.

Besides syntax and types, cadl check reports mistakes in the norms layer such as the following as errors. With even one error it prints Type check failed. Mistake Example initial, terminal, or the from / to of a transition names a state that is not in states initial: Proposed, but Proposed is not in states The transition: of on_violation / on_match is not a state name the transition id accept was written No final state can be reached from the initial state severity: is not one of Minor / Major / Critical severity: Fatal deadline: cannot be read as a duration deadline: soon A message in on: mentions an actor that is not declared HUB in "ROBOT[i] -> HUB : ack" is not declared An observe: entry is neither an attribute of a declared actor nor a message name DRONE in DRONE.battery is not declared For example, when the transition: of on_violation names a transition id, cadl 0.3.22 reports: [ERROR]: on_violation.transition 'accept' of the lifecycle transition 'accept' of contract 'DELIVERY_SLA' is not a state listed in states (L-5); it names the target state, not a transition id Type check failed: 1 error(s), 0 warning(s) A transition with a deadline: but no on_violation: gives a warning. With warnings only, the file is valid and Type check passed is printed. cadl verify does what cadl check does and, in addition, examines the assumptions and guarantees of each contract with an SMT solver (Z3 [8]). If the assumptions list both ROBOT[i].battery > 20 and ROBOT[i].battery < 10, which can never hold together, it reports that the contract can never apply: [FAIL] Contract 'DELIVERY_SLA' assumptions: Assumptions contradict each other; the contract can never apply The procedures of this textbook do not use cadl verify, but you can use it to check contracts you write yourself. Details: Appendix E, Section E.4, and Chapter 6, Section 6.3, of the specification.
documents.s: 3.9 What cadl check and cadl verify check

documents.t: With what you have read so far, read the contract of robot delivery. It is the example of Section E.6 of Appendix E of the specification, cut down to one transition and one monitor. In Chapter 5 you will write something very similar yourself. contracts: - id: DELIVERY_SLA parties: [DISPATCHER, "ROBOT[*]", "CUSTOMER[*]"] assume: - "ROBOT[i].battery > 20" guarantee: - "delivery_time <= 300s" lifecycle: states: [Proposed, Assigned, Accepted, Delivering, Completed, Violated, Terminated] initial: Proposed terminal: [Completed, Violated, Terminated] transitions: - id: accept from: Assigned to: Accepted on: "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : ack(accepted)" deadline: 5s on_violation: transition: Violated severity: Major monitors: - id: battery_guard observe: "ROBOT[i].battery" sampling: periodic(500ms) rule: "ROBOT[i].battery < 20 AND state == Assigned" on_match: transition: Violated severity: Major

Without looking at the example, can you answer these four questions aloud? What is the initial state of the delivery contract? → Proposed What happens if a robot does not acknowledge within 5 seconds? → a violation of severity Major, and the instance is forced to Violated From when are those 5 seconds counted? → from the moment the instance enters Assigned Which monitor acts when the battery falls below 20% while the instance is still Assigned? → battery_guard If you can answer all four, you know enough to start writing in Chapter 4.

A CADL file has two floors: the structure layer (actors / contracts / protocols), which says what exists, and the norms layer (lifecycle / monitors inside a contract), which says what must be kept. A contract is a class of agreement written in assume-guarantee form; the contract instance created for each order moves between states following the transitions, deadlines and monitors of the lifecycle. A missed deadline or a monitor whose condition holds is a violation and forces the instance to the state named in transition:. cadl check checks the file you wrote, and cadl verify looks for contradictions between assumptions and guarantees.

To look up these constructs, including the parts this textbook does not use, read: What you want to know Specification The structure of a whole file and the levels of detail Chapter 5, Section 5.1 Every key of actors, contracts and protocols Chapter 5, Section 5.2 The formal syntax (EBNF) Appendix A Syntax, static rules and behaviour of the lifecycle and monitors Appendix E, Sections E.3–E.5 The fields written to the IR Appendix E, Section E.7 Terms the Glossary and Appendix A of this textbook

This chapter generates Unity C# code from the specification and runs the same IR in the Python reference runtime to check the results (about 15 minutes). In the exercises you change a deadline or the environment, predict the outcome, and then observe it.
documents.s: Chapter 7 — Generating code and running the reference runtime

documents.t: In the procedure: How a single CLI command turns your CADL into a Unity-ready C# tree. Why there are two runtimes with the same semantics: a Python reference runtime that interprets the IR, and the generated C#. In the exercises: Run the Python reference runtime against your spec, multi-robot. Read NDJSON traces and aggregate them into per-robot summaries. Vary one parameter at a time and predict before observing.

The Python runtime in cadl-raspimouse-simulator/cadl/runtime/ consumes the IR and gives you deterministic, replayable discrete-time simulation. The five-robot multi_robot_demo.py is your fixed test bench: Robot Scripted outcome Why it matters robot-0-1 Completed sanity check that happy path works robot-1-1 Violated via deadline:accept demonstrates detection of a missed deadline robot-2-1 Violated via monitor:battery_guard demonstrates periodic monitor robot-3-1 Violated via monitor:deadline_watch demonstrates declarative monitor robot-4-1 stays Proposed demonstrates "instance never advances" is also a valid trace This is your ground truth to validate any spec change you make. The table describes the bundled fixture, which declares both monitors, battery_guard and deadline_watch. When you run the demo on your own IR (--ir, from Exercise 7.2 on), a monitor your file does not declare cannot fire. With the v2 of Chapter 5, which has battery_guard but no deadline_watch, robot-3-1 ends in Delivering with no violation, not in Violated. If your v2 has no battery_guard either, robot-2-1 is still Violated, but via deadline:accept.
documents.s: The reference runtime as a test bench

documents.t: The repo provides a single end-to-end script. Run it: cd ~/program/cadl_repo ./scripts/sos_dsl_handson_e2e.sh \ examples/sos_dsl_robot_delivery.cadl \ --unity ../cadl-raspimouse-simulator/unity Without the simulator repository you can still run the pipeline up to code generation: pass --unity "" and the script stops after generating the C# tree under output/sos_dsl_handson/. Replace the input with my_delivery.cadl if you want to use your own specification — note that your file will need a lifecycle.transitions[*].on: matching the bridge's event names, so for the very first run we recommend the bundled example.

$ ./scripts/sos_dsl_handson_e2e.sh examples/sos_dsl_robot_delivery.cadl \ --unity ../cadl-raspimouse-simulator/unity == INPUT == source : .../examples/sos_dsl_robot_delivery.cadl size : 166 lines == Step 1/4 — parse + type-check (cadl check) == OK == Step 2/4 — emit Sim-IR JSON (cadl sim-ir) == output/sos_dsl_handson/sos_dsl_robot_delivery.ir.json contracts : 1 states : 7 monitors : 3 == Step 3/4 — codegen Unity C# (cadl codegen --target unity-csharp) == output : output/sos_dsl_handson/unity-csharp runtime : 5 files generated : 3 files total lines : 783 == Step 4/4 — drop into ../cadl-raspimouse-simulator/unity/Assets/Scripts/SoSDsl/ == installed: .../Runtime, .../Generated preserved: .../Demo (if it existed) == DONE == Next steps for the student: 1. Open the Unity project at .../unity in Unity 6 (6000.2) 2. Open Assets/Scenes/C-SoS.unity 3. Add a ContractRuntimeHost GameObject (Demo/ContractRuntimeHost) 4. Attach PilotContractBridge to each robot that has Pilot_CSoS 5. Press Play and watch the Console for [lifecycle ...] / [violation ...] See the textbook for the full walkthrough (Chapter 8 covers these steps): https://www.ertl.jp/cadl-spec/docs/textbook/ Look at the generated tree: output/sos_dsl_handson/unity-csharp/ ├── Runtime/ # constant per generation, common to all contracts │ ├── Severity.cs # enum Minor / Major / Critical │ ├── ContractEvent.cs # struct used for both lifecycle & violation events │ ├── EventBus.cs # tiny FIFO publish-subscribe │ ├── PredicateEvaluator.cs # CADL expression evaluator (mirrors the Python one) │ └── ContractRuntime.cs # registry + tick loop └── Generated/ # one set of files per CADL contract ├── DeliverySlaState.cs # public enum DeliverySlaState { Proposed, Assigned, ... } ├── DeliverySlaContract.cs # IContractInstance impl for DELIVERY_SLA └── DeliverySlaMonitors.cs # one Eval_xxx method per monitor After the script has run, the generated files are in the Unity project. Open the project in Unity (Section 8.2 describes how) and look at the Project window: they appear under Assets/Scripts/SoSDsl/Generated. Selecting DeliverySlaContract shows the generated C# in the Inspector (you do not edit this file; it is overwritten every time you regenerate):

The same IR drives both, in different ways. The Python reference runtime (cadl/runtime/engine.py in the simulator repository) is a hand-written interpreter that loads the IR JSON when it starts; the C# contract classes are generated from the IR by cadl codegen: ┌──────────────────────┐ │ multi_robot_demo.py │ ← run today as Python │ (Python runtime) │ │ │ ┌──────────┘ │ IR JSON ──────►│ │ └──────────┐ │ │ DeliverySlaContract │ ← run later in Unity │ (Unity / C#) │ └──────────────────────┘ If both runtimes are correct, they must produce the same trace for the same inputs. We can sanity-check this without Unity: cd ~/program/cadl-raspimouse-simulator python3 -m cadl.runtime.multi_robot_demo --summary $ python3 -m cadl.runtime.multi_robot_demo --summary # multi_robot_demo summary (20 events) robot-0-1 state=Completed violations=[(none)] robot-1-1 state=Violated violations=[deadline:accept] robot-2-1 state=Violated violations=[monitor:battery_guard] robot-3-1 state=Violated violations=[monitor:deadline_watch] robot-4-1 state=Proposed violations=[(none)] kind counts: {'lifecycle': 17, 'violation': 3} cause counts: {'open': 5, 'event': 9, 'monitor': 2, 'deadline': 1} Five robots, five different outcomes. This is a scripted Python scenario, built so that every outcome a contract can reach (normal completion, deadline violation, monitor violation, still unassigned) is visible in a single run. The Unity run in Chapter 8 assigns deliveries at different times and gives the robots different battery settings, so these five rows will not be reproduced as-is (in Unity, typically the one robot whose battery you lowered violates via battery_guard while the rest progress to Completed). What you should be matching is not the per-robot outcomes but the mechanism — that the same lifecycle transitions, deadline, and monitor behave with the same meaning. 🛠 Troubleshooting: multi_robot_demo not found​ Run the command from the root of cadl-raspimouse-simulator. Python finds cadl.runtime relative to the current directory; from anywhere else it finds only the cadl compiler package, which has no runtime module, and reports No module named cadl.runtime. cd ~/program/cadl-raspimouse-simulator git pull # make sure the checkout is current python3 -m cadl.runtime.multi_robot_demo --summary To look at one contract instance at a time, demo_delivery exercises the same three mechanisms (happy path, deadline violation, monitor violation) on one contract instance (its output is for a single contract, so its shape differs from the 5-robot table above): PYTHONPATH=. python3 -m cadl.runtime.demo_delivery --scenario happy # accepted, stops at Accepted PYTHONPATH=. python3 -m cadl.runtime.demo_delivery --scenario late # 5s deadline missed -> Violated via deadline:accept PYTHONPATH=. python3 -m cadl.runtime.demo_delivery --scenario battery # battery drops -> Violated via monitor:battery_guard

Following the bundled example examples/sos_dsl_robot_delivery.cadl (166 lines), this section traces where one line you write ends up. You do not need it to follow the procedure; read it when you want to know what the commands produced. (1) Spec → IR. The deadline: 5s in your .cadl file is parsed by cadl_repo/src/cadl/parser.py, and once sim/lower.py lowers it into the IR it becomes the JSON "deadline_ms": 5000 (the whole IR is 297 lines). The IR is an intermediate representation that discards the "human-friendly notation" and keeps only the "form that machines can easily execute". (2) IR → C#. codegen/unity_csharp/contract_emitter.py reads the IR and generates three files per contract: the state enum (DeliverySlaState.cs), the state machine itself (DeliverySlaContract.cs), and the monitoring rules (DeliverySlaMonitors.cs). Together with 5 shared runtime files (listed below), a total of 783 lines is placed under unity/Assets/Scripts/SoSDsl/.
documents.s: 7.6 Inside the generated code and the reference runtime

documents.t: File What it contains Approx. lines Runtime/ContractRuntime.cs Instance registration, event delivery (to one instance or to all), the Tick loop. The heart of the system ~100 Runtime/PredicateEvaluator.cs Evaluator for predicate strings like "battery < 20 AND state == Assigned" ~250 Runtime/ContractEvent.cs Shared struct for lifecycle / violation events. The Console lines come from its ToString() ~40 Runtime/EventBus.cs / Severity.cs Lightweight pub-sub and the severity enum Small Generated/DeliverySlaContract.cs The transition table itself. Rows of if statements: "when this event arrives in this state, go to that state" ~220 Generated/DeliverySlaMonitors.cs Monitoring rules. Evaluates a predicate on each period (e.g. 500ms) and emits a violation if true ~100

File What it contains engine.py A Python implementation with the same semantics as the C# runtime (~720 lines). Reads the IR and drives state machines, deadlines, and monitors multi_robot_demo.py A scripted run in which 5 robots reach 5 different outcomes (completed, response deadline expired, battery violation, delivery delay, unassigned)
documents.s: The Python reference runtime — cadl/runtime/ (for cross-checking)

documents.t: Read examples/sos_dsl_robot_delivery.cadl from top to bottom (10 min). It is heavily commented, and it doubles as the answer key for Chapters 4–5. Read HandleEvent in Generated/DeliverySlaContract.cs (10 min) and confirm that the transitions of the .cadl file became if statements as they are. Read ContractRuntime.tick in engine.py (10 min).

cd ~/program/cadl_repo pip install pytest # once; Chapter 2 does not install it PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m pytest tests/test_unity_csharp_structural.py -q # 9 passed These nine tests catch the structural bugs that would prevent Unity from compiling the generated C# (mismatched braces, missing namespaces, name collisions, etc.). If they fail, the codegen has a regression.

You now have: A 297-line Sim-IR JSON (for the bundled example). A 783-line Unity-ready C# tree, dropped into the Unity project. A Python proof-of-concept showing what the C# trace must look like once it runs.

Goal: Run multi_robot_demo --summary against the bundled fixture (not your my_delivery_v2.cadl — yet), capture the output verbatim, and explain each row. Procedure: cd ~/program/cadl-raspimouse-simulator python3 -m cadl.runtime.multi_robot_demo --summary > session4_baseline.txt python3 -m cadl.runtime.multi_robot_demo --log session4_baseline.ndjson Check: All five robots' final states match the table above.

Goal: Shorten the accept deadline in my_delivery_v2.cadl step by step — 5s → 1s → 100ms → 50ms — and find the point at which the outcome changes. Does any robot still complete? Procedure: Edit my_delivery_v2.cadl, change deadline: 5s to deadline: 1s on the accept transition (the scenario's time scale is milliseconds: the robots acknowledge about 100 ms after assignment). Regenerate the IR and run the demo on it with the --ir option (without --ir the demo loads the bundled fixture): cd ~/program/cadl_repo cadl sim-ir my_delivery_v2.cadl --format json > my_delivery_v2.ir.json cd ~/program/cadl-raspimouse-simulator python3 -m cadl.runtime.multi_robot_demo --ir ~/program/cadl_repo/my_delivery_v2.ir.json --summary Compare the summary with the one you get from the same file with deadline: 5s, then repeat steps 1–2 with 100ms and 50ms. With the v2 of Chapter 5 you should see: deadline What changes 5s, 1s Nothing: the summaries are identical. The deadline is not what limits these runs. 100ms robot-2-1 is still Violated, but the cause changes from monitor:battery_guard to deadline:accept — the deadline now fires before the monitor does. 50ms No robot completes: robot-0-1 to robot-3-1 are all Violated with deadline:accept. my_delivery_v2.cadl has no deadline_watch monitor and no late_failure transition, so robot-3-1 ends in Delivering instead of Violated at 5s, 1s and 100ms: your own v2 reproduces four of the five outcomes of the bundled example. Reflection: An overly tight deadline (50ms here) turns every contract into a violation, regardless of effort. An overly loose one (5s and 1s behave the same) masks misbehaviour. What process would you use to pick a deadline value for a real SoS? (Hint: data from baseline runs, plus a target false-positive rate.)

Goal: Run the same scenario but with different per-instance battery / speed / deadline values. Capture how the violation pattern changes. Procedure: Make a copy of multi_robot_demo.py, modify _seed_battery(...) and update_instance_world(...) calls, run with --summary. Try at least three configurations. Submit: A small table showing config-name → terminal-state-per-robot.

Before the session. my_delivery_v2.cadl and its IR. (Optional) violation_trace_view.py from Chapter 6. Wrap-up and homework. Bring to the next session (Chapter 9): session4_baseline.txt + session4_baseline.ndjson. Your multi_robot_demo parameter-sweep table (3+ configurations). 1 sentence: which violation pattern surprised you most, and why?

documents.t: This chapter decides, from the results observed in Chapter 7, where to change the specification, and checks the change by running it again. The chapter consists of exercises only.
Use observations from simulation to identify which knob to turn. Adjust the spec at the right layer (deadline / monitor / lifecycle / actor / runtime). Validate the change with a re-run.

Each layer of the design has its own kind of fix: Symptom in trace Layer that fixes it Example fix Deadline expires for every robot Spec — relax deadline 5s → 7s One robot's monitor fires too often (false positive) Spec — tighten rule < 20 → < 15 Robots reach Violated because the world model is wrong Runtime — fix world snapshot keys check update_instance_world calls Reward never gets paid Runtime — implement reward execution extend engine.py All robots succeed but the aggregate is wrong (e.g., late) New monitor or new contract add FLEET_THROUGHPUT_SLA This is a small but useful typology of regressions in normative SoS specs.
Goal: Pick one violation from your Chapter 7 traces. Explain in 1 paragraph: which layer would you change, and how. Submit: session5_diagnosis.md (1 page).

Goal: Implement your diagnosis. Save the fixed spec as my_delivery_v3.cadl. Procedure: Make the change you diagnosed in Exercise 9.1. Generate the IR of the new file and re-run the demo against it, as in Exercise 7.2: cd ~/program/cadl_repo cadl sim-ir my_delivery_v3.cadl --format json > my_delivery_v3.ir.json cd ~/program/cadl-raspimouse-simulator python3 -m cadl.runtime.multi_robot_demo --ir ~/program/cadl_repo/my_delivery_v3.ir.json --summary Confirm the violation you fixed is gone and you didn't break anything else. Submit: my_delivery_v3.cadl + diff against v2.

Goal: Currently a reward is written in the spec (incentives.rules) but never applied — and the rule text does not even reach the runtime. When the spec is lowered to the IR (cadl_repo/src/cadl/sim/lower.py), only lambda and incentive_type are kept, under the contract's governance; the rules list is dropped. Make the Python runtime maintain a per-actor balance and credit a reward when a contract reaches Completed. Procedure: Extend ContractRuntime with balances: dict[str, float], accessor runtime.balance(actor_id), and a way to receive the rules, for example ContractRuntime(ir, log_path=None, reward_rules=[...]). Get the rules. Because the IR does not carry them, read them from the .cadl source with the cadl parser in a separate script that writes them to JSON (if your file has no incentives: block, add the one from Chapter 4): # dump_rules.py — run with the Python environment where cadl-lang is installed import json, sys from cadl.parser import parse_file sos = parse_file(sys.argv[1]) rules = [{"contract": c.id, "rule": r.description} for c in sos.contracts if c.incentives for r in c.incentives.rules] json.dump(rules, open(sys.argv[2], "w"), indent=2) # python dump_rules.py my_delivery_v2.cadl rules.json # -> [{"contract": "DELIVERY_SLA", "rule": "reward(ROBOT[i], 10) when on_time_delivery"}] The script has to be separate: the simulator repository has its own top-level cadl/ package, which shadows cadl-lang, so from cadl.parser import parse_file fails with No module named 'cadl.parser' inside the runtime, its tests, or anything run with python -m from the simulator root. Run the script from another directory and pass rules.json to the demo (add a --rewards rules.json option to multi_robot_demo). Each rule is a raw string. Parse entries of the form reward(<actor_ref>, <amount>) when on_time_delivery yourself (a regular expression is enough) and skip the others (the bundled example also has a penalty(...) rule). Stretch variant: instead of reading the source, extend lower.py (and GovernanceParams in sim/ir.py) so that the IR carries the rules, for example as governance.incentive_rules. Run cadl from your edited checkout (pip install -e .; the PyPI release does not have the key), confirm that the rules appear in the output of cadl sim-ir --format json, and let the runtime read them from the IR. Decide who is paid. The runtime knows only the instance id (robot-0-1); a contract instance has no actor field. Pass the actor when the instance is opened (for example open_instance(..., actors={"ROBOT": "robot-0"})) and map the rule's ROBOT[i] to it. Credit on entry to a terminal state. An instance is closed in two places — StateMachineEngine.fire_transition (ordinary transitions, including complete) and ContractRuntime._fire_state_jump (deadline and monitor jumps) — so hook both. Define on_time_delivery yourself as "the instance entered Completed and has no violation record"; the runtime's predicate evaluator cannot decide it, because it treats a bare identifier as true. Add cadl/runtime/tests/test_rewards.py with at least: One test: a robot earns 10 on a Completed delivery. One test: no reward is paid on a Violated delivery. Update multi_robot_demo --summary to print final balances. With the bundled scenario, robot-0 ends with 10 and the other four with 0. Reflection: The CADL spec already says reward(ROBOT[i], 10) when on_time_delivery, but until this exercise the runtime ignored it — the IR did not even carry it. Where is the line between "the spec says so" and "the runtime does so"?

Goal: A 3-page report covering the entire course. Page Content 1 Initial CADL model (v1), the question your model is asking, and what was missing in v1. 2 Simulation results — baseline vs your modifications. Tables and at least one screenshot from cadl-explorer. 3 Reflection: what did adding norms buy you? What did running the simulation teach you that the spec alone could not? Where do you think SoS-DSL could go next?

Before the session. All deliverables from Chapters 4–7. Wrap-up and homework. Submit by the end of the last session (Chapter 9): my_delivery_v1.cadl / v2.cadl / v3.cadl. session5_diagnosis.md + final report (3 pages). (Optional) test_rewards.py and the modified engine.py.

documents.t: Overview. In Chapters 4–9 you wrote the contracts by hand. In this advanced exercise you build and evaluate a loop in which an LLM generates the CADL contract from natural-language operating rules ("respond within 5 seconds", "never assign a low-battery robot") and is auto-corrected until the draft passes cadl check, with the diagnostics fed back on every failure. The essence: the LLM proposes, the type checker gatekeeps — no LLM output takes effect until it passes. Keep in mind that passing cadl check is a syntactic and type-level check, not a safety guarantee: it says the draft is well-formed CADL, not that its deadlines and rules are the right ones. Key points. A draft that passes the check is not necessarily what you meant. Compare the accepted draft's deadline values and monitor rules against the contract you hand-wrote in Chapter 5 — noticing that "passes ≠ matches intent" is the single biggest lesson here. Feed failure diagnostics back to the LLM verbatim. Record what it managed to fix and what it could not. Evaluate with counting statistics: first-pass rate, pass@K, and mean rounds to pass. Hints. Spelling out the CADL grammar constraints in the system prompt (only four SoS types, ASCII identifiers, deadline: 5s duration format, ...) can be expected to raise the first-pass rate; measuring it with and without the constraints makes a good experiment. cadl check can be invoked as a subprocess (inspect the exit code and output). No reference implementation is publicly available at present (the authors' own, step_a_design.py and measure_step_a.py in the cadl-ai-governance repository, is not public), so writing the loop and a small measurement script is part of the exercise. Start with a deterministic mock in place of the LLM (a function that returns a fixed sequence of drafts) to watch the loop run, then switch to a real LLM.

Layer We wrote We didn't write Spec a CADL file of about 110 lines (Chapters 4 and 5) nothing — the spec was the only source IR nothing generated JSON (297 lines for the bundled example) Visualisation nothing the Lifecycle View page Implementation nothing generated Unity C# (783 lines for the bundled example) Runtime semantics nothing a working state machine + monitors + deadline timers Why does this matter for SoS? The same specification powers everything: the docs, the diagram, the simulation, the code. When the specification changes — say, you tighten the deadline from 5s to 3s — you edit one file and re-run the generation commands (cadl sim-ir, cadl codegen, or the e2e script); the IR, the diagram and the generated C# then all follow from that single source, with no second copy of the rule to edit by hand. Keeping one source for all of them helps keep a large SoS design maintainable.

Each chapter from 4 to 9 ends with the exercises of one class session (19 exercises in total, graded ★ to ★★★), and Chapter 10 adds one optional advanced exercise. They rebuild and then modify the system you just built one axis at a time — tighter deadlines, new monitors, new lifecycle states, reward execution, a violation-trace view. Appendix C shows how to run them as a 5-session (or 3-session) class. To try the workflow on a fresh problem, go on to the other courses of the hands-on materials: Course B — Urban Mobility: the same CADL syntax with another domain and runtime (SUMO). Course D — Robot Town: rules, regulation and contracts amended toward a KPI while the system runs: a human sets the KPIs and decides what an LLM proposer should not decide alone. Course C — Your own SoS: an open-ended, self-directed track given as an outline. Pick a different domain (food delivery, smart traffic, data sharing between organisations, …), write its CADL from a blank page, exercise it with a small simulation harness of your choice (a Python discrete-event harness such as SimPy is the suggested default), and compare results across parameter sweeps.

This chapter adds the lifecycle and the monitors of the SoS-DSL extension to the contract written in Chapter 4 (about 15 minutes). In the exercises you add states and monitors and make two contracts coexist.

In the procedure: The seven lifecycle states a contract instance can occupy. How to write a deadline + on_violation that puts a time bound on a transition and says where the instance goes when the bound is missed. How to write a periodic monitor with a predicate over the world snapshot. In the exercises: Add a per-instance lifecycle: to a structural contract. Add declarative monitors: with predicates and sampling specs. Read cadl sim-ir JSON output and locate your additions in it.

A class-level contract spec (Chapter 4) describes the agreement, but a real SoS has many concurrent instances of that agreement — one per delivery request. Each instance has its own state that progresses over time: The same lifecycle is reused for every delivery request — only the data (which robot, which customer) differs.

A class-level contract spec says "this is the kind of agreement we make." But every concrete delivery is its own instance of that agreement, going through: Two new keys make this explicit: lifecycle: — defines states, initial / terminal markers, and transitions with deadline + on_violation. monitors: — declarative observers that are evaluated periodically or on events. When a monitor's rule matches, it records a violation (on_match.violation), moves the contract instance to the named target state (on_match.transition, e.g. Violated), or both.

First declare, near the top of my_delivery.cadl, that the file uses the SoS-DSL extension. Appendix E asks for this declaration (SHOULD), and the bundled example has it: sos: name: "MyDelivery" type: Acknowledged # central authority + autonomous agents version: "0.1.0" extensions: # ← NEW: this file uses the SoS-DSL extension - sos-dsl: 0.1 Then append the two highlighted blocks below to the DELIVERY_SLA contract. Indentation matters (YAML). contracts: - id: DELIVERY_SLA parties: [DISPATCHER, "ROBOT[*]", "CUSTOMER[*]"] assume: - "ROBOT[i].battery > 20" guarantee: - "delivery_time <= 300s" incentives: type: task_completion lambda: 0.5 rules: - "reward(ROBOT[i], 10) when on_time_delivery" # ╔═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗ # ║ NEW BLOCK 1: per-instance lifecycle ║ # ╚═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝ lifecycle: states: - Proposed - Assigned - Accepted - Delivering - Completed - Violated - Terminated initial: Proposed terminal: [Completed, Violated, Terminated] transitions: - id: assign from: Proposed to: Assigned on: "DISPATCHER -> ROBOT[i] : route_assignment" - id: accept from: Assigned to: Accepted on: "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : ack(accepted)" deadline: 5s # ⏱ must happen within 5s on_violation: # otherwise → Violated transition: Violated severity: Major - id: start_delivery from: Accepted to: Delivering on: "ROBOT[i].status == InTransit" - id: complete from: Delivering to: Completed on: "ROBOT[i].status == Delivered" # ╔═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗ # ║ NEW BLOCK 2: declarative monitors ║ # ╚═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝ monitors: - id: battery_guard observe: "ROBOT[i].battery" sampling: periodic(500ms) rule: "ROBOT[i].battery < 20 AND state == Assigned" on_match: transition: Violated severity: Major Re-run the type-checker: cadl check my_delivery.cadl

$ cadl check my_delivery.cadl Type check passed: my_delivery.cadl Lower to IR and verify the new fields are populated: cadl sim-ir my_delivery.cadl --format json \ | python3 -c " import json, sys d = json.load(sys.stdin) c = d['institution']['contracts'][0] print(f'lifecycle.initial : {c[\"lifecycle\"][\"initial\"]}') print(f'lifecycle.states : {c[\"lifecycle\"][\"states\"]}') print(f'monitors[0].id : {c[\"monitors\"][0][\"id\"]}') print(f' rule : {c[\"monitors\"][0][\"rule\"]}') " lifecycle.initial : Proposed lifecycle.states : ['Proposed', 'Assigned', 'Accepted', 'Delivering', 'Completed', 'Violated', 'Terminated'] monitors[0].id : battery_guard rule : ROBOT[i].battery < 20 AND state == Assigned

The diff between Chapter 4 and Chapter 5 is only the extensions: declaration and the two new blocks. No actor changed. The IR's "lifecycle": null is now a populated object; "monitors": [] is now a 1-element list.

Symptom Why cadl check passes, but the IR has "lifecycle": null and Chapter 6 shows no states The lifecycle: block has wrong indentation, so it is not read as part of the contract. lifecycle: must sit at the same level as assume: / guarantee:, with states: one level below it. The checker does not report the indentation itself; it reports it only indirectly, when a monitor names a lifecycle state (an M-3 error, because the contract then has no lifecycle). Parser silently treats on: as a boolean YAML 1.1 quirk; the example file works because the parser has a workaround (_yaml_on_key). If you're writing your own parser, watch for this. monitor.rule "always false" The right-hand side of state == Assigned is a bare identifier by CADL convention; \"Assigned\" in double quotes means the same. Single quotes ('Assigned') are not part of the rule grammar: cadl check warns that the rule "is not a valid rule (Appendix E.3) and is kept as text", and the monitor never fires.
The same file now describes both the structure (Chapter 4) and the rules (Chapter 5). The IR is no longer "structural-only" — it carries enough information to build a runtime.

Goal: Save my_delivery_v1.cadl as my_delivery_v2.cadl, then add a lifecycle: block to DELIVERY_SLA with the 7 states of Section 5.3. Procedure: Copy v1 → v2. Add lifecycle.states, lifecycle.initial, lifecycle.terminal, and 4 transitions (assign, accept, start_delivery, complete). On accept, set deadline: 5s and on_violation.transition: Violated (the value is the target state). Also declare extensions: [sos-dsl: 0.1] under sos:, and copy the monitors: block (battery_guard) of Section 5.3: Chapter 7 runs the v2 of this exercise and expects that monitor. Run cadl check my_delivery_v2.cadl, then cadl sim-ir my_delivery_v2.cadl --format json | grep -n -A3 '"lifecycle"' (the "lifecycle" key sits well past the first screen of the IR — line 90 for the file of Section 5.3, later if you added actors or contracts in Chapter 4 — so head would cut it off). Confirm in the output that "lifecycle" is no longer null: the line now reads "lifecycle": {, followed by "states": [ and the first state names. If you added MAINTENANCE_SLA in Exercise 4.2, grep prints a second match for that contract, which still reads "lifecycle": null; that is expected, because only DELIVERY_SLA has a lifecycle.

Goal: Detect a robot that drives faster than 1.5 m/s while delivering and move the contract instance to Violated with severity Critical. Procedure: Add a monitor under monitors:: - id: over_speed observe: "ROBOT[i].speed" sampling: periodic(200ms) rule: "ROBOT[i].speed > 1.5 AND state == Delivering" on_match: transition: Violated severity: Critical Reflection: You have just added a new normative rule without changing a single line of the robot's control code (Unity's Pilot_CSoS.cs). What does this say about the separation between the structural code and the normative spec? (Compare [Maier 1998] criterion (4), emergent behaviour: here a norm constrains it without redesigning the parts.)

Goal: Let a customer cancel a delivery while it is still Assigned, routing the contract to a new Cancelled terminal state. Procedure: Add Cancelled to lifecycle.states and lifecycle.terminal. Add a transition customer_cancel from Assigned to Cancelled triggered by "CUSTOMER[i] -> DISPATCHER : cancel_order". Decide: should Cancelled be a violation? In CADL, terminal states are not implicitly violations — they are just closed. Reflection: When you added Cancelled, did the existing simulation break? Why or why not? (Adding a state is backward-compatible; adding a deadline is not.)
documents.s: Exercise 5.3 (★★) — Add a Cancelled lifecycle state

documents.t: Goal: Beside DELIVERY_SLA, add a FLEET_SAFETY contract whose lifecycle is independent of any delivery — it is always on while a robot is operational. Procedure: Define a 3-state lifecycle: Operational → Degraded → OutOfService. Add a monitor that fires Degraded when battery < 10% (regardless of delivery state). Run cadl check. Are there any conflicts with DELIVERY_SLA rules? Reflection: A robot can be a party to both contracts simultaneously. What semantics do you want when one contract says "you may proceed" and the other says "you must stop"?

Before the session. my_delivery_v1.cadl from Chapter 4. 30 min of pre-reading: Sections 3.7–3.9 of this textbook (for more detail, Appendix E of the specification). Wrap-up and homework. Bring to the next session (Chapter 6): my_delivery_v2.cadl (with at minimum Exercises 5.1–5.3 done). The IR JSON snapshot saved as my_delivery_v2.ir.json (run cadl sim-ir … --format json > my_delivery_v2.ir.json). (Optional) my_delivery_v2_with_safety.cadl if you tackled Exercise 5.4.

documents.t: This chapter writes the structure of the robot-delivery SoS (its actors, contract and protocol) in CADL and checks it with cadl check and cadl sim-ir (about 15 minutes). In the exercises at the end you add an actor, give the protocol conditions, and write the structure of a domain you do not know yet.

In the procedure: How to declare actors with id, role, autonomy, interface. How to declare a contract's parties, A/G clauses (assume / guarantee), incentives. How to declare a protocol: the messages of one order, as a sequence of sender -> receiver : message steps. In the exercises: Identify the actors of an SoS and declare them yourself, including one for a domain you do not know yet. Run cadl check and explain its diagnostics.

Think of a CADL actors: block as a UML class diagram for the SoS — each actor type has ports (interface.input / interface.output) and a degree of self-direction (autonomy: low | medium | high). The contracts: block is the agreement between named subsets of those actors.

A CADL file says who participates and what they expect from each other, before saying anything about when or how often. The structural building blocks are: In this chapter you write actors, contracts and one protocol. transitions are optional stretch material.
documents.s: The building blocks of a structure

documents.t: Create a new file my_delivery.cadl in the root of cadl_repo (that is, ~/program/cadl_repo/my_delivery.cadl; the bundled example it resembles is examples/sos_dsl_robot_delivery.cadl), and paste the skeleton below. The commands in Chapters 4–6 are run from ~/program/cadl_repo. Read the comments — they explain what each block does. # my_delivery.cadl ─── My first SoS specification # (this file just describes structure; norms come in Chapter 5) sos: name: "MyDelivery" type: Acknowledged # central authority + autonomous agents version: "0.1.0" context: environment: grid_size: 30 # abstract parameter (not the Unity road graph) num_robots: 3 time_step_ms: 100 # ── WHO exists in the SoS ───────────────────────────────────── actors: - id: DISPATCHER role: "central_coordinator" autonomy: low # follows policy, no roaming capabilities: [assign_tasks] interface: input: [delivery_request, position_report, task_completion, ack] output: [route_assignment, delivery_notification] - id: "ROBOT[1..N]" # parametric: N copies role: "delivery_agent" autonomy: high capabilities: [follow_path, pick_up, deliver] interface: input: [route_assignment] output: [position_report, task_completion, ack] - id: "CUSTOMER[1..M]" role: "service_requester" autonomy: medium capabilities: [submit_order] interface: input: [delivery_notification] output: [delivery_request] # ── The agreement between them ──────────────────────────────── contracts: - id: DELIVERY_SLA parties: [DISPATCHER, "ROBOT[*]", "CUSTOMER[*]"] assume: - "ROBOT[i].battery > 20" # input precondition guarantee: - "delivery_time <= 300s" # output postcondition incentives: type: task_completion lambda: 0.5 rules: - "reward(ROBOT[i], 10) when on_time_delivery" # ── HOW they talk: the messages of one order ───────────────── protocols: - id: DeliveryOrder trigger: "new_delivery_request(CUSTOMER[j])" steps: # "sender -> receiver : message" - "CUSTOMER[j] -> DISPATCHER : delivery_request" - "DISPATCHER -> ROBOT[i] : route_assignment" - "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : ack" - "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : task_completion" - "DISPATCHER -> CUSTOMER[j] : delivery_notification" Run the type-checker: cd ~/program/cadl_repo cadl check my_delivery.cadl

$ cadl check my_delivery.cadl Type check passed: my_delivery.cadl Now lower it to IR JSON. The output is about 150 lines long; the listing below is abridged to the parts that matter here: cadl sim-ir my_delivery.cadl --format json { "name": "MyDelivery", "sos_type": "Acknowledged", "description": "", "environment": { "grid_size": 30, "num_robots": 3, "time_step_ms": 100 }, "institution": { "actors": [ ... ], "contracts": [ { "id": "DELIVERY_SLA", "parties": ["DISPATCHER", "ROBOT[*]", "CUSTOMER[*]"], "assume": ["ROBOT[i].battery > 20"], "guarantee":["delivery_time <= 300s"], ... "lifecycle": null, ← we have NOT written it yet "monitors": [] } ] },

Verify both: cadl check my_delivery.cadl prints Type check passed: my_delivery.cadl (and no [ERROR] lines). The IR JSON has "lifecycle": null and "monitors": []. These two lines sit near the end of the contract (around line 90 of the output), just before "norms" and "counts_as", which belong to the norms extension and stay empty here. To print just them: cadl sim-ir my_delivery.cadl --format json | grep -n -A1 '"lifecycle"' 90: "lifecycle": null, 91- "monitors": [], These two null / [] are the gap we will fill in Chapter 5 — they are why the structure-only specification cannot say "the robot must ack within 5 seconds".

Symptom Cause YAML parse error: while parsing a flow sequence You wrote a subscripted identifier without quoting, e.g. [ROBOT[i].battery, ...]. Quote it: ["ROBOT[i].battery", ...]. Parse error: Invalid SoS type: 'Centralized'. Must be one of: Directed, Acknowledged, Collaborative, Virtual CADL accepts only these four values for type:. [ERROR]: Undefined actor 'CUSTMER' referenced in contract 'DELIVERY_SLA' parties A name under parties: (or inside a predicate, e.g. CUSTMER[i].x) is not declared under actors:. Usually a typo. An actor declared as CUSTOMER[1..M] is referred to as "CUSTOMER[*]" (all) or CUSTOMER[i] (one).

You now have a CADL file that describes the structure of your SoS. It compiles, it lowers to IR, and the IR confirms there is exactly one contract called DELIVERY_SLA and one protocol, DeliveryOrder. Next we add the norms that let a runtime check that contract.

Goal: Reproduce the actors, contract and protocol of Section 4.3, by hand, into a fresh file my_delivery_v1.cadl. Procedure: Create my_delivery_v1.cadl in the root of cadl_repo (the bundled example to compare with is examples/sos_dsl_robot_delivery.cadl), and run the commands below from that directory. Declare three actors: DISPATCHER, ROBOT[1..N], CUSTOMER[1..M]. Choose sensible autonomy levels for each. Declare one contract DELIVERY_SLA with parties: [DISPATCHER, "ROBOT[*]", "CUSTOMER[*]"], assume: ["ROBOT[i].battery > 20"], guarantee: ["delivery_time <= 300s"]. Declare the protocol DeliveryOrder with the five steps of Section 4.3, and list each message in the interface of its sender (output) and its receiver (input). Run cadl check my_delivery_v1.cadl and confirm it prints Type check passed: my_delivery_v1.cadl. Check: The file passes the type check, and the IR JSON shows 3 actors, 1 contract and 1 protocol.
documents.s: Exercise 4.1 (★) — Build the baseline structural model

documents.t: Goal: Introduce a MAINTENANCE actor that periodically inspects robots, and declare a separate contract MAINTENANCE_SLA between MAINTENANCE and ROBOT[*]. Procedure: Add MAINTENANCE (single, low autonomy, capabilities [inspect, repair]). Add a contract MAINTENANCE_SLA with parties: [MAINTENANCE, "ROBOT[*]"]. Decide whether assume should include ROBOT[i].battery > 0 or something stronger. Re-run cadl check. Reflection: When you have two contracts on the same actor, which assume clauses apply? (Hint: both must hold simultaneously — this is exactly the interdependency concern that Dahmann (2014) [9] calls out as SoS pain point #5.)

Goal: Extend the protocol DeliveryOrder of my_delivery_v1.cadl with a condition that must hold before it starts and one that holds when it ends, and confirm that both reach the IR. Procedure: Find DeliveryOrder under protocols:. A protocol has no separate list of participants: who takes part follows from the senders and receivers named in steps. Add precondition: "ROBOT[i].battery > 20" above steps: and postcondition: "ROBOT[i].status == Delivered" below them (the other optional keys are safety_invariant and timing). Run cadl check my_delivery_v1.cadl, then confirm that the two conditions really reached the IR: cadl sim-ir my_delivery_v1.cadl --format json | grep -n -E '"(precondition|postcondition)"' should print two lines. Do not rely on cadl check alone here — it silently ignores keys it does not know, so a misspelt key (pre:, post_condition: …) still passes. protocols: - id: DeliveryOrder trigger: "new_delivery_request(CUSTOMER[j])" precondition: "ROBOT[i].battery > 20" steps: - "CUSTOMER[j] -> DISPATCHER : delivery_request" - "DISPATCHER -> ROBOT[i] : route_assignment" - "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : ack" - "ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : task_completion" - "DISPATCHER -> CUSTOMER[j] : delivery_notification" postcondition: "ROBOT[i].status == Delivered" Reflection: Why is the protocol described as a sequence of messages, not as code? What does this give you that a Python function would not? (Hint: think about who implements each step.)

Goal: Without copying any existing file, write a CADL skeleton for a delivery drone fleet (instead of ground robots). Same domain shape, different actors and capabilities. Procedure: Create my_drone_delivery.cadl from scratch. Decide who the actors are. Hint: a DRONE needs different capabilities than a ROBOT (consider altitude, no-fly zones, weather). Run cadl check. Reflection: How much of your file is the same as the robot delivery one, and how much is genuinely different? The same lifecycle could be reused with minor modifications — that is exactly the design intent of SoS-DSL.
documents.s: Exercise 4.4 (★★★) — Write a domain you don't know yet

documents.t: Before the session. Chapter 2 done (repositories cloned, cadl installed). 30 min of pre-reading: Chapter 3 of this textbook. Wrap-up and homework. Bring to the next session (Chapter 5): my_delivery_v1.cadl (compiles cleanly). A short note (3–5 lines) describing what is missing in v1 — i.e., what the structural-only file cannot express. (Hint: timing, what counts as a violation, what the consequences are.)

documents.t: This chapter explains the path by which diagrams, code and execution results are produced from a CADL file (the toolchain) and the four repositories it consists of, and then sets the tools up on your machine (Section 2.4).

You only need to write the leftmost box (a CADL file). Everything to its right is generated from it by the toolchain commands. ┌────────────────────────┐ │ Your CADL source │ ← You write this in Chapters 4 & 5 │ my_delivery.cadl │ └──────────┬─────────────┘ │ │ cadl check → catch typos / type errors │ cadl sim-ir → emit a JSON Intermediate Representation (IR) │ ▼ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ Sim-IR JSON │ │ (cadl-spec App. E.7) │ └─────┬──────────────┬───┘ │ │ │ └──────────────┐ │ cadl-explorer │ cadl codegen --target unity-csharp │ Lifecycle View │ ▼ ▼ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ State machine │ │ Unity C# tree │ │ diagram │ │ Runtime/ Generated/ │ └─────────────────┘ └────────────┬────────────┘ │ drop into ▼ ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ Unity scene + arbitrator │ │ → live contract events │ │ in the Console │ └──────────────────────────┘ There are two worlds — the side where specifications are written and the side where they run — with a compiler connecting them. Three points to keep in mind: The .cadl file is the only contract logic a person writes. The IR, the C# contract classes and the diagrams are generated from it by the toolchain commands. Two runtimes execute the same IR with the same meaning. The C# contract code is generated from the IR; the Python reference runtime is a hand-written interpreter that reads the IR directly and is used to cross-check results. The robot control code and the contract code are separate. Contracts only observe the robots. The robot controller Pilot_CSoS.cs contains no contract logic; the only hand-written link is a thin bridge (PilotContractBridge.cs) that turns changes of the robot state into contract events. The tools used in this textbook, and the chapters that use them: Tool What it does Chapters cadl check Checks the syntax, the types and the static rules of the SoS-DSL extension 4, 5 cadl verify Does what cadl check does, and in addition uses an SMT solver (Z3 [8]) to find contradictions between assumptions and guarantees and deadlocks in protocols introduced in 3 cadl sim-ir Turns the file into the JSON of the three-layer intermediate representation (IR) 5–7 cadl-explorer Draws the state machine (Lifecycle View) from the IR 6 cadl codegen --target unity-csharp Generates Unity C# code from the IR 7 Python reference runtime Reads the IR and replays how contract instances move between states 7, 9 Unity and the arbitrator Run the generated contract code inside the robot-swarm simulation 8

The CADL toolchain is split across four repositories so that each part can be developed independently. All four are public, and this textbook can be followed with public repositories only. Repository Role Branch to use How this textbook uses it cadl-spec The language specification and the learning site that contains this textbook (Docusaurus) main (default) Read only (viewing it locally is optional) cadl (cloned as cadl_repo) The compiler: parser, checks, IR, code generators master (default) Used as a command cadl-explorer A Streamlit app that edits and checks CADL, draws state machines and compares governance designs main (default) Used as a web app (Chapter 6) cadl-raspimouse-simulator The simulator: Unity project, Go arbitrator and Python reference runtime main (default) Where you mainly work in Chapters 7–9 The simulator keeps the Unity project (unity/), the Go arbitrator (arbitrator/) and the Python reference runtime (cadl/runtime/) together in one repository. A note on names: the Unity scene (C-SoS.unity), the robot controller (Pilot_CSoS) and the arbitrator directory (C-SoS/) carry the label "C-SoS". In the simulator, C-SoS stands for Collaborative SoS (its config has sosType: collaborative) and names the operating mode used in this textbook, in which the robots claim deliveries and the arbitrator/C-SoS arbitrator decides which robot gets each one. The repository also contains a D-SoS.unity scene for reference; its arbitrator is not included. That label is set by the simulator and is unrelated to the type: in a CADL file. The CADL file of this textbook declares type: Acknowledged, and that declaration is what the textbook means when it classifies the robot-delivery SoS (Chapter 1, Section 1.4).

Tool Version Why Python 3.9+ runs the cadl CLI Unity 6000.2.9f1 (Unity 6.2) runs the simulation Go 1.23+ builds the arbitrator NATS Server latest message bus between robots ⇄ arbitrator Node.js 20+ renders the spec website (optional) # macOS via Homebrew brew install python@3.11 go nats-server node # Unity is installed via Unity Hub.
The repositories that make up the toolchain and which branch of each one to use.
Clone the four repositories of Section 2.2 under ~/program and make the cadl command available.

mkdir -p ~/program && cd ~/program # 1) Clone the repositories. # cadl-spec, cadl and cadl-raspimouse-simulator stay on their default # branches (main / master / main). git clone https://github.com/ertlnagoya/cadl-spec git clone https://github.com/ertlnagoya/cadl cadl_repo git clone https://github.com/ertlnagoya/cadl-explorer git clone https://github.com/ertlnagoya/cadl-raspimouse-simulator # 2) Install the cadl CLI in editable mode so changes are picked up. cd ~/program/cadl_repo python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate python3 -m pip install --upgrade pip # editable install needs pip 21.3 or later pip install -e . cd ~/program

$ cadl --help usage: cadl [-h] [--version] {parse,check,verify,codegen,regime-map,iec62853,sim-validate,sim-ir,sim-gen,ai} ... CADL: Contract Architecture Description Language toolchain positional arguments: {parse,check,verify,codegen,regime-map,iec62853,sim-validate,sim-ir,sim-gen,ai} Available commands parse Parse a CADL file and report errors check Parse and type-check a CADL file verify Parse, type-check, and verify a CADL file codegen Generate runtime code from a CADL file ...
If cadl codegen --help lists unity-csharp among the --target choices ({python,solidity,opa,unity-csharp}), your install is correct.

After setup you can see that CADL is really four cooperating repositories — the spec site, the compiler, the visualizer, and the simulator. Everything that follows assumes each repository is on the branch listed in the table of Section 2.2 (main everywhere, and master for cadl_repo); most trouble at this stage comes from a wrong branch.

Check your branches (the most common pitfall). All four repositories are used on their default branches: main, and master for cadl_repo. If a page or a command described here is missing, first check that you have not switched to an older branch. Verify: cd ~/program echo "cadl-spec: $(git -C cadl-spec branch --show-current)" # main echo "cadl_repo: $(git -C cadl_repo branch --show-current)" # master echo "cadl-explorer: $(git -C cadl-explorer branch --show-current)" # main echo "simulator: $(git -C cadl-raspimouse-simulator branch --show-current)" # main For any repository on the wrong branch, switch with git -C ~/program/<repo> checkout <branch>. pip install -e . fails with File "setup.py" or "setup.cfg" not found. The pip in the venv is too old. On macOS, /usr/bin/python3 (Python 3.9 from the Command Line Tools) creates venvs with pip 21.2.4, which cannot do an editable install of a pyproject.toml-only project such as cadl. Upgrade pip inside the venv and install again: cd ~/program/cadl_repo source .venv/bin/activate python3 -m pip install --upgrade pip pip install -e . cadl reports bad interpreter, or cadl --help shows an older command list. The shell found a different cadl than the one in cadl_repo/.venv. Check with which cadl; it should print ~/program/cadl_repo/.venv/bin/cadl. In a new terminal, run source ~/program/cadl_repo/.venv/bin/activate first. If the venv itself reports bad interpreter (the Python it was built with has been removed), delete .venv and repeat step 2.
This chapter puts the generated contract code into the Unity robot-swarm simulation and watches violations being detected in the running simulation (about 15 minutes).
documents.s: Chapter 8 — Running the simulation in Unity

documents.t: How to wire ContractRuntimeHost and PilotContractBridge into an existing scene. How to read live contract events in the Unity Console.

In two separate terminals: # Terminal 1 — NATS message broker nats-server -p 4222 […] [INF] Starting nats-server … […] [INF] Listening for client connections on 0.0.0.0:4222 […] [INF] Server is ready # Terminal 2 — C-SoS arbitrator (Go) cd ~/program/cadl-raspimouse-simulator/arbitrator/C-SoS/main go run . [Config] Loaded from ../../../unity/Assets/streamingAssets/cadl_config.json: nats_url=nats://localhost:4222 numAgents=5 [Config] init=init next=next ret=ret fin=fin disp=disp resource=resource [Config] taskArbitration.enabled=true protocol=fcfs intervalSec=5.0 If that third line reads taskArbitration.enabled=true, the arbitrator has loaded its configuration and is ready to start handing out deliveries. If it says false, or the [Config] lines do not appear at all, the config file was not read — pass its absolute path with -config as shown in the note below. A further line, [Motivation] Disabled (baseline behavior), follows; it only says that the motivation extension is off. 🛠 Restart the arbitrator before every Play (important)​ The Go arbitrator initializes robot count and delivery state once at startup and does not reset when you stop and re-enter Play in Unity. It keeps the previous session's "busy / assigned" state and stops broadcasting new deliveries, so all robots stay Proposed and get Violated by deadline_watch after ~5 minutes. Restart the Terminal-2 arbitrator (Ctrl+C, then re-run) before every Play (restart NATS too if unsure). Start order is always NATS → arbitrator → Unity Play. Pass the config as an absolute path to be safe (the default is relative and depends on the launch directory): cd ~/program/cadl-raspimouse-simulator/arbitrator/C-SoS/main go run . -config ~/program/cadl-raspimouse-simulator/unity/Assets/streamingAssets/cadl_config.json If [Config] … taskArbitration.enabled=true … prints at startup, the config loaded correctly.

Launch Unity Hub. Open ~/program/cadl-raspimouse-simulator/unity with Unity 6000.2.9f1 (Unity 6.2). First open takes several minutes (package download and Library import). In the Project pane, double-click Assets/Scenes/C-SoS.unity. You should see a road network (graph) made of 11 nodes and 17 edges, with five robots — Red / Blue / Green / Yellow / Purple — driving on it. The node count, edge count, and robot count are all loaded from Assets/streamingAssets/cadl_config.json, so the Console also prints [GraphDefinition] Loaded from CADL config: 11 nodes, 17 edges. (The grid_size: 30 under context.environment in the CADL file is an abstract environment parameter that is carried into the IR; the Unity scene does not read it — its road graph is the one defined in cadl_config.json.) If the road looks small in the Scene view, select road in the Hierarchy, move the mouse over the Scene view and press F to frame it. During Play, the Game view follows one robot (m1) and shows the road around it, with that robot's own camera in the lower-right corner; the Scene view is where you can look at the whole road at once. 🛠 Mind the Unity version​ The project is saved with Unity 6000.2.9f1 (recorded in ProjectSettings/ProjectVersion.txt), and this textbook is checked with that version. Install it from Unity Hub; when you add the project, Unity Hub offers to install the matching Editor if it is missing. Do not open the project with Unity 2022.3 or older: Packages/manifest.json lists packages that exist only in Unity 6. A newer Unity 6 release will ask to upgrade the project on first open; that has not been checked for this textbook.

For each one: Inspector ▸ Add Component ▸ "PilotContractBridge" (CADL.SosDsl.Demo.PilotContractBridge) The Inspector now shows: Pilot Contract Bridge (Script) └── World keys (must match the contract's predicates) ├── Robot Battery [───────●───] 90 ├── Request Deadline Ms 300000 └── Assigned Dwell Ms 700 Assigned Dwell Ms is the minimum time the contract dwells in Assigned before accepting. It gives periodic monitors gated on that state (e.g. battery_guard, sampled every 500 ms) at least one evaluation window. Leave it at the default 700 ms — setting it below the monitor period would make violations undetectable. In the Console, lines like the following should appear continuously. You can filter them by typing lifecycle DELIVERY_SLA or violation in the Console search box. The screenshot was taken about 22 seconds into Play, with DELIVERY_SLA typed in the Console search box and the Scene tab selected: robot-2-1 (battery 15) has just been moved to Violated by battery_guard, and robot-1-1 has been assigned five seconds later. During Play the host is listed as ContractRuntimeHost under DontDestroyOnLoad; in this capture the scene part of the Hierarchy still shows the object added in "Add ContractRuntimeHost" (Section 8.2) as "New Game Object", although the Inspector shows its name. A closer look at the road during the same run, with the five robots on their way: The Game view during Play: the camera follows robot m1, and the small picture in the corner is what that robot's camera sees. [lifecycle DELIVERY_SLA/robot-2-1 Proposed -> Assigned (assign, event) @ 16112ms] [violation DELIVERY_SLA/robot-2-1 battery_guard Major monitor:battery_guard @ 16112ms] [lifecycle DELIVERY_SLA/robot-2-1 Assigned -> Violated (<jump>, monitor) @ 16112ms] [lifecycle DELIVERY_SLA/robot-1-1 Proposed -> Assigned (assign, event) @ 21675ms] [lifecycle DELIVERY_SLA/robot-1-1 Assigned -> Accepted (accept, event) @ 22479ms] [lifecycle DELIVERY_SLA/robot-1-1 Accepted -> Delivering (start_delivery, event) @ 22479ms] [lifecycle DELIVERY_SLA/robot-1-1 Delivering -> Completed (complete, event) @ 46361ms] Each robot's contract moves only on that robot's own events. The arbitrator hands out one delivery about every 5 seconds, so the robots reach Assigned one after another (in this run at about 5, 11, 16, 22 and 27 seconds). Note the 700 to 800 ms between assign and accept for robot-1-1: that is the Assigned Dwell Ms set in "Add PilotContractBridge to every robot" (Section 8.2). robot-2-1, with battery 15, is caught by battery_guard in the same frame as its assign.

The C# runs in Unity. The ContractRuntimeHost in the scene calls Runtime.Tick(now) every frame, evaluating deadline expirations and monitoring rules. A PilotContractBridge attached to each robot translates the robot's state changes (won a delivery bid, finished a delivery) into contract events (route_assignment, Delivered) and feeds them to that robot's own contract instance. Violations and state transitions appear line by line in the Console: [lifecycle DELIVERY_SLA/robot-2-1 Proposed -> Assigned (assign, event) @ 16112ms] [violation DELIVERY_SLA/robot-2-1 battery_guard Major monitor:battery_guard @ 16112ms]

Observes Pilot_CSoS and translates into contract events. Assigned Dwell Ms (700ms) is a wait time so that the periodic monitors don't miss the Assigned state

documents.t: When you feel like modifying things, there is one place to touch per goal (everything else is either generated or should not be edited by hand). What you want to do What to touch Change a deadline, add a monitor, add a state The .cadl file (→ regenerate with the e2e script) Change how robots move Pilot_CSoS.cs (the contract side needs no change as long as the events the bridge observes stay the same) Change the translation into contract events PilotContractBridge.cs Change the shape of the generated C# contract_emitter.py (advanced) Change the robot count or the map cadl_config.json Places you must not touch: hand-editing the contents of Generated/ and Runtime/. The next run of the e2e script will overwrite them (if something needs fixing, fix the generator).
