documents.t: Read PilotContractBridge.cs and see how thin the translation from observation to event is.

Confirm all of these: Check Expected There are [lifecycle ... robot-{id}-1 ...] events for all five robots Yes The robot with battery 15 has a monitor:battery_guard violation Yes Every robot's first transition is Proposed -> Assigned Yes The robots reach Assigned one at a time, about every 5 seconds (the arbitrator hands out one delivery at a time), so the last one takes about 25–30 seconds Yes A robot's contract reaches Completed when that robot finishes its delivery; the other robots' contracts do not move with it Yes The same kinds of events as Chapter 7's Python run (lifecycle transitions, violations) appear with the same meaning Yes

Symptom Fix Console: [PilotContractBridge X] ContractRuntimeHost.Instance is null You forgot to place the host. Redo "Add ContractRuntimeHost" in Section 8.2. Console silent — no contract events at all NATS or arbitrator not running. Check that Terminal 1 shows Server is ready and Terminal 2 shows the [Config] … taskArbitration.enabled=true … line. No delivery is ever assigned (no WON delivery in the Console) The arbitrator probably did not load its config. Restart it passing the absolute path of cadl_config.json via -config, and confirm taskArbitration.enabled=true in its startup output (the shipped config already has it true). Compile error in Console after Play: The name 'CADL.SosDsl.Demo.ContractRuntimeHost' could not be found Generated/Runtime files not picked up. Re-run the e2e script. Or in Unity, Assets ▸ Reimport All. All robots stay Proposed, then get Violated by deadline_watch (~5 min) The arbitrator carried over state from the previous Play (no deliveries offered). Stop Play, restart the arbitrator (and NATS if unsure), then replay. It must be restarted before every Play (see the note "Restart the arbitrator before every Play" in Section 8.2). Compile error ... already contains a definition for ... with paths under Generated/Generated/… or Runtime/Runtime/… The generated tree was copied nested (duplicated). Delete Assets/Scripts/SoSDsl/Generated/Generated and Runtime/Runtime (the current e2e script self-heals this). The battery=15 robot also completes instead of violating The bridge fired assign and accept in the same frame, so the contract never dwells in Assigned long enough for the periodic battery_guard to sample. The shipped PilotContractBridge fixes this via assignedDwellMs (default 700 ms); if you replace the bridge, keep it above the monitor period.

You have just witnessed the end-to-end story of an SoS contract: written in CADL, lowered to IR, generated to C#, executed in a real-time simulation, and observed detecting missed deadlines and battery-rule violations and moving the affected contract instances to Violated. (The runtime detects and records violations; it does not prevent the robots from misbehaving.)

Goal: Validate that the C# runtime produces the same trace shape as the Python one. Procedure: Follow Sections 8.2–8.3. Compare the Console output to your Python session4_baseline.ndjson and confirm that the event format is the same. (The per-robot breakdown of terminal states will not match the Python scenario — only the shape of the events does.)

This chapter draws the lifecycle of the contract with cadl-explorer and reads the diagram (about 15 minutes). In the exercises you compare the specification before and after adding the norms, and build a page that shows violations on a timeline.

In the procedure: How to read the Contract Lifecycle page of cadl-explorer (this textbook calls what it shows the Lifecycle View). How visual conventions (double circle, dashed border, red edge) map to the spec. In the exercises: Explain the visual conventions to an audience that does not know CADL. Compare two specs (v1 vs v2) using diagrams.

Software engineers debug code. SoS engineers debug diagrams — because the system is too distributed to step through with a debugger. The Lifecycle View is your debugger. Visual element What it means Double circle lifecycle.initial Dashed box, green fill terminal state Completed Dashed box, red fill terminal state Violated Dashed box, grey fill other terminal states (e.g., Terminated, Cancelled) Solid edge with Δ 5s transition with a deadline Red dashed edge the forced move to the on_violation target state

Install into the virtual environment you activated in Chapter 2 (cadl_repo/.venv); requirements.txt asks for the same cadl-lang package that Chapter 2 installed from the clone, so nothing is replaced. cd ~/program/cadl-explorer pip install -r requirements.txt streamlit run app.py # Browser opens at http://localhost:8501 In the list of pages at the top of the sidebar, switch from the default page (Explorer) to Contract Lifecycle. (Before v0.4.0 the page was called SoS DSL Lifecycle. If the sidebar has neither, your checkout of cadl-explorer is out of date; run git pull on main.) Two ways to load IR JSON: (a) Upload the IR of your own file. Save it first with cadl sim-ir my_delivery.cadl --format json > my_delivery.ir.json (run in ~/program/cadl_repo), then drag-and-drop my_delivery.ir.json into the file uploader. (b) Use the bundled example sos_dsl_robot_delivery.ir.json. It is shown as soon as the page opens; the dropdown (Bundled example) is there to return to it after an upload has been removed. Shortcut. The Designer page draws the same diagram straight from a .cadl file, without the cadl sim-ir step: open the file under Open an existing CADL file and switch the view to Lifecycle. It can also step through one contract instance. This step uses the IR on purpose, because the IR is what the simulator and the generated runtime read.

The screenshot below shows the page with (b), the bundled example: the sidebar with the uploader and the example selector on the left, the lifecycle diagram in the middle, and the lifecycle metadata on the right. The diagram itself, enlarged (bundled example: 5 transitions; the red dashed edge is the forced move to Violated when the accept deadline expires): Below the diagram, the page lists the monitors of the contract: The sketch below reflects (a), my_delivery.cadl (4 transitions, 1 monitor). If you instead load (b), the bundled example sos_dsl_robot_delivery.cadl, you'll see 5 transitions (it adds late_failure) and 3 monitors (battery_guard / collision_watch / deadline_watch). The page is split into two columns. The sketch is schematic: on the real page the diagram runs left to right, each edge is labelled with its trigger (the on: text, such as ROBOT[i] -> DISPATCHER : ack(accepted), then Δ 5s and any [when] condition) rather than the transition id, the metadata lists the state names, and the Monitors table also has a rule column. ┌──────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐ │ Lifecycle — DELIVERY_SLA │ Lifecycle metadata │ │ │ │ │ ┏━━━━━━━━━━┓ │ states : 7 │ │ ┃ Proposed ┃ ←initial(double) │ initial : Proposed │ │ ┗━━━━┳━━━━━┛ │ terminal : 3 │ │ │ assign │ transition_count: 4 │ │ ▼ │ │ │ ┌──Assigned──┐ │ │ │ │ │ accept Δ 5s │ │ │ │ ▼ │ │ │ │ ┌Accepted┐ │ │ │ │ └────┬───┘ │ │ │ │ violation │ │ │ │ │ (red dash)│ start_delivery │ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ │ ╔Violated╗ ┌Delivering┐ │ │ │ ╚════════╝ └────┬─────┘ │ │ │ (red, dashed) │ complete │ │ │ ▼ │ │ │ ╔Completed╗ │ │ │ ╚═════════╝ │ │ │ (green, dashed) │ │ └──────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Monitors │ ├──────────────┬──────────────────────┬─────────────┬──────────────┤ │ id │ sampling │ on_match │ severity │ ├──────────────┼──────────────────────┼─────────────┼──────────────┤ │ battery_guard│ periodic(500ms) │ Violated │ Major │ └──────────────┴──────────────────────┴─────────────┴──────────────┘ Visual conventions: Element Meaning Double circle lifecycle.initial Dashed box, green fill terminal state Completed Dashed box, red fill terminal state Violated Dashed box, grey fill terminal state Terminated Solid edge, label Δ 5s transition with deadline_ms = 5000 Red dashed edge with label violation Major the forced move to the on_violation target state Terminated stands alone in the diagram: both (a) and (b) declare it as a terminal state, but no transition leads to it. If you open either file on the Designer page, the same fact is reported as a Lifecycle warning (State 'Terminated' cannot be reached from the initial state 'Proposed'.). It is a warning, not an error: cadl check passes, because a lifecycle only needs one terminal state that can be reached.

Take a screenshot of your lifecycle (or just look carefully) and confirm: The only double-circle node is Proposed. There is exactly one red dashed edge going from Assigned to Violated. That is the forced move to Violated when the accept deadline expires. (The bundled example also draws three solid now > request.deadline edges into Violated, one for each state the late_failure transition can leave.) The monitors table shows battery_guard with sampling periodic(500ms) and severity Major.

The diagram is generated directly from the IR JSON with zero hand-coding. If you change deadline: 5s to deadline: 10s in your CADL file, regenerate the IR, refresh the page — the edge label will read Δ 10s.

Goal: Open cadl-explorer and load both v1 and v2 IR files. Identify exactly what the Lifecycle View shows for v1 vs v2. Procedure: Run cadl-explorer (streamlit run app.py). Generate IR for v1 too: cadl sim-ir my_delivery_v1.cadl --format json > my_delivery_v1.ir.json. Open the Contract Lifecycle page (in the list of pages at the top of the sidebar). Upload v1 first, then v2. Take screenshots. Check: For v1, the page should display a warning that the contract has no lifecycle. For v2, it should render a state machine with 8 states (7 if you skipped Exercise 5.3, which adds Cancelled).

documents.t: Goal: Write a 1-page A/B comparison report: the same contract, before and after Chapter 5's normative additions. Procedure: A 1-page Markdown document, with: A screenshot of the v1 visualisation (likely "no lifecycle" message). A screenshot of the v2 lifecycle. A table listing: number of states, transitions with deadlines, monitors, terminal states. 3 sentences on what kinds of failures the v2 spec catches that v1 silently allows. Submit: session3_comparison.md + the two screenshots.

Goal: Add a new Streamlit page to cadl-explorer that ingests an NDJSON log produced by multi_robot_demo --log <path> (you'll have one in Chapter 7) and displays it as a Gantt-style timeline. Procedure: Produce a log to develop against (from the simulator repository): cd ~/program/cadl-raspimouse-simulator python3 -m cadl.runtime.multi_robot_demo --log session4_baseline.ndjson Each line is one JSON record. The fields you need are instance_id, kind (lifecycle or violation), to_state, t_ms, and, on violations, detected_by. Create cadl-explorer/cadl_sim/sos_dsl/violation_trace_view.py. Parse each NDJSON line and group by instance_id. A state segment runs from one lifecycle record's t_ms to the next one of the same instance. The log has no end-of-run record, so close each instance's last state at the largest t_ms in the log (otherwise an instance that never leaves Proposed has no bar). Draw with Plotly — no new dependency required: go.Bar(orientation="h", base=start, x=duration) for the state segments and go.Scatter(mode="markers", marker=dict(symbol="x", color="red")) for the violations (Bar alone cannot draw the markers). Wire it in as a page. cadl-explorer has no pages/ directory: pages live in views/ and are registered explicitly in app.py. Create cadl-explorer/views/violation_trace.py (use views/lifecycle.py as a model), let it read the log with st.file_uploader(..., type=["ndjson"]) (the repository bundles no sample log), then add one entry to the st.navigation([...]) list in app.py: st.Page("views/violation_trace.py", title="Violation Trace", url_path="violation-trace"), With the baseline log you should get five rows, robot-0-1 to robot-4-1, and three red markers. This builds on what you would expect to see in advance — by the time Chapter 7 runs simulation, you'll have a viewer ready for its output.

documents.t: This chapter explains what a System of Systems (SoS), the subject of this textbook, is, why its rules need a language of their own, and what CADL (Contract Architecture Description Language) is a language for. The hands-on work starts in Chapter 2.

An SoS is a set of systems, each operated independently, that together achieve a goal none of them can achieve alone. The subject of this textbook is a robot-delivery SoS made of a fleet of delivery robots, a central coordinator that assigns deliveries (the dispatcher), and the customers who place orders. Each has its own goals and its own software. The robot we simulate is the Raspberry Pi Mouse ("raspimouse"), a small autonomous mobile robot — hence the simulator name cadl-raspimouse-simulator. (The physical robot runs on ROS; this textbook uses the simulator only.) The job of an SoS designer is not to write all the code of the constituent systems. It is to decide the rules of the game they all follow: who can ask whom for what, what counts as a violation, and what happens when one occurs. You will learn three things: Describe the structure of an SoS in CADL: who exists, and who exchanges what with whom (Chapter 4). Describe the norms of an SoS in the SoS-DSL extension of CADL: what each individual agreement must do, by when, and what happens on a violation (Chapter 5). Build working artefacts from one specification: from the same specification, produce a diagram, executable code and a simulation configuration, and watch violations of the norms being detected in a running simulation (Chapters 6–8). Finally, revise the specification from what you observed (Chapter 9).

Before turning to robot delivery, look at an SoS you already know. Actor What they do Who owns or commands them? Restaurant Cooks the meal and hands it over Itself. It sets its own hours and prices. Courier (gig worker) Delivers by bike or scooter Themselves. They choose their own working hours. Platform (the app) Matches orders to couriers The app company — which employs neither the restaurants nor the couriers. Customer Orders and pays Themselves. The behaviour of the whole — "the food arrives within 30 minutes" — is not designed and delivered by any single party. It results from independent actors each acting on their own interests. That state, in which independently operating systems together form a larger whole, is a System of Systems.
documents.s: 1.2 A familiar example: a food-delivery app

documents.t: Whether something can be called an SoS is usually decided with Maier's (1998) five criteria [1]. The classification of SoS itself is standardised in ISO/IEC/IEEE 21841:2019 [2]. # Criterion What to check In food delivery 1 Operational independence Does each part work on its own when the SoS as a whole is "off"? A restaurant can run as a restaurant without the app 2 Managerial independence Does each part have its own owner or decision-maker? Couriers are gig workers, not employees of the app company 3 Geographic distribution Are the parts spread out and exchanging information rather than matter or energy? Restaurants, couriers and customers are all in different places 4 Emergent behaviour Does the whole do something no part can do alone? "Delivered in 30 minutes" is a collective property nobody designed explicitly 5 Evolutionary development Do parts join, leave or change while the SoS is in use? Restaurants and couriers come and go every day (1) and (2) are essentially mandatory; (3)–(5) usually accompany them. A coffee shop, for example, whose staff work in one place and whose owner manages everyone, fails (2) and is not an SoS.
documents.s: 1.3 Telling whether something is an SoS: Maier's five criteria

documents.t: For the robot delivery of this textbook: ✓ (1) each robot can roam on its own even with no delivery assigned. △ (2) all robots share a single dispatcher, so managerial independence is weak. ✓ (3) the robots are distributed over a graph-shaped road network. ✓ (4) the delivery throughput of the fleet is something no single robot can produce alone. △ (5) the robot count is fixed in our scenario, but the simulator supports changing it. Because (2) is weak, this subject sits closer to a problem of controlling several robots in parallel than to a textbook SoS. It is still a manageable size for practising how contracts govern behaviour. A domain where managerial independence clearly holds, such as food delivery, is the subject of Course C, which follows this textbook (Chapter 11).
documents.s: Applying the criteria to robot delivery

documents.t: SoS differ by how strong their central authority is. ISO/IEC/IEEE 21841 [2] defines four types: the three types Maier proposed (Directed, Collaborative, Virtual) [1] and Acknowledged, added by Dahmann and Baldwin [3]. Type Central authority Examples Directed Strong, top-down, centralised management An air-defence network Acknowledged An authority for the SoS as a whole exists, but each constituent keeps its ownership and its own management An international space mission; the robot delivery of this textbook; a large ride-hailing platform Collaborative No single authority; the parts cooperate voluntarily through shared agreements (protocols, rules) The Internet Virtual Neither central management nor an agreed purpose; coordination arises on its own The World Wide Web; the shelters that open one by one right after a major disaster The CADL file for robot delivery in this textbook declares type: Acknowledged: it models each robot as a constituent system that keeps its own control software and autonomy but accepts the dispatcher as the SoS-level authority for assigning deliveries. The type is not fixed by the subject alone. The same food delivery is closer to Acknowledged if you focus on the platform's authority, and closer to Collaborative if you focus on the voluntary cooperation of the participants. Types also shift over time: right after a disaster the response starts as Virtual, becomes Collaborative once the municipal disaster headquarters is running, and approaches Acknowledged once the command authority is fixed by law. The type: of a CADL file is a descriptive label. The tools record it and write it to reports and generated configurations, but do not check it against anything else in the file.

If you try to write the rules of an SoS in an ordinary programming language such as C++ or Python alone, you run into problems like these. What you want to say How you would write it What goes wrong A robot must answer an assignment within 5 seconds A comment, or a verbal agreement It lives apart from the code, and the two drift apart After 5 seconds it is a violation An if statement somewhere Which 5 seconds (from sending, or from receiving?) depends on the context of the code A robot below 20% battery must not be given a new delivery An if statement in each implementation The same rule ends up scattered over many places Check the same rule in two runtimes, Unity and Python A separate implementation per language One of them falls out of date Ordinary languages offer no direct way to write both at once: that the parts act independently, and that the whole must still keep certain rules.
documents.s: 1.5 Why ordinary programming languages are not enough

documents.t: CADL is a description language for writing the rules that several systems must follow in one file, apart from their implementation code. The file is written in YAML. CADL key What it describes In robot delivery actors: The participants of the SoS and how autonomous they are DISPATCHER, ROBOT[1..N], CUSTOMER[1..M] contracts: Agreements between participants (assumptions and guarantees) The delivery service-level agreement DELIVERY_SLA protocols: The procedure of an interaction between participants assignment → acknowledgement → completion report lifecycle: The state machine one agreement goes through Proposed → Assigned → Accepted → Delivering → Completed monitors: Rules watched while a contract is running Has the battery fallen below 20%? From this one file the toolchain produces: Check results: cadl check finds mistakes in how the file is written, and cadl verify finds contradictions between assumptions and guarantees. An intermediate representation (IR): cadl sim-ir turns the file into JSON. The other tools read the IR. A diagram: cadl-explorer draws the state machine from the IR. Code: cadl codegen generates Unity C# code from the IR. A reference execution: the Python reference runtime reads and interprets the IR directly; it is not generated. Because all of these come from the same file, a rule is written in one place, and changing it means editing that file only.

actors:, contracts: and protocols: in the table belong to the core of CADL and describe what exists in the SoS (structure). lifecycle: and monitors: are added by the SoS-DSL extension and describe what should happen (norms). If you only want to describe structure, the core is enough, so the parts that treat norms as first-class concepts are kept in an extension. A file that uses the extension declares it with sos-dsl: 0.1 under extensions:. Chapter 3 explains how both layers are written; Chapter 4 writes the structure layer and Chapter 5 the norms layer.
documents.s: The structure layer and the norms layer

documents.t: An SoS is a set of independently operated systems that together do something none of them can do alone. Operational and managerial independence are the key criteria of Maier's five, and the strength of the central authority divides SoS into four types; the robot delivery of this textbook is modelled as Acknowledged. Rules written inside implementation code end up scattered and differ between runtimes. CADL avoids this by writing the rules in one file and producing checks, diagrams, code and executions from it.

You can go on with this textbook alone. For more background, see: International standards for SoS (ISO/IEC/IEEE 21839 [4], 21840 [5], 21841 [2], 15288 [6] and 42010 [7]), related research areas, and a reading list: "Why SoS-DSL?" in the hands-on materials. Comparison with existing languages: Chapter 3 of the specification.
